Title: Swiss-system chess tournaments and unfairness
Authors: László Csató, Alex Krumer
Abstract: Abstract The Swiss system is an increasingly popular competition format as it provides a favourable trade-off between the number of matches and ranking accuracy. However, there is no empirical study on the potential unfairness of Swiss-system chess tournaments if an odd number of rounds is played. To analyse this issue, our paper compares the number of points scored in the tournament between players who played one game more with the white pieces and players who played one game fewer with the white pieces. Using data from 28 highly prestigious competitions, we find that players with an extra white game score significantly more points. In particular, the advantage exceeds the value of a draw in the four Grand Swiss tournaments. A potential solution to this unfairness could be organising Swiss-system chess tournaments with an even number of rounds, and guaranteeing a balanced colour assignment for all players using a recently proposed pairing mechanism.

Title: Information asymmetry and cross-class coalitions in economic liberalization: Theory and evidence from post-communist transition
Authors: Shiyan Cao
Abstract: After the collapse of Soviet-style planned economies, the liberalization of Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) was considered critical for fostering technology adoption and achieving economic development. On the political side, the naïve expectation was that workers would welcome FDI, whereas the current industrial elite would oppose it. In reality, however, workers and managers often formed a powerful bloc against liberalization. This paper develops a formal model to explain why managers and labor unions may form political coalitions during periods of reform and how information asymmetry between managers and workers influences their policy choices. Since managers possess more information about economic conditions, they can sometimes persuade workers to perceive the managers’ preferred policy as the best option for workers’ welfare. If workers believe that managers’ interests are somewhat aligned with theirs and that managers possess a moderate informational advantage, managers can persuade workers that protectionist policies are in their best interest. In contrast, a misalignment of interests or an excessively large informational disparity might lead to excessive liberalization. The logic of this model can help inform policy debates on how domestic politics affect FDI policies.

Title: Legacy of Soviet-aided industrialization in China: A quasi-experiment
Authors: Clair Yang
Abstract: A large portion of the developing world has pursued big-push industrialization to promote growth over the past century. This paper utilizes a quasi-experimental design to investigate the long-term impact of such programs. From 1950 to 1959, the Soviet Union sent thousands of experts, engineers, and machinery to China to aid with the first Five-Year Plan of national development and to help establish a network of state-owned industrial plants across China. This massive program was brought to an abrupt standstill following the Sino-Soviet split in the early 1960s. This paper takes the unforeseen termination of the Soviet projects as an exogenous shock and investigates its impact on local economic development in the long run. Counties with more Soviet projects completed by the 1960s are shown to have larger state sectors today and, surprisingly, also enjoy better developmental outcomes overall and in the private sector in particular. Five mechanisms are examined as potential causes. I find no evidence of innovation spillover or differential infrastructure, but strong support for human capital externality and agglomeration through production networks. Resource allocation also continues to favor these localities: even private businesses in counties with more Soviet projects enjoy better access to the financial market.

Title: Material footprint accounting: addressing its scientific limitations
Authors: Mathis Wackernagel
Abstract: Material footprint (MF) accounting has gained prominence as an indicator of human pressure on the environment, particularly in policy discussions on resource efficiency and circular-economy strategies. While material footprint can be useful as a descriptive measure of industrial metabolism, this note argues that it exhibits several fundamental scientific limitations that distinguish it from other widely used indicators of human demand such as carbon footprints, ecological footprints, or human appropriation of net primary productivity. These limitations arise primarily from the absence of a biophysically grounded aggregation principle and the lack of an intrinsic upper bound. As a result, material footprints are analytically weaker as a sustainability metric, even though they remain valuable as a throughput indicator. To remedy, this paper outlines strategies to reduce misuse and to deploy material footprint more effectively as a tool for the sustainability transformation.

Title: Collaborative optimization of transmodal seafood cold chain transportation and pricing: a Freshness-Decay-Driven approach
Authors: Yu Sun, Feng Lian, Zhongzhen Yang
Abstract: In the transmodal seafood cold chain, seafood perishability and uncertainty in consumers’ freshness perceptions create a trade-off between freshness preservation and sales revenue. This study considers the channel choice behaviors influenced by consumers’ perception of freshness and develops a joint optimization model for fresh-keeping transportation and pricing based on freshness-decay dynamics to determine the fresh-keeping strategy, transportation routing, and pricing scheme with the objective to maximize retailers’ sales profit. Seafood freshness indicators are first calculated using kinetic models parameterized with experimental data obtained under controlled time–temperature conditions in existing studies. A back propagation neural network is then adopted to establish the nonlinear mapping between these physicochemical indicators and perception of freshness based on corresponding sensory evaluation data, while a nested logit model is used to capture the price-freshness trade-offs during selling. It is revealed through numerical analysis that: (1) E-commerce platforms will adopt higher transportation temperatures (3.05°C) to reduce costs, enabling aggressive pricing (54.76 CNY/kg), but contribute only about 5.72% of the retailer’s total profit; (2) Brick-and-mortar stores will implement stricter temperature control (0.37°C) leveraging location advantages, supporting premium pricing despite incurring fresh-keeping costs about 4.30 times as high as those of the e-commerce platform; (3) AVS is priced higher than SM (129.05 vs. 109.54 CNY/kg), reflecting its added service value as a store-affiliated online-to-home channel; (4) Ambient temperature changes induce coordinated operational adjustments, with total system profit changing by only 0.06% under both low- and high-temperature scenarios, while higher ambient temperatures impose greater fresh-keeping pressure. The model provides actionable transportation protocols: temperature-driven cargo allocation, refrigeration investment benchmarks, and dynamic pricing tariffs aligned with real-time freshness metrics.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Reverse logistics contract design under market uncertainty: An analysis of value-preserving repurchase policy for electric vehicles
Authors: Chaorui Huang, Hoi-Lam Ma, Xin Wen, Tana Siqin, Sai-Ho Chung
Abstract: This study proposes a reverse logistics framework by introducing a value-preserving repurchase (VPR) policy for electric vehicle (EV) makers. Under VPR, users pay a service fee and retail price and can return EVs after a specified period. To motivate returns, EV makers guarantee refunds exceeding typical secondhand prices. EV makers can offer repurchase, exchange (crediting the refund toward a new EV), or mixed options. However, market uncertainty can inflate secondhand prices beyond contract refunds, driving users to sell directly in secondary markets instead of returning. This undermines EV makers’ value recovery and new-vehicle demand. While the existing literature focuses on post-purchase returns from valuation discrepancies, we integrate volatile secondhand market prices into the VPR design. Methodologically, we develop an analytical framework for the EV reverse logistics channel, characterize the participants’ utilities through three VPR modes, and derive how secondhand prices reshape optimal VPR terms under different market structures. Furthermore, the EV makers’ mode preferences across monopoly and competitive settings are identified, thereby providing a rigorous analytical foundation for when and why different VPR options are chosen. From a managerial perspective, the results offer actionable guidance for EV makers designing VPR contracts under uncertain resale values: in a monopoly, the exchange mode emerges as dominant, and the mixed mode exhibits subtle efficiency; whereas the mixed mode prevails under competition, even it does not dominate in a monopolistic market. Overall, the findings extend beyond EVs by offering a transferable framework for value-preserving trade-in policy design in other industries facing uncertain secondhand prices.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Reducing early secondary school leaving: experimental evidence on information, tutoring, and incentives from Burkina Faso
Authors: Jan-Walter De Neve, Somkeita Pascal Zabré, Günther Fink
Abstract: Despite major gains in primary school enrollment across low- and middle-income countries, secondary school completion remains low. We conducted a randomized controlled trial in Burkina Faso to evaluate the effectiveness of three interventions designed to reduce early secondary school leaving: (i) information on the economic and health returns to education, (ii) tailored tutoring, and (iii) conditional cash incentives. The cash intervention significantly increased school enrollment, any school attendance, and regular attendance, and reduced the total number of school days missed. Tutoring significantly increased school enrollment, while its effects on regular attendance and academic progression were imprecisely estimated. The information intervention generated limited evidence of impacts, with no statistically significant effects on the primary outcome or academic progression and only marginal evidence of an increase in any school attendance. Financial and academic support can help adolescents who left school early re-enroll, but larger studies are needed to identify which interventions most effectively sustain regular attendance.

Title: Do coupled population, economic, and land use dynamics explain household energy transitions in Malawi?
Authors: Katerina E.B. Beach, Varun Goel, Yu Wu, Barbara Entwisle, Pamela Jagger
Abstract: In sub-Saharan Africa, population growth coupled with weak or missing markets for clean energy means that the absolute number of people relying on woodfuels for cooking is growing. Charcoal, which has distinctly different environmental and economic implications from firewood, has become one of the most consumed fuels in the region. However, among rural populations, the drivers and consequences of charcoal use remain under-studied. We examine rural woodfuel dynamics in Malawi, a majority rural country with high poverty, rapid population growth, lagging economic development, and abundant but rapidly declining forest resources. We examine how household energy transitions are influenced by concurrent demographic, economic, and land use changes. Using four waves of national household surveys and satellite-derived forest cover datasets, we investigate trends in household energy consumption, identify factors driving rural household fuel choices, and characterize geographic patterns of forest cover loss during 2004–2020. During this time, the share of rural households using charcoal grew from 3.9% to 13.4%. Rural households that are smaller, headed by younger individuals, and are asset-rich but land-poor had greater odds of using charcoal compared to firewood, indicating that rural livelihood dynamics have important consequences for household energy transitions. Several protected areas have experienced > 20% forest cover loss since 2001, characterized by geographic patterns consistent with unsanctioned woodfuel extraction. These findings emphasize a renewed need for integrated natural resources, energy, and livelihoods management strategies. Our insights provide information for policy makers to better predict and understand the continued growth of charcoal’s popularity in Malawi and similar contexts.

Title: The role of education in international migration decisions
Authors: Catalina Amuedo-Dorantes, Avinandan Chakraborty
Abstract: We estimate the effect of education on international migration using a fuzzy regression discontinuity design that exploits Mexico's 1993 compulsory schooling reform, which increased mandatory education from six to nine years. Combining Mexican and U.S. census data, we examine how completing lower secondary education affects migration to the United States during the last major wave of Mexican emigration in the 20th century. We find that completing lower secondary education increases migration to the United States, measured as residence in the United States in 2000, by about 15 percentage points, or roughly five percentage points per additional year of schooling. The effect is larger for men than for women and remains positive across alternative bandwidths and specifications. Moreover, the increase is concentrated in migration associated with work rather than migration associated with school enrollment, consistent with improved labor-market opportunities abroad. The estimates suggest that, where migration corridors are already established, a reform that raises lower secondary completion can also increase international mobility when domestic opportunities are limited.

Title: The dynamic impact of parental death on child labour: panel data evidence from Ethiopia
Authors: Gidisa Lachisa Tato
Abstract: Despite international consensus and actions, child labour remains prevalent and a global agenda. This paper uniquely examines the dynamic impact of parental death on child labour using rich longitudinal data from Ethiopia, while acknowledging limitations for making full causal interpretation. The empirical analysis, based on a conditional staggered difference-in-difference estimator, reveals a statistically significant impact of parental death on child labour. I specifically documented four key results. First, the cumulative effect of parental death outweighs the immediate effect. Second, the findings suggest a relatively higher impact of parental death around the age of 12 than earlier or later ages. Third, parental loss appears to push children toward unpaid household services rather than economic activities. Finally, maternal death has a stronger association with child labour than paternal death. These findings highlight the need for context-specific policy interventions and long-term support initiatives to mitigate the negative consequences of orphanhood on child development. Future research should explore multi-country analyses to provide a more comprehensive understanding and enable broader generalization of the impact of parental death on child labour.

Title: The reverse information paradox: When AI platforms retain too much or too little data
Authors: Vijaya Bhaskar Marisetty, Varsha Mamidi
Abstract: When do AI platforms retain too much or too little user data? Users disclose proprietary context to obtain useful generative-AI output, but retention of that context creates exposure and may improve future systems. We formalize this user-side analogue of Arrow’s information paradox. The disclosure cap separates two regimes. Outside the capped region, behavioral adjustment is strong enough for equilibrium harm to fall with retention, so the planner’s optimum is a boundary choice. Within the capped region, the ratio of benefit appropriability to harm internalization governs platform retention: the platform under-retains when the ratio is below one and over-retains when it is above one. When retained inputs also raise AI quality, retention and disclosure become complements once quality feedback is sufficiently strong. Retention regulation corrects the platform’s choice; an interior disclosure choice generally requires an additional disclosure-side instrument to implement the joint first best.

Title: How to determine key players when spillovers are large
Authors: Yves Zenou
Abstract: This paper examines the behavior of Katz–Bonacich centrality and key-player intercentrality in linear–quadratic network games when spillovers are large. This question is both important and empirically relevant, as it greatly simplifies the empirical testing of peer-effect models. We show that Katz–Bonacich centrality converges (up to scale) to the Perron eigenvector, while intercentrality diverges and loses all discriminatory power across nodes. Consequently, designing key-player policies becomes problematic: key-player rankings collapse, and no agent is more important than another when spillovers are sufficiently large.

Title: GVC participation and inflation in the European Union
Authors: Mariam Camarero, Antonia López-Villavicencio, Cecilio Tamarit
Abstract: This paper examines how participation in global value chains (GVCs) shapes inflation in the European Union over 1995–2023. Using local projections, we trace the dynamic response of producer- and consumer-price inflation to total, backward, and forward GVC shocks across core, peripheral, and CEEC economies. The aggregate response at the producer-price level is disinflationary and concentrated in the backward channel, supporting the discipline-on-prices hypothesis. A marked PPI–HICP wedge emerges in peripheral economies, where producer-level gains do not reach consumers, while forward linkages feed demand-pull pressures on consumer prices in both core and CEEC suppliers.

Title: Endogenous syndicate formation in (rent-seeking) contests
Authors: Kyung Hwan Baik, Dongwoo Lee
Abstract: We study a (rent-seeking) contest in which some players form syndicates and compete collectively, while others compete individually, to win a prize (or rent). A syndicate competes, as a single entity, with the other contestants to win the prize. The organizer of a syndicate chooses the syndicate’s effort level. The members of a syndicate share both the cost of effort and the prize (if it wins), according to the syndicate’s sharing rule. We first examine the profitability of being a syndicate member, assuming that the sizes of the syndicates are exogenously given. Then we consider the endogenous formation of syndicates and its effect on prize (or rent) dissipation. We show that, for any given number of players, there is a unique equilibrium size for the syndicate when only one syndicate is formed, and unique equilibrium sizes of the syndicates when two syndicates are formed. We also show that the endogenous formation of syndicates is beneficial both to the syndicate members and to the singletons, and the endogenous formation of syndicates reduces prize dissipation, compared with the individual (rent-seeking) contest.

Title: A new partial-equilibrium approach to approximating the welfare effects of market power and taxes
Authors: Till Gross, Paul Klein
Abstract: The traditional deadweight-loss (DWL) formula rests on a usually unstated, strong assumption: that all other markets are undistorted. We extend the DWL formula to cases where the surplus in other markets is non-zero. It involves an additional term of the same order of magnitude as the DWL; this term does not go to zero even when the directly affected market is small relative to the rest of the economy. In examples, we show that the DWL may get the sign of the surplus change wrong when a substantial share of the economy is monopolized or subject to commodity taxes.

Title: What social groups drive more and pay more? An equity analysis of interurban road pricing in Spain using cellphone data
Authors: Amirhossein Baghestani, Juan Gomez, José Manuel Vassallo
Abstract: Despite the extensive body of research on road pricing, relatively little attention has been paid to interurban tolling and its equity implications, particularly in the European context. This paper aims to characterize interurban road travel behavior based on the use of cellphone-based mobility data with the aim of evaluating the social and spatial equity effects of several road pricing schemes. For the case of Spain, the study identifies how different socioeconomic and geographic groups contribute to total toll payments relative to their income. Three distance-based tolling scenarios are considered, including uniform, geography-adjusted, and income-adjusted rates to assess distributional outcomes. Travel pattern analysis reveals that lower-income and rural residents travel longer interurban distances, specifically on weekdays, while metropolitan residents and individuals with higher incomes travel longer miles on weekends. The results from equity metrics such as the Gini and Kakwani indices confirm that the uniform distance-based scheme is regressive, with the burden disproportionately falling on lower-income and residents in peripheral areas. However, the inclusion of income- or geography-based exemptions, substantially improves fairness, shifting the system toward vertical equity. The study demonstrates the value of integrating large-scale cellphone mobility data with equity-focused modeling to develop socially balanced interurban tolling systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Explaining temporal and spatial variability in shared e-scooter ridership in Christchurch, New Zealand
Authors: Wai Chi Goldie Leung, Katarzyna Sila-Nowicka, Lindsey Conrow, Grant McKenzie, Simon Kingham, Vanessa Brum-Bastos
Abstract: Shared electric scooters (e-scooters) are widely adopted, yet their ridership patterns remain insufficiently understood. Existing studies rely on origin–destination (OD) inferred trips and use global models, which overlook true paths and spatial heterogeneity effects. This constrains understanding of spatio-temporal patterns and drivers of shared e-scooter ridership, reducing the effectiveness of transport planning and policy interventions. We address these limitations using observed street-segment-level trip counts to identify spatio-temporal ridership profile by clustering hourly ridership curves. We also apply Geographically Weighted Poisson Regression (GWPR) to examine spatial associations between ridership and contextual factors. Results reveal clear temporal differences from cycling behaviour and strong spatially varying associations between ridership and built environment, which global models fail to capture. Our findings show that data-driven clustering can classify micromobility behaviour without assuming trip purpose. Although focused on Christchurch, the methodological framework is transferable and applicable to other cities with similar data.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Floorspace price discontinuities and taxation in cross-border commuting areas
Authors: R. Kudashev, P.M. Picard
Abstract: Cross-border housing markets have become more prevalent in Europe since the establishment of the European Union. Using data from the functional urban area of Luxembourg, we document significant floorspace price discontinuities at the borders of Luxembourg with Belgium, France, and Germany. Employing a quantitative spatial urban model and spatial regression discontinuity techniques, we show that differences in tax rates and tax importing account for 8% and 13% of the observed price jump, respectively. The remaining price discrepancy is explained by differences in productivity and amenities.

Title: A relax-and-fix and fix-and-optimize algorithm for physician scheduling in emergency rooms
Authors: Valdemar A.P.A. Devesse, Kerem Akartunalı, Marcio da S. Arantes, Claudio F.M. Toledo
Abstract: Balancing physician workload in emergency departments is a significant problem in practice due to its major impacts in a hospital setting, from severe cost implications to its effect on vital patients’ care. From a theoretical perspective, the problem involves simultaneously addressing several inherent and often conflicting challenges, such as ensuring a fair distribution of workload among physicians, respecting the availability of staff and minimizing costs in a rather expensive sector. In this paper, we propose a matheuristic to address this challenging problem. Based on a mixed-integer programming model from the literature, we first incorporate the modelling of least absolute deviation in a set of workload constraints. Our approach integrates relax-and-fix and fix-and-optimize heuristics that are effectively used in other domains such as production planning. We present detailed computational results that compare our approach with standard mixed-integer programming model using benchmark instances from the literature. Our approach has resulted in 1) a higher degree of satisfaction with demand requirements, 2) a more accurate estimation of working hours and a fairer distribution among physicians, and 3) shorter computational times to find feasible solutions.

Title: How do misperceptions about non-monetary and monetary aspects of government jobs influence bureaucratic selection?
Authors: Bo Feng, Qiwei He, Hanzhang Liu

Title: Issue Information
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Issue Information
The good old days? Mental health across birth cohorts
Authors: Sabrina Lenzen, Luke B. Connelly, William Whittaker
Abstract: Abstract The share of young Australians reporting poor mental health has risen sharply over the past two decades, a pattern mirrored across many high-income countries. A central question is whether this reflects a genuine deterioration in underlying mental health or shifts in how different birth cohorts report their symptoms. Using 22 years of nationally representative longitudinal survey data from Australia (2002–2023), we construct a predicted mental health index from respondents’ socioeconomic characteristics, childhood conditions, physical health, life events, and financial circumstances, and compare it against self-reported mental health to isolate cohort-specific reporting differences. We find that the answer is both, namely, that younger cohorts apply lower thresholds when reporting distress, reflecting greater willingness to acknowledge poor mental health, and underlying mental health has genuinely deteriorated among recent cohorts, particularly females. Adjusting for cohort-specific reporting thresholds flattens the apparent rise in poor mental health, though a deterioration remains. After adjustment, the age gradient steepens, revealing that poor mental health peaks in mid-life, a life-cycle pattern that is obscured in raw self-reports. Our findings underscore the importance of accounting for reporting heterogeneity when interpreting mental health trends and planning health services.

Title: Sustainable transport in the climate-change era
Authors: Linchuan Yang, ChengHe Guan, Brian Caulfield
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Optimising spare parts management in hydraulic excavators: a Fuzzy CODAS and ABC analysis approach
Authors: Isik Ates Kiral, Zehra Ilke Erdem, Emre Cakmak, Sevilay Demirkesen
Affiliations: Bursa Technical University; Piri Reis University; Istinye University; Gebze Technical University
Abstract: The reliable operation of heavy construction equipment is critical for project productivity; however, spare parts inventory decisions for such equipment are often made using intuition-based or oversimplified approaches, leading to unnecessary costs and equipment downtime. In particular, construction-specific spare parts management lacks systematic, data-driven frameworks that account for uncertainty, multiple decision criteria, and operational criticality. To address this gap, this study proposes a hybrid decision-support framework that integrates Fuzzy Combinative Distance-Based Assessment (Fuzzy CODAS) with Always Better Control (ABC) analysis to optimise spare parts inventory for hydraulic excavators. The framework is applied to the hydraulic system of excavators using 22 spare parts and 13 evaluation criteria assessed by industry experts. The results indicate that pump devices, gear pumps, and regulator pumps should be prioritised as Class A items due to their high criticality, cost impact, and failure consequences, while components such as cylinders, centre joints, and certain piping systems exhibit lower stocking priority. The findings demonstrate that component-specific inventory strategies can significantly reduce operational costs and improve equipment uptime. Theoretically, this study advances spare parts management literature by introducing a construction-oriented hybrid MCDM framework, while providing an evidence-based tool for strategic inventory planning and maintenance decision-making in heavy equipment operations.

Title: Can the use of recycled powders reduce AM spare parts costs?
Authors: Mirco Peron, Luigi Panza, Mohammad Arbabian
Affiliations: NEOMA Business School; Politecnico di Torino; University of Portland
Abstract: Additive Manufacturing (AM) has attracted growing interest for spare parts production, yet its industrial adoption remains limited. A key barrier is cost, particularly the high cost of raw materials. Prior research suggests that replacing virgin powders with recycled powders could significantly reduce material costs. Recycled powders also offer environmental benefits which, under carbon reduction policies, may translate into additional economic savings. However, these advantages are offset by drawbacks: recycled powders typically exhibit lower quality, leading to reduced part reliability and higher spare parts management costs. This trade-off raises a critical question: does the use of recycled powders reduce AM spare parts costs, as suggested by the literature? Through analytical and numerical analyses supported by a case study, we show that this is only conditionally true. While recycled powders can lower total costs, their economic viability depends on the balance between material cost savings, reliability degradation, and carbon pricing. We identify threshold regions that distinguish scenarios in which recycled powders are always, never, or only conditionally preferable. Results indicate that the threshold regions are up to twice as sensitive to changes in reliability as to changes in material cost, while carbon pricing and emission reductions have only a marginal effect.

Title: A multi-period supply chain equilibrium model under tariff uncertainty and CVaR-based risk aversion
Authors: Jose M. Cruz
Affiliations: University of Connecticut

Title: Robust berth allocation and scheduling under uncertain arrival and processing times
Authors: Peng Wu, Wenxin Zeng, Andrea D'Ariano
Affiliations: Fuzhou University; Roma Tre University

Title: Supporting assembly process planning with implicit knowledge from process history: a decision support system approach
Authors: Dirk Schweers, Michael Freitag
Affiliations: BIBA - Bremer Institut fuer Produktion und Logistik GmbH at the University of Bremen, Bremen, Germany; Faculty of Production Engineering, University of Bremen, Bremen, Germany

Title: Imputing Missing Covariate Values in Nonlinear Models
Authors: Bhavna Rai
Affiliations: Indian School of Business Hyderabad India
Abstract: ABSTRACT I propose a new imputation estimator for missing covariate values in nonlinear models. The estimator provides efficiency gains relative to just using the complete cases, and is consistent for any model that falls under M‐estimation. This is unlike the commonly used dummy variable method and regression imputation, which I show to be generally inconsistent in nonlinear models. The proposed estimator is straightforward to implement, and relies only on the commonly used assumptions on missingness. To test these assumptions, I provide a novel and simple variable addition test. I show how the framework applies to nonlinear models for fractional and nonnegative responses.

Title: Information sharing and selling mode selection in a fresh e-tailing supply chain
Authors: Shuai Yan, Xia Liang, Wenchao Cheng, Yiwen Bian
Abstract: Demand information asymmetry is ubiquitous and severely undermines the performance of suppliers and online platforms in fresh e-tailing supply chains. Information sharing is vital for mitigating information asymmetry. It directly shapes members’ pricing and freshness-keeping decisions, and ultimately determines whether a platform adopts a reselling or an agency mode. We aim to study the interplay between demand information sharing strategy (sharing vs. non-sharing) and selling mode (reselling vs. agency) selection in a fresh e-tailing supply chain in this work. We find that the optimal strategy highly hinges on both consumer freshness sensitivity and prediction accuracy. Specifically, if consumer freshness sensitivity is moderate and the prediction accuracy is low, the platform prefers the agency mode and shares the demand information; otherwise, adopting the reselling mode and withholding information is the platform’s optimal choice. Under certain conditions, the platform’s optimal strategy can also improve the profitability of both the supplier and the whole supply chain. Furthermore, we examine the platform’s optimal strategy with a sophisticated supplier and find that, if consumer freshness sensitivity is moderate and the prediction accuracy is high, adopting the agency mode and sharing information will improve the platform’s profit. Interestingly, we confirm that the presence of a sophisticated supplier creates a win–win outcome for both parties under certain conditions.

Title: How does tolerance for failure impact exploratory and exploitative innovation?
Authors: Zhijian Cui, Tianxiu Zhang, Xiaojin Liu
Affiliations: International Institute of Finance, School of Management University of Science and Technology of China Hefei Anhui P. R. China; Department of Logistics and Maritime Studies, Business School The Hong Kong Polytechnic University Hung Hom Kowloon Hong Kong; School of Business Virginia Commonwealth University Richmond Virginia USA
Abstract: Abstract Prior research highlights tolerance for failure (TFF) at individual or team level, yet how firm‐level TFF shapes exploratory versus exploitative innovation remains underdeveloped. We conceptualize TFF as a stable organizational cultural norm and operationalize it via a firm's governance responses to executive underperformance, specifically, the absence of CEO dismissal or pay cuts following poor financial results. Drawing on organizational control theory, we argue that TFF influences innovation trajectories through intertwined control dynamics and resource allocation. We further examine the moderating roles of two external control forces: qualified foreign institutional investors (QFIIs) and government subsidies. Using a novel firm‐level TFF measure, we find that TFF promotes exploratory innovation while constraining exploitative innovation. Government subsidies mitigate TFF's detrimental effect on exploitation but do not moderate the TFF‐exploration relationship. For firms with heavy QFII holdings, QFIIs attenuate TFF's positive effect on exploration and weaken TFF's negative effect on exploitation. This study advances innovation literature by integrating a refined TFF construct with organizational control theory, clarifying the contingent impacts of failure tolerance on innovation and offering actionable insights for balancing risk‐taking and accountability in R&D management.

Title: Monitoring decreases discrimination
Authors: Edmund Baker, Veronika Grimm, Yuval Ofek‐Shanny
Affiliations: Friedrich‐Alexander‐Universität, Erlangen‐Nürnberg Nürnberg Germany; Energy Systems and Market Design Lab Technische Universität Nürnberg Nürnberg Germany; Department of Economics Bar‐Ilan University Ramat Gan Israel
Abstract: Abstract We study whether awareness of monitoring or study participation affects racial discrimination. Online participants rated résumés signaling either a Black or White candidate under Control, Monitoring, and Experiment conditions. Across conditions, we unexpectedly find a small average preference for Black résumés, possibly reflecting temporarily heightened racial awareness. The Control condition exhibits greater racial bias in both directions. This pattern suggests that monitoring and awareness of being studied can suppress discriminatory behavior. The findings underscore the importance of credible cover stories in discrimination experiments and indicate that subtle accountability cues may reduce bias in evaluative settings such as hiring.

Title: Targeting ride-sourcing services: Credit charge-cum-reward schemes for sustainable multi-modal mobility
Authors: Xiaoran Qin, Yushi Chen, Hai Yang
Abstract: This study examines how CCR schemes targeting ride-sourcing services influence multi-modal travel behavior in systems with public transit, ride-sourcing, and private vehicles to promote green transportation and reduce congestion and emissions. By designing Credit-Charge-cum-Reward scheme targeting ride-sourcing services, the study seeks to balance government fiscal revenue, intervention objectives, and ride-sourcing platform profitability. To rigorously capture the policy-constrained interaction between the ride-sourcing platform and travelers, a bi-level Stackelberg game-theoretic framework is developed. Within this framework, the government establishes the CCR policy environment as an exogenous intervenor. Under these policy constraints, the ride-sourcing platform acts as the leader in the upper-level problem by optimizing pricing and driver supply strategies, while travelers act as followers in the lower-level problem by making equilibrium mode choices to minimize generalized travel costs. The results demonstrate that CCR schemes effectively shift travelers toward green modes and reduce system-wide emissions while maintaining overall traffic efficiency. Interventions targeting public transit and private cars can incentivize a modal shift from high-emission private driving to ride-sourcing services. Furthermore, the study reveals the complementary functions of different credit mechanisms under fiscal neutrality, where interventions on private vehicles and transit directly determine emission reduction while those on ride-sourcing ensure fiscal neutrality in the regular equilibrium regimes, and incentive-based strategies further enhance platform profitability. Consequently, the proposed mechanism effectively reconciles the conflicts among government fiscal balance, platform viability, and traffic efficiency improvements.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Embedding space in generative freight demand models: A spatially explicit dynamic Bayesian network
Authors: Vitor Lemos, Zhenhan (Xander) Peng, Johan W. Joubert
Abstract: Freight transport demand emerges from interdependent sequences of activities unfolding across space and time, yet most large-scale models continue to represent freight as independent trips or exogenous origin-destination flows. This paper proposes a spatially explicit dynamic Bayesian network (DBN) that generates complete, synthetic freight activity chains while embedding location choice directly within the generative process. Rather than assigning destinations in post-processing, spatial behaviour arises endogenously through learned dependencies between vehicle attributes, activity context, land use, and prior locations. A central contribution is the hierarchical spatial encoding strategy, integrating a multi-resolution discrete global grid system (H3) directly into the probabilistic graphical model. By representing relative positions within nested hexagons as interdependent categorical variables, the approach captures spatial dependence across scales while keeping conditional probability tables tractable. This enables scalable, privacy-preserving synthesis of high-resolution activity chains without reproducing identifiable trajectories. The framework is demonstrated using nationwide GNSS freight telemetry from Belgium. Out-of-sample evaluation shows that the model reproduces key structural, temporal, and spatial characteristics of observed freight behaviour, including chain length and duration, origin-destination flows, border-crossing dynamics, and both global and local spatial autocorrelation. By jointly modelling sequencing, timing, and spatial structure in a transparent probabilistic framework, the proposed approach advances generative freight demand modelling and provides a flexible foundation for policy and scenario analysis and agent-based simulation in data-sensitive environments.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Macroscopic modeling and optimization of mixed-autonomy traffic in general road networks: A comprehensive and critical review
Authors: Fang Zhang, Dan Zhu, Qiang Meng
Abstract: The rapid development of autonomous vehicle (AV) technology is ushering in a new era of transportation characterized by the mixed-autonomy traffic (or mixed traffic for short), where AVs coexist and interact with human-driven vehicles (HVs). To harness the full potential of this transition, substantial research efforts over the past decade have been devoted to characterizing and managing the mixed traffic in road networks. This study provides a timely, comprehensive, and critical review of the state-of-the-art in mixed traffic network modeling and optimization. Specifically, we focus on studies that address human mobility in general congestible road networks, with an emphasis on macroscopic modeling or management of network-wide mixed traffic involving privately owned AVs and HVs. The literature search covers 136 academic journal articles published up to December 31, 2025. We classify the models developed in these studies into two main categories: mixed traffic analysis models and mixed traffic management & control models. Mixed traffic analysis models aim to investigate and predict how mixed traffic operates, evolves, or distributes over a network. We investigate these studies from three temporal dimensions: static, day-to-day dynamic and within-day dynamic. We examine the heterogeneity between AVs and HVs at the network level, translate it into ten AV-related behavioral assumptions, and highlight how these assumptions challenge and reshape modeling paradigms. Mixed traffic management & control models, on the other hand, focus on the determination of optimal management and control strategies. We overview cutting-edge strategies, including infrastructure retrofitting, participatory AV control, pricing and subsidization, among others. We elucidate how the strategy design problems are formulated and solved, and further discuss the application scenarios, advantages, limitations, and implementation barriers of these strategies. Finally, we identify critical research gaps and shed light on several inspiring directions for future investigation. This study aims to offer valuable insights for both academic research and practical decision-making regarding the deployment of AVs.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Generative Engine Optimization in AI-mediated Retail Supply Chains: Algorithmic Visibility, Fulfillment Constraints, and Platform Governance
Authors: Xiaojun Fan, Jingfan Shi, Lu Zhang
Abstract: Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) is emerging as a strategic issue in AI-mediated retail supply chains. As conversational shopping systems increasingly mediate product search, comparison, and recommendation, firms compete not only for ranked-list positions but also for being surfaced, cited, or highlighted within compressed answer interfaces. We develop a two-stage analytical Hotelling duopoly in which retailers first invest in machine-legible GEO signals and then compete in prices, while a fraction of consumers purchase through a GenAI answer engine. The model endogenizes how probabilistic answer inclusion shapes demand allocation, pricing, welfare, fulfillment-capacity payoffs, and platform governance. The analysis yields several major findings. A higher highlighting probability raises both demand share and pricing power. Yet when retailers are initially symmetric, GEO creates a defensive arms race: both firms spend to preserve answer visibility, but relative visibility, prices, allocations, and consumer surplus remain unchanged, while total welfare declines. When retailers differ in inherited algorithmic visibility capital, the content-rich retailer’s advantage may persist and be reinforced under the maintained equilibrium conditions. Extensions show that fulfillment congestion attenuates the profit value of AI-steered demand, and that quality-weighted inclusion rules can reduce low-signal escalation by tying marginal GEO effectiveness to verifiable retail and operational quality. The paper contributes to research on retail supply-chain competition by showing that GenAI answer interfaces are upstream demand-allocation mechanisms rather than merely digital-marketing channels; their economic value depends on logistics execution, service reliability, and platform scoring design.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: FDI spillovers in history: Interwar Japanese “Zaikabo” investment in China's cotton spinning industry
Authors: Holger Görg, Toshihiro Okubo, Eric Strobl, Maximilian Von Ehrlich
Abstract: We estimate productivity spillovers from Japanese cotton-spinning firms in China (known as Zaikabo) to local Chinese cotton-spinning mills based on plant-level data for 1925 to 1938. In order to capture the important role of distance in facilitating such spillovers we geo-localised the plants. Our results provide clear evidence for positive spillovers from Zaikabo to local Chinese mills, which go hand-in-hand with an upgrade in production technology towards greater use of capital. Spillovers are very localised, being strongest within a radius of up to 10 km around the Zaikabo and particularly strong for mills in Shanghai. Exploiting information on the workforce composition of the Japanese affiliates, we find suggestive evidence of a skilled-labour channel: spillovers tend to be larger from Zaikabo employing higher shares of skilled labour. We also find some evidence in line with the idea that these gains are larger for Chinese mills with higher initial productivity, consistent with a role for absorptive capacity. Our paper is the first to document FDI productivity spillovers in a historical context and to characterise the channels through which they operate.

Title: Causal forests versus penalized splines for heterogeneous treatment effects
Authors: Ivan Korolev, Abiodun Musbaudeen, Nency Dhameja
Abstract: This paper compares causal forests with varying-coefficient penalized spline estimators for heterogeneous treatment effects. We conduct simulations with randomized treatment assignment that vary heterogeneity, predictor dimension, and discrete nuisance structure. Performance is measured by out-of-sample mean squared error. Forests perform best in Wager–Athey designs with sharp treatment-effect transitions. Penalized splines tend to dominate when heterogeneity is smooth, when the baseline mean and treatment effect differ in structure, and in mixed designs with continuous, binary, and group-level covariates. As group cardinality rises, forest performance deteriorates, while mgcv random-effect smooths handle group structure effectively and remain easy to implement.

Title: Tariff shocks and land sales: evidence from China’s cities
Authors: Jiwen Guo, Jialiang Xu
Abstract: This paper studies whether local governments use land sales to buffer trade shocks. Combining land transactions for 275 Chinese cities over 2015–2023 with a Bartik measure of US tariff exposure, we find that more exposed cities raise land-sale revenue after the US-China trade war through higher average prices rather than greater aggregate land area. The price increase reflects two channels: a shift toward high-grade land driven primarily by area expansion, and a within-use price increase in commercial-residential land with no corresponding area response. Mechanism analysis shows that tariff shocks weaken local economic activity and intensify fiscal pressure.

Title: Platform-wide agreements and competition for new users
Authors: Peter Boberg, Martino De Stefano, Keler Marku, Mary Beth Savio

Title: Peer comparisons and the cost of pro-social behavior: Evidence from the lab
Authors: David Campoverde, Todd L. Cherry, David M. McEvoy, Tanga Mohr, Klaas van 't Veld
Abstract: Behavioral nudges in the form of peer-comparison information have, in many cases, proven effective in promoting pro-social behavior. The most prominent example is the use of home energy reports in electricity markets. While there is evidence that peer comparisons can induce reductions in externality-generating consumption, it is not clear through which channels the nudges operate. One possible channel is pecuniary: peer comparisons may make consumption choices more salient and prompt discovery of opportunities for financial savings. The other is non-pecuniary: peer comparisons may trigger moral motives such as guilt, social conformism, or social competitiveness. This study uses a controlled posted-price market experiment with externalities. We eliminate the “discovery” channel present in field settings by making financial incentives fixed and known. The experiment thus controls the pecuniary channel, leaving only the non-pecuniary, “moral” channel. We find that the nudge still enhances pro-social behavior, pointing to the moral channel’s importance. Two additional findings are that the nudge is equally effective across the treatments with low and high market prices (indicating that nudges and financial incentives neither complement nor crowd each other out) and that the nudge is more effective for participants with relatively cooperative worldviews.

Title: A community-driven recommender system for speed safety camera policy using large language models and knowledge graphs
Authors: Farhad Sedighi, Brian M. Staes, Benyamin Ghoreishi, Xuehan Jing, Haizhong Wang
Abstract: Speeding is a persistent contributor to roadway fatalities, accounting for over 30% of traffic deaths in the U.S., prompting the widespread use of Speed Safety Cameras (SSCs) as a proven countermeasure. However, despite their effectiveness, public skepticism, which is driven by concerns over fairness, transparency, and revenue motives, has limited the scalability and sustainability of SSC programs. Existing research lacks systematic integration of public perception into policy frameworks and fails to fully leverage advancements in artificial intelligence for context-aware recommendation. Addressing this gap, this study develops a scalable policy recommender system for SSC deployment in Oregon by fusing public sentiment with authoritative guidance using a novel hybrid framework that integrates Large Language Models (LLMs), Knowledge Graphs (KGs), and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). A statewide survey of 1,000 residents captured public opinion across six policy dimensions, which, along with state legislation (HB4109), FHWA guidelines, and best practices, formed a multi-source knowledge base stored in a Neo4j graph. The system retrieves both structured and unstructured context to support LLM-based generation of interpretable policy recommendations. Through Monte Carlo simulations, sentence similarity benchmarking, and RAGAS metrics, the proposed framework achieved the highest performance in accuracy, faithfulness, and context recall compared to baseline LLM and RAG pipelines. The results underscore the effectiveness of combining symbolic reasoning with semantic retrieval for generating transparent and community-aligned SSC policy guidance, offering a transferable blueprint for jurisdictions aiming to align traffic safety interventions with public trust and domain expertise.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Circular economy optimization of sustainable saffron supply network: integrating life cycle assessment and resource valorization
Authors: Omid Abdolazimi, Davood Shishebori

Title: Service network design with uncertainty on water levels for intermodal river transport
Authors: Bita Payami, Ioana C. Bilegan, Teodor Gabriel Crainic, Walter Rei
Abstract: . Barge transport presents a sustainable alternative to road transport, offering the potential to alleviate congestion and reduce costs. However, increasingly frequent and severe drought seasons, attributed to climate change, challenge the resilience of this mode of transport. Decreased water levels restrict navigation, impact vessel size, and reduce vessel capacity. This study introduces a novel and integrated modeling framework for tactical planning in consolidation-based barge freight transportation. By examining the relationship between water levels and vessel load capacity, with a specific focus on vessel dimensions, the framework aims to evaluate possible impacts on the efficiency and profitability of inland waterway transport. We also introduce two stochastic Water-Level-Constrained Scheduled Service Network Design with Resource and Revenue Management models to address uncertainties in resource capacities caused by water level variations, each addressing a distinct tactical plan adjustment strategy. These models aim to establish a tactical plan, given predicted water levels, that maximizes the expected carrier’s revenue while accounting for future adjustments to the plan when information is revealed and predictions are reliably updated, to fulfill the demands of shippers and optimize the utilization of the carrier’s resources. Through extensive experimentation using commercial software and a novel decision-based scenario clustering algorithm, we assess the quality of the solutions obtained with the different model variants and analyze the impact of the water level on the results.

Title: Presidents, prices at the pump, and the difference in perceptions between energy market experts and non-experts
Authors: Dylan Brewer, Matthew E. Oliver
Abstract: We conduct a survey of US-based energy market experts and non-experts and find that non-experts are significantly more likely to believe the US President plays a major role in determining retail fuel prices. Next, we analyze weekly retail gasoline and diesel price data from the US, UK, France, and Canada under different heads of state. After controlling for fluctuations in the wholesale crude oil price, country-specific long-run averages in prices, common time shocks, and national fuel excise taxes, we find that fuel prices differ systematically across leaders, though not universally. Although we do not claim to have established a causal link between executive regime change and retail fuel price variation, our fuel price analysis does help explain why many people believe political executives can influence retail gasoline prices, a phenomenon with important political and macroeconomic ramifications.

Title: Designing renewable energy auctions for high realization probability — CfD and payment-only auctions
Authors: Runxi Wang, Karl-Martin Ehrhart
Abstract: In recent years, different instruments for renewable energy expansion have been debated. Among the support and hedging instruments, two-sided contracts for difference (CfDs) have become the default in many countries and are promoted by the European Commission. On the other hand, payment-only auctions have also become established, where the electricity sales are unregulated, but the winners must pay for the right to build energy plants. Focusing on a high realization probability and the induced welfare effects, we compare two-sided CfDs with payment-only auctions. Contrary to the conventional wisdom, the non-realization risk is higher with auctioned CfDs than with payment-only auctions and is exacerbated by risk aversion, when developers can cope with both options. CfDs are particularly useful when developers need support for implementing their projects. Against this backdrop and considering asymmetric information, i.e., developers know best the economic conditions of their projects, we propose a design in which developers decide competitively between a CfD auction and a payment-only auction and which enhances the realization probability.

Title: Macroeconomic risk, political instability, and environmental sustainability risk: assessing vulnerabilities among emerging and developing economies
Authors: Rexford Abaidoo, Ayodele Julius Alade, Elvis Kwame Agyapong
Abstract: This empirical inquiry examines the impact of environmental sustainability risk (ESR) on political agitations and macroeconomic risk among emerging and developing economies in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). ESR is examined from three main perspectives: the extent of carbon emissions (denoted by CO 2 emissions), coverage or the extent of exploitation of land and water resources (denoted by the ecological footprint index), and unsustainable exploitation of natural resources (denoted by genuine sustainability risk). Data for the analysis were compiled for a sample of 36 countries from the sub-region, and empirical estimates were conducted using pooled ordinary least squares with Driscoll and Kraay standard errors, as well as the two-step system GMM framework. Empirical findings from the study show that growth in CO 2 emissions heightens macroeconomic risk among the examined economies. The results further suggest that an increase in ecological footprint exacerbates political instability for the examined economies in the sub-region. Additionally, the reported results indicate that effective governance and institutional structures can help mitigate the adverse impact of environmental sustainability risks on macroeconomic risks and political instability in the reviewed developing and emerging economies.

Title: Fuel taxes without borders: Tax-induced price changes and recorded fuel sales in the European Union
Authors: Janez Dolšak
Abstract: This paper estimates how retail fuel prices and cross-border price differentials affect recorded domestic road-fuel sales in the European Union, using harmonized monthly panel data for 24 countries from January 2008 through December 2025. We use tax-induced variation in retail prices, instrumenting domestic prices and relative price gaps with statutory fuel-tax variables in two-stage least squares models with country and month fixed effects. We complement the country-month analysis with directed dyadic IV specifications that compare home and neighbouring countries within land-border pairs. The outcome is recorded domestic fuel sales, not physical fuel consumption within national borders, so the estimates capture both changes in fuel use and shifts in the location where purchases are recorded. For diesel, the preferred country-month IV estimate implies an own-price elasticity of approximately −1.40 for recorded domestic road-diesel sales. For gasoline, the preferred estimate is also negative, approximately −0.78, although it is less stable across demanding sensitivity specifications. The clearest evidence of cross-border reallocation comes from the dyadic IV design. When the dyadic price differential is defined as the neighbour's log price minus the home country's log price, the cross-border coefficient is positive and close to +0.53 for both diesel and gasoline. This means that recorded domestic sales increase when neighbouring countries become more expensive relative to the home country. The findings imply that uncoordinated national fuel-tax changes can shift where purchases are recorded, potentially eroding domestic tax bases and complicating the interpretation of national fuel-sales statistics in integrated markets.

Title: Wildfire shrinks shelter access unevenly across California
Authors: Fatemeh Janatabadi, Alireza Ermagun
Abstract: This study advances disaster decision-making by embedding wildfire expected annual loss (EAL) into cumulative shelter access measurements across California. Departing from conventional metrics that assume full facility availability during wildfire events, it applies an EAL-weighted adjustment across multiple travel-time thresholds. Three findings emerge from the multi-scalar analysis at the census block group and county levels. First, EAL weighting consistently reduces shelter access and reveals geographically uneven proportional losses within counties. Second, county-level disparities are most persistent where extensive wildland–urban interface (WUI) development, uneven shelter distribution, concentrated wildfire exposure, and limited transportation networks coincide. Longer travel-time thresholds reduce within-county disparities in many counties yet do not eliminate structural access constraints in WUI-dominated counties. Third, although EAL-weighted access does not reveal systematic racial disparities, inequities persist by income and vehicle ownership. The framework supports mitigation-oriented identification of structurally vulnerable communities before wildfire occurrence and informs risk-aware resource allocation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Unraveling divergence in pavement LCA tools through attribution analysis
Authors: Jin Li, Wei Sheng, Yuhong Wang
Abstract: Specialized life cycle assessment (LCA) tools are increasingly used for pavement sustainability assessment, yet they can yield divergent results for the same project. This study compares five representative tools—MIT Streamlined Pavement LCA & LCCA Tool, LCA Pave, HERMES CO 2 , Athena Pavement LCA, and asPECT—using four harmonized pavement cases for a 1 km × 3.5 m lane over 50-year period. For embodied/infrastructure-related GHG emissions, project-level tools gave comparable estimates; for the asphalt freeway case, MIT, LCA Pave, and Athena ranged from 364 to 435 t CO 2 -eq/lane-km. When operational emissions were included, PVI-related use-stage effects accounted for 71 %-89 % of full life-cycle GHG in MIT and Athena. Attribution analysis shows that divergence mainly arises from system boundary, LCIA method, traffic-fuel baseline, roughness-fuel modelling, albedo treatment, and recycling-credit assumptions. Tool disagreement should therefore be interpreted modularly by life-cycle stage to guide future improvement.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Ridesharing and the redistribution of economic activity
Authors: Caitlin Gorback

Title: Equilibrium influence and pricing in duopoly competition
Authors: Reza Nazari Khanmiri, Xiao Huang, Georges Zaccour
Abstract: Competition for experience goods rarely hinges on price alone. When customers are uncertain about product fit, any attribute that shapes their posterior beliefs – brand reputation, online reviews, influencer endorsements, or money-back guarantees – becomes strategically significant. This study develops a duopoly model in which sellers compete through price and persuasion when consumers update beliefs via Bayesian persuasion and may return purchases. The equilibrium characterizes how sellers jointly craft price and influence decisions to gain competitive advantage. The seller with lower expected fit relies on influence to attract marginal consumers, while the higher-fit seller gains little from persuasion. Nonetheless, equilibrium dictates near-symmetric pricing, so competition plays out primarily through informational instruments rather than price undercutting. Influence can also reinforce rival loyalty by clarifying fit, revealing a double-edged strategic effect. Higher signal quality or tighter external price constraints compress loyal segments and increase the marginal value of persuasion. By modeling these interdependencies, the analysis clarifies how sellers can strategically align influence efforts, precision, and operational policies in competitive digital markets where consumer beliefs and transaction frictions jointly determine advantage.

Title: Labor unions and deaths of despair: Evidence from right-to-work laws
Authors: Luke Petach
Abstract: This paper examines the relationship between union membership and deaths of despair. Using state-level variation in the timing of the adoption of right-to-work laws as a natural experiment, I show that right-to-work laws are associated with a decline in union membership and an increase in deaths of despair. Two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) difference-in-differences (DiD) estimates suggest that the adoption of a right-to-work law is associated with a 2.6 percentage point reduction in union membership and an increase in deaths of despair mortality of 13 additional persons per 100,000, implying there are approximately 7.5 additional deaths of despair for every 1,000 workers who lose union membership. An analysis of mechanisms suggests the increase in mortality is largely driven by increased opioid usage and a concomitant increase in overdose deaths. I support the TWFE results with estimates from two alternative estimators robust to concerns about treatment effect heterogeneity and variation in treatment timing. Estimates from the Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) estimator and the Borusyak et al. (2024) estimator support the TWFE findings: right-to-work laws reduce union membership and increase deaths of despair.

Title: Job attribute dissatisfaction and turnover: New job or no job?
Authors: Femke Cnossen, Davide Lunardon
Abstract: We show that dissatisfaction with different job attributes predicts workers’ job mobility, using ten waves of the Dutch Working Conditions Survey (2014–2023) linked to administrative records covering over 360.000 workers. We find that dissatisfaction with non-wage attributes, such as interesting work, leadership and job security, is a strong and robust predictor of turnover across subsamples, related to a 30% higher probability of job separation. Overall, they explain 33% of the total explained variation. Different types of dissatisfaction are associated with different exit destinations: monetary and contractual dissatisfaction is primarily associated with job-to-job mobility (new job), while dissatisfaction with non-wage attributes, in particular intangibles, is more strongly linked to exits into non-employment (no job): unemployment, self-employment, and education. Our results are partly cyclical: the relationship between intangible dissatisfaction and turnover is stronger in tighter labour markets. Taken together we show that the type of job attributes a worker is dissatisfied with predicts both the likelihood of leaving and the kind of labour market transition that follows.

Title: Punching out, not down: The impact of paid sick leave on child maltreatment
Authors: Zhuoyu Qiu
Abstract: Child maltreatment has lasting consequences, but little is known about how flexible workplace protections affect child safety. This paper examines whether paid sick leave (PSL) mandates reduce reported maltreatment. Using incident-level data from the National Incident-Based Reporting System from 2007 to 2019 and an event study design, I find that PSL mandates lead to an annual 10 percent decline in reported child victims per agency, driven primarily by reductions in physical abuse. The effects are larger for cases involving female offenders and differ by victim gender: boys are less likely to experience physical abuse, while girls are less likely to experience sexual abuse. The impacts are greatest among Black children and in counties with higher poverty and lower median income. Mechanism analyses suggest two key pathways: limited exposure to higher-risk male caregivers and improved maternal well-being through greater financial security and health.
