Stricter environmental regulation in origin relative to the destination lowers trade costs for certain waste by 7%–77.7%. Per‐unit externality costs increase but gains from waste trade decrease with income, with PHE contributing substantially.

Title: Credits for Exporters: How Firm Characteristics and Loan Frequency Shape Policy Effectiveness
Authors: Álmos Telegdy, Szilárd Benk
Affiliations: Corvinus University of Budapest Budapest Hungary; Faculty of Economics and Business Administration Babeş‐Bolyai University Cluj‐Napoca Romania
Abstract: ABSTRACT We estimate the impact of Eximbank Hungary's working capital loans on firm exports using matching and panel methods. Loans increase export value by about 20% and export share by 6.5%. The strongest point estimates are associated with first loans. Export gains persist over time, but robust long‐run effects are detectable only at the full‐sample level, not among firms that receive a single loan. The estimated coefficients decline by initial export share but do not vary by firm size and productivity. Loans raise sales and employment by about 10% but do not affect productivity and profitability.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Calibration of electric vehicle energy consumption models: A context-Integrated transfer bayesian optimization approach
Authors: Chengqi Liu, Xinyu Shi, Jinbiao Huo, Yuhao Zhang, Yinke Sun, Zibo Ai, Hongtao Hu, Zhiyuan Liu
Abstract: Precise modeling of electric vehicle (EV) energy consumption is fundamental to the efficient design and management of modern transportation systems. While physics-based models offer superior interpretability, they often struggle with limited adaptability to dynamic driving conditions and heterogeneous vehicle platforms. To bridge this gap, achieving real-time and accurate calibration of physical model parameters becomes essential. This paper proposes a novel two-stage Bayesian optimization framework that integrates Contextual Bayesian Optimization (CBO) and Transfer Bayesian Optimization (TBO). In the first stage, the CBO module learns a context-aware mapping between operating conditions and physical parameters within a source domain. In the second stage, the TBO module leverages the learned prior knowledge to achieve rapid adaptation to a target vehicle domain with minimal data requirements. We evaluate the proposed framework using real-world datasets from BMW i3 and Tesla Model 3. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a per-second WMAPE of 17.27% in cross-condition scenarios. For cross-vehicle transfer, the primary out-of-sample evaluation on the held-out 70% of the Tesla trips yields a WMAPE of 24.82% and a total energy error of 12.65%. The CBO results further demonstrate rapid convergence under a limited online evaluation budget. This research provides a scalable and sample-efficient solution for high-fidelity energy modeling across diverse driving conditions and vehicle platforms.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Marine data-assisted motion control for unmanned surface vehicles in dynamic unknown environments: A distributed deep reinforcement learning approach
Authors: Chongwei Gong, Yusheng Zhou
Abstract: Unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) are increasingly deployed in modern logistics and transportation systems, supporting applications such as port surveillance, offshore logistics, and maritime infrastructure inspection. However, reliable navigation in dynamic marine environments remains challenging due to complex environmental disturbances and the conventional separation between path planning and motion control in existing approaches. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a marine-data-assisted distributed deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework for two coupled USV navigation tasks: path planning and path following. Rather than assuming a single universal policy, the proposed framework introduces a task-aware shared learning architecture called DTD3-CPER. It formulates path planning and path following as task-specific Markov decision processes while coordinating their training, experience management, and environmental interaction within a common learning framework. Moreover, an ERA5-informed marine simulation environment is developed by integrating spatially varying ocean-current and wind-field data into a grid-based navigation model. A distributed Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) algorithm enhanced with categorical prioritized experience replay (CPER) is then designed to support task-aware experience management, improve sample utilization, and enhance training stability. Simulation experiments indicate that the proposed framework achieves competitive performance against mainstream DRL baselines and conventional control methods in terms of learning efficiency, navigation safety, tracking accuracy, and disturbance adaptability. The results suggest that integrating marine environmental data with task-aware distributed reinforcement learning is a promising direction for data-driven USV navigation. From a managerial perspective, the proposed framework provides insights for developing data-driven decision-support systems for autonomous maritime logistics and intelligent maritime transportation systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Logic-based benders decomposition for multi-Period line planning with vehicle transfers
Authors: Amin Ahmadi Digehsara, Güvenç Şahin, Sina Rastani, Ralf Borndörfer
Abstract: This paper studies the multi-period line planning problem with vehicle rotation, a fundamental challenge in public transportation system design that integrates line selection, service frequency determination, and inter-period vehicle transfers. The temporal coupling induced by vehicle rotation generates strong interdependencies across planning periods, resulting in large-scale, highly combinatorial optimization models that are difficult to solve with existing mixed-integer programming methods. To address this complexity, we develop two exact decomposition-based solution frameworks. The first is a constraint satisfaction algorithm that iteratively relaxes and reinstates the vehicle flow-balance constraints, progressively reconstructing feasibility through a sequence of restricted master problems. The second is a logic-based Benders decomposition framework in which the feasibility verification stage is reformulated as a max-flow and min-cut problem. This reformulation enables the efficient identification of infeasibilities and the generation of strong feasibility cuts derived from the structure of the underlying network. Extensive computational experiments on three real public transportation networks, Istanbul Metrobüs, Athens Metro , and Quito Trolebús , demonstrate the efficiency and scalability of the proposed methods. The logic-based decomposition algorithm attains optimal solutions up to 99% faster than a state-of-the-art commercial solver and successfully solves instances with more than 300 lines that remain unsolved within 24 hours by conventional algorithms. The results confirm that embedding network-flow reasoning within a logic-based decomposition framework yields a computationally tractable and structurally coherent methodology for large-scale multi-period line planning with vehicle rotation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Multiple testing in rolling-window analysis via p-value combination
Authors: Xing Ling, Qian Wu, Kun Chen
Abstract: Rolling-window methods are widely used to explore time variation in economic relationships. Testing across overlapping windows induces a multiple-testing problem and can inflate the familywise error. Existing corrections are often either overly conservative or computationally intensive. We propose a harmonic mean p[jls-end-space/]-value procedure that provides a global test together with window-level diagnostics. We establish iterated rejection-tail calibration of the global test and weak familywise error control for the associated diagnostic rule under overlap-induced dependence. Simulations using several standard time-series tests show accurate size, higher power, and substantially lower computational cost than bootstrap-based extreme-statistic procedures.

Title: Tourist taxation, Lerner symmetry, and the double dividend
Authors: Ayumu Tanaka
Abstract: This paper studies a tax on tourism services, collected from foreign visitors upon entry, in a two-sector small open economy with congestible public infrastructure. Lerner symmetry implies that the tax raises manufacturing’s relative price and reverses tourism-driven Dutch disease. Tourism tax revenue lowers resident income taxes, while the contraction in tourism output reduces congestion, generating a double dividend.

Title: Birth rates, longevity, and monetary transmission
Authors: Seungjun Baek, Myunghyun Kim
Abstract: The source of aging matters for the real-rate redistribution channel of monetary transmission in a three-generation life-cycle model. A given old-age dependency ratio can reflect higher longevity or a lower birth rate. We show that this channel depends on the source of aging and on who bears the fiscal cost, not on the ratio alone. When retirees bear a sufficiently large share of the fiscal cost, the low-birth-rate economy has the larger consumption response to a real interest-rate increase. Otherwise, the high-longevity economy has the larger response.

Title: Macroeconomic attention and stock market volatility: Evidence from dynamic forecast combinations
Authors: Xue Gong, Rong Ma
Abstract: We construct macroeconomic attention indicators (MAIs) using daily search engine data. Across multiple dynamic forecast combination approaches, the MAIs demonstrate significant predictive power for the realized volatility of the Chinese stock market. The predictive gains are primarily driven by attention to safe-haven demand (gold) and monetary policy (interest rates), with substantial heterogeneity across sectors. Moreover, MAIs become particularly informative during the high-uncertainty periods, highlighting the state-dependent transmission of macroeconomic attention to financial markets.

Title: Environmental foundations of human capital: Deforestation’s impact on early childhood health
Authors: Richard Damania, Luis Diego Herrera Garcia, Hyungju Henry Kim, Leonardo Viotti, Esha Zaveri, Stefanie Onder, Chrissie Pantoja
Abstract: The environment underpins human well-being, yet its degradation increasingly threatens recent development gains, particularly in human health. This paper examines how forest loss affects early childhood health through the hydrological services that forests provide—an important but understudied mechanism. By linking high-resolution forest cover loss data with health outcomes for 0.7 million children across 46 countries, we exploit spatial and temporal variation in upstream forest cover loss measured at different points in time to assess downstream health impacts on rural households. Our findings show that upstream forest loss significantly increases the incidence of diarrheal disease among children under five, underscoring the critical role forests play in maintaining water quality through natural filtration. The health effects are not only immediate but also persistent: upstream forest cover loss leads to higher stunting rates, a key indicator of long-term productivity and human health. Furthermore, we find that the type of land cover transitions matters. Forest degradation and conversion to grassland are particularly harmful, while conversion to urban land may mitigate health impacts—likely due to improved infrastructure and access to services. These findings highlight the essential role of upstream forest ecosystems in supporting human capital and emphasize the need to preserve and restore natural capital to improve long-term health and development outcomes.

Title: Where and how is money spent on international migration and refugees in World Bank operational projects?
Authors: David McKenzie, Charlotte Müller, Pablo Acosta
Abstract: A strong evidence base has documented the many ways that international migration can bring large development benefits. Flagship reports from international organizations have long argued that countries should actively manage migration for development. How much is this evidence and rhetoric reflected in what money actually gets spent on? We analyze the World Bank portfolio of projects financed between 2014 and 2024 to see how much money is being spent on activities related to international migration and refugees, where it is being spent, and what it is being used for. We identify 160 operational projects, totaling $40 billion overall, with $15 billion in components related to migration and refugees. However, this funding is highly concentrated in a small number of countries, and over 70 percent of World Bank clients have not received a single dollar in financing for migration in a decade. Financing is almost entirely driven by projects to support refugees and displaced populations, with funding for facilitating or increasing benefits from economic (labor) migration averaging only $11 million annually. Examination of the few projects that do relate to economic migration shows efforts to develop new migration corridors, reintegrate returnees, and improve the technical and vocational training systems of sending countries to better align and certify skills with overseas demand. These cases also provide a demonstration effect of how money can be spent proactively to enhance the benefits of international mobility. The paper concludes by discussing the barriers to more project lending and potential opportunities.

Title: Dynamic idle-time bounding mechanism for job shop scheduling problems
Authors: Christian Perez, Rubén Mas, Miguel A. Salido
Abstract: The Job-Shop Scheduling Problem (JSP) is a well-known NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem with broad relevance to industrial scheduling applications. Given its inherent computational complexity, effective filtering and bounding strategies are essential for reducing search effort. This study proposes a dynamic idle-time bounding mechanism that restricts the search to statistically plausible idle-time intervals before and during the solution process. Idle-time thresholds, conditioned on instance size, are estimated via polynomial regression on empirical solver performance data and adaptively relaxed when necessary to preserve feasibility. The resulting mechanism prunes unpromising regions of the search space and strengthens propagation within conventional exact solvers. The mechanism is implemented as a solver-agnostic augmentation for exact solvers and evaluated on Taillard’s benchmark set and JSPLIB instances using CPLEX, Gurobi, and OR-Tools. The results show substantial reductions in solving time, reaching up to 80% on several benchmark families, while maintaining competitive returned-solution quality under common time budgets; in multiple hard instances, the optimality gap is also reduced. Overall, the proposed method is particularly effective on medium and large JSP instances, where idle-time decisions introduce substantial combinatorial degeneracy, and provides a practical enhancement for scalable exact scheduling.

Title: Multi-product batch scheduling for cement mills under time-of-use electricity tariffs
Authors: Liteng An, Songlin Zhang, Xiaochen Hao
Abstract: As a high energy-consuming facility in the cement industry, cement mills require effective production scheduling strategies to reduce electricity costs under time-of-use (TOU) pricing while satisfying the demand for multiple cement products. This study develops an optimization model for cement mill scheduling based on a mixed-integer programming (MIP) approach, with the objective of reducing electricity costs while satisfying the demand for multiple types of cement. The model first ensures that the production targets for each cement type are satisfied. Subsequently, it optimizes the scheduling of production batches and the allocation of equipment to facilitate load shifting towards periods of lower electricity tariffs, thereby minimizing total electricity costs and enhancing both the economic efficiency and practical applicability of the scheduling strategy. Furthermore, the model explicitly incorporates sequence-dependent setup times and energy consumption during machine startup and shutdown processes, realistically capturing the impact of product switching and intermittent production on overall scheduling performance, thereby improving the operational and engineering applicability of the model. In terms of solution methodology, an Improved Discrete Particle Swarm Optimization (IDPSO) algorithm based on greedy insertion decoding is proposed to generate feasible production schedules. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed model, a set of computational experiments was designed. Simulation studies based on real-world data from a cement plant demonstrate that the model not only ensures timely fulfillment of cement demand but also effectively avoids production during high-tariff periods and reduces cost impacts associated with machine startup, shutdown, and setup times.

Title: How did empirical economic research improve over the last decades: Recent trends and prospects
Authors: Abel Brodeur, Stephan B. Bruns, Helmut Herwartz, Chris-Gabriel Islam

Title: Culture and constitutional compliance
Authors: Jerg Gutmann, Anna Lewczuk-Czerwińska, Jacek Lewkowicz, Stefan Voigt
Abstract: Constitutions as the formal foundation of a country’s legal and political system have important economic and political effects. Yet, we still know little about why constitutions set effective constraints on politicians in some societies, while being largely disregarded in others. Here, we ask if national culture matters for constitutional compliance. We study a cross-section of 115 countries, making use of novel indicators of constitutional compliance. We find that societies with a more individualistic population exhibit higher levels of compliance. These results are robust and extend to instrumental variable estimations. They imply a novel transmission channel from cultural traits to long-term economic development: individualistic national culture increases the credibility of constitutional self-commitments. Our analysis also supports the more general idea that the effects of formal institutions depend on the informal institutional environment in which they are embedded. Regarding religion, our results are consistent with past research that attributes the lack of development in the modern Muslim world to deficient institutional quality.

Title: Pumped hydro energy storage: Structural results and solution algorithms
Authors: Harun Avci, Ece Cigdem Karakoyun, Ayse Selin Kocaman, Emre Nadar, Parinaz Toufani
Abstract: We study a pumped hydro energy storage facility that consists of two interconnected reservoirs – an upper and a lower – where one reservoir may be fed by natural inflow. The system operator makes real-time decisions regarding the amount of water to pump or release, thereby determining the amount of electricity to buy from or sell to the market. We model this problem as a Markov decision process, accounting for uncertainties in both streamflow rates and electricity prices. We prove the optimality of a state-dependent threshold policy under positive electricity prices: The state space can be partitioned into several disjoint domains, each associated with a different action type, such that it is optimal to bring the total amount of water in the facility and the amount of water in the upper reservoir to a different pair of state-dependent target levels in each domain. For more general data-calibrated instances in which prices can be negative, we use this threshold structure as the basis for policy-approximation algorithms. These algorithms yield near-optimal solutions up to 28 times faster than brute-force optimization, with no significant drain on total cash flows compared to the optimal solution.

Title: An evaluation method for the fume emission intensity of rubber-modified asphalt binders
Authors: Guoqiang Sun, Qiyi Zhang, Jiangcheng Ai, Guangchen Wang, Weidong Ning, Bin Li, Long Cheng
Abstract: Accurately quantifying fume emission intensity from rubber-modified asphalt binders is essential for sustainable construction and air-pollution mitigation. This study proposes an evaluation method based on maximum emission rate, peak concentration, and total emission amount. Feasibility was verified through variability, sensitivity, and comparative analyses. The method was applied to rubber-modified asphalt binders at different activation temperatures and multi-source aging durations to quantify fume emission intensity. Microscopic mechanisms were analyzed using fluorescence microscopy (FM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). Results indicate good reliability, with parallel experimental variability of 4.94% and a deviation within ±0.03 in weighted sensitivity analysis. Microscopic observations corroborated the macroscopic emission trends: high-temperature activation damaged the rubber structure and increased its solubility, more than doubling fume emission intensity, whereas multi-source aging reduced light components and decreased emissions by approximately 20%.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Integrating topic modeling and heuristic optimization for customer lifetime value in multi-channel decision support
Authors: Tzu-Chien Wang, Ruey-Shan Guo, Chialin Chen, Chia Kai Li
Abstract: As data-driven marketing evolves, firms face the challenge of translating predictive insights into strategic resource-allocation decisions. This study proposes a CLV decision-support architecture that integrates semantic representation, multi-stage behavioral prediction, and budget-constrained allocation. The architecture combines BERTopic-based semantic extraction and gradient boosting for predictive modeling with a finite-difference sensitivity-guided heuristic search module. Empirically, we separate observed temporal validation from semi-synthetic and simulation-based analyses. On the real temporal split, a predictive signal is present (AUC = 0.6313), but the integrated-versus-stage-wise uplift is small and not statistically significant. Controlled analyses instead show that integrated allocation becomes more visible under tighter budgets, stronger downstream coupling, and stress conditions. Within the BDE family, finite-difference guidance improves over vanilla BDE in the tested setting, but we retain this only as a narrow application-oriented claim. Overall, the findings support a bounded, condition-dependent view of semantic-aware CLV decision support rather than a claim of uniform deployment gains.

Title: Enabling Systemic Trust in the Physical Internet: An eDSR Approach to Governance Model Design
Authors: Malte Spanuth, Rod Franklin, André Ludwig
Affiliations: Kühne Logistics University Hamburg Germany; Leipzig University Leipzig Germany
Abstract: ABSTRACT The Physical Internet (PI) envisions a hyperconnected cyber‐physical logistics system inspired by the Digital Internet, yet adoption remains limited due to persistent trust and governance challenges. This study addresses these barriers by conceptualizing systemic trust as a foundational requirement for broad participation in the PI. We apply the echeloned Design Science Research methodology to develop the Governance and Trust Orchestration Layer (GTOL), an extension of existing layered PI models that incorporates mechanisms for rule enforcement, credentialing, dispute resolution, and fair matching. Based on empirical interviews with logistics practitioners and evaluated through scenario‐based walkthroughs, the GTOL addresses core commercial, institutional, and technological trust concerns. We contribute mid‐range design theory through six design principles that provide transferable guidance for embedding trust in decentralized logistics networks. They serve as a practical and theoretical blueprint for enabling governance structures that are transparent, enforceable, and adaptable across diverse logistics contexts.

Title: Pulling Back the Curtain: Using Dependability, Credibility, Transferability, and Confirmability as Evaluation Criteria for Literature Reviews
Authors: Christopher W. Craighead, Jessica L. Darby, David J. Ketchen
Affiliations: University of Tennessee Knoxville Tennessee USA; Auburn University Auburn Alabama USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Literature review articles play a crucial role in advancing knowledge by making sense of a body of research and setting a foundation for subsequent inquiry. Because much of the work is unobservable, some readers may wonder about the underlying rigor of a literature review. This hidden element creates parallels between literature reviews and qualitative research. In response to concerns about rigor, qualitative researchers have developed and rely upon a set of criteria by which qualitative work can be judged. In this essay, we adapt those criteria—dependability (analogous to reliability), credibility (analogous to internal validity), transferability (analogous to external validity), and confirmability (analogous to objectivity)—and explain how the criteria can be used to assess and improve the rigor of literature review articles. We then introduce the 2026 Special Topic Forum articles and spotlight examples wherein the articles excelled along the evaluation criteria.

Title: Disaster Relief Through a Complex Adaptive System Perspective: Firms' Motivations, Activities, and the Role of Operations Adaptability in Overlapping Landscapes
Authors: Thu Trang Hoang, Peter M. Ralston, William J. Rose
Affiliations: Department of Information Systems and Operations Management University of Texas Arlington Texas USA; Department of Supply Chain Management Iowa State University Ames Iowa USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Natural disasters disrupt the normal functioning of both communities and businesses. However, past literature often segregates the disaster relief view from the business continuity perspective, leaving a gap in understanding how firms can proactively support relief efforts. Using an embedded case, we focus on the operations of a multinational enterprise in the Fast‐Moving Consumer Goods sector to reveal these mechanisms. Its headquarters and geographic business units represent firms within and outside the disaster's vicinity and show how they work with NGOs and government counterparts in relief efforts. We find that firms within the disaster's vicinity (i.e., local firms or firms whose markets or supplies can be disrupted by the disaster) are motivated to proactively participate in the relief effort. These firms' goals to stabilize the market and economy are well‐aligned with NGOs and the government during disaster preparedness and response. Meanwhile, firms outside the disaster's vicinity mostly report philanthropic donations to support disaster relief, with underlying motivations for branding, tax benefits, and efficiency. Analyses of qualitative interviews and quantitative data under the Complex Adaptive Systems lens also reveal interesting insights into how the non‐profit and for‐profit landscapes overlap during disaster preparedness and response, and how firms within the disaster's vicinity can play a more central role in recovery if they have better operations adaptability capabilities (i.e., coordinated changes instead of changes in individual operations factors). Our findings contribute to both the disaster relief literature and the understanding of complex adaptive systems, especially in disaster contexts.

Title: Gone with the wind: Productive response to agricultural shock
Authors: Myriam Marending, Stefano Tripodi

Title: From social savings to spatial equilibrium: Evaluating transportation improvements in quantitative spatial models
Authors: Treb Allen, Simon Fuchs, Woan Foong Wong
Abstract: How do we evaluate the welfare gains from transport infrastructure investment? We present a quantitative spatial framework that integrates traffic and economic responses to infrastructure improvements and derives the elasticity of aggregate welfare to changes in the transportation network. The resulting formula extends the traditional ``social savings'' method to incorporate route and mode choice, agglomeration and dispersion externalities, and traffic congestion. We apply the formula to the U.S. freight network and assess the benefits of reducing costs on each segment of the U.S. Interstate Highway System. The traditional and extended measures are closely related overall, but they differ in the level of estimated gains and in the ranking of some highly valued links. Where the rankings differ, network position determines how congestion and spatial adjustment alter a link's measured benefit. Title: Sustainable procurement under ESG: Optimizing carbon and social risks in inbound operations
Authors: R. Ghasemy Yaghin, B. Ghaffarnezhad

Title: Agent-based modeling of flight delay propagation: Mechanism contributions and airport-closure impacts
Authors: Kashin Sugishita, Hiroki Mizutani, Shinya Hanaoka
Abstract: Delays in air transport often cascade through interacting operational mechanisms, yet capturing the within-day, aircraft-level dependencies that produce system-wide propagation remains challenging. We develop a minute-resolution, mechanism-resolved agent-based model that integrates five channels—aircraft rotation, passenger connections, airport congestion, stochastic disturbances, and flight-time variability. The model is initialized with day-specific tail-by-tail rotations and empirically grounded rules including size-dependent turnaround times, minimum departure intervals, airport-specific minimum connection times, and seasonal route-level flight-time distributions. Applied to Japan’s 2024 domestic network, the framework reproduces observed propagation across quiet and disrupted regimes. Mechanism attribution via stepwise ablation and Shapley decomposition reveals a stable hierarchy: aircraft rotation provides the structural backbone, stochastic disturbances are the principal amplifier, airport congestion modulates mid-distribution behavior, and passenger connections are secondary. As a policy application, temporary airport-closure experiments show strong time-of-day sensitivity: early-morning closures at Tokyo International Airport are most disruptive; impacts rise nonlinearly with duration; and two-airport closures are predominantly sub-additive. Our model enables the analysis of delay propagation under a wide range of operating conditions and offers direct, actionable policy implications for building more resilient aviation systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Who Bears the cost of Digitalization? Customer digital transformation, multiplex network embeddedness, and supplier operational resilience
Authors: Xiaolong Wang, Di Wang, Yanmin Zhao, Yanhua Gong
Abstract: Operational resilience is critical for suppliers to sustain competitive advantages amid volatile market environments. While prior research emphasizes firms’ own digital transformation as a driver of resilience, the spillover effects of customer-side digitalization on suppliers remain underexplored. Drawing on resource dependence and social network theories, this study examines the relationship between customer digital transformation and supplier operational resilience, as well as the moderating role of suppliers’ multiplex network structural embeddedness. Using data from Chinese listed firms and their supply chain relationships between 2018 and 2022, we find that customer digital transformation significantly undermines supplier operational resilience, indicating a negative downstream spillover in the digital transition. Further moderating effect analysis reveals that a supplier’s structural embeddedness in both the supply chain network and the executive interlock network can effectively mitigate this negative impact. Heterogeneity analysis shows that the adverse effect is more pronounced among non-state-owned enterprises, firms with highly substitutable products, and firms with lower digital transformation. Overall, this study advances research on digital transformation and operational resilience from a customer-driven perspective and highlights the role of network embeddedness in buffering external digital shocks.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: An integrated optimization framework for energy-efficient timetabling considering rolling stock circulation in urban rail transit
Authors: Bonan Zhang, Xiangming Yao, Jie Zhang, Peng Zhao, Mei Han, Dongsheng Zhao
Abstract: Timetable optimization is a crucial strategy for reducing energy consumption in urban rail transit. However, existing research often narrowly focused on energy reduction while neglecting fundamental operational requirements such as rolling stock circulation and fixed first/last train schedules, limiting the practical applicability of the resulting optimization schemes. This study proposes a mixed-integer nonlinear programming model to jointly determine departure headways, section running levels, and rolling stock circulation plans, with the objectives of minimizing net energy consumption and depot entry/exit operations. To support the solution of this model, an optimization framework comprising two modules is developed: (1) an energy precomputation module that decouples redundant energy computations across discrete time intervals from the core optimization process; (2) a hybrid solution module that combines an adaptive large neighborhood search algorithm with the Gurobi solver to efficiently solve the large-scale integrated model. A series of real-world case studies based on Fuzhou Metro Line 5 in China demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed framework. Compared with the current timetable, the optimized timetable reduced traction energy consumption and net energy consumption by 6.12 % and 10.20 %, respectively, with a 61.32 % increase in the amount of utilized regenerative braking energy. The number of depot entry/exit operations was reduced from 20 to 19, while maintaining the required rolling stock units unchanged. Results demonstrated that the proposed optimization framework can enhance energy efficiency and operational feasibility in urban rail transit by minimizing overall operational costs, encompassing electrical energy consumption and rolling stock circulation costs.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Payroll taxes, firm dynamism, and aggregate productivity
Authors: Jin Feng, Yuting Li, Yu Liu
Abstract: This study examines the impact of payroll-tax enforcement on firm dynamism and its implications for aggregate productivity. We exploit China's Social Security Collection Agency Reform, which transferred responsibility for collecting social-insurance contributions from local social-insurance agencies to tax authorities, thereby strengthening enforcement. We show that the reform increased firms’ social-insurance contributions, shifted workers toward informal employment without reducing overall nonagricultural employment, and reduced new firm entry while weakening incumbent firms’ profitability and investment. Overall, the reform reduced measured aggregate productivity in China's registered, above-scale industrial sector by 3.3 percent, with entry into the above-scale industrial sector accounting for about 45 percent of the estimated decline.

Title: Calibrating bid screens under quantity repricing
Authors: Yisang Park
Abstract: Holding score fixed, unit-price bidders can reallocate line-item prices to hedge quantity risk. Repricing governs how this hedge affects realized payment, while a bid screen limits its size. Their interaction leaves residual exposure: baseline exposure minus effective hedge capacity, truncated at zero. Under constant absolute risk aversion (CARA), residual exposure generates a certainty-equivalent premium in the first-price score equilibrium. With a fixed binding screen, stronger repricing raises expected procurement payments when lost hedge capacity exceeds direct exposure relief. Calibrating the screen to preserve residual exposure preserves allocation, bidder utility, and expected payment under mean-level normalization.

Title: Symmetrized smooth test for the equality of distributions
Authors: Peiwen Jia, Xiaojun Song
Abstract: We develop a novel symmetrized smooth test for the equality of two distributions by incorporating information from two probability integral transform representations in a symmetric manner. This construction eliminates the dependence on the assignment of roles to the two samples. We establish the asymptotic Chi-square null distribution of the proposed symmetrized statistic and characterize its behavior under fixed and local alternatives. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed test achieves more stable size control and improved finite-sample performance, particularly when the sample sizes are small or unbalanced.

Title: Breaking Down the Barriers: Understanding Consumer Resistance to Zero-Emission Vehicle Purchases
Authors: Shoumic Shahid Chowdhury, Md Shahadat Hossain, Mahmudur Fatmi
Abstract: Canada has established ambitious goals to reduce transportation emissions, targeting all new vehicle sales to be zero-emission vehicles (ZEVs) by 2040. In this study, ZEVs refer to battery electric vehicles (BEVs), plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs), and fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEVs), consistent with Canadian policy definitions. Despite increasing policy support, a large segment of the population remains resistant to adopting ZEVs. While prior research has primarily focused on factors driving adoption, the reasons underlying non-adoption remain less explored. This study investigates ZEV resistance using data from the British Columbia ZEV Market Research Survey, comprising 3,850 respondents, of which 3,253 individuals who have never owned a ZEV are analyzed. A random parameter multinomial logit model is employed to classify resistance into five categories: cost, charging and range limitations, vehicle unavailability, environmental concerns, and other reasons, while accounting for unobserved heterogeneity. The results reveal that resistance is highly segmented across population groups. Younger and lower-income individuals are primarily constrained by cost, whereas higher-income individuals are more likely to resist due to limited availability of preferred vehicle models. Older adults and residents of multi-unit dwellings are significantly more affected by charging and range-related barriers. These findings demonstrate that ZEV resistance is not uniform but driven by distinct constraints across population segments. The results provide targeted policy insights to support more effective and equitable strategies for accelerating ZEV adoption in Canada.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Trust beyond borders: the role of non-state actors in shaping immigration preferences
Authors: Annette Idler, Isabel Ruiz, Carlos Vargas-Silva
Abstract: STATA replication files for the article "Trust Beyond Borders: The Role of Non-State Actors in Shaping Immigration Preferences"

Title: Reinforcement learning-driven non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II for in-space manufacturing energy efficient scheduling problem with power constraint
Authors: Liping Xu, Kai Li, Chuanyu Wu, Han Zhang
Abstract: As deep space exploration missions continue to expand and the operational costs of space stations rise, there is a growing need to focus on in-space manufacturing production and energy management. Addressing the complex characteristics of energy constraints, equipment multi-functionality, and multi-constrained production in space manufacturing, this paper investigates a flexible job-shop energy-efficient scheduling problem that considers power threshold and variable processing speeds, aiming to balance production efficiency and energy consumption. Firstly, a bi-objective optimization mathematical model incorporating power constraint, variable processing speeds, setup and transportation constraints is constructed. Secondly, a reinforcement learning-driven non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (RLNSGA-II) is proposed. This algorithm employs a hybrid population initialization method, combining various scheduling rules to generate the initial population. An adaptive local search strategy is designed to choose appropriate operators for individuals. Meanwhile, a Q-learning-driven strategy is applied to determine the local search depth during the evolutionary process, aiming to enhance optimization performance without increasing computational time. Finally, the performance of RLNSGA-II is evaluated using 45 test instances. Ablation experiments demonstrate that each component contributes to enhancing overall performance, thereby confirming the effectiveness of these innovative designs. Furthermore, compared with other intelligent algorithms, RLNSGA-II performs better on the Hypervolume and Inverted Generational Distance metrics in 80% and 75.6% of instances, respectively, thus validating its effectiveness.

Title: The lecture-hall quadratic assignment problem
Authors: Tal Raviv
Abstract: We study the post-timetabling lecture-hall assignment problem : given a fixed weekly timetable and realized student enrollments, assign each lecture to a compatible hall so as to minimize the walking burden of students moving between consecutive lectures, plus a penalty for feasible but non-ideal hall–lecture assignments. The problem combines a quadratic assignment objective, driven by shared enrollments and hall-to-hall distances, with interval-scheduling feasibility and hall-capacity constraints. We prove that it is NP-hard and, unless P = N P , inapproximable within any fixed rational factor, already in a single-day, two-block special case. We develop two exact mathematical-programming formulations: a bilinear mixed-integer quadratic program and a compact mixed-integer linear program with one distance variable per successor pair. To tighten the models we introduce biclique distance cuts that dominate the standard pairwise linking inequalities, complemented by Chvátal-Gomory capacity-dominance cuts; common side constraints such as SameRoom and SameAttendees are accommodated as well. In experiments on 35 daily instances derived from five large ITC 2019 competition benchmarks and a 2023 institutional dataset from Lancaster University, the biclique-strengthened compact linearized program solves every instance to proven optimality within an 1800-second limit. The direct quadratic model often finds the same incumbents but is weaker for proving optimality on the hardest instances, while the biclique cuts are the dominant modeling device behind the observed speed and robustness. On the ten Lancaster instances, optimized assignments reduce model-implied walking by 20%–45% relative to the deployed room plan.

Title: Generational war on inflation? Optimal inflation rates for the young and the old
Authors: Ippei Fujiwara, Shunsuke Hori, Yuichiro Waki
Abstract: How does a grayer society affect the political decision-making regarding inflation rates? Is deflation preferred as a society ages? In order to answer these questions, we compute the optimal inflation rates for the young and the old respectively, and explore how they change with demographic factors, by using a New Keynesian model with overlapping generations. According to our simulation results, there indeed exists a tension between the young and the old on the optimal inflation rates, with the optimal inflation rates differing between generations. The rates can be significantly different from zero, particularly, when heterogeneous impacts from inflation via nominal asset holdings are considered. The optimal inflation rates for the old can be largely negative, reflecting their positive nominal asset holdings as well as lower effective discount factor. Societal aging may exert downward pressure on inflation rates through a politico-economic mechanism.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Captured gatekeepers: Structural conflicts of interest in U.S. higher education accreditation
Authors: Bryan Cutsinger, Siri Terjesen
Abstract: This paper examines the structural ties between federally recognized programmatic accreditors and their affiliated professional and trade associations, arguing that these organizational arrangements constitute structural conflicts of interest that raise substantial concerns about the quality-assurance function accreditation is intended to serve. Drawing on a novel dataset constructed from IRS Form 990 XML filings for 32 accreditor-association pairs over a seven-year panel (2017–2023), this paper develops and operationalizes a three-part typology of capture mechanisms: structural subordination, financial entanglement, and governance overlap. This study constructs a Regulatory Capture Index (RCI) to measure the intensity of structural capture across the population of programmatic accreditors. The findings reveal that 28 of 32 accreditor-association pairs exhibit structural subordination, 88 percent of observations are financially inseparable, and the 15 Case A health-professions accreditors uniformly score 1.0; the four structurally separate Case B pairs (ACEN, CACREP, CNME, CEPH) score between 0.000 and 0.333. The authors propose four reforms: board independence requirements, financial independence standards, mandatory separate legal incorporation, and enhanced disclosure.

Title: Just transition? Exploring the climate finance, regulatory quality, trade openness and renewable energy nexus
Authors: Lili Wang, Jun Pang
Abstract: Climate finance aims to support a fair transition to renewable energy in developing countries, yet the conditions under which climate finance is associated with renewable energy development remain unclear. This study examines the relationship between climate finance and renewable energy development using a double machine learning (DML) framework that combines Lasso regression as the base learner with K-fold cross-fitting and Neyman orthogonalization to mitigate potential bias arising from endogeneity and high-dimensional confounding. Drawing on panel data from 71 developing countries over 2000–2019, the DML estimation yields a statistically significant positive association, and the positive association between climate finance and renewable energy development is particularly evident among low-income developing countries. Furthermore, dynamic panel threshold modeling identifies significant threshold values. Specifically, when regulatory quality exceeds −1.060, the association between climate finance and renewable energy development becomes positive; and when trade openness exceeds the threshold value, the positive association between climate finance and renewable energy becomes stronger. Therefore, improving regulatory quality and facilitating trade openness may create more favorable conditions under which climate finance is more strongly associated with renewable energy development.

Title: Automakers' electrification and R&D strategies under the dual-credit policy
Authors: Linyang Sun, Yuyin Yi

Title: Electricity market structure and consequences for wind and solar uptake in the EU-27
Authors: Jonas Grafström, Daniel Halvarsson, Theo Herold, Nadja Vinberg
Abstract: This paper examines whether concentration in electricity generation affects the deployment of wind and solar capacity across the 27 European Union member states over 2000–2022. Market concentration is measured by the generation share of the largest electricity producer, and wind and solar deployment is measured as installed wind and solar capacity relative to total national electricity capacity. Using a country-level panel and dynamic estimation methods that account for persistence, unobserved heterogeneity, and reverse causality—including fixed-effects OLS and Arellano–Bond GMM estimators with lagged concentration as an internal instrument—the analysis finds no systematic relationship between market concentration and subsequent wind or solar deployment. The result is robust across alternative concentration and outcome measures, bias-corrected dynamic panel estimators, balanced samples, region-specific linear time trends and heterogeneity analyses across regions, transition stages, energy-system characteristics, and policy regimes. The findings suggest that within the EU institutional setting, market concentration per se is not a first-order constraint on renewable uptake; instead, deployment is primarily driven by policy settings and the path dependence inherent in installed capacity.

Title: Regulatory architecture and shipowner investment response under overlapping carbon-pricing regimes
Authors: Angelica Kemene, Vangelis Tsioumas
Abstract: Maritime transport, responsible for roughly 3% of global greenhouse gas emissions, faces overlapping carbon-pricing regulation as the EU Emissions Trading System extends to shipping and the International Maritime Organization develops a prospective Net-Zero Framework with tradeable Remedial Units. This raises a central question: whether instrument interaction, rather than the stringency of any one measure, changes firm-level investment when carbon prices are held fixed, and how it shapes investment policy and the value of flexibility under uncertainty. We develop a correlated three-factor real-options framework using Longstaff–Schwartz continuation-value estimation with independent validation and test-sample policy evaluation, jointly modelling freight, fuel and carbon prices with calibrated cross-correlations and a Poisson hazard model for regulatory activation. We apply it to a Long Range 2 product tanker across four regimes: EU ETS phase-in, sustained regional fragmentation, and EU ETS plus IMO under netted or stacked interaction rules. Three findings emerge. First, regulatory architecture is economically material: netted versus stacked rules shift strategy NPVs by approximately $1 million at unchanged carbon prices. Second, the efficiency-first ranking is preserved across all regimes, including fragmentation where effective carbon exposure nearly doubles. Third, direct fuel-price support of about $200–300 per tonne substantially improves staged alternative-fuel pathways but does not eliminate the structural advantage of low-CAPEX efficiency retrofits, indicating that per-tonne support narrows but does not close the remaining economic gap. Results are robust across sixteen sensitivity dimensions and Capesize and feeder cross-segment checks.

Title: Legitimate decision authority and motivation in organizations
Authors: Holger Herz, Christian Zihlmann
Abstract: The allocation of decision rights—and the decision hierarchies it creates—shape incentives in organizations and thus individual motivation. We study whether the motivational effects of decision hierarchies go beyond pecuniary incentives and how they relate to the perceived legitimacy of the decision hierarchy. In a laboratory experiment, we exogenously manipulate the payoff structure of an organization in a way that leaves the pecuniary incentives of all involved parties unaffected but shifts subordinates’ perceived legitimacy of the decision hierarchy. Our data show that subordinates’ motivation to provide effort is causally affected by the organizational payoff structure, and significantly associated with the perceived legitimacy of the decision hierarchy.

Title: Motivation complementarities in prosocial behavior: Evidence from social networks of blood donors
Authors: Adrian Bruhin, Simon Haenni, Lingqing Jiang, Adrian Roethlisberger, Regula Buchli, Beat M. Frey, Lorenz Goette
Abstract: If individuals’ prosocial motivations are complements, this creates an important lever for the provision of social capital. We develop a framework to identify motivation complementarities and apply it in the context of voluntary blood donations—a key example of a purely prosocial behavior. Using quasi-random phone calls to identify causal effects, we find that a 10 percentage point increase in the donation rate for a blood drive raises a focal donor’s turnout by about 5.6 percentage points, creating a policy multiplier of 2.3. We also rule out lower costs from joint traveling as the main driver of the motivation complementarities. Rather, they result, at least partly, from more general mechanisms, such as utility from social approval, peer pressure, or social image concerns.

Title: Impact of environmental functions on electric vehicle charging experience considering contextual constraints
Authors: Chenxi Liu, Hongyuan Lu, Lingbo Liu, Peng Tian, Zhenghong Peng, Hao Wu, Zhigang Li
Abstract: As the electric vehicle market expands, improving public charging experience has become critical to the sustainability of urban transport. Using Wuhan as an empirical case, this study develops a double machine learning framework to examine how urban functional environments shape charging experience through charging behavior, while incorporating competition intensity and time-of-use tariff differentiation as contextual constraints. Based on tens of millions of charging records, three main findings emerge. First, the functional environment has a significant positive causal effect on charging experience, about 60% of which is mediated by charging behavior. Second, only a few behavior types generate disproportionate experience gains, and these behaviors are linked to the joint presence of particular nearby urban functions. Third, moderate levels of competition intensity and time-of-use tariff differentiation amplify both the total effect and behavioral mediation. These findings inform station siting, operational optimization, and charging-network planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: The Single-Row Facility Layout Problem with chance constraints
Authors: Anja Fischer, Louisa Semrau

Title: A bi-objective vehicle routing model for sustainable waste collection in a circular economy
Authors: Niama Yahiaoui, Mehdi Souier, Abdelghani Bekrar
Abstract: Sustainability and emissions reduction are crucial in modern waste management. This article explores the integration of circular economy principles with advanced optimization techniques to enhance resource efficiency and minimize environmental impact. The focus is on a multi-period bi-objective vehicle routing problem for municipal waste collection, integrating inventory dynamics at bins, capacity constraints, and service time windows to prevent overflow and ensure operational feasibility over a planning horizon. This research aims to optimize travel costs and load dependent $$CO_2$$ C O 2 emissions combining an exact multi-objective approach using Gurobi with an approximate approach based on NSGA-II, enhanced through local search, and selects final compromise solutions using TOPSIS under different decision priorities. The proposed methodology is validated on a real-world case study from a zone in municipality of Tlemcen, Algeria, across multiple instances. The results highlight clear cost–emission tradeoffs, demonstrate the scalability limits of exact solvers in multi-period settings, and show that the hybrid NSGA-II approach consistently provides high quality, near-optimal solutions for large scale sustainable waste collection planning.

Title: Forecasting oil and natural gas prices: A model combination approach
Authors: Ruben Aag, Hilde C. Bjørnland, Peder Eliassen
Abstract: We compare oil and natural gas price forecasting in a unified pseudo-real-time framework. While oil price forecasting is well established, natural gas has received far less attention: its markets remain regionalized, with prices set at separate hubs rather than in a globally integrated market. Adapting oil models to gas, we assess how market structure shapes model transferability and accuracy. Forecast combinations consistently outperform individual models for both commodities, but gains are far larger for natural gas, where localized pricing leaves more room for improvement. Optimal weighting also differs: equal weights dominate for oil, whereas performance-based weights are superior for gas.

Title: A multi-product operations-emission cost optimization model with stochastic demand
Authors: Md. Mahfuzur Rahman, Md. Abdul Hoque

Title: Fine-tuning collaboration in a Co-opetitive manufacturing supply chain
Authors: Baozhuang Niu, Chencan Lin, Fengfeng Xie, Jianhua Zhang
Abstract: In recent years, fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) have become increasingly important in manufacturers' improvement of production processes. Because of the heavy fine-tuning cost burden, firms within a supply chain have been witnessed to engage in fine-tuning collaboration, sharing efforts and results to reduce costs. Such collaboration, however, raises concerns about free-riding problems, which can be very typical in a co-opetitive supply chain. Therefore, we examine a manufacturing system including a supplier with self-brand and a manufacturer who both deploy their LLMs in production and make efforts on fine-tuning. We reveal that a higher intensity of fine-tuning collaboration creates a “suppression effect” which hampers stakeholders’ fine-tuning efforts out of the free-riding problems, and simultaneously a “synergy effect” which indicates that the overall market potential can be expanded by fine-tuning effort spillover, motivating them to invest more in fine-tuning. Driven by the dueling effects, the benefits of both the supplier and the manufacturer from fine-tuning collaboration exhibit non-monotonic relationships with respect to the collaboration intensity and the base product quality of the supplier. We further show that fine-tuning collaboration generally benefits the supplier more than the manufacturer in the co-opetitive relationship. Their incentives for collaboration are aligned if both the base product quality of the supplier and the collaboration intensity are relatively high.

Title: Human accuracy in social network analysis: The role of network characteristics in infection risk assessment
Authors: Martijn Stroom, Roselinde Kessels, Ingrid Rohde, Martin Strobel
Abstract: Understanding an individual’s human network assessment is fundamental for successful policy design when dealing with infection risk. Yet, how individuals cognitively compensate for their inability to process complex network models, remains poorly understood. Using an online best-worst ranking experiment, we investigate individuals’ perception of the risk of connecting to carefully constructed COVID-19-infected networks of 697 Dutch participants. Specifically, we consider three network characteristics that individuals can either directly access or implicitly estimate in real-life social network assessment. We show that the perceived infection risk in social networks is not solely based on the objective probability of this risk: easily assessable physical characteristics have stronger predictive power on the perceived risk than the objective probability. Heterogeneity assessment suggests that demographic differences such as the level of education interact with the order and strength of the network characteristics. The often-complex mental calculation underlying objective risk in networks is substituted by a heuristics-driven approach. Our findings facilitate more tailored, effective, and generalizable policy and economically optimal infection-mitigating campaign design.

Title: Variations in the two-step norm elicitation procedure: timing, incentives, and scope
Authors: Sabrina Plaß
Abstract: The two-step norm elicitation procedure (opinion-matching) is widely used to measure personal normative beliefs and incentivized normative expectations, yet little is known about how sensitive it is to common design variations. This study tests the robustness of the procedure by examining whether personal normative beliefs, normative expectations, and behaviour change when elements of the elicitation procedure are varied. Using an online dictator game with a four-point scale, the baseline treatment asks participants to evaluate the appropriateness of a fair allocation. Two treatments manipulate (i) the timing of elicitation (before vs. after the decision) and (ii) incentives for normative expectations, while (iii) a third treatment varies the scope by asking participants to evaluate two action subsets (fair and low-share allocations). Timing does not significantly affect behaviour, personal normative beliefs, or normative expectations, whereas incentivizing normative expectations improves the accuracy with which participants correctly identify the modal personal normative belief. Evaluating two action subsets does not significantly alter aggregate beliefs and expectations but reveals additional variation in how participants differentiate normative appropriateness across action subsets. Overall, the findings provide evidence of robustness to changes in elicitation timing and scope in environments with clear focal norms, while incentivization improves the accuracy of elicited normative expectations.

Title: Incentive-driven evolutionary game for maritime decarbonization: Evidence from Shanghai Port
Authors: Le Hong, Lang Xu, Ran Yan
Abstract: Maritime transport underpins global trade, but remains a major source of greenhouse gas emissions, posing challenges for coordinated decarbonization. This paper develops a four-stakeholder evolutionary game model (4S-EGM) to analyze strategic interactions among the International Maritime Organization (IMO), port states, terminal operators, and shipowners, with the port state as the central decision-maker. The model integrates regulatory enforcement, financial incentives, and infrastructure investment and is contextualized through liquefied natural gas (LNG) retrofitting, with parameters referenced to Shanghai Port. Replicator dynamics, stability analysis, and sensitivity analysis are used to identify conditions supporting cooperation. The model evaluates the joint effects of green subsidies, carbon-related market benefits, initial conditions, and profit-sharing arrangements. The results show that cooperation depends on coordinated incentives, initial-condition path dependence, and contractual alignment through profit-sharing. Conditional parameter-sensitivity analysis further indicates that, under a supportive incentive configuration, full cooperation remains unchanged under moderate variations in most examined parameters except the subsidy and carbon-related market benefit. However, cooperation is not unconditional: the system does not reach full cooperation when these incentives are removed, while excessive subsidy costs may disrupt it. The findings emphasize combining sufficiently strong incentives with fiscally sustainable subsidy arrangements and provide scenario-based policy implications for coordinating stakeholder actions in transitional-fuel adoption and maritime decarbonization.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Unraveling lithium dreams: Emergent imaginaries and discourses in the Altiplano’s new extractive frontier
Authors: Roger Merino, Tania Ramírez, Daniel Hernando
Abstract: Critical minerals for the energy transition are triggering new development challenges. This article contributes to understanding these challenges by discussing the emergence of socio-technical imaginaries regarding the prospects of lithium extraction in Puno, Peru. Some scholars explain how state policies in Chile, Argentina, and Bolivia rely on state officials’ lithium imaginaries related to ideas of technological development, industrialization, and sustainability. Others have delved into how the grassroots question dominant lithium imaginaries and policies. Nonetheless, between the forging of dominant imaginaries and local contestation, there are more complex forms of co-existence of imaginaries and negotiation of ontological differences. Considering the relevance of addressing this complexity, this article presents a multi-site analysis to discuss how different actors from the state, civil society, the corporate sector, and local communities appeal to similar discourses but formulate different imaginaries on lithium extraction. Based on semi-structured interviews, documentary analysis, and participatory research, this article categorizes these imaginaries in a market-led sociotechnical imaginary, mostly advanced by high state officials and corporate actors; a state-led sociotechnical imaginary, differently advanced by sub-national authorities and regional organizations; and a commodity imaginary, advanced by local leaders and communities in their pursuit to overcome poverty and exclusion. While these imaginaries overlap in a new extractive frontier, local communities do not renounce their ontological world, connected to traditional economies and livelihoods.

Title: Retraction notice to “Asymmetric impact of oil price on current account balance: Evidence from oil importing countries” [Energy Econ. 123 (2023) 106749]
Authors: Lei Chang, Muhammad Mohsin, Zhennan Gao, Farhad Taghizadeh-Hesary
Abstract: This article has been retracted: please see Elsevier policy on Article Correction, Retraction and Removal (https//www.elsevier.com/about/policies-and-standards/article-withdrawal). This article has been retracted at the request of the authors and with the agreement of the Editor-in-Chief. Post-publication, concerns were raised on PubPeer regarding the relevance of many of the references used in the article. The authors contacted the journal to report the concerns, but were unable to offer a satisfactory explanation as to the choice of references. The Editor-in-Chief has lost confidence in the integrity and validity of the article and has agreed to the retraction.

Title: Which carbon policies redirect innovation? Comparative evidence on policy instruments and policy mixes in China
Authors: Qiang Li, Lidong Chen, Wei Jin, Lin Zhang
Abstract: This paper examines how different carbon-transition policy instruments and policy mixes are associated with the direction of firm-level innovation in the presence of non-green technological lock-in. Using patent data for Chinese A-share listed firms from 2003 to 2021, we first document strong path dependence: firms with larger stocks of non-green patents are significantly more likely to produce further non-green patents than to shift toward green innovation. We then compare four policy instruments—carbon emissions trading, low-carbon city pilots, vertical environmental management reform, and green loan interest subsidies—within a unified empirical framework. The results reveal clear differences in conditional associations across instruments. Carbon emissions trading, low-carbon city pilots, and green loan interest subsidies are associated mainly with the redirection of inherited non-green capabilities toward green patenting, whereas vertical environmental management reform is the only instrument associated with both reduced non-green innovation persistence and stronger green redirection. Policy-mix results show that focused combinations are associated with more consistent redirection effects, while broad policy bundling provides no clear additional gain, suggesting that complementarity and coherence matter more than the sheer number of instruments. These findings highlight the importance of instrument design, policy complementarity, and cautious interpretation of comparative policy evidence in innovation-led decarbonization.
