Title: Small Area Consumption Estimates Combining Survey and Financial Footprints Data
Authors: Peter Levell, Lars Nesheim, Gautam Vyas
Affiliations: Institute for Fiscal Studies London UK; Economic Statistics Centre of Excellence (ESCoE) London UK; University College London (UCL) London UK; University of Bristol Bristol UK
Abstract: ABSTRACT We estimate average equivalised consumption measures across 370 local authority districts in Great Britain, using small‐area estimation methods that combine information from a household budget survey, a much larger survey of local demographics and employment, and area‐level information on bank account outflows and energy consumption. We show that including bank account data substantially improves our estimates, showing that these and other financial footprints data can play an important role in measuring local consumption and hence living standards. We also compare consumption measures that correspond to welfare under different assumptions about mobility and the capitalisation of local amenities into house prices, as well as traditional local income measures, and show that the rankings of local authorities are sensitive to the choice of measure.

Title: Hierarchical configuration decisions in transfer line balancing: Operational, tactical, and strategic effects on cycle time
Authors: Pedram Beldar, Amir Nourmohammadi, Masood Fathi, Amos H.C. Ng
Abstract: The Transfer Line Balancing Problem (TLBP) concerns the optimal assignment of tasks to workstations in automated machining lines to improve operational efficiency. This problem is particularly relevant to high-volume manufacturing industries, such as the automotive and aerospace industries, because it directly affects productivity and cost efficiency. This study examines how hierarchical configuration decisions at the operational (task assignment), tactical (joint task–tool assignment), and strategic (joint task–tool–fixture assignment) levels affect cycle time in an existing automotive machining transfer line. Three mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) models are developed to represent these configuration levels while accounting for setup times and industrial constraints, including task–machine accessibility, zoning, and technological restrictions. Because the exact models do not scale effectively to large instances, a constructive heuristic combined with a local search strategy is also developed. The proposed solution methods are evaluated using an industrial case study and 225 benchmark instances generated using a MILP-based benchmark generator. Across the benchmark size groups, operational cycle times are, on average, up to 11.87% and 12.65% higher than those obtained under tactical and strategic configurations, respectively, indicating potential productivity and economic benefits. The findings support managers in selecting an appropriate configuration level. Sensitivity analyses are also conducted to assess the effects of task–machine accessibility and task-time variability on solution performance.

Title: From scores to decision: Unveiling company maturity for Industry 4.0 using Benefit-of-the-Doubt models
Authors: Hermilio Vilarinho, André Guimarães, Eduardo e Oliveira, Teresa Pereira
Abstract: Digital maturity assessments are essential for guiding industrial firms through their transformation toward Industry 4.0. This study proposes a novel composite indicator to evaluate digital maturity using a Benefit-of-the-Doubt (BoD) approach grounded in robust and conditional efficiency techniques. Leveraging a unique dataset of 490 Portuguese firms that completed a self-assessment, following the IMPULS model adapted to the Portuguese context, we constructed firm-specific scores that account for performance heterogeneity and environmental factors. The empirical results show that firms exhibit low maturity in Smart Infrastructure, Smart Products, and Data-Driven Services, while Human Resources emerges as the comparatively most developed dimension, indicating that digital transformation remains at an early stage for most firms, especially SMEs. Importantly, this work pioneers the application of Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) to explore the non-linear influence of contextual variables, such as firm size, sector, and region, on digital maturity scores obtained via the BoD methodology. We find that conditional BoD scores differ significantly from the standard BoD and the fixed-weight IMPULS-adapted index, and that firm age category and sector exert significant effects on digital maturity, whereas financial productivity indicators do not. This innovative use of GAMs provides richer and more flexible insights than traditional parametric methods, uncovering complex interactions that affect firms’ digital maturity. Our findings offer actionable guidance for policymakers and industry stakeholders, highlighting priority areas for tailored support and capacity-building interventions. The proposed framework contributes both methodologically and empirically to the evaluation of Industry 4.0 maturity and provides a replicable approach for assessing digital transformation in other national and sectoral contexts.

Title: A supply chain digital twin for adaptive master planning under multi-source disruptions: Evidence from a dual-channel manufacturing case
Authors: Ali Rouzkhosh, S. Ali Torabi, Ali Beiki Ashkezari, Amir Ghasemi
Abstract: Conventional Supply Chain Master Planning (SCMP) approaches are poorly suited to environments characterized by simultaneous supply, demand, and sales-channel disruptions particularly in dual-channel supply chains where asymmetric shifts between online and offline demand can create inventory misallocation, service deterioration, and cost escalation. Although Supply Chain Digital Twins (SCDTs) are increasingly discussed as enablers of disruption-aware planning, limited evidence exists on how SCDT frameworks support adaptive SCMP in multi-echelon dual-channel settings. This study develops a SCDT framework for adaptive SCMP that integrates demand forecasting, machine learning-based disruption detection, discrete-event simulation, and multi-objective optimization to dynamically revise sourcing, production, and inventory decisions in response to evolving system states. The framework is instantiated in a television manufacturing supply chain and evaluated against static and rolling-horizon planning approaches under supplier, demand, and channel-shift disruptions. Results show that the proposed SCDT improves service-cost performance, supports more balanced channel-level fulfillment, and enhances adaptive recovery behavior under disruption relative to benchmark approaches. The findings further show that channel-aware SCMP is especially important when demand shifts asymmetrically across sales channels.

Title: How will we use our time in a future of sustainable wellbeing?
Authors: Seán Fearon, Ben Gallant, Angela Druckman, Simon Mair, Lirong Liu
Abstract: Time use analysis is an accessible and intuitive method for building an understanding of the greenhouse gas emissions footprint of lifestyles, and the ways in which these lifestyles impact our enjoyment and wellbeing. This study develops a novel methodology to estimate the emissions footprint and wellbeing of lifestyles in 2050 in three global north countries (Finland, France, and the UK) from a time use perspective. This modelling utilises time use analysis, wellbeing data, direct emissions data, environmentally extended multiregional input-output analysis (MRIO), and scenario building. We first construct an ambitious 2050 scenario assuming a move to sufficiency-based household consumption of commodities and energy, dietary change, systemic changes to transport habits, technological change and cleaner production, and energy efficiency improvements. Despite modelling these ambitious changes out to 2050, we estimate that the emissions intensity of global north lifestyles will remain outside planetary boundaries. We then model the specific wellbeing and emissions in three time use scenarios, or ’lifestyles’, for all three countries to understand how time use changes can improve wellbeing and lower lifestyle emissions. These scenarios are shaped by insights from functional time use theory (FTU), with further insights from the provisioning systems literature. We find that, though it is possible to improve our wellbeing and lower emissions through lifestyle change, further radical transformations are required to provisioning systems to bring emissions footprints within planetary boundaries. Moreover, without this transformation, some socially positive changes to time use may have unintended negative environmental effects.

Title: Airline-driven ground delay program with proactive slot reduction and airline precancellation
Authors: Fan Xiao, Yi Su, Hanchuan Pan, Wenbo Du, Zhe Liang
Abstract: Ground Delay Programs (GDPs) are widely used to mitigate demand-capacity imbalances in air traffic operations. However, existing studies typically address GDP planning from either the perspective of air traffic control or that of individual airlines, with limited attention to their coordination. This study develops a collaborative framework for the airline-driven GDP that integrates proactive slot reduction and airline precancellation. The problem is formulated as a two-stage stochastic program. The first determines slot reductions and flight precancellations in anticipation of various potential capacity scenarios, whereas the second adjusts slot allocations and executes airline recovery actions based on the realized slot capacity. To address the computational challenges of this large-scale problem, we propose an efficient Lagrangian dual decomposition algorithm, which reduces the computation time by 49.06% on average compared with the standard column generation approach. Numerical experiments based on real-world data show that the proposed framework consistently achieves lower expected total recovery costs than rule-based deterministic sequential strategies commonly used in current GDP practice. Moreover, when fairness constraints are imposed, allowing slot exchanges among airlines further reduces total costs by an average of 1.37%. These findings highlight the importance of collaborative decision-making between air traffic managers and airlines, providing a robust and practical tool to enhance system-wide efficiency under capacity disruptions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Predicting sparse OD flows of perishable agricultural products in logistics and transportation networks: a socioeconomic-enhanced spatiotemporal graph model
Authors: Jingni Song, Wenting Hou, Yinli Jin, Kai Du, Lixing Yang, Jinlei Zhang
Abstract: Accurate origin–destination (OD) prediction for perishable agricultural products (PAP) is crucial for enhancing the resilience of the agricultural supply chain and improving social welfare. However, most existing studies focus on passenger or general freight OD prediction, while little attention has been given to PAP. Compared with traditional OD prediction tasks, PAP freight forecasting faces unique challenges: (1) PAP transport has strong time sensitivity, frequent disturbances, nonlinear decay, and high value loss. The related factors are complex and change over time. (2) OD flow data are highly sparse and follow a long-tail distribution, making it difficult to capture complex spatiotemporal patterns effectively. To address these issues, this study proposes a Decoupled Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Network (DST-GNN) model. It integrates PAP freight big data with regional, socioeconomic, and dynamic disturbance features. The model has two main modules: spatiotemporal feature extraction and multi-task prediction. The first module uses a multi-graph learning mechanism to describe inter-city spatial interactions and adaptive spatial dependencies. A Transformer-based encoder captures long-term temporal dependencies from multi-source dynamic data, including historical flows, weather, and holidays. The second module divides the prediction into two tasks: classifying OD activity and regressing flow magnitude. A composite objective function combining mean squared error, cross-entropy classification loss, Focal Loss, and Tweedie loss is designed to jointly optimize point prediction accuracy, OD activity identification, class-imbalance mitigation, and probabilistic distribution fitting. This objective helps alleviate data sparsity, zero inflation, and long-tail effects, improving model robustness and generalization. Experiments on PAP freight data from 333 Chinese cities show that the proposed method outperforms mainstream baselines across four product categories. Further ablation and SHAP-based interpretability analyses confirm the effectiveness of key modules and highlight the importance of macroeconomic and infrastructure factors for prediction accuracy. This study provides a new paradigm for spatiotemporal prediction under zero-inflated and long-tail conditions and offers valuable insights for the refined management and dynamic decision-making of PAP logistics networks.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Multi-objective two-echelon vehicle-drone routing with load-dependent drone under pickup delivery time windows
Authors: Fan Yu, Chao Li, Qun Chen, Yange Li, Yanzhan Chen, Xu Yang
Abstract: In a two-echelon logistics transportation system involving vehicles and drones, the energy consumption rate and maximum range of drones are influenced by real-time payloads during parcel pickup-or-delivery services. Furthermore, considering customer-specific pickup-or-delivery time windows makes the two-echelon routing problem with complex decision-space constraints more challenging. To address the Two-Echelon Vehicle-Drone Routing Problem with Load-Dependent Drones under Pickup Delivery Time Windows (2E-VRPLDTW), we develop a Multi-Objective Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Programming (MO-MINLP) model and design a constrained multi-objective evolutionary algorithm with decision-space diversity enhancement (DSDE) to solve this problem. Improving population diversity in the decision space helps avoid premature structural collapse and enhances the quality of the obtained trade-off solutions. Meanwhile, an elite-solution-guided hybrid differential evolution operator, together with a dynamic constraint-tolerance mechanism, accelerates convergence while maintaining feasibility pressure. Extensive experiments on a benchmark suite demonstrate the practical value of the proposed two-echelon vehicle-drone system: under an identical first-echelon structure and the same hard time-window requirements, it achieves a more favorable trade-off between dispatch/activation cost and operational cost than courier- and unmanned-car-based second-echelon alternatives. On solvable small/medium instances, DSDE produces non-dominated sets that are competitive with Gurobi reference solutions, while on the full benchmark it significantly outperforms representative heuristics/metaheuristics and state-of-the-art CMOEAs. Ablation and sensitivity analyses further confirm the contributions of DSDE’s key components and show that solution quality varies smoothly under moderate perturbations of critical engineering parameters (e.g., drone endurance and payload). Overall, the results support the practicality of the 2E-VRPLDTW model and the robustness of DSDE for large-scale constrained planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Impact of differentiated data ownership structures on data sharing decisions in maritime digital platforms
Authors: Hanyin Zheng, Min Wu, Kevin X. Li, Xuehao Feng, Adolf K.Y. Ng, Gil Lu Wang, Yi Xiao
Abstract: Effective data sharing is essential for coordination and interoperability on maritime digital platforms, yet participation remains constrained by ambiguous data ownership arrangements and heterogeneous stakeholder incentives. This study examines how data ownership structure (complete versus separated) as a governance mechanism, interacts with stakeholder roles (carriers, port / terminal operators, and freight forwarders / ship agents) to shape data sharing willingness on maritime digital platforms. Drawing on an extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT)-based behavioral framework that operationalizes key decision drivers, an experiment involving 173 maritime professionals is conducted. Using group comparison, interaction analysis, hierarchical regression, and RF-SHAP analysis, key determinants of data-sharing willingness are identified and both structured interaction effects and non-linear predictive patterns are examined. The results reveal substantial heterogeneity in data-sharing willingness across data ownership structures and stakeholder roles, as well as a clear interaction between these two factors. Role-based differences are limited under complete ownership but become more evident under separated ownership, particularly for intermediary actors. Beyond these contextual patterns, social influence and perceived network effects emerge as the most stable determinants, while performance expectancy and facilitating conditions play conditional roles, suggesting that perceived platform benefits and support mechanisms increase willingness only when they create clear value, reduce uncertainty, and lower participation burdens. Theoretically, this study advances maritime platform governance research by conceptualizing data ownership as a role-contingent governance arrangement rather than as a uniform determinant of willingness to share data. Practically, the findings provide guidance for designing role-aligned data ownership and incentive structures to support sustainable maritime data collaboration.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Familiar faces, honest answers? The impacts of enumerator familiarity and modality on survey responses
Authors: Travis Baseler, Lipeng Chen, Thomas Ginn

Title: Neighborhoods, perceived immigration, and preferences for redistribution: Evidence from Barcelona
Authors: Gerard Domènech-Arumí
Abstract: I use registry data and an original survey with geocoded respondent addresses to investigate how neighborhood immigration influences perceptions and preferences for redistribution in Barcelona. Natives exposed to more African and Asian migrants in their neighborhoods perceive higher immigration rates in the country and in their neighborhood. Plausibly exogenous exposure to recent migrant inflows from these same origins reduces natives' demand for redistribution and increases their support for the extreme right party when inflows are sizable. Genetic distance between natives and immigrants helps explain perceptions, while income and religious distance appear to matter more for preferences. The results highlight the interplay between neighborhoods, perceptions, and preferences.

Title: Emergency department visits and temperature: Evidence from Mexico
Authors: Luis Sarmiento, Francesco Pietro Colelli, Filippo Pavanello
Abstract: We estimate the impact of temperatures on emergency department visits using daily data from the universe of public hospitals in Mexico from 2008 to 2022. We find that cold temperatures decrease visits by up to 8.9 percent on the same day, and warm temperatures increase visits by as much as 3.6 percent. Using distributed lag models, we then show that cold temperatures can reduce visits for the next 30 days by up to 16.3 percent. For warm temperatures, contemporaneous and cumulative effects are similar (limited harvesting). These findings suggest that, unlike mortality, temperatures affect the demand for emergency services linearly. Title: Zero-shot cross-city ride-hailing demand prediction leveraging transferable urban spatiotemporal dynamics
Authors: Ben Chi, Haoge Xu, Xiqun (Michael) Chen
Abstract: Accurate ride-hailing demand prediction is crucial for platform operational efficiency and transportation management. However, in emerging markets where historical trip data are entirely unavailable, conventional data-driven models as well as transfer learning approaches become infeasible, which creates a critical barrier for platform expansion and public-sector regulation. To bridge this gap, this study proposes a novel two-stage framework for zero-shot (i.e., target-data-free) cross-city ride-hailing demand prediction, in which total demand prediction is decoupled from its spatiotemporal allocation. In the first stage, a linear regression model estimates city-level aggregate demand using universally available macroeconomic indicators and built-environment features. In the second stage, a neural network learns transferable POI temporal activity patterns to allocate this demand across space and time, serving as a proxy for urban mobility rhythms without requiring target-city trip records. The framework is validated on a dataset of 5 million ride-hailing trips from 10 cities under a strict zero-shot experimental design. Results show that the method achieves superior spatial transferability and significantly outperforms baseline models, particularly when transferring knowledge from large, data-rich cities to smaller, data-scarce ones. The predicted demand accurately captures key spatiotemporal dynamics—such as morning and evening peaks—and the learned POI activity profiles are highly interpretable, aligning with known urban activity schedules. This study contributes significantly to both research and practice. Methodologically, it presents a robust and transferable solution for demand forecasting under complete data scarcity. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method reduces RMSE by up to 64.55% and MAPE by up to 66.31% compared to baseline models, particularly when transferring knowledge from data-rich metropolises to data-scarce emerging cities. For platform operators, it provides an actionable tool for strategic market entry, fleet sizing, and risk assessment. For transportation planners and policymakers, it enables proactive evaluation of traffic impacts, coordination with public transit, and evidence-based regulatory design in emerging mobility markets.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Yes to disarmament, yes to peace: Measuring the impact of Mexico city’s gun buyback initiative
Authors: Marco Méndez-Atienza, Aurora A. Ramírez-Álvarez
Abstract: This paper evaluates Mexico City's voluntary gun buyback program, Sí al desarme, sí a la paz, launched in January 2019. Using state-month data for 2017–2023, we estimate program effects with synthetic control and synthetic difference-in-differences designs. We find a statistically significant decline in our composite outcome, which combines recorded firearm-related crimes with unclassified deaths to conservatively guard against possible outcome reclassification. The estimated decline is equivalent to roughly 17% of the composite outcome's pre-treatment mean. Because unclassified deaths need not be firearm-related, this specification prioritizes robustness to misclassification over direct substantive interpretation. The more interpretable disaggregated estimates show that the effect is concentrated in intentional firearm injuries, while effects on firearm homicides are statistically indistinguishable from zero across specifications. An illustrative Phase 1 calculation implies approximately 11,354 MXN ($560 USD) in spending per estimated averted event in the composite outcome. We also find no detectable substitution into non-firearm injuries. Mechanism evidence indicates that the program primarily collected civilian handguns and is consistent with a situational opportunity-reduction channel in civilian settings: reducing immediate access to firearms can limit escalation and lower the likelihood that routine conflicts translate into gun injuries, rather than directly disrupting organized-crime arsenals. Robustness checks, including placebo timing tests around COVID lockdown and triangulation with INEGI vital statistics, suggest that the results are not driven by reporting or reclassification. The findings contribute the first causal evidence on a voluntary gun buyback in Mexico and, by focusing on non-lethal firearm injuries rather than solely on homicides, identify a margin of impact that prior Latin American evaluations have not examined (Cano et al., 2024).

Title: A pipeline methodology for neural network accelerators under a throughput constraint
Authors: Ali Oudrhiri, Alix Munier Kordon
Abstract: Neural networks have gained widespread popularity, particularly in the context of hardware accelerators. These accelerators are typically designed according to optimization criteria such as throughput, power consumption, and energy efficiency, which involve inherent trade-offs. They generally consist of a neural processing unit with a configurable number of parallel processing elements, along with internal memory resources. This paper investigates the feasibility of improving processing throughput and achieving better trade-offs by introducing an additional optimization dimension. Specifically, we explore a pipelined configuration involving multiple distinct instances of the neural processing unit.We propose a simple and generic methodology applicable to a wide range of feed-forward neural network accelerators. We show that the problem can be formulated as a specific case of the assembly line balancing problem, and we extend a well-known dynamic programming approach with polynomial time complexity to solve it exactly. The proposed methodology is validated on a real-world industrial hardware accelerator prototype, for which evaluation functions for the relevant criteria are available. Experimental results demonstrate that the pipelined configuration significantly increases system throughput without degrading the other considered criteria.

Title: Comparative advantage and the quality choice of heterogeneous firms
Authors: Antonio Navas, Dongzhe Zhang, Ian Gregory-Smith
Abstract: This paper explores the role played by comparative advantage in shaping the impact that trade has on a firm’s product quality across industries. We develop a Heckscher-Ohlin model with firm heterogeneity and endogenous quality upgrading. Trade openness increases an exporter’s product quality differently across industries, with a larger effect in a country’s comparative advantage industry. Differences in factor endowments across countries translate into differences in factor prices which affect the firm’s marginal costs of production. The cost-advantage that firms enjoy in a country’s comparative advantage industry increases the firm’s prospective market size abroad, increasing the incentives to invest in product quality. Introducing endogenous firm-level comparative advantage based on differences in factor intensity within an industry, reveals that the firm’s response to trade openness in terms of quality choice is shaped by the firm and industry determinants of comparative advantage: Firms that use more intensively the factor in which the country is more abundant will increase quality to a larger extent. Using transaction-level data from Chinese firms, we find empirical support for the model predictions; Chinese exporters produce higher-quality products in those industries in which China reveals a comparative advantage.

Title: Decomposing the pollution generation process: Who is to blame?
Authors: Aurélie Slechten, Barnabé Walheer
Abstract: We propose a production-theoretic decomposition of long-run changes in emissions per worker that explicitly models the pollution-generation process.Building on frontier-based productivity decompositions, we separate emissions changes into efficiency change, frontier-shift change, labor productivity growth, and capital-labor ratio increases.To account for heterogeneity across countries, we estimate group-specific nonparametric production frontiers and apply the decomposition to 89 countries over 1960-2019.Counterfactual distribution analysis suggests that frontier-shift components are quantitatively important for understanding the observed cross-country distribution of emissions per worker in the final period.At the country level, labor-productivity gains and the capital-labor ratio generally exerted upward pressure on emissions.Efficiency improvements played a secondary but still meaningful role, with many countries behaving as "followers": improving efficiency relative to the frontier without necessarily shifting the frontier itself.

Title: Expected revenue, risk, and grid impact of Bitcoin mining: A decision-theoretic perspective
Authors: Yuting Cai, Ruthav Sadali, Korok Ray, Chao Tian
Abstract: Most current assessments use ex post proxies that miss uncertainty and fail to consistently capture the rapid change in bitcoin mining. We introduce a unified, ex ante statistical model that derives expected return, downside risk, and upside potential profit from the first principles of mining: Each hash is a Bernoulli trial with a Bitcoin block difficulty-based success probability. The model yields closed-form expected revenue per hash-rate unit, risk metrics in different scenarios, and upside-profit probabilities for different fleet sizes. Empirical calibration closely matches previously reported observations, yielding a unified, faithful quantification across hardware, pools, and operating conditions. This foundation enables more reliable analysis of mining impacts and behavior.

Title: Elections with job-motivated bureaucrats
Authors: Jean Guillaume Forand
Abstract: Bureaucratic voters are guided both by their preferences over public goods and by their job motivation : they bear costs from policies that downsize the government workforce. Job-motivated voters lead to ( i ) nonexistence of Condorcet-winning platforms in the short run, and ( ii ) bureaucratic persistence in the long run: equilibrium outcomes converge to alternations around at most two platforms, in which parties compete over the scale of public investment but keep the size of the bureaucracy fixed. Long-run bureaucracies are never smaller than the ideal bureaucracy of median private sector workers, and parties typically underinvest, so that public goods production is inefficient.

Title: Carbon-efficient ride-pooling at intercity railway hubs: Nonlinear topological mechanisms and algorithmic insights
Authors: Zechao Ma, Tianqi Gu, Jiayan Zhang, Long Cheng, Inhi Kim, Bin Yu
Abstract: Ride-pooling (RP) can reduce transport emissions, but its carbon reduction potential across spatial contexts remains unclear, especially at intercity transfer hubs. Using citywide regulatory ride-hailing data from Suzhou, China, this study examines how meso-level path topology features are associated with carbon reductions in railway station pooling. Railway station pooled trips show 62.6% higher carbon reductions per trip than the overall pooled-trip sample average, influenced by nonlinear mechanisms and interaction patterns rather than higher pooling intensity. An explainable machine learning framework shows that carbon efficiency is primarily associated with route quality, as reflected in path topology, operational scenarios, and built environment factors. In particular, detour constraints, common drop-off configurations, and their interactions with distance act as critical thresholds. Building on these insights, we develop a dual-layer classification framework that can identify pooling matches with high carbon reduction potential prior to dispatch (accuracy ≥ 96%). These findings suggest that intercity railway stations may serve as favorable contexts for low-carbon RP when demand concentration and route quality align. This insight can help guide matching strategies that are enabled by AI and informed by carbon efficient in shared mobility systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Promoting energy transition in shipping: An evolutionary game analysis of green corridors
Authors: Haiwei Gu, Michael G.H. Bell, Ze Wang, Zhiqi Shao, Veronica Schulz, Glenn Geers
Abstract: Green corridors are emerging as a practical mechanism to promote alternative fuels. This paper develops an evolutionary game model to better understand the interactions between shipping lines and cargo owners within a green corridor. A population of 15,000 TEU container ships traveling between Australia and Singapore is simulated to study the economic feasibility of three alternative fuels: liquefied natural gas (LNG), methanol, and ammonia. The results indicate that LNG and methanol have a competitive advantage, while ammonia appears less economically attractive under the assumptions and parameter settings adopted in this study, primarily because of its higher associated costs. Sensitivity analysis reveals cargo owners’ willingness to pay (WTP) for alternative fuels, port discounts, and carbon tax significantly influence the fuel transition. It confirms the shipping industry is likely to be particularly sensitive to the cargo owners’ preference for alternative fuels. The study also highlights the importance of coordination among key stakeholders.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Drive or breathe? Information-aware mode choice under real-time exposure using ICLV-CMXL approach
Authors: Rashmi Choudhary, Amit Agarwal
Abstract: Commuters in urban areas face prolonged exposure to air pollution. This study assessed whether providing commuters with real-time, trip-specific air pollution information can encourage a shift towards public transit modes. Sequential integrated choice and latent variable model with a correlated mixed logit component is developed using stated choice data and user perceptions for motorized transport users in Delhi. Real-time pollution information for current modes was obtained through a multimodal router. Perceptions included air quality awareness, availability and usability of air quality information, and willingness to change behavior for primary trips. The results indicate that people with a better understanding of air quality information and its usage are inclined to choose public transit. Motorized two-wheeler users are more sensitive to exposure compared to car users, showing a stronger preference for public transit. These findings highlight the importance of real-time information in mode shift. Policymakers can formulate strategies to reduce individuals’ exposure in public transit.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Robust low-carbon ship routing under weather uncertainty: a distributional reinforcement learning approach
Authors: Turgay Battal
Abstract: Maritime transport carries most global trade yet contributes roughly 3% of greenhouse-gas emissions, and as the IMO targets a 20–30% reduction by 2030 and the EU prices maritime carbon, deterministic routing is increasingly inadequate. This study merges distributional reinforcement learning with distributionally robust optimization for low-carbon routing under spatial weather uncertainty. A quantile-regression deep Q-network (QR-DQN) captures stochastic weather impacts, a Wasserstein-metric DRO term addresses train–deployment distribution shift, and a physics-informed reward embeds hydrodynamic resistance and carbon-intensity compliance. On the Rotterdam–New York corridor, the framework cuts fuel use by 17.9% versus slow steaming and 5.1% versus a standard DQN (about 390 tonnes of CO 2 per voyage, with direct EU ETS and CII relevance), while keeping adverse-weather exposure near zero and fuel variability low. Ablations attribute this consistency mainly to the physics-informed reward, with the critic securing stable training and efficiency and the robust layer curbing tail degradation under shift.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Price and prejudice: Housing rents reveal racial animus
Authors: Marius Brülhart, Gian-Paolo Klinke, Andrea Marcucci, Dominic Rohner, Mathias Thoenig
Abstract: We study the evolution of housing rents in the proximity of Swiss asylum seeker hosting centers whose populations differ by ethnic composition. Rental prices within 0.7km of an active center are found on average to be 3.8% lower than in the control group. The price response is significantly more pronounced when centers host a higher share of asylum seekers from sub-Saharan Africa. In contrast, neither religious affiliation nor inferred crime propensity of the center populations are found to affect local rental prices significantly. Our findings are consistent with phenotype-based racial animus as a significant driver of observed market outcomes.

Title: De-concentrating integration? Spatial concentration, trade access, local fundamentals, and welfare
Authors: Eduardo Fraga

Title: Do Higher-Cost Settings Deliver Better Outcomes? Post-Acute Care Efficiency in Medicare Skilled Nursing Facilities and Home Health Agencies
Authors: Fangli Geng, Jiaowei Gong, Pedro L. Gozalo, David C. Grabowski
Abstract: Determining the value of different post-acute care settings for clinically similar patients is important for providers and payers. This study examines the causal effect of post-acute care (PAC) setting on Medicare spending and short-term patient outcomes among beneficiaries discharged from hospitals following treatment for stroke or congestive heart failure (CHF). Using 2013–2017 Medicare claims data, we implement an instrumental variable strategy that exploits daily variation in skilled nursing facility (SNF) bed occupancy at the hospital service area level to estimate the local average treatment effect of SNF versus home health agency (HHA) care. Our findings reveal no significant differences, on average, in 30-day mortality or rehospitalization rates between SNF and HHA care among stroke and CHF patients. However, the 95% confidence intervals do not exclude clinically meaningful reductions in 30-day mortality. Meanwhile, SNF care is associated with approximately $4,700 more in Medicare spending per PAC episode. The spending gap is larger in markets with more constrained SNF capacity, particularly in states with Certificate of Need regulations, rural areas, and low-income neighborhoods. However, we do not detect statistically significant differences in short-term health outcomes across these markets on average, suggesting that supply constraints may amplify the spending implications of SNF use while the relationship between PAC setting and short-term clinical outcomes remains uncertain. These findings highlight the importance of aligning PAC discharge decisions with both clinical needs and local capacity considerations, particularly under value-based payment models.

Title: Measuring the value of blockchain adoption in supply chain management: an empirical analysis of key success dimensions
Authors: Marc Hübschke, Marius Gros, Benedikt Latos, Elmar Holschbach, Stefan Lier
Affiliations: South Westphalia University of Applied Sciences – Meschede Campus Department of Logistics and Supply Chain Management, , Meschede; Hochschule Niederrhein , Krefeld; Technische Hochschule Ostwestfalen-Lippe , Lemgo; South Westphalia University of Applied Sciences , Iserlohn
Abstract: Purpose Blockchain technology is widely discussed as an enabler of transparency, efficiency and trust in supply chain management (SCM). However, empirical evidence on which blockchain-related success dimensions translate into value perceptions remains limited. This study aims to examine how the perceived relevance of blockchain success dimensions relates to realized benefits and whether these benefits contribute to overall perceived blockchain value. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative survey of 41 companies with blockchain experience in SCM is conducted. Success dimensions are prioritized using best–worst scaling (MaxDiff). Relationships between perceived relevance, dimension-specific benefits and overall perceived value are analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Exploratory analyses assess company characteristics. Findings Contrary to dominant expectations in academic and practitioner narratives, even highly prioritized blockchain success dimensions fail to translate into measurable firm-level value perceptions. While transparency and traceability are associated with significant dimension-specific benefits, these improvements do not produce statistically significant direct or indirect effects on overall perceived blockchain value. This suggests that localized operational gains alone may be insufficient to generate overall perceived value and indicates that blockchain benefits may depend on broader organizational and technological complements. Originality/value The study moves beyond identifying potential blockchain benefits by empirically differentiating which success dimensions matter and which do not. By combining MaxDiff with PLS-SEM, it offers a structured, mechanism-oriented framework for evaluating blockchain success and highlights boundary conditions for value realization in SCM.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: Evaluating transportation improvements within cities using quantitative spatial models
Authors: Christopher Severen
Abstract: I describe the use of quantitative spatial models (QSMs) to evaluate the effects of transportation infrastructure within cities.After discussing the motivation for QSMs relative to other economic measurement techniques, I develop a simple QSM and detail the components that enter into the model.Next, I consider identification challenges and practical implementation.Finally, I highlight several shortcomings common in applications of QSMs, as well as growth areas where QSMs show promise for future development.

Title: Boosting remanufacturing adoption: proposal of a readiness model and improvement guidelines
Authors: Saverio Ferraro, Mirco Peron, Filippo De Carlo, Olga Battaïa, Leonardo Leoni
Affiliations: University of Florence; NEOMA Business School; Kedge Business School; eCampus University

Title: User-centric assembly planning and instruction development – a systematic literature review and conceptual framework for integrating digital and assistive technologies
Authors: Rieke Leder, Daniel Rippel, Michael Freitag
Affiliations: University of Bremen; BIBA – Bremer Institut für Produktion und Logistik GmbH at the University of Bremen

Title: Correction
Encroachment or not? Strategy options for third-party logistics service providers considering the freshness-keeping efforts
Authors: Guoli Wang, Youhua Lu, Junyan Wang
Affiliations: Tianjin University of Science and Technology
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Digital twins in supply chain management: Technical components, functionalities, and impact areas
Authors: Christoph G. Schmidt, Maximilian Klöckner, Stephan M. Wagner, Sara Calcagni
Affiliations: School of Management, University of Bath; Bain & Company; Department of Management, Technology, and Economics, ETH Zurich
Abstract: Digital twins lack a common understanding in the literature, and their impact on operations and supply chain management should be further explored to realise the technology’s potential value. Conducting a multi-round Delphi survey with additional expert interviews, we identify the underlying technical components, functionalities, and adoption barriers. Subsequently, we derive a detailed framework that provides an overview of the digital twin characteristics at the product, process, or system level. We examine multiple impact areas of digital twins related to operational excellence, risk management, communication, and innovation. Our Delphi ranking shows that digital twins could affect production process reliability, setup, and testing of machinery and maintenance procedures. We also employ the CIMO logic to inform our discussion of the potential underlying mechanisms. Our study works towards a shared holistic understanding of digital twins. We also derive a set of recommendations for managers and outline opportunities for future research.

Title: Managing compounding disruptions: analysis of supply chain responsiveness affordances enabled by cross-border E-commerce platforms
Authors: Yu Han, Anna Yumiao Tian, Woon Kian Chong, Antony Paulraj
Affiliations: School of Marketing and Logistics Management, Nanjing University of Finance and Economics; International Business School Suzhou, Xi’an Jiaotong-Liverpool University; S P Jain School of Global Management; Department of Information Systems, Supply Chain & Decision Making, NEOMA Business School
Abstract: How cross-border e-commerce platforms facilitate firms in responding to disruptions is growing to become important to improve supply chain responsiveness. Existing literature focuses on isolated disruptions and the adoption of static adoption of technologies; this research investigates the responsiveness affordances enabled by cross-border e-commerce platforms applied in facilitating small and medium-sized enterprises’ (SMEs) efforts to respond to compounding disruptions. This research follows a process approach, combining a retrospective and real-time perspective to report on qualitative inquiries with experienced informants from 15 SMEs in the manufacturing industry. The results offer a process model revealing how cross-border e-commerce platforms enabled affordances for SMEs’ responsiveness strategies to evolve throughout the Trade War and COVID-19, and also unpack the underlying logic behind the dynamic.

Title: Analysing domestic sourcing under the influence of economic nationalism and nearshoring
Authors: Duy Tan Nguyen
Affiliations: School of Business, Operations and Strategy, University of Greenwich Business School, Old Royal Naval College; Department of Logistics and Operations Management, HEC Montréal

Title: Strategic adoption of additive manufacturing in edible product supply chains: a resource-based view on sustainability
Authors: Wenqi Li, Banu Yetkin Ekren, Emel Aktas
Affiliations: Cranfield University School of Management, , Cranfield; Yasar University Department of Industrial Engineering, , Izmir, , and School of Management, Cranfield University, Cranfield, UK
Abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how the strategic value of additive manufacturing (AM) is created in edible product supply chains, using the resource-based view (RBV) as a theoretical lens. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on 29 semi-structured interviews with experts from the food, pharmaceutical and AM sectors, this research refines an initial, literature-based conceptual model and develops an empirically grounded framework. Findings AM’s VRIN attributes are necessary but not sufficient for strategic value; value depends on deployment within supply chain configurations. Three pathways are identified: supply chain transformation, product innovation and operational improvement. SMEs integrate AM strategically, while large incumbents often contain it within R&D. Sustainability outcomes remain conditional on economic viability, which acts as a gatekeeper for environmental and social value. Practical implications The framework offers decision guidance for practitioners: SMEs are shown the organisational prerequisites for pursuing supply chain transformation through AM, while large firms are given concrete signals for when to migrate AM from R&D into core operations. Policy levers for lowering adoption barriers are also identified. Originality/value This study extends the RBV by revealing that resources generate competitive advantage through multiple independent pathways, and that organisational context determines resource strategic status, not merely moderating effectiveness but fundamentally shaping whether resources function strategically or operationally. It provides the first interview-based evidence of these dynamics in the previously underexamined context of edible product supply chains.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: Equitable allocations in risk-averse settings
Authors: Özlem Karsu, Barkın Ekiz
Abstract: Abstract Many real life problems require making decisions that lead to benefit allocations across multiple entities, hence they can be cast as special types of multiobjective programming problems. In such settings, the decision makers often have fairness concerns alongside efficiency concerns. We propose a method for achieving equitable and efficient solutions for these multicriteria problems in the context of risk-averse behavior when the benefits are uncertain. To accomplish this, we introduce a methodology that combines two distinct concepts: Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) and equitable aggregations. By integrating these two concepts, we aim to establish a framework for equitable, risk-aware decision-making and address the important challenge of ensuring fairness in an uncertain environment.

Title: Adaptive resource sharing strategies for grassroots epidemic response: framework, inference and evaluation
Authors: Yue Feng, Ming Cong, Yingyi Zhang, Lili Rong, Michele Nguyen
Abstract: Effective epidemic response relies on well-designed emergency resource sharing among decentralized grassroots actors operating under highly uncertain propagation dynamics. However, insights into how such sharing can be structured and coordinated remains insufficiently understood. This study investigates emergency resource sharing at the grassroots level of epidemic response, addressing uncertainty in heterogeneous resource demands arising from dynamically evolving epidemic scenarios. To systematically represent the complexity of scenarios faced by grassroots decision-makers, we develop a three-dimensional scenario model that characterizes variations in epidemic outcomes. Meanwhile, we propose a resource sharing framework grounded in “actor-task-resource” relationships, which captures the scenario-adaptive and task-driven resource demands of grassroots actors. To infer coordinated resource sharing decisions under scenario uncertainty which minimise the expected total shortage and transport costs, we employ a distributionally robust optimization (DRO) approach which incorporates time-varying scenarios through switching Wasserstein ambiguity sets. The model is reformulated into a tractable mixed-integer linear program (MILP) via duality theory. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed resource sharing strategies effectively mitigate resource shortage risks for grassroots units across uncertain scenario realizations. Moreover, combining external resource support with internal resource sharing yields superior performance, especially when this prioritizes high-risk areas. Acquiring limited external support across small amounts of multiple resource types instead of restricting to a single resource is also shown to reduce shortage risks given uncertain scenarios. These findings offer practical insights for designing resilient grassroots emergency resource coordination plans that adapt to evolving epidemic conditions.

Title: Multi-directional DEA with Win-Rate aggregation: a robust approach to efficiency ranking
Authors: Yu Zhao, Qianwei Zhuang
Abstract: This paper proposes a methodology for aggregating multi-directional Data Envelopment Analysis results into a unified efficiency ranking. The directional distance function requires specification of a direction vector, and different directions can yield different efficiency assessments. We address this direction selection problem through win-rate aggregation that counts how often each unit outperforms others across multiple directions sampled from Dirichlet distributions. To distinguish among efficient units with identical win rates, we incorporate super-efficiency scores. The method provides intuitive directional outperformance probabilities for pairwise comparisons and tier classifications grouping units by performance levels. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate Spearman correlations of 0.97 with standard DEA rankings, discriminatory power of 81 percent, and full coverage of the BCC-efficient frontier within the top tier. Application to 57 Japanese regional banks reveals that efficiency is not determined by bank size but strongly correlates with profitability, with Tier 1 banks outperforming Tier 4 banks in 100 percent of directional comparisons, and that frontier-referenced win rates avoid the scale confounding exhibited by ideal-point rankings such as TOPSIS. The methodology also provides actionable diagnostics identifying each bank’s strengths, weaknesses, and appropriate benchmark institutions.

Title: The selective asymmetric traveling salesman problem with activities and workgroups
Authors: José Manuel Slater-Carrasco, Carlos Contreras-Bolton, Lorena Pradenas-Rojas
Abstract: This paper introduces the selective asymmetric traveling salesman problem with activities and workgroups (SATSPAW), a new variant of the selective traveling salesman problem. SATSPAW aims to maximize the profit collected from activities performed on visited nodes, subject to a time-constrained budget. Each activity has a profit and service time, but the route continues without waiting for completion. The objective is to determine a route that maximizes profit while respecting time constraints, ensuring each workgroup is assigned to a single node, and selecting activities within the allowed time. To solve SATSPAW, we propose two mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulations: a node-based model and a flow-based model. Additionally, we propose a tailored iterated local search (ILS) algorithm that integrates four perturbation procedures and four local search procedures. Three of these are classic local search operators, while the fourth employs exact methods to solve embedded subproblems: an assignment subproblem for optimally reassigning workgroups and a knapsack subproblem for selecting the most profitable activities subject to time constraints. Computational experiments on instances with up to 171 nodes show that the node-based MILP achieves slightly better performance than the flow-based MILP formulations, solving instances with up to 71 nodes to optimality and achieving an average gap of 12.55%. The ILS outperforms MILP models overall across all instances, achieving high-quality solutions with an average gap of 0.04% and significantly smaller computing times. Furthermore, as the problem sizes increase, ILS maintains efficiency and scalability, demonstrating its effectiveness in solving larger SATSPAW instances.

Title: Multidimensional uncertainty in commodity markets: a hybrid deep learning approach for corn futures price forecasting
Authors: Mohammad Zoynul Abedin, Petr Hajek, Ran Wu, Hongjun Zeng
Abstract: This paper introduces DLCorn, a novel hybrid deep learning framework that integrates a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN), a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN), and a Sequence-Oriented Fusion Time Series Predictor (SOFTS) to forecast U.S. corn futures prices. DLCorn systematically incorporates multidimensional uncertainty indicators, including the CBOE Volatility Index (VIX), Geopolitical Risk Index (GPR), and Economic Policy Uncertainty Index (EPU). Comparative results show that DLCorn achieves higher forecasting accuracy than the benchmark models in a market environment characterised by increasingly complex volatility. Using a dataset spanning 35 years from 1990 to 2024, the study evaluates DLCorn performance through robust tests, including comparisons before and after the COVID-19 crisis and assessments under different training-to-testing data ratios. Empirical results reveal that DLCorn achieved an impressive coefficient of determination (R^2) of 0.9928 across the entire sample period, with a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of only 1.4034%. Notably, the model maintains stable out-of-sample accuracy across the pre- and post-COVID-19 subsamples, indicating robustness to changing market regimes. SHAP analysis demonstrates that while VIX significantly increased its non-linear impact on corn futures prices post-pandemic, EPU maintains a strong positive correlation with prices and GPR exhibits a consistent negative relationship. The study’s primary contributions lie in DLCorn architecture design, multi-source feature extraction mechanisms, and complex sequence modelling capabilities. This work offers a novel paradigm for corn futures price forecasting and provides valuable practical guidance for market participants in optimising decision-making and risk management.

Title: Cluster representative formulation for the k-plex partitioning problem
Authors: João Telhada
Abstract: Cluster or community detection is a fundamental topic in network analysis and has been a relevant subject in the past few years, especially with the rising usage of enterprise information and social networks. In this context, cluster partitioning aims to analyze and group individuals within a network according to some common characteristics. The clique partitioning problem is one such approach, requiring each cluster to be fully cohesive. The k -plex partitioning problem generalizes this idea by relaxing the cohesiveness requirement, allowing each node to be non-adjacent to up to k −1 other nodes in its cluster. This paper investigates existing models and proposes new mixed-integer programming formulations for the k -plex partitioning problem, including formulations based on cluster representative nodes. Theoretical results are presented in terms of the comparison between the corresponding linear programming relaxations. Those results show that the new cluster representative formulations provide better linear programming relaxation bounds than existing approaches, and computational experiments show that the improvement can be substantial, highlighting their potential for improving exact and heuristic solution methods.

Title: Generalized Factor Neural Network Model for High-dimensional Regression
Authors: Zichuan Guo, Mihai Cucuringu, Alexander Y. Shestopaloff
Abstract: We tackle the challenges of modeling high-dimensional data sets, particularly those with latent low-dimensional structures hidden within complex, non-linear, and noisy relationships. Our approach enables a seamless integration of concepts from non-parametric regression, factor models, and neural networks for high-dimensional regression. Our approach introduces PCA and Soft PCA layers, which can be embedded at any stage of a neural network architecture, allowing the model to alternate between factor modeling and non-linear transformations. This flexibility makes our method especially effective for processing hierarchical compositional data. We explore ours and other techniques for imposing low-rank structures on neural networks and examine how architectural design impacts model performance. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated through simulation studies, as well as applications to forecasting future price movements of equity ETF indices and nowcasting with macroeconomic data.

Title: Impact of the Collection Mode on Salaried Labour Income Data: Evidence From Colombia Before and During the COVID ‐19 Pandemic
Authors: Andrés García‐Suaza, José Lobo‐Camargo, Sergio Montoya, Juan Ordóñez‐Herrera, Juan D. Oviedo‐Arango
Affiliations: School of Economics and Business at Universidad del Rosario Bogotá Colombia; Instituto de Investigación de Recursos Biológicos Alexander von Humboldt Bogotá Colombia; Independent Economist Bogotá Colombia
Abstract: ABSTRACT The strict confinement implemented by the National Government of Colombia in 2020 to contain the expansion of the COVID‐19 pandemic created challenges in data collection operations conducted through household surveys. As a result, surveys that traditionally relied on face‐to‐face collection methods transitioned to a remote mode using telephone surveys. We exploit a quasi‐experimental design based on the geographical‐temporal exogenous variation in the collection mode of the leading household survey for the Colombian labour market and the linkage of this survey to the nationwide social security administrative record to measure the impact of the change in the collection mode on the reported salaried labour income. We find that the change in collection mode reduces the measured salaried labour income by approximately 4.4 percentage points and increases its variance and dispersion, with differences between population groups. These findings have implications for the development of mixed data collection methods and the analysis of income‐based statistics.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Ecosystem restoration and rural incomes: Evidence from China's Shan-Shui Initiative
Authors: Hanxiao Xu, Tongze Liu, Zhiyang Shen, Fawaz Baddar ALHussan, Michael Vardanyan
Abstract: Besides improving environmental conditions, large scale ecological restoration initiatives carry implications for households' livelihoods. Therefore, evaluating whether restoration policies can align ecological objectives with income growth is important for promoting environmentally sustainable development. We study whether China's Integrated Protection and Restoration Project of Mountains, Rivers, Forests, Farmlands, Lakes, Grasslands, and Deserts, commonly known as the Shan-Shui Initiative, has helped promote rural income growth as well as the channels through which income effects operate. Using a panel of 1700 counties from 21 provinces, we estimate policy effects for the period 2016–2022 with a synthetic control approach that uses machine learning to construct counterfactual income paths for treated counties. Our results show that the initiative has increased rural incomes with gains growing over time. Estimated effects differ by pilot batch, with incomes rising by about 5% and 1.9% for the first two project cohorts implemented in 2016 and 2017, respectively, but decreasing by 0.9% for the final batch in 2018. After adjusting for potential anticipation effects, the estimated effect for the 2017 cohort increases to 3.7%. We demonstrate that ecological restoration promotes rural incomes via improvements in ecosystem services, infrastructure, and tourism development. Income effects are generally larger in more economically developed and less ecologically fragile areas, while differences across dominant project types are comparatively modest. The results provide insights into potential policies for aligning environmental protection objectives with rural development.

Title: Data-driven comparison of airline passenger flight supply using optimal transport theory
Authors: Qian Liu, Paul Rochet, Chantal Roucolle
Abstract: This study develops an optimal transport (OT) framework for measuring pairwise airline supply dissimilarity across heterogeneous route networks. By representing each airline as a distribution of seat capacity or flight frequency across routes and defining route-level transportation costs, the framework provides a flexible and interpretable approach to comparing carriers beyond traditional measures based on multimarket contact or aggregate concentration. To illustrate its versatility, three OT-based dissimilarity indices are introduced to capture differences in seasonal supply positioning, geographic market proximity, and route-length structure. The framework is applied to European scheduled passenger flights for 32 airlines between 2016 and 2025. The empirical results show that airline relationships are multidimensional, with different patterns of similarity emerging across carrier types and network characteristics. A longitudinal analysis relative to the 2016 baseline reveals heterogeneous adjustment trajectories across airlines and indicates post-pandemic convergence in some dimensions of network organization alongside persistent differentiation in others. Overall, the proposed OT framework provides a general tool for inferring airline similarity from transport distances, assessing resilience and recovery following shocks, and examining structural change over time. The framework can also support the construction of airline peer groups for benchmarking, and the medium- to long-term monitoring of structural network recovery following major market shocks.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Global airport connectivity and resilience: a data-driven approach and inverse-U relationship, 1996–2024
Authors: Yilin Zhang, Tommy Cheung, Anming Zhang
Abstract: This study analyzes the long-run evolution of global airport connectivity from 1996 to 2024 and examines how resilience to major shocks varies across the connectivity distribution. Using an extended Global Airport Connectivity Index (GACI) panel covering 101,049 airport–year observations and 5428 airports, it documents steady expansion punctuated by crises, a redistribution of connectivity across continents, and an increasingly multipolar hub hierarchy. The paper then develops a reproducible, multi-crisis resilience index with three components: depth (magnitude of loss), speed (pace of recovery), and adaptability (post-shock upgrading in the global hierarchy). The index aggregates realized airport performance across multiple major shocks, applies empirical-Bayes regularization to improve comparability across airports with uneven shock histories, and filters micro-fluctuations below 1% to reduce noise. Relating resilience to connectivity uncovers a consistent inverse-U relationship: resilience increases with connectivity up to a mid-scale range and declines among the most globally connected hubs. This pattern is consistent with greater exposure to synchronized shocks and scale-related operational frictions, although the analysis identifies the relationship rather than its underlying mechanisms. Robustness checks include alternative component weightings, pre-COVID estimates, crisis-specific recovery horizons, alternative adaptability definitions, region-specific COVID timing, an alternative fixed-scale connectivity construction, and non-overlapping crisis windows. These checks confirm the stability of the pattern. By embedding airport-level recovery behaviour in a three-decade network context, the GACI–resilience framework provides a systematic basis for comparing hub types and benchmarking realized resilience, and for informing route-development, infrastructure-planning, and policy strategies during pandemics, geopolitical disruptions, and other major shocks.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: The economic gains from breaking boundaries: Reformulating index insurance zones to maximize lower tail dependence
Authors: Enrique Estefania-Salazar, Michael R. Carter, Eva Iglesias, Álvaro Escribano
Abstract: Index insurance intended to help low-wealth households manage risk is hampered by downside basis risk, meaning that the insured suffers a loss, but the insurance index fails to signal a loss. Existing index insurance contracts use statistically ad hoc administrative boundaries to demarcate insurance zones. We develop an algorithm that creates zones that maximize lower tail dependence amongst individual units included in each zone. Breaking boundaries in this way minimizes basis risk. Using data from a satellite-based index insurance program in Kenya, we show that replacing administrative with optimized zones can as much as triple the value of insurance using an expected utility-based metric of insurance quality.

Title: Picking winners: Local land allocation and bottom-up industrial policy in China
Authors: Wenjia Tian, Zhi Wang, Qinghua Zhang
Abstract: This study examines the industrial preferences of local governments in China through the lens of land allocation. We analyze industrial land transactions from 2007 to 2019, a period marked by both expanding industrial policy and intensifying land market competition. Using a border discontinuity design that compares land transactions near county borders, we separate local government preferences from firm demand. We find systematic industrial favoritism: localities offer deeper price discounts to industries aligned with their existing specialization. This favoritism persists over time, is more pronounced in industries with substantial unrealized agglomeration potential, and is stronger in regions with well-developed market institutions. We further show that local governments comply with upper-level industrial policy only when it aligns with their own specialization. Together, these findings point to a bottom-up process in which local governments use land allocation to attract firms that reinforce local industrial strengths through agglomeration spillovers.

Title: Window-dressing in environmental regulation: Short-term incentives and temporary abatement
Authors: Zhengwen Liu, Hong Ma, Fangrui Zhang
Abstract: We study how short-term political incentives affect firms’ compliance with environmental regulation. In China, city mayors face a sharp drop in promotion probability after age 57, creating a transitory enforcement window. Using a regression discontinuity design, we find that firms governed by promotion-eligible mayors reduce sulfur dioxide (SO 2 ) emissions substantially more than under the same mayors after the threshold. These reductions are concentrated among firms without end-of-pipe abatement equipment and are driven by temporary cuts in operating hours and output rather than technological upgrades. We further document that government subsidies increase during the promotion window and are disproportionately directed to unequipped firms that curtail production, consistent with coordinated short-run compliance. A back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that these transitory incentives account for 5.2% of the national SO 2 decline during the Eleventh Five-Year Plan, but at a cost of 0.9% of total industrial output. We develop a dynamic model of firm compliance showing that such short-lived incentives induce inefficient output-based responses. Our findings highlight the limits of episodic regulatory pressure.
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: Correction: Application of a disaster related emergency response model to a food bank network
Authors: Faith Idoko, Lauren Davis, Chrysafis Vogiatzis
Abstract: While disaster management and preparedness has seen significant developments in both theory and practice in recent years, there is still a shortage of operations research and decision science strategies specifically for food banks and their operations. This manuscript aims to fill that void by investigating how a disaster-related emergency response model can be used to improve food bank preparedness and decision-making for food bank operations during disasters. Using realistic projections of food bank operations, this study evaluates various strategies to address unmet demand and minimize operational costs across different scenarios that depict the network’s potential state following a disaster. A framework is designed to facilitate effective decision-making by considering different levels of risk tolerance. The implementation of mobile pantries is highlighted as an effective way to meet demand with minimal increases in operational costs when the network is disrupted. This framework provides food bank managers with an array of possible solution approaches, enabling them to make optimal decisions based on their specific objectives.

Title: Bounded rationality, monetary policy, and the scars of supply shocks
Authors: Dario Bonciani, Frantisek Masek, Paolo Nanni, Giulio Tarquini
Abstract: Bounded rationality reshapes monetary-policy trade-offs in response to supply shocks in a New Keynesian model with endogenous growth. A negative supply shock depresses innovation and future productivity, which gives rise to long-run scarring and persistent inflationary pressures. Under rational expectations, tighter monetary policy eases the initial rise in inflation but amplifies the fall in demand, innovation, and productivity. Under bounded rationality, households underreact to future income losses. This weakens the negative wealth effect and mitigates the decline in demand and growth. As a result, tighter monetary policy can contain inflation without generating large scarring effects.

Title: Do you remember? Prosocial behavior declines in memory-based decisions
Authors: Sebastian Olschewski
Abstract: Many economic decisions affect other stakeholders, yet information about these consequences is often not directly available at the moment of choice and must instead be recalled from memory. Here, three studies examine how memory processes shape social behavior and whether their behavioral effects are better explained by motivated memory or rational accounts of memory allocation. In Study 1, participants made binary dictator-game decisions in which the consequences for themselves and another player were represented by pictures whose monetary outcomes had to be learned and later recalled from memory. Compared with the control condition in which all outcome information was available on the decision screen, participants chose less prosocially when decisions relied on memory. Studies 2 and 3 showed that prosocial choice in memory-based dictator games did not reliably increase either when strategic encoding of outcomes was made impossible or when accurate recall was monetarily incentivized. A structural model with a social utility function indicates that memory-based decisions reduce the weight placed on the other player’s outcome in unequal allocations that are advantageous to the dictator. Across choices, recall patterns, structural modeling, and individual differences, the results are most consistent with motivated forgetting during decision making: participants appear to selectively fail to retrieve information about social consequences when this information would make selfish choices harder to justify. These findings suggest that making consequences for other stakeholders salient at the moment of choice can promote socially beneficial behavior.

Title: Train scheduling with variable running speeds and multiple train compositions
Authors: Hanchuan Pan, Siqi Guo, Fan Xiao, Wei Liu, Zhe Liang
Abstract: In recent years, frequent small-scale emergencies, such as extreme weather events, have often led to significant passenger flow fluctuations in metro systems. To better accommodate this fluctuated demand, the operators are required to design irregular timetables where both train arrival/departure times at each station and composition modes for each train service vary dynamically. Accordingly, this paper investigates an integrated train scheduling problem that simultaneously addresses (1) the train running speed optimization strategy that seeks to find the best train trajectories for a series of trains, and (2) the multiple train compositions optimization strategy that provides sufficient transport capacity with the least rolling stock units. To this end, we propose a novel nonlinear mixed integer optimization model for minimizing the total costs of energy consumption and service quality for passengers, where the train running speed is innovatively treated as a decision variable. A conic reformulation technique is proposed, such that the nonlinear parts of the developed model can be reformulated as second-order cone constraints, which can be efficiently handled by commercial solvers. Two computational experiments involving a relatively small- and large-sized cases derived from the subway line 17 in Shanghai are tested to assess the quality of our method. The results suggest that this approach can be used by operators to derive a high-quality energy-efficient train timetable.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Truck-drone collaborative routing with flexible cross-truck operations and slot constraints
Authors: Hang Fan, Zhuxi Zhang, Tong Guo, Wenbo Du, Xuechen Gu, Tao Song, Defu Lin
Abstract: Truck-drone collaborative routing faces critical operational bottlenecks in realistic logistics scenarios due to strict return constraints and limited physical recovery slots. We address these challenges by proposing a novel Mixed-Integer Linear Programming model for the Flexible Assignment Vehicle Routing Problem with Drones and Slot Constraints (FA-VRPDSC). By decoupling drones from specific launch vehicles, the model enables flexible cross-truck operations and dynamic task assignments across the entire fleet under strict slot capacity limits. To efficiently solve this complex combinatorial problem, we develop a tailored Memetic Algorithm with Adaptive Large Neighborhood Perturbation (MA-ALNP). The algorithm leverages a dual-chain representation to jointly encode routing sequences and collaboration states. To navigate the tightly coupled temporal and spatial constraints, we integrate specialized repair operators and an adaptive destroy-and-repair shaking mechanism that effectively prevents premature convergence. Computational results confirm the algorithm’s exact optimality on small instances and its structural superiority on large-scale benchmarks, significantly outperforming advanced heuristics in minimizing total makespan. Our sensitivity analysis ultimately highlights that extended drone endurance is pivotal for activating flexible cross-truck docking and maximizing fleet coordination.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Experimental study on low-carbon supply chain management using symbolic award
Authors: Junjun Liu, Lifang Gao, Ning Li
Abstract: Symbolic awards, such as low-carbon supplier certification, actively motivate suppliers to strengthen their carbon reduction initiatives and advance sustainable supply chain management. Yet, when low-carbon suppliers remain scarce, these awards intensify buyer competition and raise the costs of maintaining supplier relationships. Notably, several suppliers leverage awards to build reputations that improve their bargaining power, creating strategic dilemmas around public disclosure. This study develops a two-stage game model and tests its predictions through controlled experiments to examine how alternative award formats influence supplier and buyer outcomes. Our results show that a symbolic award significantly encourages suppliers to reduce emissions and improve buyers’ bottom lines. However, award format shapes buyer utility in critical ways: public awards compel buyers to invest more in retaining suppliers, while private awards deliver greater financial value to buyers. In markets with few low-carbon suppliers, buyers often need to allocate more resources to relationship management, while suppliers may resist private incentives if they perceive reputational drawbacks. These findings highlight the need for carefully designed disclosure strategies to balance costs and benefits for both sides, thereby fostering more effective and sustainable supply chains.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Integrating minimum cost flow and capacitated location in global supply chains under uncertainty
Authors: Yi Zhang, Hari Nandan Nath, Stefan Nickel
Abstract: Modern supply chain networks face significant challenges in balancing operational efficiency and resilience under diverse real-world uncertainties such as demand fluctuations and disruptions.
