Title: Managing the effort-value tradeoff for integrating human judgment into surgery duration predictions
Authors: Laura Maria Poreschack, Andreas Fuegener, Dominik David Walzner, Ulrich Thonemann, Christof Denz
Abstract: Abstract For surgery duration prediction, it has been shown that integrating human judgment into algorithmic prediction models results in a higher accuracy than machine learning based approaches can achieve alone. However, since humans are a scarce resource in healthcare, their involvement in surgery duration prediction has high opportunity costs as their time could be spent more effectively on patient care and other medical tasks. This raises the question of how these costs should influence human involvement in tasks where algorithms perform reasonably well at minimal cost. This paper introduces a framework for selectively integrating human judgment based on the costs of human involvement and prediction uncertainty, which is captured using algorithmic meta features. Our framework identifies instances in surgery duration prediction where human judgment should be integrated in algorithmic predictions and those where it should not. We evaluate our framework using a data set containing 70,610 surgeries from a large university hospital. We observe that while always integrating human judgment leads to an overall higher accuracy than never integrating human judgment, employing the framework can lead to an even higher accuracy with lower human workload. In our case study planning costs could be reduced by 27% compared to the current status quo. Our results indicate that a cost-sensitive allocation policy that excludes human judgment for task instances that are easy for the algorithm allows humans to focus on medical tasks.

Title: Forecasting the impact of the viral ‘Kia Boys’ social media trend on car thefts to 2050
Authors: P. Jeffrey Brantingham, Craig D. Uchida, Fred Morstatter, George Mohler
Abstract: In 2022, Hyundai Sonatas became the most frequently stolen car model in Los Angeles, mirroring a nationwide trend. The sudden popularity of this mid-sized sedan among car thieves has, according to some, been linked to the viral spread of videos on TikTok and YouTube that showcased a security vulnerability that made certain Kia and Hyundai models easy to steal. These videos later acquired the moniker ‘Kia Boys’ or ‘Kia Challenge.’ In this work, we show that the surge in Hyundai Sonata thefts in Los Angeles was only weakly tied to the ‘Kia Boys’ trend, having begun much earlier during COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns. Any lasting effects of the viral social media trend were fully absorbed into offline car theft dynamics by the time social media interest peaked in 2022. We use historical data on Honda Civics and Toyota Camrys, car models popular among pre-social media generations of car thieves, to develop a model for the offline temporal and spatial evolution of theft preferences. The model suggests that the effects of the ‘Kia Boys’ vulnerability are likely to persist for decades, irrespective of the role social media played in its inception, and that these effects will be increasingly concentrated in low-income communities over time.

Title: Improving the simple average combined forecast via factor-adjusted regularization
Authors: Saerom Lee, Tae-Hwy Lee
Abstract: This paper addresses the forecast combination puzzle — the empirical observation that the simple average forecast combination often outperforms complex weighting schemes — by employing a factor-adjusted regularization framework. In this framework, the simple average is treated as a common factor. We identify and incorporate idiosyncratic components, defined as the deviations of individual forecasts from the simple average. Our approach effectively manages the high correlation among forecasts by focusing on idiosyncratic components that enhance predictive content beyond what is captured by the simple average. Empirical applications in macroeconomic forecasting show that this factor-adjusted approach yields significant accuracy gains over the simple average.

Title: Compositional zero-shot demand forecasting in retail via disentangled demand drivers
Authors: Zefree Lazarus Mayaluri, Sasmita Mishra
Abstract: Retail demand forecasting is central to assortment planning, replenishment, and promotion design, but many global forecasting models are evaluated mainly on configurations similar to those observed during training. This paper studies Compositional Zero-Shot Demand Forecasting (CZDF), where individual demand-driver values are observed in training but selected joint configurations are held out and appear only during evaluation. We propose DD-CZFormer, a driver-disentangled encoder–decoder that represents seasonality, price, promotion, product/category, region, and weather-related drivers in separate latent subspaces and composes them through cross-driver attention. The model is trained with forecasting, contrastive, orthogonality, and masking losses to encourage reusable driver representations. We evaluate DD-CZFormer on M5-CZDF and an anonymised Industrial-CZDF dataset using temporally ordered splits with held-out Region × Product × Month and Region × Product × Promotion configurations. On CZDF splits, DD-CZFormer reduces aggregate WRMSSE by 11.0% on M5-CZDF and 13.8% on Industrial-CZDF relative to the strongest non-proposed baseline in the reported mean results. Median series-level analyses further show lower WRMSSE in all twelve CZDF pairwise baseline comparisons.

Title: The ecological externalities of climate governance: Evidence that solar land use harms bird biodiversity
Authors: Xi Ji, Jie Lin, Pengfei Liu, Xiaoxue Zong
Abstract: Photovoltaic (PV) energy is widely promoted as a cornerstone of climate change mitigation, yet its land-intensive deployment may impose unintended ecological costs. This study provides a comprehensive empirical assessment of the impact of PV land use on bird biodiversity in China, using high-resolution county-month panel data. Using an instrumental-variable strategy with rich fixed effects, we find that a 1% increase in PV panel area is associated with a 0.659% decline in bird abundance and a 0.473% decline in species richness. Evidence on mechanisms suggests that these effects operate primarily through the loss of surface vegetation, which reduces habitat availability. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that the negative impacts are most pronounced on forest land, followed by cropland and grassland. Low-density, large-scale centralized installations have larger adverse effects than more spatially distributed installations, and the estimated impacts are most pronounced in autumn, a period that overlaps with intensive bird migration. Furthermore, we find no evidence that Key Ecological Function Zones mitigate the adverse ecological effects of PV development on birds. Our findings highlight an underappreciated trade-off between renewable energy expansion and biodiversity conservation, and underscore the importance of incorporating ecological externalities into energy planning.

Title: Green debt for nature-based solutions: aligning municipal budgeting and banking practices
Authors: Axelle Vincent, Tara Op de Beeck, Heleen Van Hecke, Tine Compernolle, Jan Cools, Tom Coppens
Abstract: Local governments face growing risks from climate change, which require substantial investments in climate adaptation to safeguard future generations. Nature-based solutions (NBS) have been recognized as a cost-efficient strategy to redevelop public space, to create greener and more climate adaptive urban environments. However, development of NBS is hindered by a lack of financial resources to fully scale up the transformation. To overcome this barrier, literature calls for clear sustainable finance frameworks and business model approaches to include private financing in the development of public NBS. In our research we consider the perceptions of municipalities and banks, as institutional lenders, towards using green debt-financing to finance NBS. We draw on sustainability transitions literature to theorize NBS as a niche innovation within established banking-municipal relations. Using qualitative interviews with Belgian banking experts and urban and financial planners from Flemish cities, we reveal competing financial logics between municipal financing practices and banking requirements, limiting the uptake of green debt for NBS. While NBS are mostly absorbed in traditional municipal deficit financing, this conceals their value and prevents market development. Alternatively, project finance remains difficult due to capacity constraints and differing valuation logics. Emerging sustainable finance frameworks create opportunities but shift administrative burdens onto municipalities. Overall, current practices mainly support NBS to fit and conform, rather than transform established debt-practices. Substantial upscaling of NBS will require changes in both banking practices and municipal financing approaches, including explicit integration of physical climate risk and collective financing mechanisms.

Title: Race-to-the-bottom dynamics in industrial land pricing: Asymmetric effects of China’s 2009 price floor adjustment policy
Authors: Ran Tao, Jialin Yu, Zhejin Zhao
Abstract: Minimum price floors are a common but understudied instrument for regulating industrial land markets in developing economies. We exploit China's 2009 adjustment of minimum industrial land prices, which lowered the minimum land price in some counties and raised it in others. Combining parcel-level land transactions with county characteristics in a difference-in-differences design, we find a striking asymmetry: easing counties experienced a 9.15% decline in industrial land prices and a 23.12% expansion in transferred area, whereas tightening counties showed no detectable change. The asymmetry reflects the floor's initial binding status: it was binding in easing counties, where competition for mobile manufacturing capital pushed prices down and expanded land supply, but non-binding in tightening counties, where the raised floor either stayed below market prices or was offset through rebates and subsidies. Easing counties also gained 15.53% more large-scale industrial enterprises relative to the sample mean and 7.90% in fiscal revenue, yet new land sales concentrated in low- and medium-low-tech, land-intensive sectors, a pattern that persisted through 2022 with no shift toward higher-tech industries. Relaxing a binding industrial land price floor thus brings short-run gains in firm entry and fiscal revenue but leaves these counties specialized in low-tech industries, consistent with race-to-the-bottom competition operating through industrial land pricing.

Title: Beyond the early era of EVs: Evidence from the staggered rollout of the HOV lane network in California
Authors: Eric Avis, Jing Li, Katalin Springel
Abstract: Local policies like high-occupancy vehicle (HOV) lane exemptions play an important role in encouraging electric vehicle (EV) adoption, a key component of climate programs. Using tract-level vehicle registrations and detailed data on HOV lane openings from 2012 to 2024, we study the causal effect of HOV policies on EV adoption in California. We find that HOV exemptions significantly increased EV uptake, with effects that were stronger in later years as EV technology and markets advanced. The impact is also greater in more congested areas with longer commutes and concentrated in higher-income tracts, highlighting both the effectiveness and distributional implications of HOV incentives.
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: Local charger availability and electric vehicle adoption: Evidence from Norway
Authors: Costanza Cincotta, Øyvind Thomassen
Abstract: We examine the effect of local public charging infrastructure on electric vehicle (EV) adoption using microdata from Norway between 2010 and 2023. We use 1.85 million new car registrations, geocoded to buyers’ residences and matched to nearby charging stations, along with individual- and neighbourhood-level controls and fixed effects, to estimate the causal impact of local charger availability. We find statistically significant, but economically negligible effects: doubling charger density in 2023 increases the probability of EV adoption by less than 1 percentage point. Of the (74 percentage-point) increase in the EV share in new registrations from 2016 to 2023, less than one percentage point is explained by new publicly available chargers. Effects are heterogeneous, and largely driven by car buyers living in multi-dwelling housing, and those residing in large urban areas.
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: Does happiness spread within organizations? Evidence from a field experiment in Norway
Authors: Torbjørn Hanson, Åshild A. Johnsen, Andreas Kotsadam, Alberto Prati
Abstract: We report the results from a large field experiment that tests if happiness spreads within an organizational setting, as predicted by the emotional contagion hypothesis. Although some studies have supported this hypothesis, no well-powered randomized controlled trial has ever tested it in the field. In collaboration with the Norwegian Armed Forces, we randomly assign over 1500 recruits to rooms during eight-week boot camps. Some recruits live with relatively happier peers while others live with relatively unhappier ones. We find no evidence of happiness convergence at the room level and reject even small contagion effects. We show that the null result is not explained by excessive stability in happiness, and prior studies in the same setting show that peer effects emerge for some non-emotional attitudes. These results call for a reconsideration of the presumed ubiquity of happiness spillovers, with subsequent implications for well-being models and policies.

Title: Two-stage distributionally robust optimization for the online retail inventory placement problem
Authors: Zhenhao Deng, Feng Li, Xianyan Yang, Xinyue Jia
Abstract: The rapid growth of online retail has transformed supply chain management, notably through fulfillment flexibility, which allows demand from different customer regions to be served by multiple fulfillment centers. To leverage this flexibility, online retailers allocate inventory for a large number of items across shared fulfillment centers while balancing fixed inventory-placement costs and transportation costs. However, because inventory placement requires advance planning, relying on deterministic demand estimates may lead to severe inventory misallocation and stockouts. Motivated by this, we study a two-stage online retail inventory placement problem under demand uncertainty. In our model, item-level inventory placement decisions are made before actual demand is observed. After demand is realized, transportation decisions are made to split demand fulfillment across multiple fulfillment centers, while shortage costs are incurred when inventory is insufficient. This problem is formulated as a two-stage distributionally robust optimization model over a moment-based ambiguity set. By applying duality theory and enumerating extreme-point scenarios for the continuous random variables, the infinite-dimensional min-max-min formulation is transformed into an equivalent mixed-integer linear program (MILP). An exact algorithm based on the column-and-constraint generation (C&CG) framework is proposed to solve the MILP reformulation. It incorporates problem-specific valid inequalities that provide explicit bounds on the dual variables, thereby tightening the master problem relaxation and improving convergence. To further accelerate convergence, an improved exact algorithm is developed by incorporating a tailored column generation (CG) procedure that identifies multiple scenarios at each iteration. Computational results demonstrate the efficiency of both proposed algorithms and the improved robustness of the distributionally robust model over traditional stochastic programming approaches.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: How construal level can shape buyer responses to supplier labor violations
Authors: Dayna Simpson, Tim Kraft, Marie Segrave
Abstract: Despite widespread organizational commitments to eliminate labor exploitation in supply chains, a substantial gap persists between stated policies and suppliers’ actual practices. Major companies pledge zero tolerance for labor violations at suppliers, yet evidence that buyers follow through with meaningful corrective action when suppliers commit labor violations has been limited. This gap between commitment and enforcement of labor policies by buyers reduces supplier compliance and undermines efforts to improve working conditions in global supply chains. We address the problem of buyer follow-through by exploring whether construal can influence buyers’ responses to supplier labor violations. Construal level is an established driver of managerial behavior in many domains, yet exploration of its role in supply chain decision-making is limited. Using three experiments we show that reducing construal can improve the relationship between buyer responsibility for its suppliers’ workers and buyer willingness to suspend the supplier for a major labor violation. Our findings contribute novel insights for more effective governance of working conditions in supply chains, by: i. identifying that construal can influence buyer willingness to respond to supplier labor violations; and ii. identifying interventions that influence construal and elicit more effective buyer action, including faster reporting, clear labor policies, concrete thinking, and increased expertise. Our research emphasizes the important role of construal in supply chain decision making and its links to managerial understanding of working conditions in supply chains. Our findings advance efforts to encourage more effective action from buyers when labor violations are reported in their supply chain.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Experience-driven value creation in digital airline self-service systems: evidence from a low-cost carrier context
Authors: Maryam Kefi Ben Chehida, Mathieu Dunes, Mourad Chouki, Marina Dabić, Tilo Halaszovich
Abstract: This study examines an experience-driven value creation mechanism in digital airline self-service systems in the low-cost carrier (LCC) context. It focuses on a setting less frequently studied in customer experience research: digitally mediated, low-contact airline services in which booking, check-in, and boarding interfaces function as customer touchpoints embedded in standardized passenger-service processes. From a passenger logistics perspective, these interfaces are part of standardized passenger-service systems through which customers complete sequenced service tasks with limited employee contact. Drawing on means-end theory and service-dominant logic, the study models customer experience (CX) as an antecedent of customer-perceived value (CPV) and behavioral intentions (BIs). Survey data were collected from 330 passengers of a European LCC operating in France and were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The analysis reports positive and statistically significant CX → CPV and CPV → BIs effects. The main empirical evidence concerns the indirect CX → CPV → BIs path, whereas the direct CX → BIs path is small in magnitude. In the final model, the CPV composite comprises utilitarian value/control and emotional value. No statistically significant generational cohort moderation is detected in this sample, and robustness checks indicate that the mediated CX → CPV → BIs path remains positive and statistically significant when value-for-money perceptions and travel frequency are considered. The study applies CX theory to low-contact airline environments and examines digital self-service interfaces as passenger touchpoints within standardized LCC service processes. For managers, the results underscore the importance of CX in digitally mediated LCC journeys and direct attention to interface clarity and low-friction task completion.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Time saved, but for whom? An intersectional analysis of travel-time differences for on-demand transit users in five countries
Authors: Jerome Mayaud
Abstract: On-demand transit (ODT) has the potential to both cannibalize and complement public transit networks. Users switching to ODT away from alternative transportation modes may benefit from travel time savings, but uncertainty remains about how these savings vary by mode and by population group. We present a multi-country, multi-city analysis of ODT's travel-time performance compared with car, public transit, cycling and walking modes in 33 locations, across the USA, Canada, Norway, Germany and Spain. Leveraging a unique dataset of 6,963 digitized trips that pairs actual ODT trip characteristics with travel survey responses, we derived realistic counterfactual alternative travel times using a publicly available routing algorithm. Our aim was to investigate how travel-time differences (TTD) between ODT and alternative modes differ across various socioeconomic and trip characteristics. We paid particular attention to the intersectional nature of these characteristics, to bring empirical nuance to our findings. We found that ODT plays a dual role as a trip-level substitute: a convenience substitute for the car on short trips (especially in North America), and a time-saving substitute for public transit on long trips (especially in Europe). However, multilevel modelling revealed significant inequities in the distribution of TTD: in our pooled USA and Canada subsample, men experienced 1.6 min higher TTD (i.e. greater time savings) than women across all alternative modes, White users experienced 10.4 min higher TTD than Black/African American users when the alternative was public transit, and high-income users experienced 4.4 min higher TTD than low-income users when the alternative was a car. We also uncovered an intersectional ‘disability penalty’, whereby the benefits accrued by men and high-income users were significantly diminished when those individuals also reported a disability. Beyond these substitution patterns, we also found that disabled riders were 1.85 times and low-income riders 3.4 times more likely than their counterparts to report taking a trip that would not have been made without ODT, indicating that ODT generates net new mobility for the most disadvantaged users. While ODT is a promising solution for addressing many challenges in public transit, our findings challenge the assumption that it inherently promotes equity. This underscores the urgent need for policymakers to apply an intersectional lens to service design, to prevent the entrenchment of existing mobility disparities.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Beyond the “supply chain” framing: Cattle ranching as a vanishing mediator of deforestation and dispossession in the Brazilian and Colombian Amazon
Authors: Mairon G. Bastos Lima, Jesica López
Abstract: Unsustainable land-use change has become an increasingly critical social and environmental issue. Over a few decades, vast expanses of land with native vegetation or devoted to mixed-farming systems have given way to large-scale agriculture, incurring considerable biodiversity and livelihood loss. Cattle ranching and the production of a handful of internationally traded commodities such as soy and palm oil play a pivotal role in that expansion. They have led to numerous sustainability initiatives to curb their negative social and environmental impacts, yet a “supply chain” framing poses important limitations, for it typically fails to consider relationships between sectors and broader landscape dynamics. For one, there may be much stronger drivers than food consumption at play. This article draws from the frontier literature and explores the concept of “vanishing mediator” to analyze the role played by cattle ranching in particular. Comparing the Brazilian and Colombian Amazon, we assess how ranching intermediates an ongoing transition between pre-frontier forest areas and capital-intensive monocultures. We draw from land-use data and the scientific literature on each of the two cases as well as on a total of 30 key-informant interviews done in Brazil and Colombia. Our results show that cattle ranching’s role in spearheading deforestation in both countries cannot be understood without reference to its broader context, for it works as a vanishing mediator between pre-frontier settings and industrial agriculture. Ranching occupies frontiers with little infrastructure, paving the way for monocultures; it is instrumental to the land grabbing that makes the endeavor highly profitable; and, crucially, it precariously absorbs and co-opts displaced smallholders. Cattle ranching introduces the latter — as well as incoming settlers — to state institutions that previously neglected them and to a market-driven approach to land use that still preserves the trappings of rural living. Ultimately, however, people migrate to sprawling cities and clear the way for capital-intensive crops such as soy in Brazil and oil palm in Colombia. We conclude that the notion of individualized “supply chains” is shortsighted for dealing with such broader dynamics. Instead, effective sustainability interventions require addressing local vulnerabilities and investing in economic alternatives that can successfully hedge against deforestation drivers.

Title: Editorial Board
The dual burden of energy poverty and climate exposure
Authors: Yuetong Zhang
Abstract: Households in the United States face compounded risks when high energy burdens intersect with heightened exposure to climate extremes. This study introduces a methodological framework to systematically identify and analyze these dual-vulnerability households. Using the 2020 Residential Energy Consumption Survey (RECS) linked with high-resolution NASA Daymet climate data, I spatially match households to localized measures of extreme climates like heatwaves and cold spells. Geospatial hotspot analysis reveals regions where economic and climatic risks converge, while Local Linear Forest models are employed to identify the primary drivers of household energy expenditures. The results show that climate-related variables, such as extreme temperature events and degree days, together with housing characteristics, exhibit greater predictive importance on energy costs than income. Policy simulations of programs, including appliance upgrades, weatherization, smart home technologies, and financial assistance programs, show heterogeneous predicted outcomes across household types, with technology-based strategies associated with the largest predicted reductions in energy expenditures. These findings highlight the importance of regionally tailored, climate-responsive policies that integrate technical upgrades with socioeconomic support to enhance resilience among households at the intersection of energy poverty and climate risk.

Title: Demand effects and welfare properties of energy efficiency standards
Authors: Junichi Minagawa, Thorsten Upmann
Abstract: We investigate how a common energy efficiency improvement across multiple energy-using activities affects demand, energy use, and emissions within a standard consumer framework. In contrast to the traditional rebound literature, which focuses on a single good or service, our analysis captures both substitution and income effects across several energy-using activities. We derive decompositions for (i) total demand for energy-using activities, (ii) the associated total energy demand, and (iii) the resulting emissions. These decompositions reveal that efficiency gains may lead to unintended increases in energy use or emissions, depending on the preference structure and relative marginal emissions. Building on these results, we derive a rule for the optimal design of energy efficiency standards. In the representative household case, this rule implies that the regulated price of each energy-using activity should be proportional to its marginal emissions and the absolute value of its own-price elasticity. We extend the analysis to heterogeneous households and show how the rule generalizes under equity considerations and aggregate emissions constraints. Our results provide a theoretical foundation for designing sector-specific energy efficiency standards in line with environmental and distributional objectives.

Title: Decarbonizing the maritime sector: cold ironing and e-fuels. Case study: Gran Canaria
Authors: Pablo Yánez-Rosales, Paula Ferreira, Julieta Schallenberg-Rodriguez, Alexis Lozano-Medina, B.del Rio-Gamero
Abstract: This research addresses the decarbonization of the maritime transport considering the services that can be provided at port, by analyzing both cold ironing and e-fuels production. To this end, the electricity demand for both processes is estimated, as well as the resulting electricity generation cost and the associated emissions, enabling an estimate of the climate neutrality cost. Two possible scenarios were considered for the renewable e-fuel production: dedicated renewable farms versus renewable surpluses coming from the island electricity system. For the cold ironing different scenarios are being considered: electricity coming from the grid and renewable farms to produce the required electricity. The island of Gran Canaria (Canary Islands, Spain) is considered as the case study. The results show a potential reduction of 483 kt of CO 2 -eq (9) % of the island’s emissions) and a levelized cost of energy ranging from 181 to 616 €/MWh, depending on the scenario and e-fuel considered.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Equity by design in electric vehicle charging infrastructure networks
Authors: Yen-Chu Wu, Eleftheria Kontou
Abstract: Public charging infrastructure extends electrified miles, reduces range anxiety, and promotes electric vehicle adoption. However, charging stations remain inaccessible to underserved and disadvantaged populations. To address this, we propose a novel location model for equitable electric vehicle charging infrastructure placement, with objectives to minimize detours for charging and improve trip completion for low-income travelers and multi-unit dwelling residents, who face shorter electric vehicle ranges and limited home charging access. A genetic algorithm-based approach with column generation is used to solve the multi-objective nonlinear bilevel programming problem and identify Pareto-optimal solutions. The proposed method is applied to the state of Illinois transportation network as a case study. We assume universal electric vehicle adoption to represent a forward-looking public planning scenario, rather than calibrating infrastructure solely to current ownership patterns that reflect existing socioeconomic disparities. The results show that our equity-by-design siting improves accessibility for disadvantaged travelers while maintaining service quality and performance for all privileged users. Through analysis of various scenarios, we offer insights into the robustness of equitable charging station placement. Our analysis indicates that (i) siting meeting only cost efficiency priorities can coincide with equitable outcomes but represents only a subset of Pareto-optimal solutions, whereas planning charging location driven by equity reveals various alternatives; (ii) the fewer the charging stations, the more missed trips that leave lower-income and multi-unit dwelling residents and travelers the most vulnerable; (iii) in the early stages of transportation electrification, when charging infrastructure is sparser, it is likely that disparities in charging access will be observed among socioeconomic groups but as the charging network grows denser these accessibility gaps will be bridged.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: On the political economy of nonlinear income taxation
Authors: Marcus Berliant, Miguel Gouveia
Abstract: The political economy setting of voting over general nonlinear income taxes with labor disincentives and information asymmetry in consumer/worker/voter types is considered. Agents do not communicate or coordinate with each other. The economy is the realization of a finite draw from a continuous distribution. The revenue required from a draw is determined by Pareto optimal provision of a public good for that draw. Assuming that the government must meet the revenue requirement for any possible draw, in other words the tax is robust, a majority rule equilibrium is shown to exist at the median voter’s preferred tax function out of this robust set. The key restrictions on utility are additive separability, quasi-linearity, and that utility from the public good is multiplicative in type.

Title: JUE Insight: Breaking ground: Can refund bonuses solve the holdout problem?
Authors: Timothy N. Cason, Alex Tabarrok, Robertas Zubrickas
Abstract: The holdout problem presents a pervasive challenge in situations that require the assembly of independently controlled assets, where due to complementarity the combined whole is worth more than the sum of its parts. One avenue for addressing holdout problems involves contingent contracts, where agreements are conditional upon reaching a predetermined threshold. This paper reports an experiment to investigate a new refund bonus contingent mechanism, in which asset owners who agree to participate (e.g., sell their asset) receive a bonus payment if the required threshold for project success is not met. The refund bonus eliminates failure equilibria and improves the frequency of successfully reaching the threshold in the symmetric mixed strategy equilibrium. In the experiment, individual asset holders choose each round whether to accept an offer to sell. Multiple owners must accept for the (contingent) sale to materialize, and holdout owners who do not sell can earn more, so the game has the strategic incentives of a volunteer's dilemma. The data show that the bonus mechanism increases agreements to sell, the frequency of successful projects, and efficiency. By the second half of the experimental sessions, the total number of sales is 35 percent higher and the threshold is met nearly twice as often with the bonus than without.

Title: The redistributive effects of transport policies
Authors: Morgan Ubeda
Abstract: Low-emission zones (LEZs) increase commuting costs by car but decrease negative traffic externalities in affected locations. High-income workers are more likely to sort in central locations where we expect the benefits of the policy to be the strongest, but are also more likely to commute by car. Thus, they should be more exposed to both the costs and benefits of driving restrictions. Using a quantitative urban model with rich worker heterogeneity and non-homothetic preferences, I argue that the redistributive effects of urban policies are indeed shaped by these differences in exposure and budget shares. After showing that the model is able to reproduce the patterns of sorting across space and transport modes observed in the Greater Paris region, I use it to compute the prospective effects of the Parisian LEZ. Results indicate that the policy would most likely increase welfare only at the top of the income distribution, while the rest of the population would suffer net losses.

Title: The geography of commodity booms
Authors: Luis Baldomero-Quintana
Abstract: I investigate how local commodity booms impact regional manufacturing in Colombia. I build a multisectoral economic geography model with industry linkages where states trade domestically and internationally. I quantify the spatial spillovers to manufacturing under several local resource boom scenarios, finding three key results. First, states that have both high domestic and international market access tend to see an increase in their manufacturing activity under booms, while less-connected states see a decline. Second, domestic trade and industry linkages can amplify or reduce these manufacturing spillovers. Third, international trade is the main determinant of the spatial spillovers to manufacturing. I also find that local commodity booms produce four patterns: (i) they crowd out manufacturing activity in the state where the boom occurs, (ii) their spatial spillovers to manufacturing change when I eliminate labor mobility frictions, (iii) they increase production costs in manufacturing sectors, and (iv) they induce worker reallocation across sectors. My findings show that geography, trade, and industry linkages crucially determine how commodity booms shape regional industrialization in developing nations.

Title: QSM: Introduction
Authors: Kristian Behrens, Gilles Duranton

Title: Can credit collections on traffic violations save lives? Evidence from Chinese vehicle insurance market
Authors: Ying Liu, Congrong Pan, Lihua Qin, Fangjie Zhang
Abstract: This paper estimates the effects on road safety of a regulation that imposed credit collections on traffic violations, thereby establishing a non-monetary sanction in addition to the penalty-point system. Using individual underwriting and claims data in the vehicle insurance industry in china and employing a quasi-experimental approach, we show that this regulation was effective in reducing fatalities and minor injuries by 22.9% and 87.1%, respectively. This result is robust to various checks including the propensity score matching approach. We compare this effect with that of monetary sanctions and find that it is uniform across wealth groups, whereas drivers with higher risk profiles are more responsive. This is in sharp contrast to the impact of monetary sanctions. We attribute the road safety effect of this regulation to the general deterrent effect exclusively.

Title: Netflix and chilling effect? The impact of streaming video licenses on paid digital downloads
Authors: Brett Danaher, Shahryar Doosti
Abstract: Digital distribution has expanded monetization opportunities for media firms, but it also introduces complex tradeoffs across channels. A central challenge for studios and networks is negotiating fixed-fee licensing deals with bundled subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) platforms like Netflix, whose flat-rate access model may cannibalize à la carte sales on transactional platforms such as iTunes.We exploit the natural experiment of Netflix’s launch in Australia to estimate the causal effect of licensing a film to the service on its digital sales. On average, licensing reduces à la carte downloads by 52.5%, with effects that persist even after titles are removed from Netflix – evidence that temporary bundling can have durable effects on competing transactional channels.Crucially, we show that this treatment effect is heterogeneous: the direction and magnitude of the effect vary systematically with a film’s à la carte price and its latent demand. Lower-priced titles exhibit positive treatment effects following Netflix inclusion, while higher-priced titles experience substantial declines. Though prices are not exogenously assigned, these patterns are consistent with theoretical models in which exposure on an SVOD platform can generate promotional spillovers, sampling, or word-of-mouth for lower-cost titles.Our findings offer rare revealed-preference evidence on how SVOD bundling interacts with underlying demand, addressing classic questions in industrial organization around bundling and channel conflict.

Title: Editorial Board
Supply chain stress testing and reconfiguration for tariff shocks: connecting operational and economics perspectives
Authors: Dmitry Ivanov
Affiliations: Berlin School of Economics and Law

Title: Nested rationality: the ecological foundations of the Fifth Hand theory of infrastructure project cost mis-performance
Authors: Peter E. D. Love, Lavagnon A. Ika
Affiliations: School of Civil and Mechanical Engineering, Curtin University; Telfer School of Management, University of Ottawa

Title: A Tale of Two Transitions: Mobility Dynamics in China and Russia After Central Planning
Authors: Kristina Butaeva, Lian Chen, Steven N. Durlauf, Albert F. Park
Affiliations: University of Chicago Chicago Illinois USA; University of California, Los Angeles Los Angeles California USA; Asian Development Bank Mandaluyong City Metro Manila Philippines; Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Hong Kong China
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines intergenerational mobility in China and Russia during their transitions from central planning to market systems. We consider mobility as movement, measured as changes in status between parents and children. We provide estimates of two key mobility measures: overall mobility, which captures total intergenerational movement including the effects of changing class distributions across generations, and steady‐state mobility, which captures the long‐run mobility intrinsic to the intergenerational process once the class distribution has stabilized. We further decompose overall mobility into structural and exchange components. We find that China exhibits more overall educational mobility than Russia, mostly due to greater structural mobility, while Russia exhibits greater steady‐state educational mobility. Overall and steady‐state occupational mobility are similar in China and Russia. Comparing these results to the US, we find that educational steady‐state mobility is substantially lower in China than in both Russia and the US, with Russia being the most mobile, but occupational steady‐state mobility is comparable across all three countries.

Title: A mathematical framework and optimization approach for strategically configuring hospitals to accommodate diverse patient caseloads
Authors: Robert L. Burdett, Paul Corry
Abstract: Abstract In many hospitals, treatment areas are typically dedicated to a single medical or surgical specialty. While shared use by multiple specialties is uncommon, it can be necessary, or even advantageous in certain situations. This article introduces a proof-of-concept mathematical framework for strategically reorganizing treatment-area functions to enhance resilience and operational flexibility. We focus on configuring a hospital so it can robustly treat a selected repertoire of patient caseloads (a.k.a., case mix) should they arise. Using mixed-integer programming and metaheuristic optimization, our solution approach determines which patient types should share each treatment area, maximizing the number of targeted caseloads that can be accommodated. When caseloads vary greatly or are infeasible, the model seeks a best-fit configuration that maximizes fulfilment across all caseload profiles. Because solving the exact model is computationally intractable, we propose and evaluate two matheuristics, one that utilises Simulated Annealing and the other Variable Neighbourhood Search. Numerical testing on a large, real-world instance demonstrates their effectiveness in finding near-optimal, practical solutions, providing strong motivation for further research and validation across diverse healthcare settings.

Title: MAEFF: missing-aware adaptive expert fusion framework for multi-sensor bearing fault diagnosis
Authors: Liang Yan, Shichang Du, Shuo Wang, Haitong Luo, Shanshan Li, Xianmin Chen
Abstract: Multi-sensor bearing fault diagnosis can take full advantage of the complementary information across heterogeneous signals; however, real-world deployments often involve sensor dropout, temporal gaps, and sporadic point-wise data loss. To improve diagnostic robustness under diverse mixed missingness conditions, this paper proposes a Missing-aware Adaptive Expert Fusion Framework (MAEFF), which enables adaptive decision-making under incomplete observations through reliability-guided multi-sensor fusion and relation-aware residual correction. Unlike methods that rely on signal reconstruction or data imputation, MAEFF directly incorporates missing-awareness into the fusion process itself, and further improves robustness and training stability through missingness-injected data and a staged optimization strategy. Extensive experiments on the Ottawa multi-sensor bearing dataset and the KAIST rotating-machine dataset show that, under three practically motivated missingness patterns, MAEFF achieves strong diagnostic performance under fully observed inputs and degrades gracefully as missingness increases. Across missingness ratios ranging from fully observed inputs to settings where every segmented signal window contains missing observations, MAEFF consistently maintains high accuracy and competitive macro-F1 scores, while outperforming advanced multi-sensor fusion baselines under severe missingness and achieving a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off. These results indicate that robust missing-aware fusion is an important direction for practical intelligent diagnosis, and that the proposed framework provides a flexible foundation for building resilient multi-sensor PHM systems in non-ideal sensing environments.

Title: Evaluating Model Performance Under Worst-Case Subpopulations
Authors: Mike Li, Daksh Mittal, Hongseok Namkoong, Shangzhou Xia
Affiliations: Decision, Risk, and Operations Division, Columbia Business School, New York, New York 10027
Abstract: The performance of machine learning models degrades when the training population is different from that seen under operation. Toward assessing distributional robustness, we study the worst-case performance of a model over all subpopulations of a given size defined with respect to core attributes Z. This notion of robustness can consider arbitrary (continuous) attributes Z and automatically accounts for complex intersectionality in disadvantaged groups. We develop a scalable yet principled two-stage estimation procedure that can evaluate the robustness of state-of-the-art models. We prove that our procedure enjoys several finite-sample convergence guarantees, including dimension-free convergence. Instead of overly conservative notions based on Rademacher complexities, our evaluation error depends on the dimension of Z only through the out-of-sample error in estimating the performance conditional on Z. On real data sets, we demonstrate that our method certifies the robustness of a model and prevents deployment of unreliable models.

Title: Turning Inward and/or Outward: Which socioemotional skills pay for agribusiness entrepreneurs in Nigeria?
Authors: Smita Das, Clara Delavallade, Ayodele Fashogbon, Sreelakshmi Papineni
Abstract: Socioemotional skills programs are widely used to promote economic empowerment, yet their returns may depend on the type of skills targeted and social context. We study this question using a randomized controlled trial (RCT) among 4,500 aspiring agribusiness entrepreneurs in Nigeria within a large-scale government program. Participants were randomly assigned to an interpersonal-skills curriculum, a combined interpersonal and intrapersonal-skills curriculum of the same length, or a control group. Both trainings substantially increase women's business performance, raising average profits by 50%. The two trainings generated broadly similar economic impacts overall. Effects are largest in communities with more liberal gender norms, where women report improvements in interpersonal skills such as empathy and negotiation, and better relational outcomes. Despite large economic gains, we find no corresponding increases in women's empowerment or intrahousehold decision-making. For men, interpersonal-skills training increases household income, while the combined curriculum raises profits but only in the most gender-liberal environments. The results show that the returns to socioemotional skills programs depend not only on which skills are taught, but also on whether prevailing social norms permit individuals to express and deploy those skills. Translating gains into broader empowerment may require complementary programs that relax gender norms.

Title: Rethinking manufacturer–dealer relationships for customer solutions: From a single to a portfolio of relationship modes
Authors: Johanna Luisa Knapp, Heiko Gebauer, Oliver Gassmann, Felix Wortmann
Abstract: ABSTRACT As manufacturers bundle products, services, and software into customer solutions, they need to rethink both customer and dealer relationships. Existing literature mainly explores changes in manufacturer-customer ties. Less is known about how manufacturers that use dealers as intermediaries for customer solutions must adapt their relationships with dealers. This article draws on an abductive qualitative study comprising 47 interviews with manufacturers, dealers, and customers across six industries, complemented by an embedded process case. The research examines how greater solution orientation reshapes manufacturer–dealer relationships. The findings reveal three relationship modes: (1) manufacturer-led enablement, (2) joint coordination, and (3) strategic co-creation. These modes differ in governance, coordination, decision-making, and power. The study extends the relational-process view of customer solutions to dealer-mediated channels. We develop the relationship mode portfolio concept and show that advanced servitization does not necessarily eliminate dealers; instead, dealers assume different roles depending on solution requirements.

Title: On competitive equilibria and cores in housing market problem with one broker
Authors: Yu Gu, Yongchao Zhang
Abstract: In the classical housing market problem, when all agents have strict preferences, Roth and Postlewaite (1977) show that the top trading cycles (TTC) mechanism yields the unique competitive equilibrium allocation and the unique strong core allocation. We study an extension of the housing market model that incorporates one broker. We propose the concepts of competitive equilibrium and strong core, and show that the outcome yielded by the trading cycles mechanism in Pycia and Ünver (2017) is the unique competitive equilibrium allocation and the unique strong core allocation.

Title: Diversity in teams: Collaboration and performance in experiments with different tasks
Authors: Ornella Darova, Anne Duchene
Abstract: The effect of demographic diversity on teamwork remains theoretically ambiguous. More diverse teams may benefit from more creativity and knowledge sharing, but they also face higher communication and coordination costs. This paper tests these competing mechanisms in the context of higher education. We exploit an experimental setting in a large undergraduate class, where students are randomly assigned to small homework groups, with varying levels of diversity in terms of race, gender, and place of birth. We find that the relationship between diversity and performance depends systematically on the task environment: more diverse groups outperform less diverse groups in open-ended, generative tasks, but underperform in more structured analytical tasks. We then address the effect of team diversity on coordination and communication, building an index of teamwork quality based on collaboration between members, the balance of member contributions, and the absence of conflicts. We find that diversity has a U-shaped effect on teamwork quality, regardless of the type of task performed. This result suggests that faultlines – dividing lines that split a group into subgroups based on demographic characteristics – can cause inter-subgroup cohesion to break down, while very homogeneous or very heterogeneous groups collaborate better. The results help provide a framework to understand optimal team composition for institutions and organizations.

Title: Organizational culture and habit formation in public procurement
Authors: Janne Tukiainen, Vesa Soini, Susmita Baulia, Jan Jääskeläinen
Abstract: We study the extent of a one-size-fits-all approach in the design of public procurement (PP) tenders using comprehensive data from Finland. We show that crucial PP design features related to auction and contract rules tend to have significant lack of variation across different tenders for different industries within a contracting authority. We show that this organizational rigidness is due to both organizational level culture and individual employee level work habit formation with the latter being more important. We find that both greater organizational rigidity and deviating from the national industry norms are associated with lower number of bids and higher probability of zero-bid tenders, pointing to a potential efficiency loss from organizational rigidness in PP, and offering a solution that buyers could mimic how other organizations typically buy similar products rather than how they themselves buy very different products.

Title: Generative AI and Machine learning collaboration for container dwell time prediction via data standardization
Authors: Minseop Kim, Takhyeong Kim, Taekhyun Park, Hanbyeol Park, Hyerim Bae
Abstract: Import container dwell time (ICDT) prediction is a key task for improving productivity in container terminals, as accurate predictions enable the reduction of container re-handling operations by yard cranes. Achieving this objective requires accurately predicting the dwell time of individual containers. However, the primary determinants of dwell time-owner information and cargo information-are recorded as unstructured text, which limits their effective use in machine learning models. This study addresses this limitation by proposing a collaborative framework that integrates generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) with machine learning. The proposed framework employs Gen AI to standardize unstructured information into standard international codes, with dynamic re-prediction triggered by electronic data interchange state updates, enabling the machine learning model to predict ICDT accurately. Extensive experiments conducted on real container terminal data demonstrate that the proposed methodology achieves a 13.88% improvement in mean absolute error compared to conventional models that do not utilize standardized information. Furthermore, applying the improved predictions to container stacking strategies achieves up to 14.68% reduction in the number of relocations, thereby empirically validating the potential of Gen AI to enhance productivity in container terminal operations. Overall, this study provides both technical and methodological insights into the adoption of Gen AI in port logistics and its effectiveness.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: The 15-minute neighbourhood and housing affordability: insights from Los Angeles
Authors: Dena Kasraian, Emma Kurihara, Ahmadreza Faghih Imani, Tom Rous, Audrey de Nazelle
Abstract: The 15-minute neighbourhood is a planning concept that aims to address urban environmental, health and social challenges by enabling residents to meet their daily needs within a 15-minute walk or cycle. While widely promoted, equity concerns have emerged regarding 15-minute neighbourhood transitions, particularly the tension between livability and accessibility gains and housing affordability protection. This work addresses two gaps in the existing 15-minute city literature. First, it presents empirical evidence on the relationship between local accessibility and housing affordability; second, it provides actionable guidance on how to ensure that interventions balance accessibility gains with affordability protection to promote just transitions that actively address, rather than exacerbate, existing inequalities. To assess the potential for 15-minute neighbourhoods to contribute to just transitions towards sustainable and healthy urban environments, we evaluate linkages between 15-minute neighbourhood status and affordable housing in Los Angeles county which faces a growing unhoused population alongside rising rent and home values. Informed by a literature review, we apply a scoring methodology that accounts for access and choice to different categories of amenities to assess 15-minute neighbourhood status, which we compare against different housing affordability metrics using geospatial analysis. Findings reveal a weak but positive correlation between 15-minute neighbourhood scores and affordable housing availability. Notably, residents of affordable housing in Los Angeles often have relatively high access to amenities traditionally perceived as less accessible to low-income populations, such as green spaces and grocery stores. Our findings suggest that cities may be able to pursue proximity-based planning without inherently exacerbating inequities, provided that affordability is explicitly considered. Beyond our immediate empirical findings, our proposal to jointly evaluate affordability and 15-minute neighbourhood scores, as well as the resulting neighbourhood typology and suggested interventions offer a practical approach to help cities support a just transition to affordable 15-minute neighbourhoods. This approach is especially relevant for other car-dependent metropolitan regions that are promoting proximity-based planning while facing affordability challenges.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: When air meets ground: Modeling the congestion externalities of urban air mobility in integrated air-ground transportation networks
Authors: Zhenwei Gong, Zhuoye Zhang, Fangni Zhang
Abstract: This study develops an integrated modeling framework to analyze the network equilibrium and congestion externalities of Urban Air Mobility (UAM) within a low-altitude air-ground transportation system. The model couples a ground transportation network with a low-altitude airspace network via vertiports, incorporating elastic traveler demand with cross-price effects and employing Macroscopic Fundamental Diagrams to capture traffic dynamics in both layers. We investigate how system controls (perimeter boundary and vertiport operations), UAM network design, and pricing strategies influence overall system performance. Analytical findings reveal significant paradoxes: well-intentioned perimeter and vertiport controls can exacerbate congestion (control paradox), airspace capacity expansion may worsen system-wide conditions (capacity paradox), and fare adjustments can produce counterproductive demand shifts (pricing paradox). These paradoxes are fundamentally driven by the interplay between demand elasticities and the coupling strength between air and ground networks. Numerical experiments based on Hong Kong Island demonstrate that the impact of UAM is highly sensitive to network design: while UAM services with very few routes have limited system-wide effects, a complex, highly connected network acts as a powerful network reconfiguration tool, redistributing demand and fostering a more polycentric and resilient urban structure. Sensitivity analyses further show that the control paradox is amplified by low own-price sensitivity and high cross-price sensitivity for ground controls, whereas airspace and vertiport controls exhibit opposite patterns. The study underscores that the primary value of UAM lies not merely in point-to-point speed but in its potential as a strategic lever for reshaping city-wide mobility. Our framework provides critical insights for policymakers and operators to navigate these complexities and design integrated management strategies that harness the benefits of UAM while mitigating unintended congestion spillovers.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Behavior and representation in open-weight Large Language Models for combinatorial optimization: From feature extraction to algorithm selection
Authors: Francesca Da Ros, Luca Di Gaspero, Kevin Roitero
Abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) open new perspectives for automation in optimization, yet little is known about whether their internal representations capture problem structure or algorithmic behavior. We investigate whether representations learned by frozen, open-weight LLMs for combinatorial optimization instances can support downstream decision tasks. The goal is not to replace exact feature extractors or to propose a new algorithm, but to assess whether such representations are reusable for feature recovery and algorithm selection. Our methodology combines direct querying , which tests explicit feature extraction, with probing analyses of whether this information is implicitly encoded in the hidden layers. The probing framework is further extended to a per-instance algorithm selection task. Experiments span four benchmark problems, three instance representations, and five open-weight models from 3B to 120B parameters across the Llama instruct and gpt-oss reasoning families, including a chain-of-thought study on Llama models. Results show a limited ability to recover features explicitly, particularly those requiring structured computation, while part of this information remains implicitly encoded in the hidden states. A consistent gap separates implicit encoding from explicit retrieval. Model scale attenuates this gap, whereas the effect of chain-of-thought prompting depends strongly on model size, and in all cases the gap remains open. Reasoning-oriented models also tend to abstain more when reliable computation is not possible. Notably, the predictive power of LLM hidden-layer representations is comparable to traditional feature extraction across all five models, indicating they can act as effective surrogate descriptors for downstream optimization tasks.

Title: Opportunistic sovereign default under a credible peg
Authors: Joao Hernandez
Abstract: In the African Financial Community (CFA) franc zones, a credible euro peg coexists with external debt denominated largely in U.S. dollars: euro–dollar fluctuations, exogenous to these small economies, directly raise the domestic-currency burden of debt. Panel regressions show that such depreciations raise sovereign default intensity by roughly 9%. In these same high-default years, consumption does not fall—evidence against the insurance motive of standard default models. I explain both facts by extending the partial default framework of Arellano et al. (2023) with foreign-currency debt, exogenous exchange rate shocks, and government heterogeneity. Exogeneity changes the nature of default: governments default not for insurance but opportunistically, exploiting the valuation gap between the higher debt burden and the higher revenue from new borrowing, generating a short-run rise in consumption. A policy counterfactual finds leaving for a self-managed dollar peg welfare-neutral on the financial side: opportunistic default insures the mismatch so effectively that a country profits from devaluations whatever their source, so the arrangement's value lies not in shielding the debt but in the exogenous-devaluation environment that makes default opportunistic.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: An explainable machine learning analysis of retail renewable premiums
Authors: Yufan Ji, Noah Dormady, Abdollah Shafieezadeh, Kathryn Diana, Matthew Hoyt, Alberto J. Lamadrid L., Samantha Fox
Abstract: Estimating the supplier’s premium on retail renewable energy is persistently challenging. 14 U.S. states and several international jurisdictions have implemented retail restructuring (i.e., ”retail choice”) through which consumers can shop for electricity supply from marketers. These marketers often offer plans with varying compositions of renewable energy supplied by renewable energy certificates (RECs). This study quantifies the renewable energy premium on residential electricity offers using comprehensive data from Ohio’s retail choice market (2014–2023). We develop an algorithm that matches renewable and non-renewable offers by the same supplier on the same day, with virtually identical offer details (e.g., maturity, monthly fee, termination fee) over 120,000 matched contracts. Using a gradient boosting model with SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations), we characterize how observable contract features and wholesale market conditions (e.g., forward hub prices) on the renewable energy premium of renewable offers. On average, renewable contracts include a markup of 7.67% (price difference of 0.642 cents/kWh). However, results also indicate that longer contract maturities and higher early termination fees are associated with lower renewable energy premiums, suggesting that renewable premiums vary systematically across contract structures. Importantly, we find robust empirical evidence for the presence of a trigger price: when forward wholesale energy prices are below $47.9/MWh, marketers obtain renewable energy premiums through higher marginal prices. Above this trigger, marketers no longer obtain a higher premium on renewable offers and instead manipulate maturities and early termination fees. Policy implications for market design and societal environmental objectives are presented.

Title: Climate change and credit risk of rural financial institutions: Evidence from China
Authors: Peng Peng, Shuo Han, Bingbing Zhang
Abstract: Extreme precipitation, as a key climate physical risk, critically affects the credit risk of the financial system, particularly in vulnerable sectors. However, existing research pays insufficient attention to its micro-level transmission mechanisms and systemic spillover effects. Using meteorological observation data and financial data of rural financial institutions in China from 2010 to 2021, this paper systematically examines the impact of extreme precipitation on the credit risk of rural financial institutions and its transmission pathways. We find that extreme precipitation raises the credit risk level of rural financial institutions, with the core mechanisms being the reduction of agricultural output and losses in housing assets. Further supplementary analysis indicates that extreme precipitation events can amplify the risk interaction and spillover effects among different types of banks, with the risk linkage between rural commercial banks and city commercial banks being the most sensitive. These findings highlight the importance for financial institutions to conduct scenario analysis and stress testing, and provide micro-level evidence for building a climate-resilient financial system.

Title: Ports in transition: rethinking hydrogen hub site selection through a multi-stakeholder lens
Authors: Lara Pomaska, Gordon Wilmsmeier, Johannes Meuer
Abstract: Green hydrogen is central to decarbonizing energy and transport systems, with ports increasingly positioned as key locations for hydrogen-related activities. However, the specific functions of ports within emerging hydrogen value chains and the evolving multi-stakeholder dynamics surrounding their development remain underexplored. The objective of this study is to develop a conceptual multi-actor multi-criteria decision-making framework for hydrogen hub site selection in ports. Drawing on a narrative literature review and expert interviews, we identify four distinct functions in the hydrogen value chain: industrial hydrogen hubs, bunkering-oriented hubs, import–export gateways, and distribution and aggregation nodes. Each function involves specific infrastructure requirements, stakeholder constellations, and decision criteria. By incorporating stakeholder salience and function-specific objectives into the decision logic, our framework structures early-stage decision-making around divergent interests and governance complexity. We contribute to the port development and infrastructure planning literature by introducing hydrogen-related port functions, conceptualizing their evolution, and integrating multi-stakeholder governance into decision-making.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Passenger-freight shared mobility for decarbonizing urban-rural bus systems: fleet and capacity optimization
Authors: Jiabin Wu, Zijian Huang, Linhong Wang, Yiming Bie, Yuting Ji, Jun Gong
Abstract: Urban-rural public transport faces a self-reinforcing cycle of declining ridership, service deterioration, and mounting deficits, while parallel diesel freight operations generate substantial carbon emissions along the same corridors. Passenger-freight shared mobility (PFSM) addresses both challenges by using idle bus capacity to co-transport parcels, yet its implementation must balance passenger service quality and freight efficiency. This study formulates a bilevel optimization model that jointly determines fleet composition, and dynamic capacity allocation, and vehicle scheduling while incorporating stochastic travel time effects of freight operations. An improved jellyfish search algorithm is developed to solve the resulting mixed-integer program. A case study of two urban–rural routes in Shanxi Province, China, shows that the optimized PFSM scheme turns a daily operating deficit of RMB 2462.16 into a profit of RMB 537.55, eliminates dedicated freight trucks, and reduces annual freight-related CO 2 emissions by 19.12 tons per route, demonstrating a viable pathway for decarbonizing rural transport.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Real-world battery electric vehicle charging and driving behavior estimation and quantification
Authors: John Merickel, Casey Quinn, Timothy Coburn, Kang-Ching Chu
Abstract: Newer, longer-range electric vehicles (EVs) drive approximately 12,000 miles annually, approaching the 14,000-mile annual average for gas vehicles, highlighting the importance to understand better EV charging and driving behavior as EVs become mainstream. Using U.S. EV driving, parking, and charging data from 2018 to 2019 and 2023–2024, we analyzed how drivers use charging infrastructure and predicted charging likelihood. A random-forest model was used to screen for key factors, informing an interpretable mixed logit model with about 80 % out-of-sample accuracy. Drivers of longer-range EVs in 2023–2024 primarily charged at home, but plugged in roughly 25 % less often at home at the end of the day than drivers of shorter-range EVs when state of charge was 50 %. Charging was more likely (∼5–9 %) in the Northeast than in other regions, particularly in winter. Additionally, greater public charging availability may also be associated with an increase in the probability of away-from-home charging.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Spatial scale of agglomeration and dispersion: Number, spacing, and the spatial extent of cities
Authors: Takashi Akamatsu, Tomoya Mori, Minoru Osawa, Yuki Takayama
Abstract: Cities have become fewer, bigger, and flatter in many countries. Better transport access has fostered the concentration of economic activities toward fewer, bigger cities, while each city has become more decentralized. We show that two types of dispersion forces against spatial agglomeration explain the dual evolution of cities. Dispersion forces within a city, such as those arising from the consumption of limited land, affect only the city's residents. A decrease in transport costs reduces the relative benefits of agglomeration in a congested central location, making the population distribution in each city flatter and more spread out to achieve a balance between the costs and benefits of agglomeration. Dispersion forces that spill over beyond a city, such as market crowding, make locations near the city unattractive. Lower transport costs promote competition for a wider area around each city, leaving fewer cities with larger distances between them. A model's comparative static results, and thus its policy implications, depend on the type of dispersion forces it incorporates.

Title: The local and aggregate effects of land-use regulation on farmland protection
Authors: Yue Yu
Abstract: This paper studies the distortionary effects of land-use regulations that preserve farmland from urban sprawl. I exploit a major policy restricting farm-to-urban land conversion in China — the Farmland Red Line Policy — to provide causal evidence on the negative impact of land-use regulation on local development, measured by GDP and population growth. To understand the aggregate impact of the policy, I develop a quantitative spatial equilibrium model that features endogenous land-use decisions. The calibrated model reveals a 7% loss in workers’ welfare due to the policy. Furthermore, a cap-and-trade platform that allows local regions to exchange farmland preservation requirements can eliminate 60% of workers’ welfare costs. The results highlight the substantial welfare costs that can arise from suboptimal land-use policies, underscoring the need for careful design in fast-growing economies.

Title: Impacts of privatization on state-owned enterprises: A tale of zombie versus healthy firms
Authors: Gang Xu, Ruiting Wang, Xue Wang, Tao Zha
Abstract: We estimate the effects of privatization on zombie versus healthy state-owned enterprises (SOEs) in China, extending our analysis beyond TFP to a broad array of financial and economic indicators. Privatizing zombie SOEs generates persistent favorable effects: it enhances labor productivity and TFP, reduces bank subsidies, lowers leverage and administrative expenses, improves liquidity, boosts profits, and accelerates sales growth, thereby increasing their probability of recovery. Privatization’s effect on reducing government subsidies, however, is generally weaker and appears to be transient. These benefits are more pronounced than for healthy SOEs and display some heterogeneity across regions and industries. Our findings offer policy implications for emerging markets, suggesting that prioritizing the privatization of underperforming, zombie-like entities can be associated with substantial economic gains and efficiency improvements.

Title: The long-run impacts of parental leave policies on the motherhood penalty: Evidence from Canada
Authors: Moyosore Sogaolu

Title: Mismatch in the 21st century: An overview
Authors: Luca Coraggio, Monica Langella, Armando Miano, Marco Pagano, Marco S. Petterson, Vincenzo Pezone, Annalisa Scognamiglio
Abstract: Technological change, demographic pressures, and the green transition are reshaping labor markets, highlighting the importance of understanding how workers’ skills align with job requirements. This paper surveys the theoretical and empirical literature on worker-job mismatch, focusing on skill mismatch and distinguishing it from related concepts including hiring difficulties, sectoral mismatch unemployment, and broader allocative inefficiency. We discuss the forms that mismatch can take in the labor market and review their empirical measures. Recent contributions highlight the importance of multidimensional skills and the potential of employer-employee data and machine-learning methods to measure mismatch when direct skill information is unavailable. We then review the main theoretical mechanisms through which mismatch arises, emphasizing search frictions and imperfect information and learning. We also survey evidence on the determinants of mismatch, including labor-market institutions, financial constraints, geography, managerial practices, technological change, and migration, and on its consequences for wages, career outcomes, productivity, and employment. Finally, we discuss policies to reduce mismatch and identify open questions for future research.

Title: Commentaries on “Discussing five decades of legacy of soft systems methodology in operational research and other fields of knowledge”—Alberto Paucar-Caceres
Authors: Giles A. Hindle, Kathy Kotiadis, Martin Kunc, David C. Lane, Hernán López-Garay, Alejandro Ochoa Arias, Chris Smith, Eliseo Vilalta-Perdomo, Mike Yearworth, Alberto Paucar-Caceres
Affiliations: University of Hull; University of Kent; University of Southampton Business School; Henley Business School; Universidad de Ibagué; Universidad Austral de Chile; The University of Manchester; Aston University; University of Exeter Business School; Manchester Metropolitan University
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Social status and Holocaust survival in Nazi internment
Authors: Matěj Bělín, Tomáš Jelínek, Štěpán Jurajda
Abstract: When does social hierarchy break down? Can social status acquired during peacetime affect the structure of mortality in prisoner societies facing long-term existential threat? We study two distinct Holocaust settings: the Theresienstadt ghetto and the Auschwitz-Birkenau concentration camp. We find that social status provided substantial survival protection in the partially self-administered prisoner society of Theresienstadt, where it was as helpful for women as for men, even under high survival pressure. However, social status was no longer effective in supporting survival in Auschwitz, where there was no semblance of prisoner self-administration.

Title: The intergenerational effect of the Food Stamp Program on marriage and fertility
Authors: Augustine Denteh, Nicardo McInnis
Abstract: Abstract This paper examines the intergenerational effects of the Food Stamp Program (FSP) on fertility and marriage in the United States. Using the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, we leverage the initial roll-out of the Food Stamp Program in the 1960s and 1970s to examine the future family formation decisions of individuals born between 1955 and 1981. The results suggest that exposure to the program has different effects on fertility and marriage based on age and gender. For men, increased exposure to the program reduces fertility at older ages, particularly for those from disadvantaged backgrounds, with limited effects on marriage. Among women, we find no statistically significant effects of increased exposure to FSP on fertility and marriage. Our study builds on a growing literature that considers the intergenerational impacts of public policies that increase childhood economic resources.

Title: Coordinated scheduling and distribution in seru production system with self-operated logistics under delivery time uncertainty
Authors: Zhe Zhang, Xiaoling Song, Yong Yin, Taixin Li
