Title: Rushing to the altar? Same-sex marriages when rights feel at risk
Authors: Mateus Maciel, Sara Parente, David Zuchowski
Abstract: Abstract The literature on same-sex marriage has primarily focused on the effects of legal recognition, overlooking other factors that influence marriage decisions among same-sex couples. This study provides novel evidence on the role of political context by analyzing how the election of a homophobic leader affects these decisions. Using the case of Brazil, we examine the effect of revealed local support for the openly homophobic Jair Bolsonaro in the presidential elections on same-sex marriage dynamics. To estimate this effect, we apply a difference-in-differences approach with varying treatment intensity. The results show a significant increase in same-sex marriages in municipalities with higher support for Bolsonaro during the period between the election and the beginning of his presidential term. These findings suggest that perceived threats of rights restrictions can trigger immediate and significant personal decisions among minority groups, even in the absence of legal changes.

Title: Exploring the supply chain resilience of food banks: a dynamic capabilities perspective
Authors: Tiloux Soundja, Karima Afif
Affiliations: Université Laval Department of Agri-Food Economics and Consumer Sciences, , Quebec
Abstract: Purpose While supply chain resilience (SCR) has been extensively studied in for-profit contexts, nonprofit supply chains (NPSCs) remain underexplored. Drawing on dynamic capabilities theory (DCT), this study aims to investigate how food banks enact and integrate resilience capabilities under systemic disruptions. Using the COVID-19 pandemic as an empirical setting, this study investigates strategies deployed across pre-crisis, crisis and post-crisis phases. Design/methodology/approach Based on 21 semi-structured interviews with Moissons and community-based organizations across Québec (Canada), this study adopts an abductive, interpretive approach to identify the dynamic capabilities (DCs) underpinning proactive, concurrent and reactive responses. Findings Nonprofit SCR is enabled by six interdependent dynamic capacities: anticipation, adaptability, agility, collaboration, recovery and learning, aligned with the sensing, seizing and transforming processes. Horizontal collaboration emerges as a pivotal mechanism enabling network-level adaptation despite severe resource constraints. Findings further show that collaboration also functions as a compensatory mechanism when formal reconfiguration capacity is limited. Practical implications Findings guide nonprofit managers and policymakers in strengthening supply chain continuity during systemic disruptions. Practitioners can enhance resilience by institutionalizing peer collaboration and leveraging digital coordination tools, while policymakers can better align regulatory frameworks and funding mechanisms with the flexibility needs of NPSCs. Originality/value This study extends DCT to resource-constrained NPSCs and develops a temporal, process-based framework of resilience. Unlike prior DCT applications in for-profit and vertically coordinated supply chains, which emphasize firm-level optimization and hierarchical coordination, this study demonstrates how resilience emerges under chronic resource scarcity, volunteer dependence and fragmented operations. Horizontal governance structures further shape how capabilities are enacted across decentralized actors. The study highlights that resilience is achieved through compensatory, network-based mechanisms rather than formal reconfiguration capacities typical of firm-centric models. It provides empirically grounded insights into how DCs unfold across crisis phases in decentralized nonprofit networks, with implications for other systemic disruptions and comparative research.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: Credence Goods, Consumer Feedback and (in)Efficiency
Authors: Mehdi Ayouni, Thomas Lanzi
Affiliations: BETA Université de Lorraine, Université de Strasbourg, CNRS Nancy France
Abstract: ABSTRACT We study how consumer feedback affects a credence good market where consumers sequentially visit a monopolistic expert. Each consumer's problem can be minor or major. Before treatment, the expert performs a diagnosis which may fail. Each consumer reveals the received treatment and its outcome. Consumers observe feedback history and decide whether to visit the expert. We find that consumer feedback can lead to inefficiency. When diagnosis fails, the expert overtreats consumers even though the probability of a major problem is low. This behavior does not arise without consumer feedback.

Title: Existence and Uniqueness Theorem of Continuous and Monotone Bayesian Nash Equilibrium and Stability Analysis
Authors: Ziheng Su, Huifu Xu
Affiliations: Department of Systems Engineering and Engineering Management, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shatin, New Territories, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, China
Abstract: Since the seminal work by Meirowitz [Meirowitz A (2003) On the existence of equilibria to Bayesian games with non-finite type and action spaces. Econom. Lett. 78(2):213–218], there has been growing attention to the existence and uniqueness of continuous Bayesian Nash equilibria. In the existing literature, existence is typically established using Schauder’s fixed-point theorem, relying on the equicontinuity of players’ best response functions. Uniqueness, on the other hand, is usually derived under additional monotonicity conditions. In this paper, we revisit the issues of existence and uniqueness, and advance the literature by establishing both simultaneously using the Banach fixed-point theorem under a set of moderate conditions. Furthermore, we analyze the stability of such equilibria with respect to perturbations in the joint probability distribution of type parameters, offering theoretical support for the application of Bayesian Nash equilibrium models in data-driven contexts. Funding: This research is supported by a CUHK start-up grant.

Title: On the macroeconomic dynamics of the circular economy: A stock-flow consistent model
Authors: Marcelo Villena, Claudia Pabón-Pereira
Abstract: This paper develops a dynamic ecological-macroeconomic model of the circular economy that integrates the core strategies of reducing, reusing, and recycling within a unified intertemporal framework. The model treats produced capital, available material stocks, waste liabilities, and dissipated residuals as physically interconnected stocks subject to material-balance constraints. Its central contribution is to show how capital depreciation, when interpreted as deferred residual generation rather than only as a loss of productive services, changes the optimal growth problem. Two macroeconomic mechanisms emerge from the analysis: a circular capital discount, reflecting the shadow cost of future residuals embodied in current investment, and a waste-liability drag, through which depreciation-related and production-related residuals lower the effective intertemporal return to capital and reduce sustainable consumption relative to a linear benchmark. We show analytically that these mechanisms imply a liability-adjusted golden rule of capital accumulation and a lower socially optimal steady-state capital stock than in the standard neoclassical model. The paper also maps the planner’s allocation into a decentralized system of circular Pigouvian incentives, derives a circularly adjusted accounting identity for comprehensive wealth, and provides calibrated transition exercises showing how Reduce, Reuse, and Recycle operate through distinct macroeconomic channels. The results suggest that circular strategies reshape growth not by eliminating intertemporal trade-offs, but by changing the shadow valuation of capital accumulation, residual generation, and material recovery.

Title: Self-medication under uncertainty: Insights on drug quality and consumer behavior in Burkina Faso
Authors: Renate Hartwig, Moumouni Koala, Lena Merkel, Salfo Ouedraogo, Fadima Yaya Bocoum
Abstract: How does drug quality affect self-medication behavior? We address this question in the context of Burkina Faso, where self-medication with antibiotics is widespread. Using chemical quality tests, we find that one in three antibiotics on the market is substandard or falsified, posing significant health risks. While consumers are broadly aware of the prevalence of poor-quality drugs, they struggle to assess quality based on observable cues such as price or packaging. To identify causal effects, we conduct a novel lab-in-the-field experiment that varies the probability of purchasing effective medicine. We find that self-medication increases as drug quality becomes more certain. These results suggest that market-level interventions to improve drug quality may unintentionally increase inappropriate antibiotic use, with implications for health policy and antimicrobial resistance.

Title: Reciprocity and state capacity: Evidence from a national pollution control reform in China
Authors: Yu Luo, Yongwei Nian, Ming-ang Zhang
Abstract: We propose a new approach to pollution control from the social contract perspective, which highlights the reciprocal obligations between firms and the government, in contrast to the conventional regulatory view. Combining granular data on Chinese industrial firms with a 2007 reform that sharply increased the government's incentives for pollution control, we show, in a difference-in-differences framework, that firms with prior government support achieved greater emission reductions than those without following the reform, primarily through costly clean technology adoption and output cuts. These effects are consistent across various strategies that account for the potential endogeneity of government support and appear to be driven by reciprocity between firms and the government, as (a) the effects are more pronounced in regions with stronger norms of reciprocity, and (b) the government, in turn, responded with continued support. Alternative explanations—including government leverage, financial constraints, regulatory enforcement, and political connections—cannot explain our findings. We further examine the aggregate implications of firm-government reciprocity at the city level, exploiting quasi-random variation in city-level support induced by plausibly exogenous mayoral rotation and across-mayor variation in support preferences in an instrumental variable design. We find that such reciprocity translated into significant declines in regional pollution concentrations, thereby enhancing the government's capacity for pollution control.

Title: Embedding resilience in biological production through functional modularity: A mixed-method approach
Authors: Huynh Thi Ngoc Diep, Ho Huy Tuu, Nguyen Thi Tram Anh
Abstract: Resilience is commonly conceptualised as a capability developed in response to disruption rather than as a property embedded in a production organisation. Drawing on evidence from biological production, specifically the shrimp-farming context in Vietnam, this study identifies a recurring structural pattern reflecting the core principles of modularity and explains how it enables resilience to emerge endogenously from the production structure. A sequential mixed-methods design combines an in-depth case study, which uncovers the organisational mechanisms through which modular structures isolate disturbances, enable functional substitution, and support adaptive recombination, with a quasi-experimental analysis that provides causal evidence of their contribution to production continuity during pandemic disruptions. The findings show that resilience is generated by the structural organisation of production while simultaneously improving operational efficiency. The study advances resilience theory by demonstrating how resilience emerges as an endogenous property of production organisation and clarifying the mechanisms through which modularity generates resilience.

Title: Reconstruction of intertemporal pricing competition in two-sided markets based on fairness concerns
Authors: Dingbo Tan, Qingmei Tan, Kebing Chen
Abstract: Digital subscription platforms such as Netflix and iQiyi frequently employ dynamic pricing, and users naturally perceive fairness concerns in response to such price changes. These fairness concerns significantly influence the equilibrium pricing structures of two-sided subscription platforms. This paper develops a two-period dynamic pricing game model to study how buyers' fairness concerns alter the platforms' pricing structure across buyers and sellers. We show that fairness concerns demonstrate flexibility in adjusting pricing strategies in the intertemporal game of two-sided markets. Different from previous studies, the side with stronger network effects will be subsidized rather than subject to more aggressive pricing decisions when fairness concerns are low. Furthermore, the platform's pricing strategy is jointly determined by retention rates and fairness concerns. Specifically, for buyers, the platforms adopt the ‘ penetration-harvesting ’ strategy when both the retention rate and fairness concerns are weak. However, if the retention rate is high, the ‘lock-in effect’ will be utilized to increase the price. For sellers, the platforms adopt an incremental pricing mechanism. We also find that the buyers' fairness concerns can lead to asymmetric pricing adoption, which alters the traditional seesaw effect (where price increases on one side correspond to decreases on the other). Additionally, the unit transportation cost of two-sided users and fairness concerns jointly determine the strategy selection of the platforms. Essentially, in two-sided markets with strong network externalities, moderate fairness concerns can enhance social welfare.

Title: Supplier competition and the incentive to purchase data
Authors: Huaxin Huang, Na Leng, Jian Ni
Abstract: We investigate suppliers’ incentive to purchase data in a supply chain where multiple competing suppliers face uncertain downstream demand and may choose to acquire noisy demand signals (data) to improve their decisions. We identify a competition-reinforcement effect: data acquisition can trigger more aggressive competition among suppliers, which in turn erodes their incentive to purchase data. We show that this competition reinforcement effect could outweigh the conventional informed-decision benefit of better demand information, especially when input substitutability is low. As a result, intensified competition could reduce suppliers’ willingness to buy data, and may even generate net welfare losses.

Title: A logic-based Benders decomposition for the traveling salesman problem with facility-based drones
Authors: Yuan Yuan, Huan Tang, Jiliu Li, Frederic Semet, Hu Qin
Abstract: This study considers a truck and drone delivery system in which a truck transports parcels from a warehouse either directly to customers or to transshipment facilities, where drones are deployed for last-mile delivery. The problem is modeled as a Traveling Salesman Problem with Facility-based Drones. We propose a mixed-integer programming formulation and a logic-based Benders decomposition (LBBD) algorithm. The master problem determines facility opening, customer assignment to the truck or facilities, and the truck route, while considering only the aggregate flight-distance budget of drones at each facility. The subproblems are formulated using constraint programming and assign deliveries to individual drones while explicitly enforcing drone-level flight-range constraints. Several feasibility and optimality Benders cuts are introduced to strengthen the LBBD algorithm. In addition, valid inequalities are derived to accelerate the master problem and are also embedded in a benchmark branch-and-cut algorithm applied to the arc-flow formulation. An initial heuristic is further developed to quickly provide a high-quality upper bound. Computational experiments demonstrate that the proposed LBBD can solve instances with up to 160 nodes and outperforms both a state-of-the-art commercial solver and the branch-and-cut algorithm in terms of solution quality, computation time, and solvable instance size. Sensitivity analyses further reveal the impact of key parameters and provide valuable managerial insights.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Investigating substitution effects of autonomous taxis using rank-ordered logit models
Authors: Hua Wang, Yutong Cai, Shukai Chen, Dian Sheng
Abstract: In recent years, autonomous vehicles (AVs), particularly in shared mobility applications, have attracted increasing attention from academia, industry, and the general public. However, most existing studies on autonomous taxi services rely on hypothetical stated preference scenarios, as large-scale real-world deployment remains limited. The city-wide operation of Apollo Robotaxis (ARs) in Wuhan, China, provides a unique opportunity to examine traveler responses in a context where autonomous ride-hailing services are widely accessible. Drawing on a stated preference survey that integrates on-site and online data collection, this study investigates how the large-scale deployment of ARs reshapes travel mode choices and competitive dynamics in the urban mobility market. Latent class and random-parameter rank-ordered logit models are employed to capture heterogeneity in traveler preferences. The results reveal substantial variation in willingness to adopt ARs across distinct traveler segments, with cost sensitivity and prior experience playing crucial roles in mode substitution between ARs, traditional taxis, and ride-hailing services. Market simulations further indicate that uniform pricing strategies may lead to uneven impacts across user groups and intensify competitive pressure on conventional drivers, whereas differentiated pricing can promote higher AR adoption while mitigating displacement effects. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of accounting for preference heterogeneity when designing Robotaxi pricing and subsidy policies, and provide empirical evidence to support a more gradual and socially balanced transition toward large-scale autonomous mobility services.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: A general framework for bi-objective user equilibrium with piecewise disutility
Authors: Zhandong Xu, Hongtai Huang, Zhengyang Li, Qianni Wang, Jun Xie
Abstract: This paper proposes a general bi-objective user equilibrium (BUE) framework with piecewise disutility functions for transportation networks. The framework is motivated by empirical evidence that travelers exhibit buffer-threshold behavior, that is, the disutility remains limited within a tolerable range but rises sharply once a critical threshold is exceeded. We introduce a piecewise disutility specification that combines buffer thresholds with flexible post-threshold functional forms, allowing diverse behavioral patterns arising in time–toll trade-offs, electric-vehicle routing, and mean–risk route choice to be modeled within a unified structure. We show that the resulting problem admits a convex optimization formulation and develop a customized column generation algorithm for large-scale computation. Numerical experiments on several real-world networks demonstrate that the proposed framework provides a unified and tractable approach for analyzing bi-objective equilibrium behavior under a range of threshold-based disutility specifications.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Value versus cost in post-experience robotaxi use: evidence from a cognitive–affective–conative model
Authors: Duy Quy Nguyen-Phuoc, Feng-Yan Wu, Thao Phuong Thi Nguyen, Diep Ngoc Su, Tuan Trong Luu, Zhi-Chun Li
Abstract: Recent advances in autonomous driving have accelerated the deployment of robotaxi services, positioning them as a key component of future urban mobility. However, existing research has largely emphasized pre-adoption intentions, offering limited insight into users’ post-experience evaluations and continued usage behavior in fully driverless contexts. To address this gap, this study examines how perceived value and perceived risk, conceptualised as higher-order constructs, are jointly associated with continued usage intention toward robotaxi services in China. Guided by the cognitive–affective–conative (CAC) framework, perceived value and perceived risk are conceptualized as multidimensional cognitive evaluations formed through actual usage experiences. Based on survey data collected from 409 users with real-world robotaxi experience in Wuhan, China, the study employs structural equation modeling to investigate how these cognitive evaluations shape affective responses, including positive emotion, negative emotion, and satisfaction and, in turn, continued usage intention. The results show that perceived value is strongly associated with higher post-experience positive emotion and satisfaction, which in turn are positively related to continued usage intention, with satisfaction emerging as the strongest direct predictor. In contrast, perceived risk is primarily associated with higher post-experience negative emotion, while its associations with satisfaction and continued usage intention remain weak. This suggests that positive affective and evaluative mechanisms play a more dominant role in sustaining usage than cost-related concerns. By extending the CAC framework to post-experience robotaxi usage, this study deepens the understanding of continued usage behavior in autonomous mobility and offers practical implications for enhancing user acceptance and supporting the large-scale deployment of robotaxi services in China.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Fare-free subway eligibility and older adults’ traffic safety: Evidence from Seoul, Korea
Authors: Eun Jin Shin
Abstract: Population aging is reshaping urban mobility and intensifying concerns about older adults’ traffic safety in many countries. Although prior studies show that transit fare subsidies can change older adults’ travel behavior, it remains unclear whether these changes translate into improved traffic safety. Focusing on Seoul, this study examines changes in age-specific crash rates around the eligibility threshold for South Korea's fare-free subway policy, which grants free subway rides to adults aged 65 and older. Using a regression discontinuity design, the analysis estimates discontinuities in neighborhood-by-age crash rates at the age-65 eligibility cutoff. The results indicate discontinuous declines in both driver-involved and non-motorized-user-involved crash rates at the cutoff. Supplementary travel survey evidence suggests that the decline in driver-involved crashes may reflect a shift from private car use to subway travel, an interpretation also broadly consistent with the comparable reductions observed in at-fault and non-at-fault driver crashes. For crashes involving non-motorized users, the decline at the age-65 cutoff is not accompanied by a reduction in walking or cycling trip frequency and is concentrated in crashes involving drivers younger than 65. Taken together, these findings indicate that fare-free subway eligibility is associated with improved traffic-safety outcomes for older adults both as drivers and as non-motorized users, highlighting the importance of considering traffic safety in evaluations and reforms of age-targeted transit fare policies.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: A design-of-designs survey framework to analyze information processing strategies in choice experiments
Authors: Jose J. Soto, Elisabetta Cherchi, Juan de Dios Ortúzar, Luis I. Rizzi
Abstract: This study introduces a novel design-of-designs survey framework tailored to model decision-making processes involving the presence of alternative choice heuristics. Often based solely on a utility maximization framework, traditional choice models fail to account for the diverse heuristics that individuals may employ when faced with varying task complexity and choice contexts. The design-of-designs framework allows capturing potential alternative heuristics by systematically varying task complexity along meta-dimensions such as the number of alternatives, attributes, and choice contexts in different transport-related choices (of route, holiday destination, and residential location). The survey framework incorporates advanced features, including dynamic presentation schemes, perceptual indicators, and cognitive effort metrics, to elucidate how survey complexity may shape heuristic adoption. In particular, residential location alternatives are displayed on interactive maps, enabling respondents to filter alternatives based on selected attribute values and providing insights into selective information processing and the use of choice paths. Additionally, stated non-attendance indicators and response times are registered to evaluate cognitive load and attribute importance. Finally, the survey design also includes the possibility of considering latent constructs, such as engagement, thinking styles and trust in institutions, which have proven important in modelling with alternative heuristics. The paper highlights the importance of integrating non-compensatory behaviour into discrete choice models to enhance behavioural realism by capturing the dynamics of heuristic-driven decision-making. Finally, the paper discusses how the different survey elements can support future research on information processing and heuristic use in stated choice surveys.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: A residential e-bicycle parking mismatch? Unpacking a neglected issue in cycling policy
Authors: Ugo Lachapelle, Patrick Rérat, Emmanuel Ravalet
Abstract: To support bicycling, cities have focused on providing infrastructure to ensure safe movement. Much less research assesses the provision of adequate bicycle parking, especially residential parking. Because of their higher weight and costs, e-bicycles especially require safe, sheltered and accessible parking. The paper describes the features of home-based bicycle parking for Swiss individuals with and without e-bicycles and assesses variations and discrepancies in residential bicycle parking availability and e-bicycle ownership across land use and household characteristics. The 2021 Swiss Mobility and Transport Microcensus (MTMC) provides a representative national sample of data on e-bicycle ownership and residential bicycle parking (n = 10,154). Variations in logit-based estimated probabilities of e-bicycle ownership and quality parking access across predictor variables are assessed. The probability of having accessible sheltered and secured bicycle parking in a locked room, the golden standard of safety, protection from the elements and ease of use, is low and below that of e-bicycle ownership probabilities, regardless of socio-demographics and location features. Across group characteristics, specific mismatches between parking access and e-bicycle ownership are identified. The largest mismatches are found for homeowners and residents of areas poorly served by public transit. Current housing stock is ill-equipped for parking of e-bicycles, especially in areas where regular cycling is historically low. While existing standards can help shape new housing stock, retrofitting existing residential buildings is an important policy challenge. On street veloboxes may be more feasible. The variety of observed bicycle parking forms also points to the limits of current survey instruments. Improvements to survey instruments are proposed.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Corrigendum to “Development and interdisciplinarity: additional insights on the ‘economics silo’” [World Dev. 205(2026) 107435]
Authors: Matthias Aistleitner

Title: The development studies divide: fierce fault lines or fruitful frictions?
Authors: Arnim Scheidel
Abstract: The concept of development has deeply divided the social sciences concerned with peoples and earth's future. For many researchers and practitioners, variants of development are crucial normative cornerstones to frame and guide research and policy. Many critical scholars and activists associate the term with colonial, capitalist, extractivist, and patriarchal threats, and see it as the root cause of environmental degradation. In short, some study development as a solution, others as the problem. I call this rift the Development Studies Divide. After tracing diverse disciplinary roots, I discuss where the fault lines run and whether fruitful frictions could enrich the future of (critical) development studies. Despite stark differences in ideological, epistemological, and conceptual orientations, there is room for mutual learning, specifically across methodologies. A reflexive integration of critical perspectives with quantitative methods can substantiate critical claims beyond isolated case studies, address them at larger scales, and generate robust knowledge on alternatives to development beyond largely theory-driven proposals. It could also correct global empirical analyses that become problematic when their assumptions and interpretations are not grounded in the diverse histories, worldviews, and values of non-Western realities.

Title: A contingent behavior approach for estimating price elasticities
Authors: Richard T. Carson, Jiajun Lu, Thomas Sterner, Dale Whittington
Abstract: Abstract ​Analysis of many policy interventions depends on the availability of accurate estimates of price, income and other elasticities. Economists typically use revealed preference data to estimate these elasticities ex-post. We propose a simple survey-based contingent behavior approach for estimating ex-ante (expected) elasticities as well as their distributions in the population. Ex-ante and ex-post estimates of eleasticities may differ for legitimate reasons; both are relevant to policymakers. We illustrate this CB approach using data from seven Global South countries. Results show that it is possible to develop contemporaneous country-specific estimates of ex-ante elasticities quickly and inexpensively in data-poor environments. We also discuss how these ex-ante elasticities may inform policy acceptance.

Title: The West-to-East Power Transmission project and corporate green productivity: Evidence from Chinese industrial enterprises
Authors: Li Xie, Zhisheng Huang
Abstract: Against the backdrop of advancing high-quality development and green transition, the construction of cross-regional power transmission projects has emerged as a pivotal initiative for fostering a green, low-carbon, and high-quality spatial pattern. This study focuses on Chinese industrial enterprises, treating the commissioning of the West-to-East Power Transmission (WEPT) project as a quasi-natural experiment of cross-regional power resource allocation. Employing a multi-period difference-in-differences (DID) model, we empirically investigate the mechanism by which cross-regional power resource allocation through the WEPT project affects enterprises' green productivity. The findings indicate that the WEPT project has a significant positive effect on enterprises' green productivity, primarily through improved efficiency in allocating green resources. This project alleviates the cost burden on enterprises by mitigating regional electricity price distortions and facilitating industrial agglomeration, thereby stimulating their investment in emission-reduction equipment and enhancing their green productivity. Meanwhile, the impact of the WEPT project on enterprises' green productivity is asymmetric: it primarily improves green productivity in power-importing regions, at the terminals of thermal power transmission lines, and among state-owned and small- and medium-sized enterprises. Furthermore, the capacity enhancement enabled by the technological iteration of the WEPT project and the expansion of the layout scope facilitated by its technological selection have notably propelled the green transformation and development of enterprises. This driving effect not only fosters enterprises' green development through energy-saving effects but also operates via emission-reduction effects, with the latter being more prominent.

Title: Editorial Board
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Convergent validity in incentive-compatible contingent valuation: Bid-vector and elicitation format effects
Authors: Wojciech Zawadzki, Mikołaj Czajkowski, Jens Rommel, Julian Sagebiel, Christoph Schulze
Abstract: : This study investigates convergent validity between elicitation formats within contingent valuation methodology, focusing on theory-driven formats designed to align with incentive compatibility. While earlier literature endorsed the single binary choice (SBC) format as the only incentive-compatible option, recent studies outline theoretical conditions under which payment card (PC) and open-ended (OE) formats may also encourage truthful preference revelation. We contribute to this debate by directly comparing these three theory-driven formats and assessing their robustness against bid-vector effects and other biases such as anchoring, yea-saying, and strategic misrepresentation. We conduct a large-scale, multi-country survey with 12,343 respondents across Poland, Sweden, Hungary, Spain, Germany, and the Netherlands, examining consumers’ willingness to pay (WTP) for an EU-wide biodiversity-enhancing program. The results indicate limited convergent validity across formats, with substantial discrepancies in WTP estimates. However, analysis of choice frequencies suggests that convergent validity holds for lower bid levels, whereas higher bids introduce differences. We argue that these differences stem from both behavioral biases and methodological factors, including bid vector design and econometric assumptions. Our results underscore the critical influence of bid structure on WTP estimates and highlight the need for further research to refine elicitation formats and econometric methods used in contingent valuation studies.
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: Procompetitive effects of vertical mergers? Evidence from the European Union
Authors: Chiara Bellucci, Armando Rungi
Abstract: This study examines the relationship between mergers and firm-level financial measures using a sample of 4,482 acquisition targets in the European Union from 2007 to 2021. Findings suggest that horizontal mergers lack statistically significant results, whereas vertical mergers entail changes in markups (-0.7%), market share (+2.5%), Return on Fixed Assets (ROFA) (+2.3%), and capital intensity (-7.2%). The result for vertical mergers increases over time, and is larger when the number of pre-existing subsidiaries is greater. Our results suggest the elimination of double profit margins as a potential explanation.

Title: Commercial banking in the fintech era: A triadic efficiency analysis of technology, governance, and region using network DEA-window and Tobit regression
Authors: Nannan Liang, Yu Shi, Yao Chen
Affiliations: Nanjing Audit University; Pace University; University of Massachusetts at Lowell
Abstract: This study develops a triadic framework to evaluate operational efficiency in commercial banking and examine how digital finance and Fintech innovations shape performance across institutional and regional contexts. We integrate a two-stage network Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) with window analysis (3-year window width) and Tobit regression, distinguishing between productivity and profitability and accounting for ownership structures: state-owned banks (SOBs), joint-stock banks (JSBs), and city commercial banks (COBs). The analysis reveals heterogeneity in digital finance impacts: SOBs benefit from regulatory support but exhibit institutional inertia; JSBs leverage agility to offset structural gaps; COBs face persistent profitability inefficiencies. Regional patterns show infrastructure-driven gains in the West, market saturation in the East, and decline in the Northeast. More critically, digital finance exhibits opposite U-shaped impacts across operational stages: it follows a U-shaped trajectory with productivity efficiency initially suppressing then enhancing, and an inverted U-shaped with profitability efficiency initially boosting then eroding. This divergence underscores the need for ownership- and region-specific digital strategies, improved risk governance, and coordinated regulatory efforts. The proposed framework reconciles the technological, institutional, and spatial dimensions of digital transformation and offers actionable insights for sustainable financial innovation in emerging economies.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Stratified acceptance-probability-based adaptive simulated annealing for efficient optimization: applications in econometrics and graph analytics
Authors: Foued Saâdaoui, Hana Rabbouch
Affiliations: International University of Rabat; King Abdulaziz University; Lab: LR18ES15 Algebra, Number Theory & Nonlinear Analysis; Higher Institute of Management of Sousse
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Breaching 1.5 °C: Give me the odds
Authors: J. Eduardo Vera-Valdés, Olivia Kvist
Abstract: This paper develops a probability framework to convey the uncertainty surrounding predictions of when the temperature thresholds established by the Paris Agreement will be breached. The motivation for reporting probabilities is that they enable policymakers to make timely and informed decisions. The method can be summarised as predicting future temperatures under different scenarios and calculating the proportion of predicted outcomes that exceed the specified limits. These probabilities can be computed for different time horizons and updated as new data become available. We illustrate our method using two forecasting mechanisms. The first model links temperature anomalies to effective radiative forcings, enabling the assessment of how emissions scenarios affect breaching probabilities. The second model relies solely on the time series dynamics of observed temperatures and does not require additional inputs for forecasting. Our methodology is simple to implement and can be readily adapted to more complex climate models. We encourage climate model developers to include probabilities of breaching these limits in their reports.

Title: Willingness-to-pay for bacteriophage-treated rainbow trout: A comparative study of Denmark and Germany
Authors: Miho Maezono, Julia Bronnmann, Rasmus Nielsen, Max Nielsen
Abstract: The use of antibiotics in aquaculture contributes to the development of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), which poses serious public health risks. Bacteriophages offer a promising alternative for preventing and treating bacterial diseases in fish, effectively replacing antibiotics without fostering antibiotic resistance. However, little is known about consumer perceptions and acceptance of bacteriophage-treated seafood. This study examines consumer willingness to pay (WTP) for bacteriophage-treated rainbow trout using a discrete choice experiment. On the basis of responses from 1918 Danish and 1914 German consumers, our findings reveal a positive mean WTP for bacteriophage-treated trout (€3.03 in Denmark and €3.76 in Germany per 250 g fillet, respectively) relative to the reference level (vaccine-treated), whereas the mean WTP for antibiotic-treated trout was significantly lower. Substantial heterogeneities in WTP for health control across consumers were confirmed, as the estimated standard deviations were statistically significant. However, at least 75.6% of Danish respondents and 64.2% of German respondents demonstrated a positive WTP for phage-treated trout. These findings highlight consumer openness to bacteriophage-based disease control and provide valuable guidance for policy-makers and the aquaculture industry in their transition toward potentially more sustainable and health-conscious alternatives to antibiotics.

Title: The case for a green financial transaction tax
Authors: Gunther Capelle-Blancard
Abstract: The aim of this article is to assess whether and how the financial transaction tax (FTT) could be “greened” – that is, adapted to support environmental objectives and the transition towards a more sustainable economy. While traditionally conceived as a regulatory tool, the FTT holds unexploited potential as an instrument for climate finance and broader environmental alignment. This paper outlines five complementary arguments in favor of a green FTT: (1) its capacity to mobilize stable, international funding for global public goods; (2) its relevance in light of the financial sector's role in recent economic, social and environmental crises; (3) its ability to modestly lengthen investment horizons and counteract excessive short-termism; (4) its potential to enhance public trust in finance by matching rhetoric about sustainable finance with contributions; and (5) its use as a differentiated tool to reward environmentally responsible investors and issuers. The paper also includes an exploratory calibration of potential revenues from a tiered green FTT, intended to provide illustrative orders of magnitude rather than forecasts, and to show how such a mechanism could operationalize the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities in climate finance. While recognizing practical limitations (in terms of governance, data reliability, and risk of complexity), the paper concludes that a well-calibrated green FTT could be a simple and useful complement within the broader climate policy mix.

Title: Cognitive-cultural biodiversity amidst environmental uncertainties: A coevolutionary proposal
Authors: Richard B. Norgaard, Jalel Sager
Abstract: As compounding systemic global crises push modernity toward collapse, the dominant epistemological and economic frameworks are proving fundamentally inadequate. This commentary revisits and expands upon early coevolutionary thought in ecological economics to diagnose the current crisis of “collective cognizance.” We argue that fragmented, atomistic modern science fails to grasp whole-system dynamics, while mainstream economics—functioning as a global belief system of “economism”—has constructed a brittle, destructive monoculture optimized for short-term market efficiency. Drawing on the biological mechanisms of evolution, where profound diversity supports resilience, we propose a shift toward cognitive biodiversity. To navigate an unpredictable, post-crash future and help ensure intergenerational equity, humanity must abandon the monolithic pursuit of a single global blueprint. Instead, we advocate cultivating a rich pluriverse of diverse, coevolving learning cultural experiments, bound together, within and across groups, by caring relationality. To avoid epistemological tribalism and maintain cooperation, this pluriverse must be underpinned by a shared commitment to methodological pluralism—an ecology of knowledges that allows different ways of understanding the world to cross-pollinate without demanding a unified theoretical framework.

Title: Strategic information sharing in platform-based consumer-to-manufacturer customization
Authors: Qing Zhang, Yan Zhang, Yini Zheng, Yong He
Abstract: As consumer demand diversifies, consumer-to-manufacturer (C2M) customization has emerged as a new production paradigm. It leverages data collection and analysis of consumer preferences to inform the tailored product design and manufacturing. This paper investigates a platform-based C2M customization mode in which the platform can choose whether to share information to empower the manufacturer’s C2M customization production. By introducing a two-dimensional product matching framework that decomposes consumers’ matching preferences into functional matching and personalized matching, we examine the interplay between the manufacturer’s C2M customization and the platform’s information sharing strategy and investigate how the interaction impacts the supply chain members’ decisions and profits. We obtain several main results. Firstly, the platform’s information sharing does not consistently incentivize the manufacturer to invest in C2M customization, and may not always yield mutual benefits for both parties. Secondly, when the manufacturer’s C2M investment efficiency is low, the platform is more inclined to share consumer preference information with the manufacturer, thereby facilitating the manufacturer’s C2M customization investments at equilibrium. Conversely, the equilibrium strategy compels the manufacturer to collect consumer information to promote C2M customization, as the platform withholds information. Lastly, a win–win outcome occurs when the manufacturer’s C2M customization investment efficiency is not excessively high. We extend the model in several ways to verify robustness. Our findings provide managerial insights for manufacturers and platforms considering engagement in C2M customization.

Title: Editorial Board
Integrating prompt-based zero-shot learning into Bayesian network for maritime cybersecurity risk analysis
Authors: Yunfeng Zhao, Huanhuan Li, Trung Thanh Nguyen, Christian Matthews, Zaili Yang
Abstract: The increasing digitalisation of maritime ecosystems, including vessels, ports, offshore facilities, and shore-based organisations, has expanded the attack surface of maritime operations and increased exposure to cyber threats. Cyber incidents affecting these interconnected systems may propagate across global logistics networks, highlighting the need for systematic cybersecurity risk analysis in maritime transport. However, existing studies often rely on expert judgement or limited datasets, which restrict scalability and hinder comprehensive identification of Risk Influential Factors (RIFs). This study develops a data-driven framework that integrates Large Language Model (LLM)-assisted text classification with Bayesian Network (BN) modelling to analyse maritime cybersecurity risks. A structured taxonomy of RIFs is defined to capture temporal, regional, operational, and technical attributes of cyber incidents. LLM-based prompt engineering is then employed to automatically extract these factors from unstructured incident reports. The reliability of the automated classification process is evaluated through manual annotation on a sampled subset of incident reports and comparative experiments across multiple LLMs. The BN model is further assessed using repeated cross-validation to evaluate predictive performance and robustness. The results reveal key dependencies among cyber incident characteristics and consequence types, providing probabilistic insights into maritime cyber risk patterns. The proposed framework offers a scalable approach for analysing cyber risks in maritime transport systems and supports risk-informed cybersecurity management.

Title: Locus of control, climate change adaptation and perception: Evidence from rural Ethiopia
Authors: Halefom Yigzaw Nigus, Martin Paul Jr Tabe Ojong, Kibrom A. Abay
Abstract: Despite an overwhelming scientific consensus about the adverse effects of climate change and potential adaptation strategies, the uptake rates of climate adaptation practices fall short of expectations and public perceptions about the drivers and implications of climate change remain mixed. This paper examines whether farmers’ psychological traits, particularly locus of control, predict climate adaptation strategies. We focus on adoption of drought-tolerant varieties, fast-maturing varieties, early/late planting varieties, crop diversification, conservation agriculture, and water harvesting technologies using a large household survey from Ethiopia. We also explore climate change perceptions, and whether and how they align with actual climatic records. We find that farmers with a higher degree of internal locus of control are more likely to adopt various climate adaptation practices and are more likely to perceive changes in mean precipitation and temperature, while those with a higher level of external locus of control are less likely to perceive climate change and hence less likely to adopt climate-resilient practices. One standard deviation increase in internal (external) locus of control is associated with 3–5 percentage points higher (lower) probability of adopting alternative climate adaptation practices. We also find suggestive evidence that farmers’ climate adaptation responses are consistent with their climate perceptions and actual climatic records. These findings highlight the important role of behavioral attributes, including psychological traits, in explaining climate perceptions and subsequent climate actions.

Title: Resource-constrained project scheduling for construction dust emission reduction
Authors: Yifei Li, Lihui Zhang, Zongyu Yao, Jinrong Zhu
Abstract: Construction dust is a primary source of urban particulate matter pollution, posing a significant threat to public health and the urban environment. Based on the fugitive emission characteristics of construction dust, this study proposes a novel control method. Unlike existing research that relies on changing activity execution modes to reduce environmental impact, the core of this method lies in leveraging dynamic variations of meteorological conditions to mitigate construction dust pollution solely by optimizing activity execution times. Building on this, the study introduces a novel Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling Problem with Construction Dust Emission Reduction (RCPSP-CDER). By introducing a piecewise linear function to characterize the time-varying attributes of the meteorology-driven dust emission factor, a bi-objective optimization model for project duration and dust emissions is established. Two complementary solution approaches are developed: an ε[jls-end-space/]-constraint Constraint Programming exact method (ε C-CP) and an NSGA-II metaheuristic. The high-rise building case study reveals that significant reductions in construction dust emissions can be achieved through scheduling optimization, even under resource constraints and with no extension to project duration or increase in cost. Sensitivity analysis reveals the impact of meteorological conditions and resource capacity on the emission reduction potential. Computational experiments on PSPLIB benchmark instances across four scales show that ε C-CP attains solution quality comparable to NSGA-II on small-scale instances and recovers the exact Pareto front on a subset of them, thereby serving as a reliable benchmark; on medium- and large-scale instances, NSGA-II consistently outperforms ε C-CP in both Pareto front quality and computational efficiency. This study provides project managers with a robust quantitative decision-making tool to achieve dust reduction targets under practical engineering constraints.

Title: Bidding wars in the housing market: When directed search becomes stock-flow matching
Authors: Melvyn Coles, Eric Smith
Abstract: This paper considers equilibrium trade in a real estate market. When search is directed, buyers have private independent values, and sellers compete on asking prices, stock-flow matching characterises equilibrium outcomes. Consistent with the data, equilibrium not only generates large and variable price spikes for new listing sales; unsuccessful sellers lower their asking prices over time; and there is equilibrium asking price dispersion. Bidding war data demonstrate that the match surplus is substantial: a lower bound equals 3.3% of house price, whereas ballpark examples suggest match surplus is around 10%.

Title: Oil news shocks and the U.S. consumer sentiment and spending
Authors: Zeina Alsalman
Abstract: This paper examines the impact of oil news shocks on U.S. consumer sentiment and spending using a monthly Proxy-VAR model estimated over 1978:1–2019:12. Oil news shocks generate a delayed fall in both the Index of Consumer Sentiment (ICS) and Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE), with declines emerging about one year after the shock. ICS sub-indices and related measures reveal persistent falls in expectations about personal finances, business conditions, and buying conditions, and a significant increase in inflation expectations. Disaggregated PCE responses show that durable-goods spending increases briefly, consistent with intertemporal substitution, before turning negative, while nondurables, services, and energy-related spending fall immediately and persistently. Extending the sample through 2024 yields generally similar responses, though household behavior shows a short-lived improvement. A forecast-error variance decomposition indicates that oil news shocks explain meaningful medium- and long-horizon variation in inflation expectations, sentiment toward major purchases, and major consumption components, underscoring their role as expectation-driven disturbances.

Title: Does real-time pricing deliver lower carbon emissions?
Authors: Magdalena Strasburger, Tracey Dodd, Tim Nelson
Abstract: This study examines the relationship between household electricity consumption and carbon (CO₂) emissions costed in terms of real-time pricing (RTP) versus a static tariff. The analysis is based on 57 million hourly observations taken between February 2024 and January 2025 from 10,751 German households, each equipped with some kind of energy management system and most with a home battery. Overall, we find that RTP customers do not consume electricity with lower CO₂ intensity than customers on static tariff. In fact, both groups have negative price coefficients, but the effect is much stronger for RTP households. Customers on a static tariff show little response to price changes, whereas RTP customers reduce their consumption much more noticeably when prices rise. However, static customers have slightly lower CO₂ emissions per unit. Hence, while RTP might encourage customers to shift their usage patterns to lower-priced periods, this does not necessarily align with periods of low CO₂ output. Our results also illustrate that batteries and electric-vehicle chargers are critical enablers of load shifting. Yet, even with these technologies, the times at which people use electricity rarely coincides with the cleanest grid hours. These findings challenge the assumption that RTP inherently reduces emissions without also installing ancillary physical technologies, like batteries. Most importantly, this research shows the importance of integrating real-time carbon intensity signals with pricing and better access to enabling technologies to align electricity use with cleaner grid conditions.

Title: The Way Forward in Fashion e‐Commerce Returns: Enhancing Eco‐Efficiency
Authors: Claudia Colicchia, Maria Concetta Carissimi, Stella Viscardi, Martina Farioli, Pietro Evangelista, Fabrizio Dallari, Alessandro Creazza
Affiliations: Department of Management, Economics and Industrial Engineering Politecnico di Milano Milano Italy; School of Industrial Engineering LIUC University Castellanza Italy; Institute for Studies on the Mediterranean (ISMed) National Research Council (CNR) Naples Italy
Abstract: ABSTRACT In fashion e‐commerce, about one in three orders is returned; however, firms keep offering free, fast returns driving these volumes even as they acknowledge the economic and environmental costs. Why do inefficient return practices persist? We argue that the answer is not a failure to optimize but a collective trap in which no single actor can afford to break away alone. Adopting a supply chain perspective and drawing on Extended Institutional Theory (EIT), through a qualitative multiple‐case study of Italian fashion e‐commerce firms, we examine how the interaction of legitimacy‐seeking and profit‐seeking logics across producers, retailers, and logistics and transport providers reproduces these practices. Upstream legitimacy‐driven decisions, aimed at maintaining high service levels, propagate downstream through contractual‐operational constraints, limiting the autonomy of logistics and transport providers. These interdependencies generate reinforcing decision‐making loops stabilizing dominant return practices, notwithstanding their inefficiencies. The study identifies outcome‐based imitation mechanisms, such as omnichannel return management, return consolidation, and differentiated return policies, as levers to disrupt these loops and enhance eco‐efficiency while maintaining legitimacy. The paper extends EIT to supply chain contexts and offers prescriptive insights. Practically, it highlights the need for sector‐based actions to rebalance legitimacy and profit motives for sustainable returns management.

Title: Supply chain complexity and innovation ambidexterity: Thresholds, role differentiation, and coordination regimes
Authors: Jingwei Xu, Fengwen Chen, Yinghua Shen
Abstract: Supply chain complexity reshapes firms’ innovation choices, yet its implications for innovation ambidexterity remain unclear. This study develops a biform game model to examine how complexity influences the balance between exploration and exploitation within and across firms. We show that complexity has a dual effect by expanding innovation opportunities while increasing coordination frictions. This trade-off generates threshold conditions under which within-firm ambidexterity becomes less sustainable and specialization becomes more attractive. Even so, the weakening of internal ambidexterity does not necessarily eliminate ambidexterity at the system level. Under heterogeneous participation conditions, role differentiation across firms can preserve an ambidextrous supply chain structure. We further show that coordination regimes, including standards, platforms, and integration investments, can mitigate frictions and shift these thresholds. Numerical analysis illustrates these patterns over a broader parameter range. The study extends research on innovation ambidexterity to complex interorganizational settings and offers implications for collaborative supply chain design.

Title: Strategy uniqueness and stock price crash risk
Authors: Xin Li, Zhenzhen Sun
Abstract: This paper examines how corporate strategy uniqueness influences stock price crash risk. Using portfolio analyses and panel regressions, we find that firms pursuing more unique strategies exhibit significantly lower crash risk. Channel analyses suggest that strategically unique firms face lower competitive pressure and weaker incentives to withhold bad news, thereby mitigating crash risk. Cross-sectional results further indicate that this negative relationship is stronger among firms with greater information asymmetry and weaker corporate governance. Overall, our findings provide important evidence on the role of corporate strategy in shaping firms’ downside tail risk.

Title: Travel time models incorporating zone boundaries in SBS/RSs with multiple shuttle carriers
Authors: Jingjing Yang, Ran Chen, Hu Yu
Abstract: Shuttle-based Storage and Retrieval Systems equipped with shuttle carriers (SBS/RS-SC) are an emerging alternative to traditional shuttle-based storage and retrieval systems. In SBS/RS-SC, storage racks are partitioned into multiple zones, each comprising several tiers and served by a dedicated shuttle carrier. Unlike conventional shuttles, these carriers can move horizontally and vertically simultaneously, enabling more efficient load transport within each zone. To evaluate the performance of this system, this paper develops closed-form travel time models for both single-command (SC) and dual-command (DC) operating modes. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the developed models approximate the discrete system with high accuracy, with deviations of less than 3.51%. Building on these validated models, a zone boundary optimization model is further proposed to determine the optimal rack partitioning that minimizes expected travel time. The optimization results show that the performance gap between optimal zoning and equal-sized zoning is less than 4.07% for the SC mode and 0.087% for the DC mode, indicating that simplified equal-sized zoning can provide near-optimal performance in practice. Furthermore, sensitivity analysis reveals diminishing returns to improvements in equipment speed, identifies a practical range for the shuttle speed ratio, and shows that the optimal rack layout depends strongly on the interaction between system kinematics and the shape factor. Finally, the framework is extended to incorporate system throughput, investment cost, class-based storage, and alternative dwell-point policies, thereby providing comprehensive decision support for SBS/RS-SC design and operation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Exploring joint travel-charging adaptation responses of battery electric vehicle users under varying weather conditions
Authors: Yueyi Yang, Xinghua Li, Don Mackenzie, Yuntao Guo
Abstract: Understanding how battery electric vehicle (BEV) users respond to adverse weather requires accounting for the interdependence between travel and charging decisions, as weather conditions directly influence battery efficiency, driving range, and charging availability, thereby constraining both mobility and energy replenishment. A two-stage analytical framework is proposed to investigate integrated travel–charging responses under varying situational contexts by jointly considering trip purpose, initial battery state of charge, and weather conditions, including temperature, wind, and rainfall. First, latent class analysis identifies four distinct joint response patterns—status quo maintenance, cautious adjustment, adaptive rescheduling, and protective withdrawal. Second, an interaction-extended integrated choice and latent variable model is estimated to examine how scenario attributes, sociodemographic characteristics, and latent psychological constructs shape response selection. The framework is implemented using a scenario-based stated adaptation experiment conducted in Shanghai, China, yielding 1,506 valid responses from private BEV owners. Results show that weather conditions systematically reshape joint responses through distinct but consistent patterns: rainfall and wind primarily induce protective or avoidance-oriented responses, temperature variations shift the balance between maintenance and adjustment, and extreme conditions generally increase non-status quo behaviors. Psychological factors further differentiate responses, with higher perceived risk and coping willingness increasing the likelihood of adaptation, while anticipatory preparedness reinforces status quo maintenance. The findings provide a behavioral evidence base for policymakers and charging-service operators to improve infrastructure resilience, operational guidance, and user-facing interventions in response to increasingly variable and uncertain weather conditions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Are telework and teleservices the solution for reducing traffic congestion and emissions? Findings from a comprehensive activity-based modeling analysis
Authors: Qinhua Jiang, Brian Yueshuai He, Qiao Yu, Yifang Zhu, Jiaqi Ma
Abstract: The telework and teleservices (Tele-X) are becoming increasingly popular with the development of Information and Communications Technologies, and the COVID-19 pandemic significantly changed the trend. As post-pandemic society increasingly embraces Tele-X and conducts more activities online, Tele-X's potential to alleviate congestion and reduce traffic-related emissions remains unclear. This study investigates the impacts of Tele-X adoption on travel behaviors and evaluates the potential to decrease Vehicle-Miles-Traveled (VMT) and emissions. We developed an integrated modeling framework that includes a hybrid survey, discrete choice models, dynamic travel demand and supply models, and environmental analysis. A case study focusing on Los Angeles (LA) County revealed that about 45% of workers telework at least once a week. However, the reduction in commuting trips is counterbalanced by an increase in non-work trips induced by the flexible schedules of telework, resulting in minor changes total daily activity numbers (+0.2%). The VMT decreases by 3.9% after the pandemic, accompanied by similar reductions in emissions: NOx by 2.1%, PM2.5 by 3.1%, and greenhouse gases by 3.1%. This indicates that Tele-X can be an effective mitigation strategy. Furthermore, a community-level analysis of the Westwood region in LA County shows that while further promotion of Tele-X could reduce local travel, it may induce more passing-by traffic, leading to higher emissions in sub-region.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: From announcement to operation: The changing impact of light rail transit on housing prices across implementation phases
Authors: Hisham Negm, Rodrigo Victoriano-Habit, Mylene Riva, Ahmed El-Geneidy
Abstract: New public transit infrastructure can significantly influence housing prices. While most studies examine impacts only after construction or compare a limited number of implementation phases, little is known about how transit-induced property value capitalization evolves dynamically throughout the implementation process. This study investigates the impact of Montreal’s new light rail project (the REM) on housing prices across four stages: announcement, construction, testing, and initial operation. The phased implementation of the REM also allows us to examine whether the operation of one branch generates anticipatory price effects along branches that remain under construction. Drawing on panel data of 14,711 residential property transactions over eleven years (from 2013 to 2023), we employ a natural experiment design through a difference-in-differences (DiD) approach to isolate the project’s net effect at different stages on housing prices. Our findings show that the four stages of REM implementation affect property values differently across catchment areas along operating and non-operating branches. The project announcement raised housing premiums within 800 m of some parts of the corridor, and this effect persisted throughout the construction period. REM-related premiums around the branch that underwent testing remained positive throughout the construction period. However, during testing and early operation, these gains were largely offset, possibly due to operational impacts such as noise and vibration. While premiums dissipated near the operating branch, properties along unopened branches remained stable or continued to appreciate compared to the rest of the region. By highlighting how home values evolve across different stages of implementation of large-scale transit investments, this study provides insights that can inform the design of Land Value Capture policies to capitalize on property gains while mitigating externalities.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Why do eligible individuals fail to enrol for social assistance programmes? A systematic narrative review of factors affecting take-up
Authors: Mariona Tres Vilanova
Abstract: Why do so many eligible individuals fail to sign up for government social assistance benefits? While non-take-up of social benefits is of great concern both for the effectiveness and equity of social policies, academics and policymakers continue to be puzzled by the lack of clarity on why people forgo increases in disposable income. Focusing on literature from the Global South, this review puts forward an analytical framework that identifies how structural conditions shape the context in which individual and institutional factors operate. Together, these interact to mitigate or exacerbate compliance, learning, and psychological costs as well as perceived relative benefits. Findings are synthesised around the three cost types. Overall, this review concludes that individual characteristics alone rarely explain non-take-up as their effects are moderated by the structural, programmatic and institutional conditions in which they operate. This helps explain why the literature often produces inconclusive or even contradictory findings regarding the determinants of take-up. These findings prompt further investigation into the structural conditions and programmatic and institutional factors that shape take-up gaps, and that policies aiming to close these gaps should consider.

Title: Heritage-sensitive interventions to support Indigenous peoples’ forest conservation: Evaluating an origin-label for highland produce in northern Thailand
Authors: Marco J. Haenssgen, Navaporn Sunanlikanon, Prasit Leepreecha, Mukdawan Sakboon, Putthida Kijdumnern, Giacomo Zanello, Daniele Asioli, Parichart Chawiwong, Pattarawadee Op-Ai, Inthanon Sutjathammawong, Phatsakorn Kiatsuntikun, Peter Petkoff, Anne Hertzog, Elizabeth Auclair, Ivo Vlaev
Abstract: Global conservation policies increasingly recognize the vital role of local and Indigenous communities in ecosystem protection, but mechanisms to support such communities’ livelihoods in a conservation context remain limited. Based on participatory engagement with diverse highland communities in the northern Thai tropics, we co-designed a highland origin label with the intention to alleviate Indigenous livelihood pressures. This study assessed whether this label can positively influence downstream urban consumers’ willingness-to-pay for Indigenous highland communities’ produce, using cross-sectional, qualitative, and choice experimental data. The study was implemented between February and April 2025 across four urban markets in Chiang Mai City, Thailand, including actual buying decisions for strawberries and chayote fruits and experimental exposure to background information on Indigenous highland livelihoods. The results from 888 real-market consumers revealed a substantial willingness-to-pay premium for origin-labelled products, with +11.6 Thai Baht/+56.3% on average (chayote: +10.4 Thai Baht/+50.0%; strawberries: +12.6 Thai Baht, +61.1%). Higher willingness-to-pay was positively associated with prior experience of purchasing labelled products and interest in Indigenous rights, negatively with price-conscious shoppers, and not associated with exposure to livelihood information. Large classes of shoppers (at least 75.9%) exhibited high utility for the origin label. Qualitative responses indicated strong positive sentiment and label credibility, although with a risk of overinterpretation. We conclude that co-developed origin labels can elicit substantial consumer willingness-to-pay, but translating it into tangible support for Indigenous livelihoods would require further considerations of agricultural value chain optimisation, cooperative support, channels for direct and consumer-segment-specific marketing, and tackling problematic Indigenous stereotypes.

Title: Centralized and competitive extraction of distributed renewable resources on networks with nonlinear aggregate growth
Authors: Filippo de Feo, Giorgio Fabbri, Silvia Faggian, Giuseppe Freni
Abstract: We study the optimal and strategic extraction of a renewable resource that is spatially distributed over a network, migrates across nodes (with no loss of biomass during transit), and evolves according to a nonlinear (concave) aggregate growth function. A subset of nodes hosts extractors, while the remaining ones serve as reserves. We analyze a centralized planner's problem and a non-cooperative game with stationary Markov strategies. For three canonical growth families (logistic, power, and log-type saturating laws) paired with corresponding utilities, we derive closed-form value functions and feedback rules for the planner, and we construct a symmetric Markov equilibrium for the game on strongly connected networks.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Corrigendum to “The impact of financial stress, governance, and geopolitics on Europe's energy transition mineral trade” [Energy Economics, 146 (2025) 108523].
Authors: Oleg Mariev, Md. Monirul Islam
Abstract: A brief replication package was originally submitted with the paper. It has now been expanded to enable exact reproduction of the results, as verified by the authors and the editor-in-chief. The authors gratefully acknowledge the journal's initiative in encouraging authors to provide detailed replication packages.Supplementary materialSupplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eneco.2026.109533.

Title: Total cost of ownership for CO2 carriers under alternative fuel price uncertainty
Authors: Kyunghwa Kim, Wook Kim
Abstract: As environmental regulations become more stringent, the maritime industry faces increasing pressure to make informed decisions on alternative fuels and power systems amid substantial uncertainty in fuel costs and regulatory shifts. This study develops a techno-economic assessment framework for a CO 2 carrier operating under stringent phased European Union (EU)’s environmental regulations. Economic dispatch analysis combined with Monte Carlo simulation evaluates three conventional genset systems and six alternative-fueled fuel cell (FC) systems. This study adopts the mean and the 95% value at risk (VaR 95% ) of the total cost of ownership (TCO) as comparative metrics. The results indicate that the blue liquid hydrogen (b-LH 2 ) FC system achieves the lowest mean TCO and VaR 95% , while the electro-methanol (e-MeOH) FC system has the highest in both metrics. Notably, VaR 95% rankings differ from those based on mean TCO, underscoring the importance of risk-based evaluation. This framework supports risk-aware investment decisions for shipowners facing market volatility.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Direct and indirect impacts of road networks on vegetation cover
Authors: Ziheng Huang, Qingjie Fu, Huixin Lin, Jingyang Liu, Lanyi Zhang, Min Wu, Xisheng Hu
Abstract: Road expansion balances socio-economic growth with ecological threats to vegetation cover, yet quantifying and comparing direct and indirect effects remains a challenge. This study analyzes road-vegetation dynamics (2015–2023) in Fujian, China’s first Ecological Civilization Pilot Zone, using a direct/indirect impact framework coupled with geospatial explainable artificial intelligence (Geo-XAI). Results show rising road density alongside slight vegetation recovery. Direct impact exhibits a strong negative linear correlation with road density, governed by nighttime light in cities and population density in rural areas. In contrast, indirect impact is predominantly positive, nonlinear and spatially heterogeneous, primarily governed mainly by land use intensity. Nonlinear thresholds exist nighttime light intensifies direct losses above 35 but promotes indirect gains only above 60.5; population density exacerbates direct impact up to ∼ 5,070 persons/km2, while supporting indirect benefits only below ∼ 1,270 persons/km2. The findings underscore the need for spatially targeted, pathway-specific management to harmonize infrastructure and conservation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: A multiobjective framework for optimising Home Health Care districts
Authors: William Emiliano, Maria do Sameiro Carvalho, Lino Costa, Vitor Eduardo Molina Junior, Géremi Gilson Dranka, José Telhada
Affiliations: School of Technology, University of Campinas; ALGORITMI Research Center, School of Engineering, University of Minho; Federal University of Technology
Abstract: Home health care (HHC) services provide a practical alternative to traditional healthcare, especially in ageing populations, where demand for home-based medical care is rising. However, ensuring equitable and efficient service delivery poses significant logistical challenges, including balancing workload, minimising travel distances, and maintaining district contiguity. This study presents a novel multiobjective optimisation model to address the districting problem in HHC, through real-world data from Portugal. The proposed simultaneously optimises service efficiency, workload distribution, and geographic compactness while preserving district contiguity. The results demonstrated significant improvements with reductions in travel distances ranging from 10% to 40% and workload deviation minimised by up to 100%, leading to more balanced and operationally efficient districting plans. Additionally, it successfully preserved district contiguity, a crucial aspect for the practical implementation of districting solutions. The model adaptability across various scenarios underscores its potential as a decision-support tool for healthcare administrators, establishing a new benchmark for optimising HHC service planning and improving healthcare accessibility across different geographical contexts.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: The role of sufficiency in aligning European sovereignty and sustainability in the lithium value chain
Authors: Pauline Bucciarelli, Vincent D’Herbemont
Abstract: The transition towards low-carbon and digital technologies is set to profoundly reshape metals markets, particularly those required for battery manufacturing. Amid growing geoeconomic fragmentation, this shift is accelerating the implementation of public policies aimed at securing supply and strengthening the resilience of strategic technology value chains. In the European Union, the recently adopted Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA) aims to ensure secure and sustainable access to critical raw materials. By integrating the entire lithium value chain into an Integrated Assessment Model, we analyse the interplay between lithium supply, demand, and recycling within decarbonisation scenarios. Our findings suggest significant challenges in meeting the CRMA reshoring targets without reducing industrial demand. We show that sufficiency strategies could help achieve these benchmarks, while cutting European lithium imports by at least 44% between 2030 and 2050 and reducing cumulative final demand by 1.2 Mt, a 46% decrease relative to current policy trajectories. Beyond securing supply, sufficiency reduces the energy footprint of the lithium chain, improves spatial extractive justice, and strengthens overall robustness under uncertainty. Integrating sufficiency into Europe’s material security framework offers a pathway to more closely align strategic autonomy with sustainability objectives.

Title: Residential relocation decisions under sea level rise and incentives from insurance: A discrete choice experiment study of France
Authors: Moongyeom Kim, Sem Duijndam, Jeroen C.J.H. Aerts, Jens de Bruijn, Veronica Lupi, W.J. Wouter Botzen
Abstract: This study examines household preferences for staying versus relocating under future coastal flood risk in metropolitan France, using a discrete choice experiment. By embedding Protection Motivation Theory (PMT) into a mixed logit framework, we account for both economic and cognitive drivers of residential decision making.
