To address inconsistent preferences in the group, we introduce measures of support and opposition that help identify and adjust conflicting information. When decision-makers agree to revise their inputs to achieve consistency, the recommended alternative is identified through three complementary procedures: (i) a representative compatible value function, (ii) net flow scores from the necessary preference relation graph, and (iii) extreme ranking analysis. If consistency cannot be reached, the recommended alternative is determined by the rank-acceptability indices derived for individual decision-makers using stochastic multiobjective acceptability analysis. An illustrative case involving the multiple-criteria evaluation of teachers by a committee of experts demonstrates the feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed method.

Title: Worker skills, firm dynamics, and productivity
Authors: İlhan Güner, Christian Siegel
Abstract: We develop a general equilibrium model of firm dynamics with multiple labour skills to analyse the productivity implications of skill shortages. Firms employ cognitive, interpersonal, and manual skills in both operational and overhead tasks, with sectoral variation in skill intensities, and within sector firm size heterogeneity due to idiosyncratic technology draws. Calibrated to UK data, the model reveals that cognitive skills are a binding constraint on productivity. A reduction in the supply of cognitive skills lowers labour productivity at all levels – firms, sectors, and in the aggregate. About half of the sectoral effects are due to changes in the within-sector distribution, whereby larger firms grow in relative size but become less productive. Sectoral heterogeneity in skill intensities amplifies these effects.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Relative income and global inequality: Evidence from the United Kingdom
Authors: Anca Balietti, Diego Marino Fages
Abstract: This paper provides a direct replication of Fehr et al. (2022), who examine whether information about individuals’ position in the global income distribution affects preferences over global inequality. Whereas the original study draws on a representative sample from Germany, we analyze a broadly representative UK sample ( N = 2116 ). UK respondents underestimate their global rank by about 2.4 deciles on average, yet randomly providing accurate rank information has no detectable effect on real-stakes donations to international anti-poverty NGOs or on policy attitudes toward global redistribution, international organizations, globalization, or immigration. The estimated average treatment effects are small, close to zero, and precisely estimated. A data-driven heterogeneity analysis reveals no sizable or systematic differences in subgroup responses. Overall, the results reinforce the evidence that correcting global income misperceptions alone is unlikely to shift preferences over global inequality in the European settings studied so far.

Title: Co-exportation of products by multi-product firms
Authors: Peter H. Egger, Corinne L. Jones, Leandro Navarro
Abstract: The attention on multi-product firms has focused primarily on firms’ product scope, i.e., how many products firms sell, rather than on which products they co-produce and sell. We address this by developing a stochastic heterogeneous-firm model that allows for correlations in production efficiencies across products and in consumers’ tastes across products and destinations. Our estimation strategy centers on a novel extension of generalized score matching. We use Chinese export data for the leather sector. The estimates reveal a clustered co-exportation structure consistent with correlated efficiency shocks across products sharing similar production processes.

Title: Minority Protection in Voting Mechanisms — Experimental Evidence
Authors: Dirk Engelmann, Hans Peter Grüner, Timo Hoffmann, Alex Possajennikov
Abstract: Under simple majority voting an absolute majority of voters may choose policies that are harmful to minorities. It is the purpose of sub- and super-majority rules to protect legitimate minority interests. We study how voting rules are chosen under the veil of ignorance. In our experiment, individuals choose voting rules for given distributions of gains and losses that can arise from a policy, but before learning their own valuation of the policy. We find that subjects on average adjust the voting rule in line with the skewness of the distribution. As a result, a higher share of the achievable surplus can be extracted with the suggested rules than with exogenously given simple majority voting. While the rule choices are not significantly biased towards underor overprotection of the minority, towards majority voting or towards status-quo preserving rules, they only imperfectly reflect the distributions of benefits and costs.

Title: The impact of environmental regulation on clean innovation: Are there crowding out effects?
Authors: Nicola Benatti, Martin Groiss, Petra Kelly, Paloma Lopez-Garcia
Abstract: We examine the extent to which environmental regulation affects innovation and which policy types provide the strongest incentives to innovate. Using a local projection framework, we estimate the regulatory impact on patenting activity over a five-year horizon. As a proxy for environmental policy exposure, we estimate firm-level greenhouse gas emissions using a machine learning algorithm. At the country-level, policy tightening is largely associated with no statistically significant change in environmental technology innovation. At the firm-level, however, environmental policy tightening leads to higher innovation activity in technologies mitigating climate change, while the effect on innovation in other technologies is muted. This suggests that environmental regulation does not lead to a crowding-out of non-clean innovations. The policy type matters, as increasing the stringency of technology support policies and non-market based policies leads to increases in clean technology patenting, while we do not find a statistically significant impact of market-based policies.

Title: Grid connection costs as a barrier to new generation: Evidence from PJM and implications for transmission policy
Authors: Sarah Johnston, Yifei Liu, Chenyu Yang
Abstract: Meeting projected growth in electricity demand and climate goals will require building new electricity generators. The grid connection process is seen as a key constraint on this development. We collect new data on grid connection costs for PJM, the largest regional grid operator in the United States. We geographically match these costs to transmission spending to study their determinants. Using regression analysis, we find that these costs, and especially the network upgrade portion, are difficult to predict: generators with similar characteristics can have very different costs. We also find that planned generators with high network upgrade costs are much more likely to be canceled. Finally, prior transmission spending by the grid operator is associated with lower network upgrade costs for connecting generators. These findings emphasize the critical role of transmission capacity in expanding electricity generation capacity.

Title: The natural level of oil prices
Authors: Daniel Cuzzi, João Victor Issler
Abstract: This paper makes two original contributions. First, it introduces the concept of the natural level of oil prices, defined as the real price consistent with long-run supply and demand fundamentals in the absence of transitory shocks. Based on a cointegration framework linking oil prices to global industrial production, OPEC production, and non-OPEC production, the natural level provides a long-run anchor for oil prices, distinguishing temporary dislocations from permanent changes in oil markets.Second, splitting oil production between OPEC and non-OPEC producers in cointegration analysis is essential for identifying the natural level of oil prices, since their respective long-run impact on oil prices is not homogeneous.Empirical evidence indicates that transitory deviations from the natural level typically dissipate within 18–24 months. When we evaluate the out-of-sample forecasting performance of the proposed framework against the random walk, Hodrick–Prescott and Hamilton filters, and futures prices, the cointegration-based error-correction model consistently delivers the most accurate medium-term forecasts, reducing RMSE and MAE by 13%–22% relative to the random walk at 12–24-month horizons. We also derive a tractable decomposition of the oil risk premium as a function of the gap between observed and natural prices, showing how the natural level shapes expectations through the futures term structure.The proposed framework helps policymakers to distinguish persistent from transitory oil-price movements. It also provides investors and energy-market firms with a benchmark for assessing commodity-price risks, investment decisions, and long-term capital planning.

Title: Energy flexibility procurement strategy in competitive demand response markets: Dual-channel supply chain perspective
Authors: Xinyue Fei, Cheng Lyu, Yibo Ding
Abstract: The Demand Response (DR) market is crucial for smart grids to procure energy flexibility, thereby achieving supply–demand balance. This paper establishes a game-theoretic framework for dual-channel flexibility procurement in the DR market, where a grid operator (GO) procures load flexibility from energy consumers (ECs) both directly (the direct channel) and through the service provider (SP) (the wholesale channel). We examine the strategic interaction between the two channels and show that introducing the direct channel can mitigate double marginalization in the incumbent wholesale channel, thereby improving total channel surplus. Under certain channel cost conditions, the direct channel even benefits its competitor, the SP. We also unravel the strategic role of the direct channel as a credible threat: when channel costs are moderate, it disciplines the SP’s behaviors even though it is inactive. The equilibrium is further validated in a case study. The results show that dual-channel procurement expands the DR market by over 60% when channel costs are low, and can increase the SP profits by 28%, and improve the social welfare at a probability of 54.41%.

Title: When closer is not better: travel well-being among peri-urban older adults
Authors: Panyu Peng, Yibin Ao, Yangxi Lv, Mingyang Li, Hao Zhu
Abstract: Transportation-related subjective well-being captures emotions and satisfaction during travel and is increasingly used to evaluate the social benefits of transport and spatial policies. Using survey data from older adults in peri-urban Chengdu, China, we examine the associations of objective accessibility, perceived built-environment quality, perceived accessibility, and mobility capability with travel well-being and overall well-being. This study combines structural equation modeling, explainable machine learning, and robust interaction regressions to examine structural pathways, nonlinear patterns, and conditional associations. Perceived built-environment quality and mobility capability are positively associated with travel well-being, which is, in turn, positively associated with overall well-being. By contrast, higher objective accessibility is associated with lower travel well-being on average. This negative association tends to weaken at higher levels of perceived built-environment quality and mobility capability. The findings suggest that improvements in proximity alone may be insufficient and should be accompanied by safe, comfortable, continuous, predictable, and barrier-free walking conditions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Editorial Board
Substituting storage for transmission: Implications for renewable energy
Authors: J. Scott Holladay, Ben Meadows, Tim Roberson, Charles Sims
Abstract: We analyze the potential for electricity storage to substitute for transmission capacity. We develop a spatial-dynamic model of the grid where a utility manager dispatches generators and batteries to serve load at the lowest possible cost. The addition of storage requires the manager to optimize charging and discharging across the day, making the problem dynamic. We identify general conditions under which transmission and storage can serve as substitutes. When transmission is constrained and the battery is being charged or discharged, storage and transmission are substitutes at that instant. The investment-relevant capacity value depends on the aggregation of these instantaneous scarcity values across all hours of the day: storage substitutes for transmission investment when additional storage capacity reduces the time-averaged shadow value of the transmission constraint. This suggests storage can serve as transmission in markets where transmission is frequently constrained and the battery rarely sits idle. We calibrate our model to the electric grid in Texas and show that transmission and storage are substitutes even when wind generation is curtailed. The ability to substitute storage for transmission enables utilities to forgo costly and contentious grid expansion projects.
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: Algorithmic wage setting on online labor platforms
Authors: Herbert Dawid, Philipp Harting, Michael Neugart
Abstract: Online digital labor platforms are increasingly important as tools for matching employers and workers. They reduce labor market frictions and provide the opportunity for remote work, but concerns have been raised about whether workers receive adequate incomes. We study how the use of machine-learning based algorithms for the determination of wage offers affects workers’ wages on online labor platforms by setting up a simulation framework and analyzing outcomes under different assumptions about platform and algorithm design. Firms use reinforcement-learning to update posted wages on the platform, and heterogeneous workers send applications based on the posted information. We show that, if firms use a deep Q-network (DQN), a state-of-the-art machine learning algorithm, collusive wages emerge when the number of competitors is small, and no experience replay is used. Our findings are robust across many features of the model, including the design of the online labor platform.

Title: Gay varsity: Subject choices, grades, and early careers for UK LGB university students
Authors: Jefferson Frank, Alexander Vickery
Abstract: Using data on UK students attending university from 2012 – 2020, we look at how LGB students differ from their heterosexual counterparts. LGB men and women both have large shifts towards Humanities subjects, and away from LEM (law, economics, management) and STEM. Gay and bisexual men do well in degree outcomes in the Humanities, and about the same as heterosexual men in other subjects. Lesbian and bisexual women do about the same as heterosexual women in the Humanities and poorly in other subjects. Male and female LGB students suffer in salaries in their early career.

Title: Editorial Board
Leverage constraints and bank monitoring: Bank regulation versus monetary policy
Authors: Florian Böser, Hans Gersbach, Sebastian Zelzner
Abstract: Bank leverage constraints can arise from regulatory capital requirements or from central bank collateral requirements in reserve lending. We compare these two policy channels within the so-called “bank money creation” approach. We show that monetary policy via collateral requirements leads to a novel and unique collateral leverage channel . Through this channel, banks facing liquidity constraints can expand loan supply and deposit issuance by raising the collateral value of their loans, which they achieve through tighter loan monitoring. The collateral leverage channel can improve welfare beyond standard bank capital regulation and inform the design of central bank collateral frameworks.

Title: Stochastic supplier selection and order allocation: A conditional value at risk approach
Authors: Nitin Sahu, Garima Mittal
Affiliations: Decision Sciences Area, Indian Institute of Management Lucknow
Abstract: In the current business landscape, global supply chain networks are becoming increasingly unpredictable and are focused on risk management. The supplier selection process within a supply chain network is inherently exposed to various risks, and it is essential to minimise these risks and the associated potential losses. This study focuses on modelling risk within the supplier selection process. Thus leading to more informed supply chain procurement decisions. Specifically, the study proposes a bi-objective, risk-averse supplier portfolio model based on Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR), a key financial risk management measure. The proposed model aims to optimise the supplier risks in the worst-case scenario corresponding to critical parameters like total procurement cost, supplier quality level, and supplier service levels. Additionally, the proposed model addresses operational uncertainty in supplier parameters using a chance-constrained approach. The proposed methodology is validated through a numerical illustration that demonstrates the practical applicability of the model. Further, the sensitivity analysis is performed through the computational experimental design to assess the robustness of the proposed model and the solution approach. Results demonstrate that the CVaR-based modelling approach effectively addresses the downside risk associated with service and quality objectives while accounting for operational uncertainties in the supplier selection process.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Beyond the supply chain: digital ecosystem orchestration to advance circular strategies for food waste
Authors: Mutala Mohammed Fuseini, Madeleine Pullman, Maneesh Kumar, Vasco Sanchez Rodrigues, Laura Purvis
Affiliations: Cardiff University Cardiff Business School, , Cardiff; Portland State University Department of Business, , Portland; Cardiff University Department of Business, , Cardiff; Cardiff University Department of Logistics and Operations Management, , Cardiff
Abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how digital platforms enable orchestration across circular food supply network ecosystems to support food waste reduction. Focusing on ecosystem-level coordination rather than individual firms or dyadic relationships, the study explores how digital platforms facilitate the orchestration of actors, resources and circular practices across interconnected organisations. Design/methodology/approach An embedded single-case study of a UK food supply network ecosystem was studied. The ecosystem comprised six embedded sub-cases involving 27 organisations across hospitality and food service, food technology, food supply, food charities, food upcycling and recycling and policy influencers. Semi-structured interviews and secondary data were analysed. Findings The study highlights how digital platforms enable circular food waste reduction through orchestration across supply network ecosystem partners. The findings reveal three interconnected mechanisms of digital platform orchestration: digital coordination, capability redistribution and legitimacy alignment, which collectively enable actors to synchronise actions, share capabilities and institutionalise circular practices across the ecosystem. Originality/value This empirical study enriches the supply chain literature by extending the focus on circular food waste reduction from a firm-level capability perspective to an ecosystem-level orchestration process. The findings reveal three recursive mechanisms of digital platform orchestration – digital coordination, capability redistribution and legitimacy alignment – that explain how interconnected actors collectively enable and institutionalise circular practices across food supply network ecosystems.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: Energy-efficient lot-sizing in grid-connected production with on-site renewables and limited energy storage
Authors: Stephan Köppel, Florian Sahling
Abstract: Abstract Sustainable energy technologies and efficient energy usage are important drivers for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. The manufacturing industry, with its high energy consumption, is particularly important. Integrated energy-oriented production planning becomes essential with the adoption of on-site renewable energy technologies such as photovoltaics, wind power, hydropower, and energy storage systems. However, energy-oriented planning approaches, particularly in terms of lot-sizing, are limited. Hence, we present a novel energy-oriented dynamic lot-sizing model for multiple products in a capacity-restricted production system. Decentralized renewable energy sources supply energy, which can be stored temporarily in an energy storage system. Connections to the national power grid and energy trading are included, assuming that power generation and energy prices are known. The model aims to minimize inventory, setup, and energy costs. Numerical results highlight the superiority of our model in terms of solvability over a model formulation based on the PLSP presented by Liao and Gicquel (2024). Furthermore, we explore strategies to improve the lower and upper bounds of the monolithic model. The proposed hybrid matheuristic, which combines a Fix-and-Optimize heuristic with local branching, achieves high solution quality. Comparisons with traditional (consecutive) planning approaches underscore the benefits of energy-oriented lot-sizing, including better utilization of renewable energy and cost reductions of up to 19%. These findings demonstrate the potential for significant economic and environmental benefits through integrated energy-oriented production planning.

Title: Strategic Bonding Curves in Automated Market Makers
Authors: Álvaro Cartea, Fayçal Drissi, Leandro Sánchez-Betancourt, David Šiška, Łukasz Szpruch
Affiliations: Mathematical Institute, University of Oxford, Oxford OX2 6ED, United Kingdom; and Oxford-Man Institute of Quantitative Finance, University of Oxford, Oxford OX2 6ED, United Kingdom; Oxford-Man Institute of Quantitative Finance, University of Oxford, Oxford OX2 6ED, United Kingdom; School of Mathematics, University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh EH9 3FD, United Kingdom
Abstract: The bonding curves of decentralized exchanges (DEXs) define with mathematical formulae the relationship between liquidity supply and prices. Most DEXs use the bonding curves of constant function markets (CFMs) to clear the supply and demand of liquidity. At present, liquidity providers (LPs) operate at a loss in CFMs on average. We generalize CFMs and introduce decentralized liquidity pools (DLPs), which provide LPs with the tools to design dynamic bonding curves according to strategic preferences. In DLPs, impact functions encode how orders affect prices, and quote functions determine the price of liquidity. To illustrate the strategic flexibility of DLPs, we develop models for bonding curves when prices form across multiple venues, within the DLP, or in a competing venue. In fragmented markets, the DLP estimates the fundamental price from the trading flow to adjust the bonding curve and reduce arbitrage losses. Our models may be used as hooks in Uniswap v4 when the DLP’s impact functions are the constant product function.

Title: Decoupled Functional Central Limit Theorems for Two-Timescale Stochastic Approximation
Authors: Yuze Han, Xiang Li, Jiadong Liang, Zhihua Zhang
Affiliations: Center for Applied Statistics and School of Statistics, Renmin University of China, Haidian District, Beijing 100872, Peoples Republic of China; School of Mathematical Sciences, Peking University, Haidian District, Beijing 100871, Peoples Republic of China
Abstract: In two-timescale stochastic approximation (SA), two iterates are updated at different rates, governed by distinct step sizes, with each update influencing the other. Previous studies demonstrate that the convergence rates of the error terms for these updates depend solely on their respective step sizes, a property known as decoupled convergence. However, a functional version of this decoupled convergence has not been explored. Our work fills this gap by establishing decoupled functional central limit theorems for two-timescale SA, offering a more precise characterization of its asymptotic behavior. Our results show that, on each timescale, the limiting dynamic has the same form as in standard SA, and the coupling between the two iterates enters the limit only through the associated coefficients. To achieve these results, we leverage the martingale problem approach and establish tightness as a crucial intermediate step. Furthermore, to address the interdependence between different timescales, we introduce an innovative auxiliary sequence to eliminate the primary influence of the fast timescale update on the slow timescale update. Funding: This research was supported by the National Key Research and Development Program of China [Grant 2022YFA1004002], and the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 12501417 and 12350001]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/moor.2025.0876 .

Title: Strongly Connected Orientations and Integer Lattices
Authors: Ahmad Abdi, Gérard Cornuéjols, Siyue Liu, Olha Silina
Affiliations: Department of Mathematics, The London School of Economics and Political Science, London WC2A 2AE, United Kingdom; Tepper School of Business, Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania 15213; Mathematical Sciences, Mellon College of Science, Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania 15213
Abstract: Let [Formula: see text] be a digraph whose underlying undirected graph is two-edge connected, and let P be the polytope whose vertices are the incidence vectors of arc sets whose reversal makes D strongly connected. We study the lattice-theoretic properties of the integer points contained in a proper face F of P not contained in [Formula: see text] for any [Formula: see text]. We prove under a mild necessary condition that [Formula: see text] contains an integral basis B (i.e., B is linearly independent) and any integral vector in the linear hull of F is an integral linear combination of B. This result is surprising as the integer points in F do not necessarily form a Hilbert basis. In proving the result, we develop a theory similar to matching theory for degree-constrained dijoins in bipartite digraphs. Our result has consequences for head-disjoint strong orientations in hypergraphs and also, to a famous conjecture by Woodall that the minimum size of a dicut of D, say [Formula: see text], is equal to the maximum number of disjoint dijoins. We prove a relaxation of this conjecture by finding for any prime number [Formula: see text], a p-adic packing of dijoins of value [Formula: see text] and of support size at most [Formula: see text]. We also prove that the all-ones vector belongs to the lattice generated by [Formula: see text], where F is the face of P satisfying [Formula: see text] for every dicut [Formula: see text] with minimum size. Funding: This research was supported by the Office of Naval Research [Grant N00014-22-1-2528] and the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council [Grant EP/X030989/1].

Title: When wages rise, quality falls: Minimum wages and the hidden trade-off in competitive e-commerce markets
Authors: Xinyu Liu, Han Xiao, Songqing Jin
Abstract: We show that product and service quality serve as a hidden margin of adjustment to minimum wage hikes in hyper-competitive digital markets. Leveraging granular transaction data from 2628 Tmall stores in rural China from 2015 to 2020, combined with household surveys and firm-level data, we exploit staggered city-level minimum wage increases and find that in the short run, firms neither reduce employment nor significantly raise prices. Instead, they systematically degrade quality, as evidenced by worse product ratings, slower logistics, and poorer customer service, starting within two quarters and persisting over time. The reduction in intermediate inputs compromises product quality, while cuts to outsourced IT services undermine service quality by weakening operational efficiency. Crucially, this decline is driven by high-quality incumbents, whereas low-quality firms show no change but are more likely to exit the market following the shock. These results reveal a trade-off between labor income and consumer welfare, a cost that is invisible in traditional labor market evaluations but central to a complete welfare assessment.

Title: Optimal investment and fair sharing rules of incentives in virtual renewable energy communities
Authors: Almendra Awerkin, Paolo Falbo, Tiziano Vargiolu
Abstract: Abstract This paper examines two interconnected challenges in Renewable Energy Communities (REC) optimization: investment in renewable technologies and equitable sharing of incentives, usually offered by a central authority. Focusing on a REC under the so-called virtual framework and composed of a household and a biogas producer — common in rural and urban contexts — we analyze how investment decisions and incentive-sharing mechanisms impact community profitability and self-consumption. The household invests in photovoltaic panels to reduce energy purchases and monetize surplus generation, while the biogas producer either converts biogas into electricity or sells it on the gas market. We model this interaction as a leader-follower problem: an administrator (leader) defines the incentive-sharing rule, while a household and a biogas producer (followers) determine their optimal investments. Modeling the objective of the leader as a Nash bargaining problem and a Nash equilibrium for the followers’ static game, we provide model-based insights into efficient REC design and policy implications for fostering sustainable community energy systems. The model is applied to this stylized case of a REC, under realistic data about the random variables and investment costs. We obtain structural insights into how specific incentive policies and members’ investment decisions interact within this specialized configuration, highlighting trade-offs that can guide the strategic organization of similar community energy frameworks.

Title: Competitive pricing and cooperation mode strategies on E-commerce platforms with reference price effect
Authors: Ningning Wang, Jing Li, Lin Wei
Abstract: Manufacturers are increasingly inclined to distribute products through multiple e-commerce platforms simultaneously. This trend provides strategic consumers with more opportunities to compare retail prices across different platforms, thereby generating a reference price effect. The manufacturer may cooperate with each platform under either an agency mode or a reselling mode. Besides, a uniform pricing or a differentiated pricing can be adopted. Motivated by this emerging practice, this paper investigates the competitive pricing and cooperation mode strategies by considering reference price effect. We focus on a platform-based supply chain comprising one manufacturer and two e-commerce platforms. The results indicate that: (i) From the perspective of manufacturer and platform profits, differentiated pricing is more preferable with unilateral reference price effect while uniform pricing can conditionally dominate differentiated pricing with cross reference price effect. (ii) A strong reference price effect can aggravate double marginalization under mode (R, A) but alleviate it under mode (A, R). Besides, it can mitigate platforms’ price competition between platforms with a low commission rate. (iii) When the commission rate is moderate, both reference price effect and platform competition jointly determine cooperation modes strategy. (iv) There exists a triple-win situation for the platform supply chain members. Our extended models indicate that the main findings are robust.

Title: Complementarity, congestion and information design in epidemics with strategic social behaviour
Authors: Davide Bosco, Luca Portoghese
Abstract: In the context of an epidemic where the risk of death post-infection depends on demography and social behaviour, this paper characterises how the degree of congestibility of the social environment and the public/private nature of the available information about health states jointly affect the strategic social distancing of demographically heterogeneous agents. Key result is that the joint presence of congestibility and private information is necessary and sufficient for social-distancing decisions to be strategic complements. Strategic substitutability ensues in every other case. Within the limits of the proposed model, the analysis provides a sound theoretical rationale for the heterogeneity in the results provided by the extant literature on the issue. Implications ensue for optimal information design. First: limiting private information (e.g. by forbidding self-tests) is always socially optimal. Second: if private information cannot be limited, the second-best policy crucially depends on environmental congestibility: with high congestibility, providing the maximum extent of public information (e.g. via mass screening campaigns) is desirable, whereas the converse is true with low congestibility.

Title: Collaborative multi-depot vehicle routing problem with time windows, split delivery, and uncertain demands
Authors: Yong Wang, Mengyuan Gou, Siyu Luo, Lu Zhen, Xiuling Hei
Abstract: With the rapid development of e-commerce and information technology, customers can add, cancel, or restore orders in real time, and an order can contain multiple incompatible types of commodities that need to be split for delivery. The increasingly uncertain and diverse customer demands have driven a shift from single-depot to multi-depot urban logistics networks. By systematically analyzing the various service area configurations in the multi-depot network, this study rigorously demonstrates that multi-depot collaboration can reduce delivery costs for customers requiring split deliveries. Then, a collaborative multi-depot vehicle routing problem with time windows, split delivery, and uncertain demands (CMDVRPTW-SDUD) is proposed and investigated. To reduce the frequency of vehicle route adjustments during service, the working day is divided into consecutive time slices, transforming CMDVRPTW-SDUD into a series of temporally segmented sub-problems. A time-slice-based mathematical model is formulated to minimize the total operating cost and the number of second-echelon vehicles. An improved K -means++ clustering algorithm is integrated with a multi-objective jellyfish search algorithm with genetic operations (MOJS-GO) to solve the model. The MOJS-GO incorporates a population evolution mechanism and a local search operator to balance convergence speed and solution quality adaptively. An uncertain demand response strategy is designed to address the temporal variability of customer requests, while a vehicle resource sharing strategy reallocates idle second-echelon vehicles to improve utilization. The performance of the proposed method is benchmarked against the CPLEX solver, multi-objective particle swarm optimization, multi-objective difference evolution, and non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II. A real-world case from Chongqing City, China, is used to validate the model and algorithm. Comparative analyses across varying uncertain demand response methods, time slice lengths, reserved second-echelon vehicle loading proportions, and algorithm ablation experiments confirm the robustness of the approach. By jointly considering split deliveries due to incompatible items and real-time demand variation, this study offers a practical solution for building cost-efficient, resource-optimized, and flexible multi-depot transport systems in uncertain environments.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: TrajCleaner: An end-to-end framework for systematic cleaning and completing vessel trajectory data
Authors: Huimin Qiang, Wenlong Niu, Xiaodong Peng, Huanhuan Li
Abstract: Reliable vessel trajectory data are fundamental for maritime situational awareness and intelligent port management, yet Automatic Identification System (AIS) records frequently suffer from drift errors, temporal gaps, and fragmented sequences. Existing studies on AIS trajectory cleaning and gap completion remain limited by fragmented workflows, weak integration between detection and completion, and insufficient adaptivity across heterogeneous maritime environments. To address these challenges, this paper proposes TrajCleaner, a systematic end-to-end framework for trajectory anomaly detection, repair, and event-based completion. This framework integrates adaptive multi-feature detection to identify missing or abnormal segments across diverse vessel types and port operational regimes. A multi-factor weighted similarity mechanism enables robust candidate retrieval, while a spatio-temporal joint completion strategy enforces port-specific navigational constraints and performs density-aware temporal allocation to ensure behavioral plausibility. Unlike prior approaches that treat drift correction, gap detection, and interpolation as independent tasks, TrajCleaner provides a unified pipeline from anomaly recognition to event-level trajectory completion. Experiments using AIS data from the port of Los Angeles (LA) demonstrate that TrajCleaner substantially enhances detection accuracy, completion fidelity, and temporal realism compared with state-of-the-art baselines. By generating eventized and behaviorally coherent vessel trajectories, TrajCleaner improves the analytical depth of downstream maritime applications, including vessel behavior profiling, port operational efficiency assessment, and channel and berth planning. These capabilities provide a more reliable data foundation for predictive, adaptive, and decision-support systems in next-generation smart ports, ultimately strengthening maritime safety, operational efficiency, and environmental sustainability.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: A logic-based Benders decomposition algorithm for anchor position allocation problem
Authors: Baoli Liu, Fan Zhang, Di Wu, Xiaotian Zhuang, Zhongshuai Wang
Abstract: An imbalance between the growing demand for vessel access to anchorage areas and the rigid, scarce supply of anchorage capacity has led to persistent “anchoring difficulties” in port waters. In this paper, we consider the anchor position allocation problem (APAP) that arises from anchorage operations and management. The problem is concerned with serving the demand of a set of calling vessels with the available anchor positions at minimum cost, where some vessels may be denied service if allocation is not cost-effective. The APAP extends traditional variants of the bin packing problem by incorporating practical features: anchor position heterogeneity, vessel navigation directions, and traffic flow control. Despite its theoretical significance and wide-ranging practical relevance, the APAP has received little attention in the literature. We formulate this problem as a mixed-integer linear programming model. General-purpose solvers can handle the model in small-scale scenarios. To address the computational intractability of practical-sized problems, we propose a tailored logic-based Benders decomposition (TLBBD) algorithm with problem-specific optimality cuts, complemented by an exact polynomial-time allocation procedure. Through computational experiments based on the operational data from Zhoushan Port, China, we show that the proposed TLBBD significantly outperforms the Gurobi solver and current industry practices for anchor position allocation. In particular, our algorithm obtains optimal solutions for instances with up to 75 vessels and 30 anchor positions in under ten minutes. Extensive experiments are further conducted to derive managerial insights.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Ride-hailing platform operations and blockchain adoption under service quality uncertainty: quality-, quantity-, and risk-sensitive passengers
Authors: Jing Sun, Shifeng Liu, Daqing Gong, Xiaojie Yan
Abstract: Ride-hailing platforms have become a mature mode of transportation, yet service quality on the supply side remains volatile. Passengers display different risk attitudes toward such fluctuations, making joint pricing and service-quality governance decisions nontrivial. This paper studies how the platform should operate and whether to adopt blockchain in the presence of risk-sensitive passengers. Blockchain enables the platform to better identify passengers’ risk types and implement differentiated decisions. We develop a game-theoretic model with network externalities and further capture the sensitivity of both supply-side and demand-side users to service quality. We find that passengers’ relative sensitivities to service quality and driver quantity shape both the ranking of optimal service-quality governance intensity across risk types and the platform’s overall operating strategy. In particular, higher service quality is not always optimal, as higher prices can still be associated with user growth. Moreover, the same sensitivity structure governs how blockchain adoption modifies the platform’s optimal service-quality governance intensity. In addition, blockchain adoption always benefits drivers; when passengers are highly sensitive to service quality, it can generate mutually beneficial outcomes among passengers, drivers, and the platform. We also emphasize the role of government subsidies when passengers’ sensitivity to service quality is moderate, as the platform has no incentive to adopt blockchain in this case. The main insights remain robust when the platform is risk-averse to profit fluctuations. These findings provide implications for both platform and government.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: How can public concerns shape eVTOL policy design? A knowledge graph-enhanced large language model (LLM) framework
Authors: Tianlin Liu, Cheng Yang, Hyungchul Chung, Manman Zhu, Ke Han, Hongliang Ding
Abstract: Electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft (eVTOL) may provide faster and more flexible connections for intracity and intercity trips, but their adoption depends on more than aircraft performance. Although prior studies have examined eVTOL acceptance and potential demand, the link between behavioral evidence and policy design remains underdeveloped. Using stated preference survey data from six Chinese low-altitude mobility pilot cities, covering a 30-km intracity setting and intercity settings at 60, 100, 160, and 300 km, we first construct a three-layer causal network to examine how individual characteristics, psychological attitudes, and travel-scenario attributes jointly shape eVTOL mode choice. The results show that travel cost, waiting time, and ground access/egress distance constrain eVTOL adoption, whereas perceived convenience, perceived usefulness, income, and congestion experience increase adoption potential; network analysis further identifies income and perceived usefulness as key leverage points in the decision system. Building on these behavioral findings, we develop a knowledge graph-enhanced large language model (KG-enhanced LLM) framework that integrates causal evidence and literature-based knowledge to translate the identified concerns into policy recommendations. A comparative experiment shows that the KG-enhanced LLM produces recommendations with higher evidence reliability, scenario relevance, logical coherence, and overall quality than a standalone LLM. Guided by these findings, the study recommends that eVTOL deployment prioritize transparent safety governance, accessible pricing, door-to-door integration, and differentiated communication across user groups. The study thus advances a structured approach for linking public acceptance analysis with policy design and offers methodological implications for emerging mobility systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Operating room planning problem under uncertainty: A regret minimization model
Authors: Mohsen Roytvand Ghiasvand, Amin Ahmadi Digehsara, Amir Ardestani-Jaafari, Babak Mohamadpour Tosarkani, Pooya Pourrezaie-Khaligh
Abstract: Operating room (OR) planning presents a significant challenge for hospital managers due to inherent uncertainty in surgery durations, which are unknown at the time of scheduling. Decisions regarding the number of ORs to open and the assignment of surgeries must be made in advance, and inaccurate estimates can lead to idle capacity, excessive overtime, or delayed procedures. This study develops and compares three complementary optimization frameworks for OR planning under uncertainty: classical robust optimization (RO), regret minimization (RM), and a data-driven distributionally robust optimization (DRO) approach termed mean robust optimization (MRO). The RM model is designed to limit the maximum performance loss relative to an ex post optimal benchmark, thereby reducing excessive conservatism associated with worst-case planning. We show that both the RO and RM formulations admit equivalent robust counterparts and propose efficient column-and-constraint generation (C&CG) algorithms to solve large-scale instances. To leverage historical surgery duration data, we further incorporate the MRO framework, which constructs data-driven ambiguity sets through clustering and provides a tunable balance between robustness and data adaptivity. Extensive computational experiments demonstrate clear behavioral differences among the models. While RO yields the most conservative schedules, RM achieves lower worst-case costs at the expense of higher regret exposure under severe uncertainty, and MRO consistently delivers intermediate solutions that reduce conservatism while maintaining numerical stability. The results highlight how uncertainty severity, overtime cost structure, and data availability jointly influence model performance. From a managerial perspective, the proposed unified framework offers practical guidance for selecting OR planning models that align with institutional risk preferences and data maturity.

Title: Coordinating pilotage services across ports: A tri-objective optimization framework for cost, fairness, and safety
Authors: Baoli Liu, Yaomei Qiao, Dian Sheng, Jianfeng Zheng, Yuwei Xing
Abstract: Regional ports that are geographically adjacent or share overlapping pilotage waters can coordinate their pilotage operations to achieve more efficient and intensive use of resources. In this study, we consider the multi-port pilotage allocation and scheduling problem (MPPASP), in which a pilot dispatch center (PDC) manages a heterogeneous team of pilots, together with a fleet of pilot boats and helicopters, to provide pilotage services across a regional port cluster. The MPPASP is a generalization of the simultaneous pick-up and delivery vehicle routing problem with time windows, incorporating unique features such as diverse pilot requirements, multi-pilot synchronization, port-specific work regulations, and transport mode trade-offs. The objectives are to simultaneously minimize total operational costs, maximize service fairness across ports, and maximize pilotage safety. Despite its practical significance for regional port management, the MPPASP has not been well studied as reported in the literature. We formulate this new problem as a tri-objective mixed-integer program, based on which we develop a hybrid solution framework to solve it. The framework integrates evolutionary multi-objective search, guided by reinforcement learning for objective-oriented initialization and operator exploration, with optimization modules implemented via GUROBI to improve solution performance. Numerical experiments based on the field data from Beibu Gulf Port (comprising Qinzhou, Beihai, and Fangcheng Ports) in Guangxi, China, demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed solution framework compared to both the state-of-the-art solver and the benchmark algorithms from the literature. Sensitivity analyses provide managerial insights for PDCs, examining the optimal pilot grade composition together with the most suitable regional port cluster size and resource adjustments under seasonal demand fluctuations.

Title: Decision-aware robust Markov decision processes with distance-based uncertainty sets
Authors: Jun Zhou, Yisha Xiang, Ming Zhao
Abstract: Markov decision processes (MDPs) are widely used to model sequential decision-making under uncertainty, with applications such as maintenance optimization and inventory control. However, in many real-world settings, transition probabilities must be estimated from limited and noisy historical data, leading to significant estimation errors. Robust MDPs address this challenge by constructing ambiguity sets that, with high confidence, contain the true transition probabilities. While effective in guarding against worst-case scenarios, these models often produce overly conservative policies, especially when data are scarce. In this paper, we propose a novel decision-aware robust MDP framework that reduces conservatism by incorporating information from nominal policies and their performance. Specifically, we introduce a second ambiguity set centered at an alternative reference distribution, identified through an inverse MDP that enhances nominal performance. The intersection of this set with the conventional ambiguity set (centered at empirical distributions) forms a decision-aware uncertainty set. We provide tractable reformulations for ϕ[jls-end-space/]-divergence-based ambiguity sets and develop an efficient algorithm to seek robust yet less conservative policies. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the decision-aware approach achieves improved out-of-sample performance and yields worst-case distributions closer to the true distribution, highlighting its advantage over conventional robust MDPs.

Title: Nominal GDP targeting and the tax burden
Authors: Michael Hatcher, Juyi Lyu
Abstract: Recent work suggests that nominal GDP targeting may raise social welfare, but fiscal considerations have largely been ignored. We study an overlapping generations model with government debt and distortionary taxes. Nominal GDP targeting has two opposing effects on the tax burden: mean taxes increase, but tax volatility is reduced. Differently to previous works, we find that nominal GDP targeting lowers social welfare relative to inflation targeting. A key mechanism is that nominal GDP targeting makes inflation countercyclical, thereby raising long run inflation risk and consumption risk of retirees while increasing the inflation risk premium paid on government debt.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Noise, ferries patterns and residents’ perception: the port of Las Palmas case
Authors: Eduardo Hernández-Pérez, Beatriz Tovar, Salvador del Saz-Salazar
Abstract: Managing acoustic externalities at the port-city interface requires integrating source emissions with community perception. This study develops a framework to characterise ferry noise during hotelling, combining high-resolution monitoring with social analysis. Methodologically, AIS-synchronized measurements characterised vessel emissions, while a stratified survey evaluated resident annoyance. Results reveal L den levels of ∼67.5 dBA, exceeding industrial limits due to tonal and low-frequency penalties. These findings demonstrate that strategic maps and point measurements serve complementary purposes: the former for urban planning and the latter for designing market-based mitigation incentives to supports the ’polluter pays’ principle. Furthermore, despite low self-reported noise disturbance, hierarchical regression analysis identified residents’ health risk perception and pro-environmental behaviour as key predictors of annoyance. Specifically, the model established health risk perception as the primary factor driving heightened sensitivity. Within normalised urban noise context, concern for physical well-being acts as the principal catalyst for perceived annoyance, surpassing both ideological and contextual factors.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Public child care and mothers’ career trajectories
Authors: Katrin Huber, Geske Rolvering
Abstract: This paper studies how public child care affects the quality of mothers’ careers in Germany, a setting characterized by low female labor force participation and traditional gender norms. Leveraging administrative data and quasi-experimental variation in child care expansion, we analyze occupational and employer mobility, task content, leadership, and within-firm wage positions. We show that while child care increases maternal employment, its effects on career quality are selective and context-dependent. Improvements are observed in employment in high-skilled occupations involving more complex, non-routine tasks and tend to be more pronounced among mothers in time-flexible occupations and family-friendly firms, highlighting complementarities between public policy and workplace conditions.

Title: Greedy work: Signaling and the design of demanding jobs
Authors: Jaesoo Kim
Abstract: This paper develops a theory of greedy jobs in which rigid, high-intensity work arrangements arise as an equilibrium response to asymmetric information rather than as a purely technological necessity. Firms differ in their returns to demanding work, but these returns are privately known, while job demandingness is observable to workers. When workers are homogeneous, firms separate efficiently and job design reflects productivity alone. Once workers differ in their tolerance for demanding work due to caregiving responsibilities, equilibrium sorting interacts with signaling incentives: to deter imitation and attract non-caregivers, high-return firms distort job design beyond the surplus-maximizing level, generating excessively rigid jobs and higher wage premia while excluding caregivers. The framework also shows how technological convergence, caregiving-targeted innovations, and minimum flexibility requirements reshape signaling incentives, helping explain why excessively demanding jobs persist in elite labor markets and why regulation and technological progress can have ambiguous effects when job design serves as both a signal and a sorting device.

Title: The Case for Doing Less: Rethinking Communication With Consumers During Logistics Service Failures
Authors: Haley Paluzzi, Micah J. Marzolf, Travis Tokar, Haozhe Chen
Affiliations: Department of Management, College of Business Colorado State University Fort Collins Colorado USA; Department of Supply Chain Management, Debbie and Jerry Ivy College of Business Iowa State University Ames Iowa USA; Department of Information Systems and Supply Chain Management, Neeley School of Business Texas Christian University Fort Worth Texas USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Existing research highlights that proactive communication of logistics service failures can positively affect consumer attitudes and behaviors. However, we explore how strategic restraint (i.e., doing less ) during service failures can serve as a powerful design principle for improving performance, highlighting the need to reconsider when and how firms intervene in such situations. Grounded in attribution theory, this study uses two scenario‐based experiments to explore the role of proactive communication in shaping consumers' attributions of blame and subsequent repurchase intentions. Findings indicate that in a logistics service context, when retailers refrain from communicating delivery delays with consumers directly (i.e., proceed with no delay communication or allow carriers to manage delay‐related communication), consumers place less blame on the retailer and increase repurchase intentions. These results hold across varying levels of service criticality and prior patronage.

Title: Issue Information
Housing restriction policies and internal migration
Authors: Xueying Lyu, Siqiang Yang
Abstract: This paper investigates the impacts of housing purchase restrictions on internal migration and household tenure choices in Chinese cities. We develop a spatial model that incorporates individuals’ migration and tenure decisions across cities. The model predicts that potentially affected homebuyers will either switch destinations or change tenure choices, depending on heterogeneous city characteristics. Utilizing the China Migrants Dynamic Survey and a difference-in-differences approach, we examine the model’s implications and find that the restrictions lead to a decrease in migration inflows and a reduced proportion of homeowners among migrants in the restricted cities relative to the unrestricted ones. However, this overall pattern masks important heterogeneity across cities: incoming migrants are more likely to adjust their tenure choices when restricted cities offer better development prospects or desirable living conditions, and they are more inclined to relocate to alternative destinations when such attributes are lacking. These findings highlight the importance of considering unintended consequences on migration when designing housing policies.

Title: Defining covert supply chains
Authors: George A. Zsidisin
Abstract: Most published research has focused on advancing knowledge associated with supply chain practice among entities that are visible or, in other terms, overt in their operations. However, not all supply chains can be readily seen or observed and instead operate covertly in order to conceal their product, service, financial and information flows from another entity. This note will begin exploring this under-studied facet of supply chain management by providing a preliminary definition and typology of covert supply chains. This phenomenon differs from related topics such as illicit supply chains, hidden operations and resilience under threat by arguing how these “hidden” supply chains exist regardless of legal standing, extend beyond operations, and can be used as one of many available tactics to sustain resilience from external threats by avoiding detection. Managerial implications for purchasing and supply management professionals include considering how and when covert supply chains can support operations and corporate strategy, incorporating a wider external context beyond the buyer-supplier dyad in decision-making, and deriving learning lessons from similar disciplines outside the business context.
Journal: Journal of Purchasing and Supply Management

Title: Handling processing time uncertainty in flexible job shop scheduling with variable sublots: a CVaR-enhanced MILP and multi-agent reinforcement learning approach
Authors: Chuanzhao Yu, Youshan Liu, Chunjiang Zhang, Weiming Shen
Affiliations: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
Abstract: The utilisation of variable sublots in scheduling increases machine efficiency through operation overlap, yet its performance is vulnerable to processing time uncertainty, which can propagate delays and erode robustness. This paper tackles the flexible job shop scheduling problem with variable sublots (FJSP-VS) under such uncertainty, seeking to harness lot streaming efficiency while rigorously managing downside risk. We propose a risk-aware, integrated framework coupling multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) for adaptive coordination with a scenario-based, conditional value-at-risk(CVaR)-enhanced mixed-integer program (MILP) for robust sublot planning. The MARL component handles dynamic, operation-level scheduling across flexible routes, while the CVaR-enhanced MILP provides a formal hedge against severe makespan outcomes in sublot partitioning, machine assignment, and timing decisions. Computational results on established benchmarks reveal that the proposed framework consistently surpasses risk-neutral and alternative robust schedulers. The method reduces the CVaR0.9 of makespan by up to about 2% while maintaining competitive average makespan performance, resulting in more stable scheduling outcomes under processing-time uncertainty.

Title: Who should set cosmetic standards in agricultural live-streaming supply chains: farmer or live streamer?
Authors: Baofeng Zhang, Li Lan, Jiawei Xu, Chenchen Zhao
Affiliations: China Agricultural University
Abstract: Live streaming is increasingly being applied in the agricultural industry by directly connecting farmers with consumers and shifting supply chains from wholesale contracts to revenue-sharing contracts. This transformation grants farmers greater authority over product selection, including decisions regarding cosmetic standards for produce. Motivated by this practice, this study explores cosmetic standard authority and its supply chain implications within an agricultural live-streaming context involving a farmer and a live streamer. We find that under either authority model, when consumer additional utility for high-standard produce is high, the decision maker prefers selling high-standard produce and otherwise opts for low-standard produce. Surprisingly, a higher agency fee rate makes both parties more likely to sell low-standard produce. When consumer additional utility for high-standard produce is either very high or very low, consensus on unified cosmetic standards can be reached; otherwise, their preferences diverge. In such conflicting cases, live streamer-controlled standards lead to greater farmer effort but also to higher food loss and lower consumer welfare. Interestingly, under certain conditions, either party controlling the decision right can improve overall supply chain profit. This study highlights live-streaming's role in transforming agricultural supply chains and offers managerial insights into cosmetic standard authority and food loss.

Title: Charging-bay reservation in single battery swapping stations under demand regime shifts with meta-learning and adaptive switching
Authors: Bo Zhang, Yanchao Zhang, Tao Wang, Zhihua Chen, Guoliang Shi, Rui Miao, Zhibin Jiang
Affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Hunan University

Title: Assessing system reliability in multi-grade production under different demand fulfilment policies via a multistate flow network
Authors: Hsuan-Yu Chen, Yi-Kuei Lin
Affiliations: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University; National Chin-Yi University of Technology; Chaoyang University of Technology; Asia University
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Learning from the development of digital maturity models in manufacturing: a Design Science Research approach
Authors: Paolla Polla Pontes do Espírito Santo, Néstor Fabián Ayala, Alejandro G. Frank
Affiliations: Organizational Engineering Group (Núcleo de Engenharia Organizacional – NEO), Department of Industrial Engineering, Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul; School of Engineering and Science, Tecnológico de Monterrey
Abstract: This his study examines how digital maturity models can more effectively guide Industry 4.0 implementation in manufacturing contexts. Despite the proliferation of maturity and readiness models, firms still struggle to translate assessments into actionable improvements aligned with operational objectives. Existing models tend to emphasize specific technologies or isolated dimensions, limiting their ability to capture the systemic nature of digital transformation and the learning processes embedded in its implementation. This study adopts a Design Science Research approach to develop a maturity assessment framework grounded in operational targets. The model departs from technology-centric perspectives and structures digital maturity around recurring manufacturing challenges across four dimensions: Smart Manufacturing, Smart Supply Chain, Smart Working and Smart Consumption. The framework was co-developed and validated through an iterative, longitudinal process with a large manufacturing company, integrating literature analysis, field observations, interviews, benchmarking and real-world applications. The resulting model defines sixteen operational targets across six maturity levels, enabling firms to link technology adoption to measurable operational improvements. The findings also emphasize the role of the development and implementation process as a source of organizational learning.

Title: Optimal timing of climate adaptation investment: a stopping-time approach under stochastic climate loss
Authors: Ron Dembo
Abstract: We examine the optimal timing for climate adaptation investments as a continuous-time optimal stopping problem. Physical climate risk produces heavy-tailed loss distributions whose extremes grow with climate uncertainty; adaptation is an irreversible expense that provides a permanent reduction in those losses. We incorporate this structure within the Climate Capital Option Theory (CCOT) framework, which models adaptation as a protective put option on a stochastic climate-loss process. The investment decision reduces to: exercise the option the first time a climate- or financial-stress indicator exceeds an endogenous threshold τ*. We derive τ* explicitly, analyse its comparative-static properties concerning climate uncertainty, the regulatory capital cost coefficient η, and the adaptation cost I_0, and demonstrate that τ* is non-decreasing with the variance of the loss process. A formal sensitivity analysis reveals that increasing climate uncertainty, understood as a mean-preserving spread on the loss distribution, decreases the optimal threshold, thereby making early investment unequivocally optimal. A numerical example involving a multi-hazard manufacturing asset in the Philippines supports the theory: the tail-risk capital benefit, V_tail, accounts for over 47% of the total adaptation value, a component overlooked by expected-loss approaches. This paper advances the literature on real options, climate finance, and stochastic optimization by presenting the first rigorous treatment of adaptation timing through a stopping-time approach with an explicit role for regulatory capital.

Title: Multi-agent deep reinforcement learning-based flexible flow shop scheduling of household paper production
Authors: Zhenglei He, Zejun Liu, Xiuli He, Jigeng Li, Mengna Hong, Kim Phuc Tran, Yi Man, Xianyi Zeng
Abstract: Due to the growing market demand for product differentia, the household paper production has to adapt to be more flexible in recent years, while it is challenged by uncertainty and complexity in dynamic scheduling. The objectives of minimizing maximum completion time and energy consumption are equivalent to the household paper firms, while traditional tools relied on expert knowledge and human intervention with multiple objectives in this issue. This paper mathematically identified and summarized the household paper workshop scheduling based on its process characteristics of high requirement on flexibility and energy efficiency, and innovatively proposed a deep reinforcement learning-based optimization system via formulating the problem into a Markov game. The optimal solutions are attained through interactions between multiple agents, representing different objectives, in the production scheduling environment. To validate the proposed approach, case studies were conducted using industrial data derived from a household paper company. The results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method in multiple aspects. Future study could explore deeper to strengthen the model’s generalizability, scalability, and handling uncertainty to validate its applicability in real-world environments.

Title: Disruption-resilient lot-sizing and scheduling using multimodal deep reinforcement learning and distributionally robust evaluation
Authors: Mohammad Asghari, Mohamad Y. Jaber, Cory Searcy, Hamid Afshari
Abstract: Modern manufacturing systems face increasing pressure to remain cost-efficient, responsive, and resilient amid operational uncertainty and disruptive events. While traditional scheduling methods offer limited adaptability, existing AI-based solutions often overlook robustness and risk sensitivity in complex production settings. This study addresses this gap by developing a multimodal deep reinforcement learning (MDRL) framework that learns data-driven scheduling policies under routine stochastic variability and evaluates them through distributionally robust and tail-risk-based disruption stress tests. The proposed approach leverages a transformer-based algorithm enhanced with transformer encoders and cross-modal attention to processing diverse data sources. Robustness is assessed through scenario-based disruption stress testing and CVaR/DRO-based robustness scoring for post-training checkpoint selection. Experimental results reveal that the MDRL agent consistently favors mid-sized lot sizes (peaking around 58 units) and reduces setup activations by approximately 30%, promoting stable and efficient operations. Analyses for robustness show that while increasing the CVaR threshold from 0.5 to 0.99 raises worst-case cost by over 50%, it leads to a 26% drop in service level, highlighting critical trade-offs between risk aversion and responsiveness. These findings highlight the potential of MDRL to optimize operational performance while supporting systematic robustness evaluation in real-time production environments. The framework offers a scalable and intelligent decision-making tool for next-generation smart factories, with implications for operational efficiency, sustainability, and supply chain resilience.

Title: Dictator game giving: Money vs. effort — women are more generous with money but more selfish with effort
Authors: Petr Krautwurm, Lena von Deylen, Philipp C. Wichardt
Abstract: The data reported in this paper show that dictator game transfers depend crucially on whether money or effort are to be distributed. In a standard (monetary) version, giving is far more generous (close to equal sharing); behaviour is highly selfish in the effort version. Moreover, women are more altruistic then men when distributing money but are more selfish when distributing effort. The results suggest that the common focus on monetary transfers covers only part of the story.

Title: Monetary policy transmission under supply-chain disruptions: Evidence from a time-varying BVAR
Authors: Sungjun Huh, Insu Kim
Abstract: This paper examines the time-varying effects of monetary policy and global supply-chain disruptions on U.S. inflation and GDP during the COVID-19 pandemic. To this end, we estimate a time-varying parameter Bayesian Vector Autoregressive (TVP-BVAR) model. We find that expansionary monetary policy shocks’ impact differs significantly between pre- and post-pandemic periods. Specifically, inflationary effects of supply-chain disruptions increased substantially after the pandemic, while output effects remained stable. Furthermore, monetary policy pass-through to inflation strengthens as supply-chain pressures intensify. Finally, statistical evidence shows that supply-chain disruptions steepen the Phillips curve, with the effect most pronounced for durable goods inflation.

Title: Do prediction markets price events or adjudication? Evidence from the disputed Polymarket markets
Authors: Guangzhe Wang
Abstract: A prediction-market share is read as a probability about an event. In an oracle-settled market the cash flow is fixed not by the event but by the outcome that the resolution mechanism certifies, so the price can come apart from the event. We test whether prices forecast the event or the adjudication by reading them inside the on-chain settlement window of disputed Polymarket markets, the interval between a bonded proposer’s assertion of the outcome and the UMA token vote that fixes the payoff. Inside that window the real-world event is already frozen while the payoff is still pending, so a discount on the asserted-correct claim cannot be ordinary forecasting of an unrealized event. Using 233 disputed markets with a clear audited rule-correct winner, coded by a search-grounded language-model audit formed independently of how the oracle ruled and matched to each market’s UMA Optimistic Oracle lifecycle, we find the token vote overturns the audited winner in 12.4 percent of markets, an upper bound inherited from the coding model. Six hours after the first dispute the audited-correct claim already trades at a discount that is 0.83 higher in markets the oracle will overturn, and the discount climbs toward one as the vote approaches while the upheld claim falls toward zero. The pricing pattern survives the choice of coding model, the removal of deadline questions, restriction to the markets that escalate to the vote, and a treatment limited to the hand-verified overturns. The complete UMA voting record shows the deciding votes to be broad and near unanimous, and the dispute-time price predicts the vote share itself. Prices in contested prediction markets are therefore best read not as beliefs about the world but as forecasts of how a decentralized rule will be adjudicated.

Title: Point scale framing and student performance: Evidence from a field experiment
Authors: Puneet Arora, Arihant Jain, Ishita Tripathi
Abstract: Does the numerical scale used to score an exam affect how hard students try? We test this question with a preregistered natural field experiment in which 1235 university students in India took identical tests framed as scored out of either 20 or 100 points. Exploiting both a high-stakes graded quiz and a zero-stakes additional test, we find no statistically or economically meaningful effects of the point-scale manipulation on test scores or on four effort measures, regardless of stakes, gender, or prior ability. These consistently null results, robust across settings, outcomes, and subgroups, identify a boundary condition for the numerosity heuristic: when scoring units are transparently arbitrary and evaluation ultimately rests on percentages, numerical rescaling does not shift behavior. The findings support the behavioral neutrality of a widely used and easily modified feature of assessment design.

Title: Gender differences in teacher grading across school subjects: Evidence from Germany
Authors: Sebastian Otten
Abstract: This study examines whether gender differences in teacher-assigned grades vary systematically across subjects. Using data from German secondary schools, I compare teacher-assigned grades with anonymously graded standardized test scores within a difference-in-differences framework. Across six core subjects spanning the humanities and STEM, I find systematic grading differentials favoring female students. The estimated differential is largest in German and Math and substantially smaller in English and the sciences, indicating considerable cross-subject heterogeneity. The differential also varies markedly by school track and teacher experience, with systematically larger estimates in the academic track and particularly pronounced differentials among novice teachers.

Title: Revisiting patience and achievement: evidence from matched parent–child preferences
Authors: Ernan Haruvy, Ying Yang
Abstract: This paper examines whether children’s time preferences independently predict academic achievement using matched incentivized measures for parents and children linked to standardized mathematics performance. Reduced-form regressions replicate prior findings that more patient children perform better academically. However, once parental time preferences are included, children’s patience no longer predicts achievement, while parental patience remains strongly significant across specifications. These results suggest that previously documented links between children’s time preferences and academic performance may reflect intergenerational behavioral transmission or household inputs rather than child-specific traits. The findings highlight the importance of jointly modeling parent and child characteristics when studying non-cognitive skill formation.

Title: Platform competition and driver multi-homing in ride-hailing markets
Authors: Yaqian Zhou, He Huang, Hai Yang
Abstract: This paper explores platform competition and driver multi-homing in ride-hailing markets. We propose an equilibrium model of a two-platform system with price- and time-sensitive customers and earnings-sensitive drivers. We consider two separate settings: single-homing where drivers work only for the platform that offers higher earnings, and multi-homing where drivers simultaneously work for two competing platforms. Our framework segments the customer market into two groups: loyal customers, who stick with their preferred platforms, and competitive customers, who always choose the platform that yields higher utility. Within this framework, we first examine how two key features of competitive markets—customer loyalty and platform substitutability—can affect equilibrium prices and wages and resulting market outcomes. We find that, ceteris paribus, an increase in customer loyalty makes all stakeholders worse off, while an increase in platform substitutability benefits customers and drivers at the expense of platforms. Building on this, we explore how multi-homing would impact the interests of different stakeholders. A major result in the multi-homing literature on on-demand service platforms is that both customers and drivers are worse off when drivers multi-home. We show that this result largely depends on assuming away the “pooling effect”—matching becomes more efficient when demand and supply increases proportionally—that is prevalent in on-demand service platforms. By incorporating the “pooling effect”, the findings suggest that multi-homing could make both customers and drivers better off in markets with high competition characterized by low customer loyalty and high platform substitutability. Moreover, our results indicate that all stakeholders could be better off when drivers multi-home in markets where drivers are less heterogeneous in their reservation earnings and the degree of competition is moderate.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: The Braess-like paradox in airline network design: Insights from two case studies
Authors: Yueer Zhou, Yahua Zhang, Linbo Li, Kun Wang, Xiaowen Fu
Abstract: Designing airline networks that enhance profitability through higher load factors and improved revenue generation is a challenging task. Although progress has been made, several issues remain unresolved, particularly regarding the adaptability of existing models to large-scale networks and routing inefficiencies caused by network paradoxes such as the Braess paradox. This study proposes a multi-objective framework for hybrid airline network design based on a self-regulated ant colony optimization (SRACO) algorithm. Case studies of Qantas Airways and China Southern Airlines demonstrate the framework’s applicability across different network settings. The results reveal that the occurrence of a Braess-like paradox in the simulation may lead to resource inefficiency during passenger assignment approaches equilibrium, particularly when network routes and frequencies are optimized.
