Fortunately, this phenomenon can be mitigated by adjusting hub locations. These findings indicate that network performance is constrained by hub location and highlight the importance of the joint optimization of hubs and routes. Moreover, incorporating hub location adjustments during the design process can mitigate the paradox and enhance airline revenue.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: The politics of climate adaptation in Nepal: authority, knowledge, and resource inequality in multi-level governance
Authors: Suman Acharya
Abstract: Contemporary approaches to climate change adaptation increasingly emphasize multi-level stakeholder engagement. These approaches seek to advance sustainability, equity, and inclusion while addressing the social, environmental, economic, and political needs of present and future generations. Although technocratic adaptation addresses biophysical climate risks, it often neglects socio-political forces that shape vulnerability and can intensify long-term climate risks and inequalities. This paper utilizes a multi-level governance framework to examine the political dimensions of climate adaptation, focusing on the dynamics of authority, knowledge, and resource access. Building on literature on the political dimensions of climate change adaptation, this study draws on ethnographic data to examine how power is exercised, negotiated, and resisted across multiple governance scales in Nepal. Focusing on the Karnali region, it shows that despite formally democratic multi-level institutions, adaptation authority remains centralized at the federal level and shaped by corruption, reinforcing exclusion and elite capture. As federal, provincial, and local governments compete over authority, knowledge production, and resource control, Nepal's multi-level adaptation governance reinforces power differentials and elite influence while marginalizing vulnerable communities, thereby limiting transformative and just climate adaptation. This paper argues that effective adaptation requires accountable multi-level governance rather than decentralization alone. Meaningful subnational authority must be matched by cross-scale coordination, transparency, and oversight so that decision-making, resources, and knowledge are not captured by elites at any level.

Title: Identifying the types of government interventions that work in the sanitation sector
Authors: Britta Augsburg, Habiba Djebbari, Molly Lipscomb, Tetsushi Sonobe

Title: A double-stage heuristic algorithm for the antibandwidth maximization problem via the linear bottleneck assignment optimization
Authors: Jintong Ren, Jin-Kao Hao, Eduardo Rodriguez-Tello, Zequn Wei
Abstract: The antibandwidth maximization problem is a classic graph layout problem arising in applications such as multiprocessor scheduling, radio frequency assignment, and obnoxious facility location. It involves assigning distinct integer labels to the vertices of a graph such that the minimum absolute difference between the labels of adjacent vertices is maximized. To solve this NP-hard problem, we propose a double-stage heuristic algorithm integrating a local optimization stage with a dedicated reduced neighborhood, and a greedy optimized perturbation stage including a greedy assignment step as well as an optimized assignment step. Crucially, we demonstrate that the optimized assignment step can be transformed into solving the linear bottleneck assignment problem, which is solvable in polynomial time via a threshold algorithm. Experimental results across 256 benchmark instances show that our algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art methods by achieving 42 improved lower bounds while matching the best-known results on the majority of the remaining instances. Additional analysis confirms the critical contribution of the algorithm’s key components to its overall performance.

Title: Contagion-based safety premium in bank networks
Authors: Zhongjie Fan, Ping He, Zehao Liu
Abstract: We examine safety premiums through the lens of financial contagion in interbank networks. In our model with endogenous collateralized lending contracts, safe assets command premiums because they relax funding constraints without amplifying default propagation. Multiple equilibria characterized by distinct lending volumes and safety premiums emerge exclusively in networks containing directed cycles. The safety premium thus serves as a tractable, price-based statistic of systemic fragility. Comparative statics show that conditions weakening contagion—most notably a sufficiently high safe-to-risky-asset ratio—can eliminate equilibrium multiplicity. Pure-strategy high-lending equilibria survive only when collateral quality is sufficiently high. Network structure critically influences these dynamics: increased density introduces competing effects (amplified contagion risk versus enhanced liquidity coinsurance), with their relative dominance determined by loan sizes and collateral quality. Core-periphery networks generate higher safety premiums than complete networks, as peripheral banks respond defensively to the amplified contagion risk circulating within the core. A greater number or larger size of peripheral banks leads to a higher safety premium.

Title: Gatekeepers and the endogenous design of consumer preferences under personalized pricing
Authors: Rosa Branca Esteves, Nicolas Pasquier
Abstract: We develop a Hotelling duopoly model of competition on a gatekeeper platform in which firms choose between uniform pricing and personalized pricing. Implementing personalized pricing requires access to a platform-provided pricing technology and entails a per-transaction fee set by the platform. The platform also designs rankings and recommendations that affect the distribution of consumers between loyal and marginal types. We show that the platform may strategically reshape the demand environment to make personalized pricing more attractive to firms and thereby raise the fee it can charge. By reallocating mass from loyal to marginal and more disloyal consumers, the platform intensifies competition under uniform pricing and relaxes firms’ adoption constraint. Excessive centralization, however, erodes the rents that sustain fee extraction, so the platform chooses an interior degree of demand centralization. Relative to a no-manipulation benchmark, this reallocates surplus toward the gatekeeper and away from firms and consumers. When the platform also appropriates a share of seller profits, its incentives may reverse: it may favor loyalty-enhancing designs that soften downstream competition. The analysis highlights how platform monetization and recommendation design jointly determine downstream competition and its welfare consequences.

Title: Consolidation of Local Health Authorities and mortality in the Italian NHS
Authors: Silvia Balia, Rinaldo Brau, Sara Pau
Abstract: This paper studies the health consequences of administrative centralization in healthcare, focusing on the consolidation of Local Health Authorities (LHAs) within the Italian National Health Service. This type of reform fits within a broader set of cost-containment efforts aimed at reducing administrative expenditures and exploiting economies of scale. In the Italian case, the reform centralized governance and expanded the scale of health administration, creating authorities with substantially larger catchment areas and shifting decision-making to more heterogeneous jurisdictions. Such changes may affect the responsiveness of healthcare provision to local needs, the coordination of service delivery, and access to care. Using an event-study Difference-in-Differences design, we estimate the policy’s impact on municipal mortality rates, accounting for heterogeneous treatment effects and co-occurring fiscal adjustment policies. We find a significant increase in mortality starting four years after implementation, with an average treatment effect on the treated of 2.1%. The effects are concentrated in municipalities belonging to absorbed LHAs and in those exposed to mergers involving relatively large pre-reform LHAs and substantial post-merger expansions in catchment areas; they are also unevenly distributed, creating new vulnerable areas. Welfare estimates based on life-years lost indicate that the monetary costs of increased mortality exceed plausible administrative savings by roughly an order of magnitude.

Title: Issue Information
Driver‐Centric Vehicle Routing for Parcel Delivery
Authors: Yoshinori Suzuki, Bo Lan
Affiliations: Department of Supply Chain Management, Debbie and Jerry Ivy College of Business Iowa State University Ames Iowa USA; Department of Marketing and Operations, Scott College of Business Indiana State University Terre Haute Indiana USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT One issue parcel delivery drivers are facing in their workplace is the limited access to restrooms. Because drivers are constantly pressured to meet the demanding performance standards called work quotas, they have little time to visit restrooms while working, often forcing them to urinate into bottles in the back of their trucks. This paper presents a new vehicle routing approach for parcel deliveries using the driver‐centric concept , the aim of which is to improve the drivers' level of comfort at the workplace. We propose a vehicle routing model that allows a driver to stop at either a business customer permitting restroom access or a public restroom every M minutes, where M is the driver‐specified parameter indicating the tolerable time between restroom stops. We show that, contrary to what some practitioners believe, our driver‐centric approach can give benefits not only to delivery drivers but also to parcel carriers under many practical conditions, thereby providing a win‐win solution for both parties. Drivers benefit from using driver‐friendly routes that allow them to visit restrooms at their desired intervals, while also increasing the chances of meeting work quotas. Parcel carriers benefit from reduced delivery time and operating costs in each vehicle route.

Title: Artificial Intelligence in Public Procurement: Aligning Operational Capacity, Legitimacy, and Public Value
Authors: Giovanna Culot, Matteo Podrecca, Andrea S. Patrucco, Guido Nassimbeni
Affiliations: Polytechnic Department of Engineering and Architecture University of Udine Udine Italy; Nottingham University Business School Nottingham UK; Department of Economics and Management “Marco Fanno” University of Padova Padova Italy; Department of Operations Management Copenhagen Business School Copenhagen Denmark
Abstract: ABSTRACT Public procurement is adopting artificial intelligence (AI) more slowly than private‐sector procurement, despite similar operational opportunities. We analyze this gap through Moore's Strategic Triangle (ST), focusing on public value, operational capacity, and legitimacy and support. Based on 38 expert interviews and a follow‐up resonance questionnaire, the study identifies three tensions: (i) contested performance gains versus social and environmental costs; (ii) data access for model performance versus stewardship duties for public and supplier data; and (iii) opacity versus accountability and contestability requirements. We elaborate the ST for AI‐enabled procurement by showing that AI changes how the three existing conditions must be held together. The tensions surface as practical questions about whether gains can be evidenced as public value, who controls procurement data and vendor learning, and whether AI‐supported recommendations can be explained and challenged. The strongest mitigation levers sit in agencies' contracting and decision practices, including work design, data rights and portability, audit trails, and supplier challenge mechanisms.

Title: Application of a disaster related emergency response model to a food bank network
Authors: Faith Idoko, Lauren Davis, Chrysafis Vogiatzis
Abstract: Abstract While disaster management and preparedness has seen significant developments in both theory and practice in recent years, there is still a shortage of operations research and decision science strategies specifically for food banks and their operations. This manuscript aims to fill that void by investigating how a disaster-related emergency response model can be used to improve food bank preparedness and decision-making for food bank operations during disasters. Using realistic projections of food bank operations, this study evaluates various strategies to address unmet demand and minimize operational costs across different scenarios that depict the network’s potential state following a disaster. A framework is designed to facilitate effective decision-making by considering different levels of risk tolerance. The implementation of mobile pantries is highlighted as an effective way to meet demand with minimal increases in operational costs when the network is disrupted. This framework provides food bank managers with an array of possible solution approaches, enabling them to make optimal decisions based on their specific objectives.

Title: Further developments on stochastic dominance for convex combinations of infinite-mean random variables
Authors: Keyi Zeng, Zhenfeng Zou, Yuting Su, Taizhong Hu
Abstract: In recent years, stochastic dominance for independent and identically distributed (iid) infinite-mean random variables has received considerable attention. The literature has identified several classes of distributions of nonnegative random variables that encompass many common heavy-tailed distributions. A key result demonstrates that the weighted sum of iid random variables from these classes is stochastically larger than any individual random variable in the sense of the first-order stochastic dominance. This paper systematically investigates the properties and inclusion relationships among these distribution classes, and extends some existing results to more practical scenarios. Furthermore, we analyze the case where each random variable follows a compound binomial distribution, establishing necessary and sufficient conditions for the preservation of the aforementioned stochastic dominance relation.

Title: Beyond heuristics: an experimental study on the impact of math self-efficacy and cognitive reflection on newsvendor decision-making performance
Authors: Sina Zare, Yasaman Ghasemi, Kay-Yut Chen
Affiliations: Loyola Marymount University (LMU); The University of Texas at Arlington (UTA)
Abstract: Behavioural newsvendor research has documented persistent deviations from optimal ordering – demand chasing, pull-to-center, and anchoring – yet the psychological foundations underlying these biases remain underspecified. We distinguish two constructs: cognitive reflection (CRT), the disposition to override intuitive responses, and math self-efficacy (MSE), a domain-specific motivational belief supporting the persistent application of rule-based reasoning under uncertainty. Using a repeated-round laboratory newsvendor experiment (N = 43 participants, 100 incentivized rounds), we examine the associations between CRT, MSE, and profit, whether MSE attenuates demand-chasing bias, and whether MSE moderates round-by-round learning. CRT and MSE are positively associated with profit, and the estimates are consistent with an indirect association linking CRT to performance via MSE. MSE significantly attenuates demand-chasing bias, primarily in later rounds as participants gain task experience. By contrast, MSE does not moderate the rate of learning but is associated with greater within-subject stability and consistency of ordering behaviour, consistent with motivational stability rather than cognitive bias correction. These findings indicate that reasoning style and motivational beliefs play complementary roles in reducing decision biases: CRT supports analytic override of intuitive responses, whereas MSE sustains consistent rule-based ordering under uncertainty. The study advances the psychological foundations of behavioural operations and informs training and decision-support systems.

Title: A multi-objective MILP approach for coordination and communication scheduling in resource-constrained multi-agent systems
Authors: Félicien Barhebwa-Mushamuka, Tomas Ménard
Affiliations: University of Caen Normandie
Abstract: Cooperative Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) are increasingly deployed in automated warehouses, robotic fulfilment centres, and smart logistics environments, where agents must coordinate under communication, energy, and operational constraints. Inefficient communication policies can increase energy consumption, create bottlenecks, and overload specific agents, reducing long-term system robustness. This paper proposes a multi-period coordination and communication scheduling framework for industrial MAS formulated as a Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model. The framework jointly optimises coordination efficiency, communication-energy consumption, and workload balance (Fairness) while considering finite coordination capacities, bounded communication durations, dynamic communication conditions, and coordination-communication dependencies. Two multi-objective solution approaches are developed: a desirability-based reformulation to identify balanced compromise solutions and an ε-constraint formulation to analyze Pareto trade-offs among efficiency, energy use, and fairness. Industrial-scale benchmark instances inspired by autonomous warehouse operations are generated to evaluate the framework under heterogeneous capacities, workload variability, sparse communication topologies, and dynamic energy conditions. Computational experiments and sensitivity analyses show that communication energy is a major operational bottleneck. Results reveal scarcity and saturation regimes in which moderate increases in communication-energy availability significantly improve coordination performance, whereas further resource relaxation yields diminishing returns. The framework provides a tractable and interpretable tool for robust coordination and communication management in large-scale industrial MAS.

Title: The innovation payoff of AI in production: evidence from German manufacturing
Authors: Djerdj Horvat, Heidi Heimberger, Angela Jäger, Christian M. Lerch
Affiliations: Department Innovation and Knowledge Economy, Fraunhofer Institute for Systems and Innovation Research ISI; Department of Innovation Management, University of Hohenheim
Abstract: This study examines the relationship between the implementation of artificial intelligence (AI) in production processes and product innovation outcomes in manufacturing firms. It contributes to the literature by providing empirical evidence on the role of AI in innovation while accounting for firm-level heterogeneity in established innovation drivers, including R&D intensity, workforce qualifications, human-centric practices, and structural characteristics. Using data from 1,334 firms in the 2022 German Manufacturing Survey, we find that AI implementation in production is positively associated with innovation-enhancing processes that complement existing organisational resources and capabilities. However, this relationship is limited to product innovations that are new to the firm and does not extend to innovations that are new to the market. Furthermore, distinguishing between product innovation types relevant to the twin transition, we find that AI implementation is primarily associated with a higher likelihood of digital product innovations, whereas eco-oriented product innovations are more strongly linked to the adoption of human-centric practices. These findings suggest that AI in production should be viewed not merely as an operational technology but as a strategic capability whose innovation potential depends on its integration with complementary organisational resources and capabilities.

Title: Dairy cow simulation model to assess the economic impact of twin calving
Authors: Osvaldo Palma, Lluis M. Plà-Aragonés, Alejandro Mac Cawley, Víctor M. Albornoz
Abstract: This study presents a discrete-event stochastic simulation model designed to represent the productive and reproductive dynamics of a dairy herd. The model is first validated by comparing its steady-state outcomes with analytical results available in the literature, showing a close agreement that confirms its consistency and supports its use for more complex analyses. Once validated, the model is applied to examine the economic consequences of different management decisions, particularly those related to twin calvings. The results indicate that, under the most profitable voluntary culling strategy, herds without twin births achieve a monthly net profit of $134.55 per cow, while those experiencing twin calvings reach $113.89 per cow, which represents a loss of $185.98 per animal per parity. This magnitude is consistent with values commonly reported in previous studies. In addition, the sensitivity analysis shows that reducing the probability of twin births increases profit almost proportionally, with an improvement of around $2.06 per cow per month for every ten percent decrease. Altogether, these findings shed light on the economic impact of twin calvings and illustrate how simulation offers a flexible and practical framework for evaluating herd-level decisions under uncertainty.

Title: Harnessing the ripple effect: the role of digitalization and network position in building viable supply chains
Authors: Jianyu Zhao, Zhiwei He, Xi Xi, Wei Liu
Abstract: In an era of recurrent and severe disruptions, understanding how firms sustain supply chain viability has become a central question in operations and supply chain management. While prior research has extensively examined the ripple effect and supply chain resilience, less is known about why firms exposed to similar upstream disruptions exhibit heterogeneous viability outcomes. Drawing on the supply chain viability (SCV) framework, this study investigates whether internal digital capabilities and external network power buffer the adverse effects of upstream ripple propagation on firm-level supply chain viability. Using panel data on 222 Chinese publicly listed firms and their supply chain networks from 2011 to 2023, we examine how digitalization and upstream bargaining power shape firms’ ability to withstand cascading disruptions. The results show that the ripple effect significantly undermines supply chain viability, but this negative relationship is attenuated for firms with higher levels of digitalization and stronger upstream network positions. These findings advance SCV research by providing empirical evidence on the buffering roles of digital capabilities and network structure in sustaining viability under systemic shocks. The study also offers managerial implications for building viable supply chains in environments characterized by deep uncertainty.

Title: Exploitation vs. Exploration: How knowledge spillovers shape healthcare practices and innovation
Authors: Yinan Liu, Chen Lin, Zixiao Li, Jing Zhang
Abstract: Improving public service quality is a central challenge in developing countries. A common policy tool is to transfer expertise and protocols to lower-tier institutions, with the expectation that such spillovers improve both current performance and long-term innovative capacity. We study this policy logic using a Chinese reform that mandated knowledge transfer from elite to lower-tier hospitals. Our analysis combines a novel measure of lower-tier hospitals’ alignment with elite hospitals’ clinical practice, developed with a large language model applied to clinical texts and prescription decisions, with measures of physicians’ exploratory activity based on academic publications. Using a difference-in-differences design, we find that the policy increased practice alignment at targeted hospitals by 0.29 standard deviations, yielding immediate efficiency gains. At the same time, this gain in exploitation was accompanied by a decline in exploration: physician academic output fell, with publication counts declining by 7% and citation impact by 13%. Our findings highlight that policies promoting existing knowledge can close practice gaps and improve care efficiency, while also creating a potential trade-off with professionals’ incentives to generate new knowledge.

Title: From augmentation to action: AI-LLM–enabled improvisation and reactive capability in digital manufacturing supply chains
Authors: Soumyadeb Chowdhury, Sachin Kumar Mangla, Guo Li
Abstract: Amid global disruptions and rapid technological change, digital manufacturing supply chains face growing pressure to develop reactive capabilities. This study examines the relationships among artificial intelligence large language model (AI-LLM) augmentation, supply chain improvisation, and reactive capability. Grounded in the dynamic capabilities view (DCV), we propose and empirically test a conceptual model in which supply chain improvisation mediates the association between AI-LLM augmentation and reactive capability, while digital innovation resistance and supply chain decisiveness act as moderators. Survey data from 224 UK supply chain managers were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). The results show that AI-LLM augmentation is positively associated with reactive capability via supply chain improvisation. Digital innovation resistance weakens the AI-LLM–improvisation relationship, underscoring the importance of an digital innovation-supportive culture, and supply chain decisiveness strengthens the relationship between improvisation and reactive capability, highlighting the value of prompt decision-making mechanisms. Overall, this study extends DCV by clarifying AI-LLM augmentation as a micro-foundational capability that supports improvisation in uncertain supply chain environments, and thus offers guidance for managers seeking to leverage AI-LLM augmentation to build reactive capabilities while managing resistance and fostering decisiveness in digital manufacturing supply chains.

Title: Resilient supplier selection and order allocation under disruption risk over a Wasserstein ambiguity
Authors: Xin Li, Xuan Vinh Doan, Juergen Branke
Abstract: Supply chain resilience is increasingly important for safeguarding operations against disruption risk, presenting decision-makers with the challenge of balancing cost efficiency and effective risk mitigation. We study the problem of resilient supplier selection and order allocation under uncertain disruption impact. Probability distributions of the actual disruption impact are unknown, and only a possibly small set of historical realizations may be available. To handle the distributional uncertainty, we first construct an ambiguity set that encompasses all possible distributions of disruption impact within a 1-Wasserstein distance from the empirical distribution. We then define a two-stage distributionally robust supplier selection and order allocation problem to determine optimal sourcing and contingency decisions among available suppliers under capacity constraints. The objective is to minimize the total cost consisting of the fixed cost related to contracting suppliers plus the worst-case mean-CVaR associated with disruption over all distributions defined in the ambiguity set. Using the model structural properties, we derive a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) reformulation that can be implemented and solved using off-the-shelf optimization software. We conduct numerical experiments based on synthetic data inspired by a real-world case taken from the literature. The experiment results demonstrate that our proposed model yields robust solutions and achieves superior out-of-sample performance over the stochastic approach.

Title: A single-axiom cardinal characterisation of quadratic utility
Authors: Leo Kurata
Abstract: In the cardinal part of their analysis of spherical preferences, Chambers and Echenique (2020) characterise quadratic-plus-linear utility using two axioms concerning changes from a status quo: Status Quo Independence (SQI) and Eventual Linearity (EL). We show that the two axioms are not independent. Specifically, SQI implies EL and, indeed, forces the additivity condition in EL to hold at every status quo, not merely at some status quo. Consequently, under continuity and normalisation, SQI alone characterises the representation, implying that their cardinal theorem remains valid when EL is dropped. The respective roles of continuity and normalisation are also clarified.

Title: News shocks and seafood exports: Evidence from the Fukushima ALPS-treated water release announcement
Authors: Fan Feng, Faqin Lin, Mengxun Liu, Qianqian Zhang
Abstract: News shocks are often characterized as a form of external uncertainty, which could drive consumer behavior by shaping cognitive processes. However, news coverage often coincides with real-world events, making it difficult to identify whether observed effects are driven by the news itself or by the underlying events. Based on the announcement of the planned release of ALPS-treated water from Fukushima, news concerning future events, this paper identifies the economic consequences of news shocks and incorporates salience theory into international trade. Applying a difference-in-difference method, we find that Pacific Rim countries and regions near Japan experienced a significantly greater decrease in seafood exports than those further away in the post-news period. The negative effects could be attributed to demand-side factors, including consumer sensitivity to news, heightened fear of unknown risks, and a shift toward substitute products.

Title: Give enough or not at all
Authors: Jean Zhang, Gal Smitizsky, Marta Serra-Garcia, Ayelet Gneezy
Abstract: We study the prosocial preferences of givers and receivers when giving involves small amounts. Focusing on this lower bound of generosity, we propose that people may prefer to give nothing, rather than give a small amount, while receivers prefer receiving small amounts to nothing. We further suggest that this asymmetry is driven by givers’ signaling concerns. Evidence from four studies—two survey experiments (N = 1,656), one incentivized lab experiment (N = 296), and one field study (N = 77 fundraising sessions lasting 30-60 minutes)—supports our proposition, revealing a mismatch between givers’ and receivers’ preferences. Importantly, we find that explicitly conveying to givers that small amounts are acceptable significantly increases the likelihood of giving.

Title: Resource-oriented optimization of electric vehicle systems: A data-driven survey on charging infrastructure, scheduling, and fleet management
Authors: Hai Wang, Baoshen Guo, Xiaolei Zhou, Kun Ding, Shuai Wang, Zhiqing Hong, Tian He
Abstract: Driven by growing concerns over air quality and energy security, electric vehicles (EVs) have experienced rapid development and are reshaping global transportation systems and lifestyle patterns. Compared with traditional gasoline-powered vehicles, EVs offer significant advantages, including lower energy consumption, reduced emissions, and lower operating costs. However, several core challenges remain to be addressed: (i) charging station congestion and operational inefficiencies during peak hours, (ii) high charging costs under time-varying electricity pricing schemes, and (iii) conflicts between charging needs and passenger service requirements. To address these challenges, this paper presents a comprehensive review of resource-oriented optimization models and approaches proposed in the literature. The reviewed studies cover the entire life cycle of EV systems, including charging station deployment, charging scheduling strategies, and large-scale fleet management. In addition, we compare successful and challenging real-world EV deployment cases worldwide to highlight the practical necessity of tailoring optimization algorithms to local infrastructure conditions. Moreover, we discuss the broader implications of EV integration across multiple domains, such as human mobility, smart grid infrastructure, and environmental sustainability, and identify key opportunities and directions for future research.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: The location-routing problem for UAV monitoring under time-varying noise constraints
Authors: Yuping Li, Kewei Xiang, Mingjie Li, Xingyu Wang
Abstract: Noise pollution has emerged as a critical bottleneck hindering the sustainable deployment of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) in urban environments. Current research largely treats facility location and noise-aware routing in isolation, failing to capture the interdependence between strategic infrastructure decisions and tactical compliance operations. This paper bridges this gap by introducing the Location-Routing Problem with Time Windows of the UAVs in Noise-Constrained zones (NC-LRPTW), a joint optimization framework designed for urban UAV monitoring networks. The core innovation lies in modeling flight altitude as a discrete endogenous decision variable, enabling the system to autonomously balance the trade-off between energy-intensive high-altitude flights required for noise abatement and time-penalty costs associated with low-altitude hovering. We formulate this problem as a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming model and propose a tailored two-stage hybrid heuristic algorithm for solving large-scale instances. This algorithm integrates Tabu Search for strategic facility siting with Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search, enhanced by a Departure Time Optimization mechanism, for tactical multi-constraint routing. Computational experiments demonstrate competitive performance against Gurobi on small- and medium-scale instances and effective scalability to complex city-level scenarios derived from real-world data. By internalizing environmental externalities into network design, this study provides a practical decision-support tool for governing the urban low-altitude economy.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Digital twins for low-altitude transportation and logistics: A barrier-centric survey of UAV and eVTOL systems
Authors: Yunshi Zhang, Yuhao Wang, Weimin Zhen, Chunlin Wang, Xiaobo Qu
Abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) platforms are increasingly considered for urban air mobility (UAM), last-mile logistics, and emergency-response operations, yet large-scale low-altitude deployment remains limited. Digital twin (DT) technology supports real-time monitoring, prediction, and control, while existing studies provide limited explanation for why some low-altitude DT application domains advance toward deployment more readily than other domains do. This survey interprets application maturity through a barrier-centric framework that combines a four-layer architecture, feedback-loop timing distinctions, and an application taxonomy organized around three recurring constraints: the Fidelity-Latency Paradox, Information-Theoretic Limits, and the artificial intelligence (AI) Verification Challenge. Scenario comparison across urban UAM, rural or peri-urban logistics, and emergency response shows that the same DT architecture can imply different deployment boundaries depending on operational role, feedback timing, and non-technical conditions. Across applications, predictive maintenance and diagnostic functions appear comparatively mature, whereas path planning, traffic management, and safety-critical real-time control remain more constrained by computational, communication, and assurance requirements. For transportation and logistics research, the main implication is that DT deployment should be assessed by how computational limits, communication capacity, and certification requirements interact with regulation, infrastructure, and business conditions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Balancing competition and collaboration in carbon-regulated supply chains through shared green logistics
Authors: Salman Piri, Bahman Manafi, Hadi Gholizadeh
Abstract: This paper examines how competing firms can balance competition and collaboration in carbon-regulated supply chains through shared green logistics. The study considers an integrated supply chain network involving facility configuration, supplier selection, shared green distribution centers (DCs), inventory positioning, multimodal transportation planning, and dynamic pricing decisions under competitive and cooperative interactions among firms. The proposed framework explicitly integrates logistics infrastructure sharing, transportation mode selection, and carbon-compliance mechanisms to support efficient freight operations across multiple distribution echelons and market channels. A bi-level game-theoretic optimization model is developed in which firms simultaneously determine strategic network configuration, logistics collaboration, carbon-compliance decisions, and channel-specific pricing policies. The upper-level captures strategic interactions through a generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) framework, whereas the lower level determines firm-level operational decisions under capacity, demand, and emission constraints, including carbon tax and cap-and-trade mechanisms. Building upon this supply chain network design foundation, the model evaluates three strategic interaction regimes. Non-cooperation (NC), full cooperation (COOP), and a novel hybrid competitive–cooperative (HYB) setting in which firms share logistics infrastructure and environmental investments while retaining pricing autonomy in downstream markets. This hybrid coopetitive structure, largely absent from the supply chain network design literature, enables firms to exploit logistics synergies while preserving competitive incentives. To solve the resulting multi-level mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem, a master–oracle solution architecture is developed that combines Logic-Based Benders with Equilibrium Oracles (LBB-EO) and Dual-Calibrated Equilibrium Cuts (DCEC). The framework is validated through a real-world consumer electronics supply chain case study that incorporates empirical demand data, carbon-pricing benchmarks, and logistics infrastructure constraints. Results demonstrate that the HYB maximizes profit in typical parity/competition settings by monetizing service gains while exploiting pooled logistics. Furthermore, COOP is most robust when rail is scarce, quotas bind, or parity tightens, achieving the smallest profit drawdowns and deeper abatement at low marginal cost. Sensitivity analyses reveal that service- and carbon-aligned levers (higher service weight, lead-time penalties, rail capacity, and green-DC effectiveness) shift flows from fragmented trucking to consolidated rail via the shared hub, lowering operating costs and emissions with smooth, monotone responses.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Trade-in strategy: the impact of strategic consumers on competitive supply chains
Authors: Tao Jiang, Kaigeng Shen, Youwei Guo, Xingzheng Lu
Abstract: Advancements in data technology enable firms to collect consumer purchase history data on a broader scale. This not only facilitates the recycling of old products (trade-in programs) but also supports the implementation of behavior-based pricing (BBP) using historical data to boost sales of new products. However, this has also intensified competition among firms. This paper constructs a two-period dynamic pricing model to examine the interactive effects of BBP and cross-brand trade-in strategies under different closed-loop supply chain channel structures. The research findings reveal changes in trade-in rebate, product prices, channel member profits, consumer surplus, and social welfare. We find that, first, BBP may either intensify or alleviate competition in trade-in rebate schemes. Second, firms adopting uniform pricing (UP) should implement price increases in the second period, while those adopting BBP should adopt price decreases to counter competition. Third, UP generates greater total supply chain profits, while BBP consistently increases consumer surplus; however, BBP leads to inferior social welfare. Finally, we extended the model in six dimensions. Finally, we extended the model in six dimensions to capture more realistic competitive scenarios and test the robustness of key findings. These extensions include asymmetric channel structures, salvage values of old products, consumer switching costs, discount factors, consumer retention of old products, and market partial coverage. This work provides some theoretical insights for government agencies in developing a competition regulatory framework that balances firm profits and consumer welfare.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: The role of expressway roadside rest areas in truck arrival behaviors at ports with truck appointment system
Authors: Ying Jiang, Fengqian Guo, Zhiming Lin, Huanyu Yang, Linghan Zhang
Abstract: The Truck Appointment System (TAS) has emerged as an effective management strategy for mitigating congestion at container ports. However, existing studies have rarely examined TAS-induced behavioral adjustments among truck drivers, particularly changes in their use of expressway roadside rest areas. To address this research gap, this study investigates how different TAS time-window settings influence truck drivers’ use of en-route service facilities, including rest areas, restrooms, dining services, and refueling stations, during trips to a port. The empirical analysis results of Colombo Port truck arrival data show that TAS implementation can stabilize both rest-area utilization and port-gate arrival rates. A series of agent-based simulation experiments were conducted to investigate changes in container truck drivers’ time-use behavior at rest areas and their subsequent arrival behavior at port gates under various scenarios. Additionally, TAS effectively influences the utilization of roadside rest areas, highlighting the underdevelopment issues of truck service facilities in Sri Lanka. The simulated utilization of service facilities is highest for restrooms, followed by rest areas and refueling stations, whereas dining facilities are used less frequently. The results also indicate that a one-hour appointment window provides the most effective performance among the tested scenarios for the case-study port. When the TAS time window is shorter than two hours, its impacts on rest-area operations should be explicitly considered. These findings provide theoretical and practical insights into the coordination of port appointment policies and expressway rest-area infrastructure planning, and demonstrate how TAS can influence both en-route facility utilization patterns and external container truck arrival dynamics at port gates.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: An analytical heterogeneous agent macro model of concentration, markups, and falling labour shares
Authors: Karsten Kohler, Jo Michell, Ayoze Alfageme
Abstract: This paper presents a small-scale analytical heterogeneous agent model (HAM) to explore firm concentration dynamics and the aggregate effects on distribution and growth. It contributes to recent work on tractable macroeconomic agent-based models (ABMs) by comparing two versions of the model: an ABM with bilateral firm-customer matching, and a simplified HAM without direct agent interaction. The HAM replicates key ABM results while allowing for analytical solutions. The model captures how pricing, investment, and market concentration evolve at the micro level and affect macro-level outcomes. Firms differ in capital size and market share. Larger firms benefit from lower unit costs due to economies of scale, gain larger market shares, and charge higher markups. At the same time, customers seek lower prices, creating competitive pressure. These mechanisms drive endogenous changes in the firm size distribution. More profitable firms temporarily grow faster, leading to concentration of capital, market shares, and markups. These dynamics lead to right-skewed distributions, producing a divergence between the average profit share across firms and the aggregate profit share, which is driven up by the biggest firms. The fall in the labour share reduces consumption and slows down growth. Despite its simplicity, the model captures key empirical patterns related to superstar firms and declining labour shares.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Introduction to the special issue on market power: A search-theoretic approach
Authors: Sephorah Mangin, Nicolas Petrosky-Nadeau, Petr Sedlacek, Shengxing Zhang

Title: Climate justice: Historical accountability vs. international Paretianism
Authors: Hyunwoo Hong, Biung-Ghi Ju
Abstract: We examine two principles of allocative justice in the climate agreement - historical accountability (Neumayer, 2000) and international Paretianism, IP (Posner and Weisbach, 2010). The former requires that a country’s emissions rights be limited by its historical (emissions) debt. The latter is forward-looking and requires that the agreement should not make any country worse off. The international protocols satisfying historical accountability impose drastically greater burdens on advanced countries in Europe and North America than the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement. Interestingly, the protocol supported by IP, despite being forward-looking and supposedly more favorable to advanced countries, also demands significant emissions reductions from them—often even more than the equal per capita allocation. This finding counters Posner and Weisbach’s earlier IP-based argument against the Kyoto Protocol (and the equal per capita rule).

Title: Assessing the public charging serviceability for electric vehicles: an accessibility-based approach
Authors: Yuzheng Xie, Wenying Ji
Abstract: This study proposes a serviceability assessment framework for public electric vehicle charging infrastructure (EVCI) that evaluates tract-level supply–demand gaps using charging miles per public-charging-dependent electric vehicle (EV) per day. In this framework, user exposure to reachable charging opportunities is estimated using a customized Gaussian two-step floating catchment area accessibility model that incorporates mobility-informed spatial competition. This exposure is then converted into a physically interpretable serviceability metric to provide a planning-level indicator of the estimated balance between accessible public charging service and expected charging demand. A case study in Arlington, Alexandria, and Falls Church, Virginia, USA, shows strong sensitivity to detour tolerance, with the median gap shifting from 4.54 under a 5-minute detour to − 4.45 under a 15-minute detour. Cross-scenario diagnosis indicates three decision-relevant deficit drivers: sparse supply presence in residential and suburban tracts, throughput limitations in mixed-use activity centers, and competition-sensitive coupling effects along major corridors under expanded reachability.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Have inputs been substituted for each other? Nonparametric tests for factor substitution in banking data envelopment analysis
Authors: Darold T Barnum
Abstract: ABSTRACT Standard Data Envelopment Analysis radial models such as CCR and BCC assume that inputs are substituted for each other along the efficiency frontier. However, this assumption is rarely verified empirically, creating the risk of specification bias if factors are not substituted. This paper introduces a nonparametric testing protocol to determine whether inputs have, in fact, been substituted for each other along the efficiency frontier. It employs Local Weighted Quantile Regression to estimate the partial derivatives of the input frontier directly from the data, classifying input pairs as substitutes or non-substitutes based on the sign and statistical significance of the estimated frontier slopes. The methodology is illustrated using Monte Carlo simulations of known substitute and non-substitute technologies. When applied to 2,534 U.S. commercial banks, the protocol finds no evidence of substitution for any input pair: 13 of 15 specifications classify the inputs as non-substitutes that increase and decrease together, and the remaining two yield positive but imprecisely estimated slopes. The paper then shows that applying the standard CCR model to the bank data results in substantial biases in bank efficiency scores. Finally, the paper identifies models that have been used to account for fixed proportion technologies.

Title: What works in digital transformation for agro-industry? Evidence from meso-institutional governance in the tomato value chain
Authors: Maria Teresa Cappella, Eleonora Sofia Rossi, Emanuele Blasi
Affiliations: University of Tuscia Department for the Innovation in Biological, Agro-food and Forestry Systems, , Viterbo
Abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine behavioural and organisational factors influencing farmers’ acceptance of digital farming technologies within hybrid agri-food chains. Focusing on the Italian processed tomato supply chain, it analyses how producer organisations (POs) combine technical, contractual and relational governance to foster decision support systems (DSS) adoption. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on the technology acceptance model and supply chain governance theory, the study integrates two analytical strands: (i) survey data from 260 tomato producers analysed through two parallel structural equation models distinguishing DSS users from non-users; and (ii) a structured descriptive-comparative analysis of existing contracts and farmers’ preferred contractual clauses, following a sequential explanatory logic linking behavioural profiles to governance expectations. Findings Results reveal clear asymmetries between adopters and non-adopters. For non-users, adoption intention is driven by perceived support and peer influence; for users, ease of use and attitude explain continued utilisation. Contractual preferences diverge correspondingly: non-users prioritise minimum-price guarantees, while users favour quality-based incentives and multiannual commitments. Originality/value Methodologically, two parallel SEMs identify stage-dependent adoption mechanisms typically obscured in pooled applications. Analytically, combining behavioural modelling with contractual governance analysis links adoption profiles to heterogeneous governance preferences, offering actionable insights for designing differentiated contractual bundles and support systems aligned with farmers’ heterogeneous risk profiles.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: Integrated construction scheme and critical path search for scheduling with reentrant and skippable operations in real-world hybrid flowshop
Authors: Xueteng Zhang, Xuchu Jiang, Biao Zhang, Hongyan Sang, Leilei Meng
Affiliations: Liaocheng University; Zhongnan University of Economics and Law
Abstract: This paper investigates a complex scheduling problem originating from real-world pharmaceutical workshops, characterised by the coexistence of reentrant and skippable operations, which we define as the hybrid flowshop scheduling problem with reentrant and skippable operations (HFSP_RAS). The core challenge lies in effectively handling cross-stage operational dependencies, along with strict machine cleaning and transfer time constraints. To accurately capture these complex industrial constraints and to provide highly effective exact benchmarks, two mathematical models are developed: a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model and a Constraint Programming (CP) model. Considering the demand for real-time computational efficiency in modern manufacturing, we further develop a heuristic approach that integrates a Construction Scheme (CS) and Critical Path Search (CPS), named CS-CPS. Specifically, the CS adopts a dual-job encoding and a two-phase active decoding mechanism to generate high-quality initial schedules. The CPS further improves the solutions by introducing a critical-path-based search and a neighbourhood pruning strategy. This paper compares the CS-CPS with the MILP and CP models, constructive heuristics, and metaheuristics. The results demonstrate that the proposed CS-CPS, while bridging the computational gap of exact solvers, consistently outperforms the compared algorithms in terms of solution quality and stability. Finally, validation based on real-world production data further confirms its superiority.

Title: On the use of large language models for methods-time measurement
Authors: Gurhan Ceylan, Haluk Yapicioglu, Martin Benter, Constantin Eckart, Peter Kuhlang
Affiliations: Eskişehir Technical University; MTM Institute, MTM Association e. V.
Abstract: Manual operations remain a significant part of modern manufacturing, maintaining the role of Methods-Time Measurement (MTM) as a framework for improving productivity and standardising work processes. Despite its usefulness, conducting MTM analysis is a labour intensive task requiring specialised expertise. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) provide a promising path for streamlining MTM analysis. This study establishes a performance baseline for LLMs in this domain by assessing their capabilities when provided with meticulously detailed work descriptions and a comprehensive MTM knowledge base. To this end, we evaluated the analyses generated by DeepSeek-V3.2-reasoner, GPT-5.2-pro, Gemini-2.5-pro, and Qwen3-14B by comparing them against expert-validated ground truths across eleven working scenarios. Our findings suggest that LLMs can accurately perform MTM analysis when supplied with detailed work descriptions and domain knowledge. GPT-5.2-pro and Gemini-2.5-pro proved especially capable, perfectly analysing five and six scenarios, respectively, across ten experimental runs. Despite this success, challenges remain when tasks involve subtle rule applications or steps that are implied rather than stated. Although LLMs significantly reduce analysis time and effort, expert validation remains critical for reliable deployment. These results demonstrate the viability of LLMs as assistive tools for MTM practitioners.

Title: Live-streaming commerce, streamer influence, and channel strategy
Authors: Haiying Yang, Zhuang Qian, Zhengping Wu
Affiliations: RiderUniversity; Pennsylvania State University; Syracuse University
Abstract: Live-streaming commerce has emerged as a significant and powerful sales force. This new type of commerce enables consumers to engage in real-time interactions while making purchases over the Internet. An increasing number of companies, especially small and medium-sized enterprises, have adopted live-streaming commerce to attract and engage consumers. Our study investigates the supplier's optimal strategy in response to the fast-growing live-streaming commerce and explores the most effective way to collaborate with third-party livestreamers. We first analyze the impacts of inter-channel cannibalisation upon introducing the new live-streaming channel and find that suppliers should stay with the traditional online channel unless the live-streaming channel can increase the market size significantly. We then assess suppliers' choice in live-streaming mode: self-streaming versus collaborating with professional livestreamers. Our results suggest that collaboration is more profitable only if the third-party livestreamers have a substantial edge in influence level compared to self-streaming. Our analysis also explains the scenario in which suppliers initially choose to sell products through the third-party live-streaming channel but later decide to switch back to self-streaming.

Title: Unpacking the process of production relocation: a longitudinal case study
Authors: Yang Cheng, Ruihong Gao, Zheng Liu
Affiliations: Department of Materials and Production, Aalborg University; School of Business Administration, Jiangxi University of Finance and Economics; Department of Business Administration, Osaka University of Economics; Greenwich Business School, University of Greenwich
Abstract: With the trend of globalisation, manufacturing companies configure their supply networks and transfer production facilities from one location to another. Whilst current literature mainly focuses on factors affecting production relocations, less is known about the implementation process which contains evolving activities across manufacturing and supply levels. In this paper, we ask the following research question: How do firms implement their production relocation process, when considering the impacts of manufacturing and supply networks? Through a longitudinal case study of a manufacturing company in Taiwan, we develop a process-oriented framework with five phases, namely preparation, manufacturing network relocation, supply network relocation, network development, and network integration. Our study further highlights the interdependent connection between manufacturing networks and supply networks. The study provides guidance to companies which are involved in production relocation decisions in the changing international business context.

Title: The Transmission of Macroprudential Policy in the Tails: Evidence From a Narrative Approach
Authors: Álvaro Fernández‐Gallardo, Simon Lloyd, Ed Manuel
Affiliations: Banco de España Madrid Spain; Bank of England London UK; London School of Economics London UK
Abstract: ABSTRACT We estimate the causal effects of macroprudential policies on the entire distribution of GDP growth for advanced European economies using a narrative‐identification strategy in a quantile‐regression framework. While macroprudential policy has near‐zero effects on the center of the GDP‐growth distribution, tighter policy brings benefits by reducing the variance of future growth, significantly boosting the left tail while simultaneously reducing the right. Assessing a range of channels through which these effects materialize, we find that macroprudential policy particularly operates through ‘credit‐at‐risk’: it reduces the right tail of future credit growth, dampening booms, in turn reducing the likelihood of extreme GDP‐growth outturns.

Title: The Autoregressive Inverse‐Wishart Multivariate Stochastic Volatility Model and Its Factor Extension
Authors: Xin Jin
Affiliations: School of Economics Shanghai University of Finance and Economics Shanghai China; Key Laboratory of Mathematical Economics (SUFE), Ministry of Education Shanghai China
Abstract: ABSTRACT Despite its conceptual appeal, the autoregressive inverse‐Wishart (AIW) multivariate stochastic volatility model has been hindered by inefficient sampling methods. The existing samplers for the latent covariance matrix severely suffer from the curse of dimensionality and only work when the dimension is very low. In this paper, we introduce a new proposal for the latent covariance matrix in the AIW model, which demonstrates far better scalability. We introduce different extensions to the basic AIW model that capture various stylized volatility features. We further fit the AIW model into a factor structure and provide an a posteriori identification procedure without introducing order dependence. When evaluated using real datasets ranging from 10 assets to 1000 assets, the new AIW‐based models, whether the standalone versions or the factor versions, are especially suited for multivariate volatility modeling in a wide range of dimensions.

Title: An explainable FRAM–AHP–XAI framework for semiconductor supply chain risk under rare earth dependencies
Authors: Massimiliano Ferrara, Valeria Isgrò
Abstract: The global semiconductor supply chain faces unprecedented risks driven by geopolitical tensions, rare earth element (REE) concentration, and technological dependencies. This paper develops a comprehensive theoretical and empirical framework for supply chain risk management in the semiconductor industry by integrating the Functional Resonance Analysis Method (FRAM), the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP), and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). The framework is designed for decision-making under conditions of geopolitical fragmentation, where supply concentration, export control regimes, and industrial policy interventions, such as the United States CHIPS and Science Act and the European Critical Raw Materials Act, jointly shape the strategic space available to manufacturers, policymakers, and regulators. We introduce two theoretical results, the Geopolitical Concentration Risk Propagation Theorem , which formalizes how supply concentration amplifies systemic risk through the supply chain network, and the Rare Earth Criticality Equilibrium Theorem , which establishes conditions for stable multi-sourcing strategies under export control uncertainty. The framework is validated using real-world data from the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), the International Energy Agency (IEA), and the Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA), covering the period 2020–2024. The empirical analysis is built on a curated dataset of 15 critical minerals across 47 countries, with clearly specified training and out-of-sample validation partitions, and risk-prediction accuracy metrics aligned with the supply chain risk management literature. The framework achieves a 34% improvement in risk prediction accuracy compared with traditional AHP-based approaches, and SHAP-based explanations ensure transparency of the resulting policy guidance, with LIME-SHAP agreement exceeding 92% across the test scenarios considered. The findings provide actionable insights for navigating the increasingly fragmented semiconductor landscape while embedding rare earth dependencies, low-carbon transition needs, and trade policy dynamics into a single, interpretable decision architecture.

Title: A Bayesian-reinforcement learning approach for maintenance optimization under usage and maintenance heterogeneity
Authors: Siqi Qin, Xiujie Zhao, Le Gao, Min Zhang
Abstract: Maintenance is critical to ensuring the reliability of industrial systems. In practice, diverse customer usage habits lead to significant variations in system degradation paths, while the heterogeneity of maintenance personnel can also significantly impact maintenance outcomes. In this paper, we introduce a Bayesian-reinforcement learning framework to optimize maintenance policies by accounting for both customer and maintenance heterogeneity. The framework leverages sequential Bayesian inference for real time parameter updates and reinforcement learning to dynamically adjust maintenance actions, balancing exploration and exploitation. The purpose of balancing exploration is to collect more data to enhance parameter estimation accuracy. Numerical examples illustrate that increased data collection enhances parameter accuracy, and maintenance costs also tend to converge. Sensitivity analysis reveals that accurate prior information is crucial for policy convergence speed. Moreover, the optimal maintenance policy is more sensitive to maintenance costs than repair effects, emphasizing the importance of cost considerations in maintenance decision making.

Title: Global and regional long-term climate forecasts: A heterogeneous future
Authors: María Dolores Gadea-Rivas, Jesús Gonzalo
Abstract: Climate is inherently a long-term phenomenon, and reliable long-term forecasts are essential for designing effective mitigation and adaptation policies, assessing climate risk, and guiding the green transition. This paper proposes a simple methodology for generating long-term temperature density forecasts from observational data, using the realized-quantile framework of Gadea and Gonzalo (2020). By treating unconditional quantiles as time-series objects, we move beyond traditional mean-based projections and provide forecasts of the full temperature distribution. The method relies on an out-of-sample model competition and combines Pareto-superior forecasts to reduce dependence on a single model and improve robustness. Importantly, it explicitly allows for heterogeneous warming patterns across time, space, and quantiles. The resulting regional density forecasts reveal spatial disparities and asymmetric effects that are obscured in average temperature projections. Our findings highlight the need for climate agreements and policy evaluation to focus on the entire temperature distribution, rather than relying exclusively on the mean.

Title: The Teacher and the Test? an Analysis of the Short and Long‐Run Predictive Power of Achievement Indicators
Authors: Lex Borghans, Ron Diris, Trudie Schils
Affiliations: Department of Macro, International and Labor Economics (MILE) Maastricht University Maastricht the Netherlands; IZA Institute of Labor Economics Bonn Germany; Department of Economics Leiden University Leiden the Netherlands
Abstract: ABSTRACT Test scores provide objective indicators of student achievement, but are argued to neglect certain skills. Teacher assessments, conversely, are subjective but typically designed to provide a more holistic evaluation of student potential. Combining survey and administrative data for the Netherlands, we estimate the predictive power of test scores and teacher assessments measured at age 12 across the life cycle, and analyse what this predictive power reflects. We find that the non‐overlapping predictive power of both indicators is strong. While the predictive power of the teacher assessment is partially driven by socio‐economic bias, self‐fulfilling prophecy effects and, especially, test measurement error, we find that it also captures productive skills that tests do not.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Who Benefits From the Assignment of Homework?
Authors: Darragh Flannery, Dónal Palcic, Jose G. Clavel
Affiliations: Department of Economics, Kemmy Business School University of Limerick Limerick Ireland; Department of Quantitative Methods University of Murcia Murcia Spain
Abstract: ABSTRACT We examine the relationship between the assignment of homework and student achievement among 8th grade students across 23 countries using the TIMSS 2019 dataset. Exploiting within‐student, between‐subject variation in homework assignment, we find a small but statistically significant positive relationship between homework and achievement. This benefit is driven primarily by the frequency with which homework is assigned rather than its volume. Heterogeneity analyses suggest larger benefits for students with more highly qualified or more experienced teachers, while effects are broadly uniform across the performance distribution except among particularly weak students. We also document substantial cross‐country variability in these estimated effects.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Mean-Field Games of Speedy Information Access with Observation Costs
Authors: Dirk Becherer, Christoph Reisinger, Jonathan Tam
Affiliations: Institute of Mathematics, Humboldt Universität zu Berlin, 10099 Berlin, Germany; Mathematical Institute, University of Oxford, Oxford OX2 6GG, United Kingdom
Abstract: We investigate mean-field games (MFG) in which agents actively control their speed of access to information. Specifically, the agents can dynamically decide to obtain observations with reduced delay by accepting higher observation costs. Agents seek to exploit their active information acquisition by making further decisions to influence their state dynamics so as to maximise rewards. In a mean-field equilibrium, each generic agent solves individually a partially observed Markov decision problem in which the way partial observations are obtained is itself subject to dynamic control actions, whereas no agent can improve unilaterally given the actions of all others. We formulate the mean-field game with controlled costly information access as an equivalent standard mean-field game on an augmented space by utilising a parameterisation of the belief state by a finite number of variables. With sufficient entropy regularisation, a fixed-point iteration converges to the unique MFG equilibrium. Moreover, we derive an approximate [Formula: see text]-Nash equilibrium for a large but finite population size and small regularisation parameter. We illustrate our (extended) MFG of information access and of controls by an example from epidemiology, where medical testing results can be procured at different speeds and costs. Funding: J. Tam is supported by the EPSRC Centre for Doctoral Training in Mathematics of Random Systems: Analysis, Modelling and Simulation [Grant EP/S023925/1]. D. Becherer is supported by German Science Foundation DFG and Berlin-Oxford IRTG 2544, “Stochastic Analysis in Interaction” [Grant 41020858] and acknowledges funding by DFG - CRC/TRR 388, “Rough Analysis, Stochastic Dynamics and Related Fields” [Grant 516748464]. This work was also supported by the EPSRC Centre for Doctoral Training in Mathematics of Random Systems [Grant 2269738].

Title: Sustainable and inclusive wellbeing governance: Reinventing democracy after the crisis
Authors: Robert Costanza, Roberto De Vogli, Sandrine Dixson-Decléve, Lorenzo Fioramonti, Enrico Giovannini, Ida Kubiszewski, Hunter Lovins, Jacqueline McGlade, Lars Fogh Mortensen, Kate E. Pickett, Kristín Vala Ragnarsdóttir, Stewart Wallis, Richard Wilkinson
Abstract: Despite decades of advances in sustainability science, global progress on climate change, biodiversity loss, inequality, and human wellbeing remains dangerously inadequate. While these failures are often attributed to insufficient political will or contested knowledge, we argue that a more fundamental constraint lies in how collective decisions are made. Contemporary governance systems are increasingly shaped by concentrated economic and political power, undermining their capacity to act in the collective interest and to pursue long-term sustainability goals. At the same time, there is growing evidence that citizens broadly support transformative policies aimed at sustainable and inclusive wellbeing. We argue that governance design itself has become a critical leverage point for sustainability transitions. For example, deliberative democracy offers an alternative by representing shared societal values and goals through randomly selected citizens' assemblies. Such assemblies operate independently of partisan and special-interest control and have demonstrated success at several scales. Advances in communication technology now make their broad application increasingly feasible. In parallel, new decision-making methods, such as sociocracy, emphasise consent over majority rule and provide tools to reduce polarization and foster inclusive agreements within deliberative processes. Viewed historically, today's governance challenges resemble recurrent crises and may offer a critical opening to adopt more sustainable and inclusive forms of governance, grounded in deliberation, consent, and collective wellbeing.

Title: Indiscriminate barriers: The trade effects of due diligence policies in global timber markets
Authors: Valentin Mathieu, Clément Nedoncelle
Abstract: This paper offers the first comprehensive assessment of the trade effects of due diligence policies (e.g., the U.S. Lacey Act and the EU Timber Regulation) which are motivated by concerns over illegal logging in global timber markets. We use a structural gravity model with global timber trade data from 2000 to 2021 to estimate the impact of these regulations, differentiating effects based on an exporter’s risk profile and product type. We find that these policies act as a significant non-tariff barrier. Crucially, this deterrent effect is indiscriminate: we find no evidence that high-risk exporters are more constrained than compliant, low-risk exporters. This suggests that the substantial compliance costs and procedural barriers limit trade for all suppliers. We also show that these policies most strongly affect raw and lightly processed timber. Counterfactual simulations confirm that a risk-targeted policy–one that restricts due diligence obligations to high-risk exporters–could preserve overall trade volumes while effectively shifting sourcing away from risky suppliers. Our findings offer timely insights for global trade and environmental policy design, highlighting the need for refined, risk-calibrated mechanisms in emerging regulations such as the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR).

Title: Impossibility theorem for two-tier electoral systems
Authors: Sebastian Tim Holdum, Frederik Ravn Klausen
Abstract: Abstract Two-tier electoral systems aim to balance regional representation and proportionality. Recently, the mathematical mechanisms of several Northern European two-tier systems have been challenged by increasing political party fragmentation, as evidenced by the expanding German parliament and the majority-deciding disproportionality of Denmark’s 2022 election. Regionality, proportionality, and two-tier systems are defined mathematically and used to identify the common cause behind these developments through the formulation of an impossibility theorem: no electoral system with fixed parliament size can guarantee both proportional and geographic representation. Finally, a new algorithm, geographically ranked guaranteed proportionality , is proposed to circumvent the impossibility theorem.

Title: Research on China's new energy vehicles industry chain game under tariff uncertainty
Authors: Yanxin Liu, Haoyu Wang, Xin Cai
Abstract: As geopolitical risks continue to escalate, the new energy vehicle (NEV) industry chain has become increasingly exposed to tariff shocks across multiple segments. This study develops a three-party dynamic game model based on international market game, incorporating four tariff scenarios and five bargaining power settings to analyze firms' optimal strategies. The results show that the combination of low costs for integrated firms and high costs for final product firm can generate a win–win outcome for domestic firms. Bargaining power exerts a positive effect on the prices of intermediate goods, and such effects vary distinctly under different game structures. Under the output sequential game, stronger bargaining power benefits integrated firms while reducing downstream firms’ profits. In contrast, under the price simultaneous game, stronger bargaining power benefits the profits of all firms increase simultaneously. From the perspective of national profits, the optimal strategy under the output sequential game is characterized by low tariffs, high final product costs, and low bargaining power, whereas the price simultaneous game favors high tariffs, low intermediate product costs, and high bargaining power. Although cost declines of foreign firms tend to erode the profit levels of domestic firms, excessively high tariffs can yield localization-related benefits. These findings suggest that tariff and bargaining strategies could be adjusted according to different game structures to improve domestic industrial competitiveness.

Title: Limited awareness and message feasibility in cheap talk
Authors: Zhonghao Shui, Beiqing Cui, Jian Wu
Abstract: This note studies how limited awareness affects cheap talk through message feasibility. A receiver is already aware of a new state, while the sender may be unable to formulate the associated message. We characterize monotone informative equilibria in a three-state game where the sender becomes aware of the new state with an exogenous probability before observing the payoff-relevant state. Prior awareness partially restores the common-awareness mimicking constraint. The new-state message may identify the payoff-relevant state, combine state and awareness information, or remain informative by revealing the sender's awareness even when it no longer identifies the state.

Title: Climate shocks, attitudes towards intimate partner violence, and the protective role of climate-resilience projects
Authors: Amanda Guimbeau, Xinde James Ji, Nidhiya Menon
Abstract: This study investigates the impact of climate change on intimate partner violence attitudes in Bangladesh and shows that policy can mitigate much, if not all, of the harmful consequences of climate shocks on women. Utilizing a novel dataset linking geo-referenced meteorological data with information on women’s attitudes, we find that dry shocks increase tolerance for intimate partner violence among women in poor and agriculture-dependent communities, with suggestive evidence that this happens due to the erosion of women’s outside options. Distributed-lag estimates show that these effects persist beyond the immediate period of exposure, consistent with a gradual weakening of women’s fallback positions rather than a purely short-run stress-induced or backlash response. Climate resilience projects funded by the Bangladesh Climate Change Trust (BCCT), a domestic climate fund, mitigate the negative impacts of dry shocks, highlighting the significant role of such initiatives in generating positive ameliorative spillover effects. Remotely sensed data on land use and crop-yield indicators reveal that these projects protect agriculture during dry shocks, especially in the rainfed Aman season, thus providing a credible test of the importance of the agricultural transmission channel and the pathway through which such projects buffer climate shocks. Our findings underline the crucial role of targeted policies in fostering climate adaptation.

Title: Resilient hybrid air-ground networks for disaster preparedness and response: A distributionally robust approach
Authors: Hengxing Zhao, Zijian Zhao, Pengcheng You
Abstract: Disaster relief operations are frequently paralyzed by substantial network failures that sever access to affected regions during the critical “golden period”. While traditional logistics rely on ground transport and strategic airlift, their effectiveness can be compromised by correlated infrastructure collapse or airport bottlenecks. We develop a resilient network design framework that jointly optimizes facility location, inventory pre-positioning, contingent strategic- and tactical-air capacity, and supporting charging investment for tactical air operations. Motivated by the prohibitive ownership costs of such assets, we model the acquisition of tactical capacity (eVTOLs) through contingent contracts, enabling a flexible response. The problem is formulated as a two-stage distributionally robust optimization model with a Wasserstein ambiguity set to hedge against joint uncertainty in demand and road connectivity under limited data. This ambiguity structure preserves empirical joint-scenario information and leads to an exact decomposition scheme based on sample-wise evaluation blocks. Computational experiments on the Yushu earthquake and the U.S. hurricane season show that the preferred portfolio depends strongly on disruption topology. In Yushu, the robust solution shifts toward tactical bypass capability, and the tactical layer acts as a lifeline bridge when road fragmentation blocks access. In the hurricane case, overall portfolio scale changes less, while inventory and airlift are repositioned across the regional network; there the tactical layer plays a supporting redistribution role within a broader air-ground architecture.
