Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Timing the vaccine flow: An intelligent navigator for strategic delivery and coverage
Authors: Mahsa Mohammadi, Mohsen Roytvand Ghiasvand, Babak Mohamadpour Tosarkani
Abstract: The unprecedented impacts of the COVID-19 outbreak have increased global interest in secure and efficient vaccine distribution. This study investigates the challenges of planning vaccine distribution, including demand fluctuations, limited data availability, and inequitable access to vaccines. It focuses on the allocation of vaccines to mobile and stationary Public Health Units (PHUs) and the management of demand through online registration and real-time updates. To address these challenges, we develop a data-driven Decision Support Framework (DSF) comprising a data-based and a model-based framework. The data-based framework introduces an augmented robust optimization approach that uses dynamic uncertainty sets to adapt to changing conditions. Two data generation algorithms, integrated with predictive analytics, enhance limited data, improve out-of-sample performance, and increase the explainability of robust solutions. These uncertainty sets are fed into the model-based framework, which integrates three mathematical models to dynamically configure PHUs and optimize the vaccination distribution plan. As a conceptual contribution, a new policy is proposed to maximize coverage through a Dynamic PHU Allocation (DPA) algorithm that updates mobile PHU locations. Additionally, an assignment model reallocates surplus inventory to address shortages and ensures proper storage for future use. The numerical results demonstrate that the proposed DSF enables adaptive decision-making, effectively coping with fluctuations in vaccination demand and reducing vaccination shortages by 80% compared to other approaches. The adaptability of the DSF, combined with the role of mobile PHUs in managing demand fluctuations and ensuring equitable access, offers insights for resource allocation and logistical planning in uncertain scenarios.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Seismic resilience assessment and multi‑phase optimization method of regional road networks for earthquake rescue
Authors: Yue Su, Xiushi Dong, Hongjun Cui, Minqing Zhu, Xinwei Ma, Weijie Yu
Abstract: High-resilience road networks are critical for improving rescue efficiency and reducing seismic losses. Existing studies have proposed effective seismic resilience assessment and optimization methods for single phases (pre-earthquake, during-earthquake, post-earthquake). However, the improvement mechanism and effectiveness of multi‑phase resilience optimization framework remain understudied, which limits the construction of high‑resilience road networks. In this context, this study proposes a seismic resilience assessment and multi‑phase optimization method of regional road networks for earthquake rescue. Firstly, a multi–state damage model of road networks is developed by considering complex topological connected relations and multi–state damage characteristics of road components. Then, a probabilistic method is proposed for multi-state road network performance evaluation. This performance is quantified via total travel time for rescue demand. After that, a resilience assessment framework encompassing resistance, adaptation, and recovery capacities is established by linking the rescue process to network performance. Based on this framework, a multi–phase resilience optimization model is formulated to maximize expected resilience under seismic uncertainty by integrating pre–earthquake reinforcing, during–earthquake monitoring, and post–earthquake repairing strategies. Finally, the proposed method is demonstrated using a real regional road network and more than 300,000 simulated scenarios. Under consistent cost constraints, the resilience improvement effect of the multi–phase combined optimization strategy is significantly better than any single–phase strategies. Crucially, the resilience improvement of this combined optimization strategy proves robust across diverse uncertain scenarios. This system–level resilience improvement can be explained by complementary and distinct improvement mechanisms associated with each phase. This provides theoretical and methodological support for planning high–resilience road networks and multi–phase resilience optimization strategy.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: The gender dimension of refugees’ integration in the labor market
Authors: Tobias Müller, Pia Pannatier, Martina Viarengo
Abstract: This paper examines the gender differences in labor market integration among refugees and their determinants. It focuses on a longitudinal dataset that covers the entire refugee population in Switzerland over 20 years. During the period examined, the majority of refugees came from low-income economies in Africa and Asia. The quasi-random allocation of asylum seekers across Swiss cantons, which differ in their socio-economic characteristics, provides a natural experiment to identify the effects of source country culture and the role of local initial conditions in shaping refugees’ labor-market integration trajectories. Our empirical findings show that women refugees from countries with more conservative gender norms (measured by female-to-male labor force participation ratios and fertility rates) have less favorable labor market outcomes, with these effects varying in their persistence over time. The analysis further reveals the negative role of initial unemployment and the positive role of co-ethnic networks in the cantons of arrival, with these effects varying by gender and network characteristics. Finally, local attitudes toward gender equality reduce the gender gap in labor market outcomes among refugees.

Title: Human-capital formation: The importance of endogenous longevity
Authors: Titus J. Galama, Hans van Kippersluis
Abstract: We present a theory of human capital, with health, skill, and longevity, endogenously determined. Using comparative dynamic analyses and a calibrated version of the theory, we uncover an important economic mechanism driving human-capital formation: whether individuals can influence their longevity. When they can, additional resources are invested in human capital. When they cannot, additional resources are used for consumption and leisure, i.e., “non-productively”. These findings point to the potential importance of endogenous longevity as an economic mechanism driving human-capital formation, and, by extension, human capital-based economic growth.

Title: An equilibrium theory of nominal exchange rates
Authors: Marcus Hagedorn
Abstract: This paper proposes an equilibrium theory of nominal exchange rates, which offers a new perspective on various issues in open economy macroeconomics. The nominal exchange rate and portfolio choices are jointly determined in equilibrium, thus providing a new approach to overcoming the indeterminacy results in Kareken and Wallace (1981). The distinctive features of this theory are that the nominal exchange rate is determined in international financial markets, that the risk premium and UIP deviations are fully endogenous equilibrium objects and that the real exchange rate inherits its properties from the nominal exchange rate. In terms of policy, this novel theory implies that a country with an exchange rate peg and free asset mobility faces a tetralemma and not a trilemma, because it loses not only monetary policy independence but also fiscal policy independence.

Title: Progressing towards efficiency: The role for labor tax progression in reforming social security
Authors: Krzysztof Makarski, Joanna Tyrowicz, Oliwia Komada
Abstract: This paper studies the role for progressive labor income taxation in the context of social security reform. We propose a novel reform that replaces redistributive pensions with a contribution-based system while simultaneously increasing the progressivity of labor income taxation to preserve social insurance. Using a stylized model, we show that the benefit of such reform is derived from the Frisch elasticity of labor supply. For sufficiently high values, the reform can be fiscally neutral and Pareto-improving. We then evaluate the reform in a full general equilibrium model calibrated to the U.S. economy. Quantitative results on the efficiency-insurance trade-offs are in line with our theoretical predictions. In the steady-state, for plausible values of the Frisch elasticity, the fiscal space generated by increased labor supply is sufficient to compensate through lump-sum transfers the loss of pension-based insurance. These results carry over to transition dynamics: the reform yields a Pareto improvement along the transition path. Our findings highlight the potential for tax-based redistribution to replace pension-based insurance.

Title: Oil shocks & suicide
Authors: Chandler Hubbard, Alexander James, Makenzi Scott
Abstract: We estimate the effect of positive and negative oil shocks on suicide. Using restricted-use, U.S. state-level mortality data, we find that negative shocks increase suicide risk and that positive ones have little effect. Baseline estimates indicate that from 2015 to 2020, the oil bust raised the average suicide rate in the most oil-rich states by roughly 13%. Exploring sources of heterogeneity, effects are largely driven by men and people without college degrees. Results are robust to various modeling decisions and assumptions and are not easily explained by compositional changes. Implications are discussed, especially as they relate to the clean-energy transition and the “resource curse.”

Title: Public data openness and the greening of firms’ energy consumption mix: evidence from China
Authors: Jing Liu, Mingwei Song, Tao Qiao, Qinlin Gong
Abstract: Public data openness has become an increasingly important element of digital governance, yet its implications for firms' energy use remain underexplored. Using a panel of Chinese publicly listed manufacturing firms located in 289 prefecture-level cities from 2011 to 2022, this study examines whether the launch of municipal public data platforms promotes the greening of firms' energy consumption mix. We employ a staggered difference-in-differences design with firm and year fixed effects. The results show that public data openness significantly improves the greenness of firms' energy consumption mix. Subsample analyses yield larger point estimates for firms in cities with high-quality public data openness, for state-owned enterprises, and for firms located in peripheral and non-resource-based cities. Moderation analyses indicate that government environmental policy attention and public environmental concern strengthen this relationship. Exploratory channel analyses provide suggestive evidence that public data openness may promote a greener energy consumption mix by increasing both the output and quality of green technology innovation and by promoting firms' digital transformation. These findings highlight how public data openness can support firms' transition toward cleaner energy use through the joint roles of policy signaling and data provision. They also offer policy insights for developing economies seeking to align digital governance with green-transition objectives, while recognizing that the broader applicability of the findings depends on institutional and developmental conditions.

Title: How does the renewable energy transition affect energy security and equity? Diverging effects in developing and developed countries
Authors: Yiwei Ren, Xunhuan Li, Siyou Xia
Abstract: This study investigates how the renewable energy transition differentially affects energy equity and security in developed versus developing countries. Using two-way fixed effects models and instrumental variable-generalized method of moments (IV-GMM) estimation with panel data for 65 countries over 2000–2023, we analyze the impact of power generation through renewables on five key indicators of energy equity and security. We find that power generation through renewables increases residential electricity prices and reduces electricity self-sufficiency in developed countries, but improves electricity access rates, reduces urban-rural access disparities, lowers residential electricity prices, and enhances energy self-sufficiency in developing countries. Mechanism analysis reveals that these diverging effects operate through distinct transmission channels: intermittency challenges and stranded asset problems in developed countries versus the diversification of power generation in developing countries. Our results suggest that the renewable energy transition weakens energy security and equity in developed countries but enhances energy security and equity in developing countries. This study contributes to the academic debate on the impact of the renewable energy transition on energy security and equity and calls for differentiated policies to ensure a sustainable, reliable, and just energy transition across the world.

Title: How to replace public communication with private one
Authors: Helmuts Āzacis, Péter Vida
Abstract: A sender wants to make a public announcement to three receivers but she cannot. The Byzantine agreement communication protocol (Lamport et al., 1982) prescribes that the sender instead sends the same private message to the receivers who in turn forward to each other the message they have received from the sender. Let the receivers consider the (bitwise) majority of their received messages as a pseudo public message of the sender. We show that this protocol, besides being 1-resilient, substitutes public communication in a very strong sense: every player can consistently believe (Kreps and Wilson, 1982), no matter what messages they have sent or received, that all the receivers hold the same pseudo public message which coincides with the (bitwise) majority of the messages sent by the sender. It follows that the set of sequential equilibrium outcomes of any game (with at least four players) is weakly larger with private communication than with public communication.

Title: Integrated production-distribution scheduling for perishable goods under the aerial–ground cooperative distribution mode
Authors: Feng Wang, Hongguang Bo
Affiliations: Dalian University of Technology

Title: A system-of-systems framework for digital twin-enabled real-time sustainability reporting
Authors: Yujia Luo, Juan Ramón Candia, Peter Ball
Affiliations: York St John University; University of Leeds; University of York
Abstract: The convergence of Industry 5.0 imperatives, sustainability challenges, and compulsory reporting standards necessitate advances in manufacturing analysis. Digital Twins (DTs) enable real-time manufacturing monitoring and optimization, yet remain disconnected from corporate sustainability reporting (SR). This separation restricts leveraging operational data for mandatory disclosures and seeking operational improvements from sustainability reporting insights. DT research has predominantly focused on energy efficiency, with limited attention to broader environmental dimensions. We address this gap by developing a System-of-Systems framework integrating operational DTs with SR requirements. The gap, identified through literature analysis, is confirmed using expert interviews. We identify data mismatches between DT systems with process-level data and SR using periodic, facility-level data. Applying System-of-Systems theory, we develop a four-step framework (Mapping, Matching, Measuring, Modeling) enabling systematic translation between two independent systems. The framework demonstrates how manufacturing systems DTs can both supply and respond to SR outputs. Interview cited examples using a simplified manufacturing system and exemplified SR standard demonstrate applicability. The outcome is a structured approach for integrating DTs to support SR generation, and for SR insights to inform DT-enabled operational scenarios for performance enhancement. The contribution of the DT and SR framework is both to modeling advancement as well as management practice.

Title: Robust human-robot collaborative assembly line balancing problem under task time uncertainty
Authors: Si Hu An, Byung Do Chung
Affiliations: Yonsei University
Abstract: The human–robot collaborative assembly line balancing problem (HRC-ALBP), which incorporates collaborative robots (cobots), has recently garnered considerable attention for its potential to enhance productivity and support efficient, human-centered working environments. However, the natural variability in human task times introduces uncertainty, creating challenges for task assignment in collaborative settings. To address this issue, this study proposes a robust local search genetic–particle swarm optimisation (RGP) algorithm for solving the robust HRC-ALBP under task time uncertainty. The proposed algorithm generates line configurations while mitigating excessive solution conservativeness. Numerical experiments were conducted under task time variability to evaluate the performance of the proposed algorithm. The results verify that the algorithm produces more stable line configurations. Furthermore, sensitivity analyses were performed by varying both the number of cobots and the coefficient of variation of task times. Consequently, assembly lines designed using the RGP algorithm exhibit substantially higher reliability in sustaining uninterrupted production flow. Moreover, these analyses examine the operator assignment strategies required to establish a stable assembly line, depending on the number of cobots and the coefficient of variation of task times. The results indicate that stable assembly line design critically depends on appropriate operator assignment strategies.

Title: Enhancing manufacturing flexibility and efficiency through AMR-facilitated shared robotic arms in extended robotic flow shop
Authors: Qing Zhang, Peiqi Zhuang, Yuhan Yi, Yige Sun, Sai-Ho Chung, Hoi-Lam Ma
Affiliations: Xihua University; The Hong Kong Polytechnic University; The Hang Seng University of Hong Kong
Abstract: The shift to shorter product life cycles and higher customisation demands has made manufacturing flexibility essential. However, the traditional robotic cell production method, equipped with either stationary robotic arms or robotic arms moving along railways, lacks the scalability and reconfigurability to meet volatile demand. Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs) provide a promising alternative. Thus, in this study, to enhance production flexibility and efficiency, we introduce a new feature to the traditional robotic cell scheduling method by introducing shared robotic arms facilitated by AMRs. Specifically, AMRs can serve a set of machines across cells; operations in each job are allowed to be processed in different robotic cells concurrently. Additionally, we propose a simulated annealing-based matheuristic algorithm. In this approach, the mathematical programming technique is embedded into the simulated annealing algorithm to determine the optimal heterogeneous AMR routing (HAR). Computational experiments validate the proposed manufacturing method and reveal its suitability in two scenarios: deployment in a compact production configuration and the processing of heterogeneous jobs with bottleneck operations. The effectiveness of the proposed method primarily stems from its capacity to boost machine utilisation, leading to a considerable decrease in makespan.

Title: Rework as a systemic risk amplifier: Exposure-normalized modeling of safety frequency and severity
Authors: Peter E. D. Love
Affiliations: School of Civil & Mechanical Engineering, Curtin University

Title: Input convex learning-enabled reinforced model predictive control for islanded microgrid operation under extreme conditions
Authors: Di Cao, Yu Liu, Yinfan Wang, Qin Zhang, Weihao Hu
Affiliations: School of Mechanical and Electrical Engineering, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China; Center for System Reliability and Safety, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China; School of Economics and Management, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

Title: Large Datasets for the Euro Area and Its Member Countries and the Dynamic Effects of the Common Monetary Policy
Authors: Matteo Barigozzi, Claudio Lissona, Lorenzo Tonni
Affiliations: Department of Economics University of Bologna Bologna Italy; Department of Economics, Management and Quantitative Methods University of Milan Milan Italy
Abstract: ABSTRACT We introduce EA‐MD‐QD, a new publicly available dataset comprising 1136 macroeconomic time series for the euro area (EA) and its ten largest member countries observed at monthly or quarterly frequency. Since January 2024, EA‐MD‐QD has been updated monthly and continuously revised, providing a valuable resource for policy analysis in the EA. Using EA‐MD‐QD, we study country‐specific impulse responses to an EA‐wide monetary policy shock. Results reveal moderate yet significant cross‐country heterogeneity, with differences between so‐called core countries, such as France and Germany, and peripheral countries, such as Italy and Spain, in their price and interest rate responses, together with meaningful differences in real activity, while stock price responses are relatively homogeneous. Evidence points to homeownership and saving behavior as potential drivers of the observed cross‐country differences.

Title: Effects of climate activism on firm productivity and uncertainty: Evidence from global oil extraction
Authors: Morakinyo O. Adetutu, Anthony J. Glass, Abbi Kedir, Karligash Kenjegalieva
Abstract: We present global microeconometric evidence on the impact of climate advocacy on hydrocarbon production. We construct two panel data sets by first linking climate activist campaigns to several thousand oil fields, which together account for 72% of global production. Second, we use textual analysis of over 140 million words from 1832 annual reports to compute a measure of activism-induced uncertainty for the corporations that control these oil fields. We find robust evidence that climate activism directly reduced not only oil field productivity but also increased company-level uncertainty. By utilising the ownership links between corporations and their oil fields, we also uncover an indirect mechanism in which the initial activism-induced company uncertainty leads to further productivity losses at the field level. Our findings demonstrate the presence of two pathways through which climate advocacy impacts hydrocarbon extraction.

Title: Industrial internet platform–enabled supply chain low-carbon transformation: A two-stage evolutionary game approach
Authors: Xiang Li, Zibo Lin, Yu Cao
Abstract: Climate change mitigation and net-zero targets have increased the pressure on manufacturing supply chains to reduce carbon emissions across organizational boundaries. However, supply-chain-wide low-carbon transformation remains difficult because focal firms have limited governance reach over multi-tier partners, while many small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) face capability and resource constraints. Industrial Internet Platforms (IIPs) provide a potential mechanism for addressing this challenge by transforming localized low-carbon practices into reusable modules and supporting their diffusion across supply chain networks. This study develops a two-stage evolutionary game framework to examine IIP-enabled supply chain low-carbon transformation. Stage I models a tripartite evolutionary game among the IIP, focal firms, and affiliated firms, capturing the joint evolution of low-carbon module construction, focal-firm cooperation, and affiliated-firm transformation. Stage II embeds SMEs in a scale-free network to analyze how the platform capabilities formed in Stage I affect the diffusion of low-carbon modules. The results reveal three main findings. First, stable low-carbon transformation depends on the coordinated formation of platform-enabled capabilities: stronger capability building in Stage I accelerates and stabilizes SME adoption in Stage II, whereas partial cooperation leads only to limited or fragmented transformation. Second, government policies have nonlinear and stage-dependent effects. A coordinated portfolio of subsidies, penalties, and tax incentives can reduce module-construction and transformation costs, thereby promoting the formation of a robust low-carbon capability system. Third, network structure significantly shapes diffusion outcomes. Larger networks provide more redundant diffusion paths and facilitate broader adoption, whereas excessive clustering creates information redundancy and slows convergence. This study contributes to low-carbon supply chain research by linking platform-enabled capability building with network diffusion, extends platform governance research by conceptualizing low-carbon modules as endogenous capabilities, and offers implications for policy design and supply chain management practice.

Title: Application fees and the robustness of Nash equilibria in school choice
Authors: Cyril Rouault
Abstract: We study the robustness of Nash equilibria in the preference revelation game induced by the student-optimal stable mechanism when small application fees are introduced. Assuming lexicographic preferences over outcomes, we show that introducing application fees reduces the set of Nash equilibria, to the detriment of student welfare. We provide a sufficient condition on the distribution of application fees that eliminates any Pareto improvement in which a student strictly benefits from being assigned to a given school. When all application fees are strictly positive for all applications, every Nash equilibrium induces a stable assignment.

Title: Warm-glow bequests and descendant risk
Authors: Rory McGee
Abstract: Reduced-form bequest motives are routinely assumed to exhibit decreasing absolute risk aversion (DARA). I show this is consistent with an underlying altruistic primitive: when descendant risk is unrealised at the bequest choice date, DARA of the warm-glow preference is inherited from the descendant’s continuation value under both multiplicative and additive risk, without parametric restriction. Yet the two canonical specifications differ in what is preserved beyond DARA. Multiplicative risk yields a shifter-weight decomposition and preserves CRRA form; additive income risk—the relevant case for dynastic precautionary savings—preserves DARA but not functional form.

Title: Narrow non-bank financial intermediation and economic growth: does the economic cycle matter?
Authors: Michelle Majid, Akeem Rahaman
Abstract: In this paper, we examine whether the relationship between non-bank financial intermediation (NBFI) and economic growth varies across the economic cycle. While existing studies focus on the average effects of broad measures of NBFI, the effects of the narrow measure of NBFI differing during periods of economic stress is less clear. Using a panel of 26 jurisdictions participating in the Financial Stability Board's NBFI exercise between 2006 and 2024, we find that larger narrow NBFI sectors are associated with higher real GDP growth. However, we find limited evidence that this relationship varies systematically between expansionary and recessionary periods.

Title: Learning from observed matches in two-sided markets
Authors: Suwan (Cheng) Long
Abstract: This paper asks what can be learned from observed merger pairings when acquirers and targets meet in a two-sided market with transferable utility. A compact assignment-game model implies revealed-preference inequalities: observed matches must generate at least as much total surplus as feasible counterfactual matches in the same local market. I take these inequalities to Refinitiv M&A data for U.S. same-industry transactions during 2010–2024. The final estimation sample contains 1025 completed acquirer-target pairs and 36,881 financially feasible counterfactual pairs constructed within industry-quarter cells. A benchmark linear surplus specification based on differences in profitability, leverage, sales growth, and liquidity has weak identifying content. Across 60 optimization runs, the same maximum score is obtained, but the coefficient vectors attaining it differ substantially in sign and magnitude. The result is not a general impossibility claim about revealed-preference methods. It shows that observed matches and standard financial differences alone provide limited discipline on merger surplus when transfers, outside options, and richer pair-specific synergies are unobserved.

Title: Hydropower dams, deforestation, and land use change: Evidence from Brazil
Authors: Chiara Falco, Valentina Raimondi
Abstract: In Brazil, hydropower generates more than 60% of the national electricity supply, placing the country among the most hydropower-dependent economies worldwide. This study analyses the causal impact of dam construction on forest loss in Brazil using a new municipality-level panel dataset covering 379 dams, combined with high-resolution satellite data on forest coverage, among other variables. Applying modern staggered differenceindifferences estimators and a dynamic event study, we find that dams reduce forest cover by almost 9% percent in the municipality. No anticipatory effects are detected, but postconstruction losses increase steadily over time. Mechanism show that forest loss occurs mainly through cropland expansion, with smaller increases in pasture and higher agricultural value added. Effects are concentrated in the North and NorthEast regions, amplified in municipalities with high public land shares and unequal land distribution, consistent with persistent institutional legacies. Our results highlight that while hydropower enhances energy security, it entails substantial environmental costs requiring stronger land governance.

Title: Vertiport capacity planning and operations for urban air mobility commuting
Authors: Mengxin Qin, Tie-Qiao Tang, Tao Wang, Shangwu Wen, Haijun Huang
Abstract: Urban air commuting (UAC) represents a vital phase in the evolution of low-altitude transportation. Vertiports are the core of urban air commuting, serving as the hubs that connect passengers with aircraft. Their capacity and operational efficiency directly affect service quality. Thus, understanding how vertiports, in terms of both planning and operations, impact the urban air commuting system is essential. To facilitate this understanding, we construct an aggregate model to describe the economic behavior of the UAC service. From the demand perspective, we employ the bottleneck model integrated with a discrete choice framework to characterize commuter behavior and departure time preferences. On the supply side, we adopt a profit maximization model to delineate the operator’s strategic decisions. This includes the optimal planning and allocation of vertiport land resources, ensuring efficient infrastructure utilization. We employ a queuing model with a buffer to characterize the matching process between commuters and flying car units. In this context, the buffer represents a surplus of vehicles staged at the vertiport relative to the number of available boarding gates, thereby ensuring service continuity and operational stability. The results in the analytical solutions and numerical tests reveal that excessive investment costs can deter operator participation due to sub-optimal returns. To improve system performance, we evaluate the effectiveness of various policy instruments-such as subsidies, maximum price limits, and service quality standards-in regulating and supporting the burgeoning urban air mobility (UAM).
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Prompt and sequential selection transfer based large language model for traffic prediction with limited data
Authors: Xiaojun Bi, Yuzhan Li, Yiwen Sun, Heng Chang, Ke Cheng, Delong Zhu, Bowen Du
Abstract: In the field of intelligent transportation systems, data scarcity severely constrains the generalization capability and precision of prediction models. Existing transfer learning methods often suffer from negative transfer due to discrepancies between source and target domains, compromising prediction performance. Although current LLMs exhibit strong feature learning capabilities, they primarily depend on pretrained knowledge and make insufficient use of source city data for targeted training. Moreover, they fail to conduct in-depth exploration of the characteristics inherent in limited datasets. To address this issue, we propose a Prompt and Sequential Selection Transfer based Large Language Model (PST-LLM) for traffic prediction with limited data, which represents the first effort to leverage LLMs specifically for traffic prediction under limited data without relying on conventional transfer learning frameworks. First, we develop a Source City Sequential Selection (SCSS) strategy for knowledge fusion. Combined with simulated fine-tuning on data-rich source cities, this approach precisely identifies optimal transfer paths to mitigate negative transfer induced by data scarcity. Second, we incorporate text prompts to enable deep fusion of semantic cues with spatio-temporal data. This integration guides the model to efficiently capture traffic patterns under limited data. Finally, a joint pruning and freezing strategy is adopted to streamline model parameters, suppressing overfitting during limited data training and significantly enhancing generalization capability. Experimental results show that PST-LLM consistently outperforms state-of-the-art(SOTA) across real-world datasets under identical settings. Furthermore, PST-LLM not only can generates predictive outputs but also can produces interpretable reasoning analysis and actionable travel recommendations. This is achieved through a dedicated reasoning branch that decodes the model’s high-level embeddings into natural language based on prompt engineering. The source code for PST-LLM is available at https://github.com/pku-smart-city/source:code/tree/main/PST-LLM .
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: The reverse side of online shopping: examining sociodemographic and built-environment determinants of delivery returns
Authors: Angela J. Haddad, Chandra R. Bhat
Abstract: The rapid growth of e-commerce has created new transportation challenges through increased product returns, yet the behavioral determinants of delivery return patterns remain understudied from a consumer-centric perspective. This research develops a comprehensive econometric framework to analyze online shopping frequency, delivery return rates, and the realized distribution of returns across channels using data from the 2022 National Household Travel Survey (NHTS). We employ a multivariate modeling approach integrating probit ordered-response and probit fractional response models to examine three interconnected outcomes: (1) frequency of online goods purchases, (2) proportion of online purchases returned, and (3) distribution of returns across four channels (home pickup, post office, Amazon drop-off, and physical store). The modeling framework accounts for causal relationships between outcomes while controlling for unobserved factors that lead to correlations across the three dimensions just listed. Results reveal significant sociodemographic heterogeneity in online purchasing and return behavior. Women, teleworkers, individuals with higher formal education, and those with higher incomes tend to exhibit increased e-commerce engagement. Older adults and zero-vehicle households, in contrast, have lower online purchase participation and return accessibility. Built environment factors significantly influence return behaviors, with rural residents showing reduced return rates and limited access to Amazon drop-off locations, while individuals residing in areas with high retail density exhibit increased use of Amazon drop-off and physical store returns. The analysis reveals causal relationships where higher online shopping frequency is associated with increased return rates, and both shopping frequency and return rates jointly influence return channel choices. These findings have important implications for transportation planning and urban logistics, highlighting the need for policies that ensure equitable return access and the importance of integrating e-commerce return trips into travel demand models.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: What does ETS do to real-side production activity? Firm-level evidence from Korea
Authors: Jinhyeok Yang
Abstract: This study examines the effects of Korea’s Emissions Trading Scheme (K-ETS) on real-side production activity in the manufacturing sector, using firm-level panel data from Statistics Korea’s Mining and Manufacturing Survey and a Difference-in-Differences design. It finds that K-ETS did not significantly affect the amount of value added generated by covered firms, but was accompanied by declines in both gross output and production costs during the first phase, suggesting a temporary scale-down in their production activity. Sectoral analysis reveals that the scale-down was more persistent in a few high-emission sectors. Covered firms also increased the share of electricity in their energy mix, although this adjustment was pronounced in the low-emission sector and limited in high-emission sectors. No consistent evidence of improved production efficiency was found, and employment effects were also statistically insignificant across sectors. These findings suggest that firms’ real-side adjustments to K-ETS were temporary in manufacturing as a whole, but more persistent in a few high-emission sectors. This raises concerns about long-term competitiveness in those sectors and suggests the importance of complementary support measures under a common ETS price signal.

Title: Electric vehicle driving range optimization considering vehicle-to-grid technology in China
Authors: Chikun Huang, Chaoxu Xu, Zhenhong Lin
Abstract: Determining the optimal driving range for battery electric vehicles (BEVs) is crucial to meet user needs while minimizing production mismatch costs. The introduction of vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology complicates this, as bidirectional energy flow reduces battery lifespan. This study develops a framework to determine the optimal range, considering time-of-use pricing, V2G revenues, range limitation, and battery degradation. Results show users prefer longer ranges when V2G benefits are significant. In the base case, a 400 km range meets 93.54% of user needs without considering V2G or degradation. When discharging revenue per kWh exceeds 2 times the peak-to-valley price difference, users are incentivized to choose longer ranges. Charging during shoulder periods and discharging during peak hours increases range by 4.8%; considering battery degradation, the increase is 3.4%; and when both factors are considered, the range increases by 8.8%. Waste in range, materials, and emissions is calculated based on these results.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Social tipping in electric mobility? Lessons from the electric vehicles lead market
Authors: John Thøgersen, Marianne Aasen
Abstract: In most countries of the world, the diffusion of battery electric vehicles (EVs) is still limited to “innovators.” Only in Norway have EVs been so widely adopted that they have reached the “early majority” (i.e., more than 16% of the car stock). To learn what others can do to follow the front-runner, this paper reports a study of drivers and barriers of EV adoption in Norway based on a yearly, representative rolling panel survey from 2018 to 2023, interviewing more than 4000 residents per year. In Norway, the transformation to EVs was initiated by an ambitious demand-side policy. Cross-lagged panel analyses reveal that, in this context, supportive social norms were important drivers of EV adoption, amplified by self-reinforcing feedback loops, as suggested by innovation diffusion theory and research on “social tipping.” Social norms nudging may hence be a tool to accelerate the diffusion of EVs, complementing financial and infrastructure measures.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Commute time thresholds across different city scales in urban China
Authors: Jiaxue Shang, Jianhui Yu, Li Chen, Bin Zhang, Wenzhong Zhang
Abstract: Long commutes are typically considered undesirable, yet in China’s super cities, residents endure significantly longer commutes without necessarily reporting lower satisfaction. To explain this phenomenon and systematically examine the differentiated thresholds of commute satisfaction across city scales, this study adopts reference point theory and analyzes large-scale survey data from 59 Chinese cities using a two-stage machine learning approach. Results indicate that commute time is the most influential factor, with satisfaction thresholds rising alongside city scale—from 19.0 min in small cities to 43.5 min in super cities. City size moderates satisfaction in a U-shaped pattern, with a rebound in super cities linked to better transport infrastructure and social comparison effects. Thresholds also vary across commuting modes. From a behavioral economics perspective, the research clarifies the psychological mechanisms behind commute well-being, providing a scientific basis for tailored urban transport policies that enhance residents’ health and quality of life.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Port decarbonisation readiness of container Terminals: An Interval-Valued fuzzy TOPSIS approach
Authors: Turgay Battal, Yeliz Çelik, Meltem Eken
Abstract: Ports are essential elements of global supply chains, yet their progress towards decarbonisation varies widely. This study develops a Port Decarbonisation Readiness Framework (PDRF) to evaluate the readiness of six container terminals in Türkiye. The framework integrates three components: entropy-based weighting of sustainability indicators, interval-valued fuzzy representation of uncertainty, and a fuzzy Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (fuzzy TOPSIS) ranking procedure. The PDRF assesses terminal-level readiness across Scope 1 and 2 operational emissions and Scope 3 mitigation readiness for onshore power supply (OPS). Because Scope 3 emissions from shipping operations are difficult to quantify, they are represented through mitigation-readiness indicators (OPS planning and electrification potential) rather than a full inventory. The results reveal substantial differences in decarbonisation readiness among terminals and demonstrate how the PDRF can support port authorities and policymakers in identifying priorities and aligning port strategies with climate goals.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: In This Issue
Product Liability Litigation and Innovation: Evidence from Medical Devices
Authors: Alberto Galasso, Hong Luo
Affiliations: University of Toronto, NBER and CEPR (email: ); University of Toronto (email: )
Abstract: We study the impact of product liability litigation on new product introductions by leading medical device firms. We find that the defendant firms, and other firms to a lesser extent, reduce their propensity to introduce new products in the litigated product categories during litigation years. We also show that changes to safety regulation influence the likelihood of litigation. Lastly, we show that the potential welfare loss due to litigation appears relatively contained: The decline in new product introductions is not permanent, it does not spill over beyond the litigated categories, and litigation induces firms to develop safer devices. (JEL D83, K13, L64, O31, O34)

Title: Failures of Contingent Reasoning in Annuitization Decisions
Authors: Erzo F.P. Luttmer, Priscila De Oliveira, Dmitry Taubinsky
Affiliations: Dartmouth College and NBER (email: ); Nova School of Business and Economics (email: ); UC Berkeley and NBER (email: )
Abstract: This paper studies psychological biases in take-up of annuities, using an incentivized experiment with a probability-based sample (N = 3,038). Choosing an annuity was payoff-maximizing in the experiment at all prices, but take-up was incomplete and price elastic. Reformulating decisions as insurance against a “bad” outcome rather than insurance against “longevity risk” did not increase take-up. Instead, we find substantial failures of contingent reasoning: Participants underappreciated how annuitization mitigated the need for less-efficient means of saving for retirement. Increasing the salience of the interaction with savings decisions, or eliminating the need to think through this interaction altogether, substantially increased annuity take-up. (JEL D15, G22, G23, G51, G52, J26)

Title: Liquidity Constraints and the Value of Insurance
Authors: Keith Marzilli Ericson, Justin Sydnor
Affiliations: Boston University and NBER (email: ); University of Wisconsin and NBER (email: )
Abstract: Insurance moves resources across both time and states. We study the consumption-smoothing benefits of insurance under liquidity constraints in a model where contracts span multiple consumption periods. The normative benchmarks for insurance demand under liquidity constraints differ qualitatively and quantitatively from the standard model: Individuals may only partially insure at actuarially fair prices, may benefit from insurance when premiums are very high and even sometimes when dominated, and may value insurance against events that will surely happen. Using simulations for health insurance, we highlight how these findings generate insights about how cost-sharing should be designed differently for liquidity-constrained populations. (JEL D86, G21, G51, G52)

Title: Sequential Protest Formation
Authors: Benjamin Matta
Affiliations: Sao Paulo School of Economics–FGV (email: )
Abstract: People participate in protests even though it is costly, benefits are not exclusive to participants, and each individual is unlikely to be pivotal. Building on these characteristics, I propose a sequential model of protest formation where opportunities to participate arrive stochastically, and the protest succeeds if participation surpasses a threshold. I show a unique equilibrium exists and characterize its dynamics. If the unique equilibrium involves participation, the time between participation decisions shortens as the protest progresses—a pattern observed empirically. A player with an opportunity becomes sequentially pivotal if, after abstaining, the protest will likely end before another opportunity arrives. (JEL D72, D84, D91)

Title: The Economics of Discriminatory Job Reservations
Authors: James P. Choy
Affiliations: University of York (email: )
Abstract: A society reserves certain jobs for members of a politically dominant social group to maximize the wages of workers in that group. Through an appropriate choice of reserved jobs, the dominant group chooses both the size of the set of reserved jobs and the elasticity of substitution between reserved and unreserved jobs. Optimal discrimination endogenously creates categories of “good” and “bad” jobs and assigns workers from different social groups into these different categories. The relative scarcity of labor determines whether discrimination or free labor markets are optimal. I apply the model to apartheid South Africa and other discriminatory societies. (JEL H22, J15, J22, J31, J42, J71, N37)

Title: Data Linkages and Privacy Regulation
Authors: Rossella Argenziano, Alessandro Bonatti
Affiliations: University of Essex (email: ); MIT Sloan School of Management (email: )
Abstract: We assess the efficacy of privacy regulation when consumers are privacy conscious. We develop a model of data linkages where a consumer interacts sequentially with two firms: One firm collects data on consumer behavior, and the other firm leverages the data to set a quality level and a price. A data linkage benefits the consumer in equilibrium when the recipient firm is sufficiently similar to the collecting firm. We endogenize linkage formation under several existing privacy regulations. Voluntary consent requirements benefit consumers in equilibrium, but blanket bans on discriminatory price and quality offers harm them. (JEL D11, D21, D82, D83)

Title: Rational Misspecification: Framework and Applications
Authors: Ran Eilat, Kfir Eliaz
Affiliations: School of Economics, Tel Aviv University (email: )
Abstract: This paper proposes a framework for assessing whether misspecified decision-makers would be willing to pay for information that can potentially make them less misspecified. We introduce a prior-free approach, based on “constrained” maximal regret, to derive an upper bound on the subjective assessment of potential gains from acquiring a more accurate model. The constraint stems from the information currently available to the decision-maker. We apply our approach to three prominent models of misspecified beliefs: coarse expectations, causal misperceptions, and sampling equilibria. (JEL D83, D84, D91)

Title: The Combinatorial Multi-Round Ascending Auction
Authors: Bernhard Kasberger, Alexander Teytelboym
Affiliations: Department of Economics, Johannes Kepler University Linz and Austrian Institute of Economic Research (email: ); Department of Economics and St. Catherine's College, University of Oxford (email: )
Abstract: The Combinatorial Multi-Round Ascending Auction (CMRA) is a new auction format used in recent European spectrum auctions. We show that an auction-specific version of truthful bidding leads to an efficient allocation. We then characterize different ex post equilibria that feature truthful bidding, demand expansion, and demand reduction. The truth-telling equilibrium is fragile to small asymmetries in the bidders' caps. Moreover, if bidders are sufficiently symmetric, the CMRA is vulnerable to risk-free collusion. We propose an alternative activity rule that prevents such collusive strategies while keeping other equilibria intact. We discuss outcomes of several Danish CMRAs in light of our equilibrium predictions. (JEL D44, H82, L82)

Title: Welfare of Competitive Price Discrimination with Captive Consumers
Authors: Yanlin Chen, Xianwen Shi, Jun Zhang
Affiliations: Zhongnan University of Economics and Law (email: ); University of Toronto (email: ); Department of Economics, School of Business, University of Technology Sydney (email: )
Abstract: We study the welfare effects of price discrimination in a duopoly with both captive and contested consumers. Using a unified information design approach, we characterize the best and worst market segmentations for producer surplus, consumer surplus, and social surplus. The firm-optimal segmentation, which divides the market into two nested segments, consistently reduces consumer welfare relative to uniform pricing. The consumer-optimal segmentation, which divides the market into a symmetric segment and a nested segment, may sometimes yield a Pareto improvement but does not necessarily coincide with the social-optimal segmentation. (JEL D43, D83)

Title: Collusion by Exclusion in Public Procurement
Authors: Regina Seibel, Samuel Škoda
Affiliations: University of Toronto (email: ); University of Oslo (email: )
Abstract: This paper studies bid rigging in auctions with bidder preselection. We develop a theoretical model to analyze the optimal behavior of partial bid-rigging cartels and show how commonly used two-stage auction formats, in which the first stage is used to preselect bidders, may be exploited. Based on our theoretical results, we construct a collusion marker reflecting the optimal cartel strategy and, using administrative data on public procurement auctions in Slovakia, we identify bidders suspected of collusion. We show that bidder preselection allows cartels to exclude competitive rivals and thereby increase procurement costs above what would be possible without preselection. (JEL D43, D44, H57, L12)

Title: Higher-Order Beliefs and (Mis)learning from Prices
Authors: Kevin He, Jonathan Libgober
Affiliations: University of Pennsylvania (email: ); University of Southern California (email: )
Abstract: We study misperceptions of private-signal correlation in an incomplete-information Cournot duopoly game. Exaggerating the correlation between players' demand signals is beneficial when agents hold flexible beliefs about price elasticity but is harmful when their beliefs are dogmatically correct. For agents with flexible beliefs who learn elasticity by observing prices, correlation misperceptions indirectly distort behavior through elasticity misinference. If agents know the true elasticity, this learning channel is eliminated. Correlation misperceptions have opposite direct and indirect effects on behavior, so the presence of elasticity inference can reverse an error's viability. (JEL C72, D21, D43, D81, D82, D83)

Title: Exploiting Rivals' Strengths
Authors: Giacomo Calzolari, Vincenzo Denicolò
Affiliations: European University Institute, University of Bologna, and CEPR (email: ); University of Bologna and CEPR (email: )
Abstract: We analyze oligopolistic competition in which firms use contracts contingent on what buyers purchase from their rivals. We present a new mechanism through which a dominant firm, by using these contracts, can gain more from exploiting its rivals than from foreclosing them. This exploitation is achieved by requiring buyers to source at least a certain share of their total requirements from the dominant firm, though less than 100 percent. By optimally designing these contracts, the dominant firm can earn as much as it would if it were to acquire the rivals' specific technological and marketing capabilities at no cost. (JEL D43, D82, D86, K21, L14, M31)

Title: The Effects of Sin Taxes and Advertising Restrictions in a Dynamic Equilibrium
Authors: Rossi Abi-Rafeh, Pierre Dubois, Rachel Griffith, Martin O'Connell
Affiliations: Institute for Fiscal Studies and Amazon (email: ); Toulouse School of Economics (email: ); University of Manchester and Institute for Fiscal Studies (email: ); University of Wisconsin-Madison and Institute for Fiscal Studies (email: )
Abstract: We develop a dynamic equilibrium model of firm competition to analyze the effects of counterfactual policies, such as taxes and advertising restrictions, on pricing, advertising, consumption, and welfare. Using micro-level data, we estimate how consumer exposure to television commercials influences product choice and model firms' strategic competition over advertising budgets and pricing. We exploit firms' practice of delegating advertising slot decisions to agencies to link consumer-level advertising variation to firms' strategic choices. Our results show that a sugar-sweetened beverage tax reduces advertising, while the additional impact of advertising restrictions is significantly weaker when a tax is already in place. (JEL D12, D22, H25, L13, L66, L82, M37)

Title: Optimal Design of Market Access
Authors: Takuro Yamashita, Shuguang Zhu
Affiliations: Institution of Social and Economic Research, University of Osaka, Ibaraki, Osaka, Japan (email: ); School of Economics, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Shanghai, P.R. China (email: )
Abstract: We study a data provider's problem of optimally designing and selling marketing lists that enable a retailer with private types to access consumers with heterogeneous characteristics. When virtual values satisfy a particular form of convexity (named boundary dominance), under certain regularity conditions, the optimal mechanism comprises fully revealing marketing lists, irrespective of whether the retailer's types are vertically or horizontally ordered. Moreover, in the vertical case, the optimal mechanism allows a simple “fixed-price” implementation. In the horizontal case, it exhibits no-exclusion and rotation properties. Conversely, if boundary dominance is violated, the optimal mechanism may not be fully revealing. (JEL D82, L81, M31)

Title: Front Matter
Reinforcement learning based material requirement planning for customised assemble-to-order systems with incomplete bill-of-materials information and stochastic lead times
Authors: Nanshan Qi, Zhibin Jiang, Liping Zhou
Affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University
Abstract: We study a material requirement planning (MRP) problem for customised assemble-to-order (ATO) systems in which order-specific bills of materials (BOMs) are unknown when orders are placed and are determined during design lead times, while component replenishment lead times are stochastic. MRP for general ATO systems has long been considered analytically intractable; the combination of uncertain BOMs, delayed BOM revelation, and stochastic replenishment lead times in a dynamic customisation environment further enlarges the state space and strengthens the coupling between replenishment and allocation. We propose a structure-aware deep reinforcement learning framework. Our approach utilises a graph-based encoder and a GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit) module to effectively extract features from the product-component requirements and stochastic pipeline dynamics. Leveraging these features, we employ a dual-policy head that simultaneously outputs state-dependent parameters for base-stock replenishment and allocation strategies, thereby preserving the interpretability of classical inventory rules. We further introduce structure-based regularisation terms, inspired by structural patterns suggested by simplified ATO systems, to encourage economically meaningful behaviour and improve robustness. Numerical experiments show lower cost and competitive on-time fulfillment in the base case and in stress regimes with high BOM uncertainty, long replenishment lead times, tight delivery windows, and high backlog penalties.

Title: Blockchain and AI integration in supply chains: a bibliometric and science mapping study of research trends and future directions
Authors: Gülçin Büyüközkan, Gizem Tüfekçi
Affiliations: Industrial Engineering Department, Faculty of Engineering and Technology, Galatasaray University; ING Belgium SA/NV
Abstract: Recent literature increasingly emphasizes the integration of Industry 4.0 technologies into supply chain (SC) management. Among these, Blockchain and Artificial Intelligence (AI) have attracted growing academic and managerial interest, although research remains at an early stage. This study maps the evolution, intellectual structure, and emerging themes of Blockchain and AI research in SCs. It analyzes all relevant Scopus-indexed articles published from the earliest available record through 2024. Bibliometric analysis and science mapping are conducted using VOSviewer and SciMAT. Findings indicate that research was limited and fragmented until early 2022, followed by rapid growth and thematic consolidation between 2022 and 2024. The study contributes by jointly reviewing Blockchain and AI literature in SCs, identifying major thematic clusters, comparing their separate and combined applications, and deriving managerial, operational, and future research implications. It also provides a forward-looking reference for developing planning and control strategies in Blockchain-AI-enabled SCs and practical implementation efforts.

Title: C2DAN: conditional domain adversarial network with supcon loss for mitigating class confusion in anomaly detection of DFOS
Authors: Ning Xu, Yiwei Li, Fuyang Chen, Ruihang Xu
Abstract: This paper presents C2DAN, a cross-domain anomaly detection strategy for distributed fiber optic sensing (DFOS) systems. Due to the long deployment range of optical fibers, variations in installation environments often cause the same type of event to exhibit different signal patterns across locations, resulting in significant domain shifts. Additionally, subtle differences in fiber-medium responses to identical external forces may lead to overlapping feature representations between different classes, thereby inducing class confusion. To address these challenges, C2DAN builds upon a CNN-Transformer backbone and incorporates an entropy-weighted conditional adversarial mechanism. Specifically, the extracted feature representation and the corresponding class prediction distribution are combined through a multilinear mapping to construct a joint feature-prediction representation, which is then fed into the domain discriminator. This design enables class-conditional domain alignment rather than marginal distribution alignment alone. In addition, entropy-based weighting is introduced to reduce the influence of uncertain samples during adversarial training, thereby improving the stability and semantic reliability of cross-domain alignment. Furthermore, a SupCon Loss is introduced to reduce intra-class variance and enlarge inter-class margins in feature space, enhancing the model’s ability to distinguish between overlapping classes caused by signal response variations. Extensive experiments under different deployment scenarios and operational conditions demonstrate that C2DAN outperforms existing methods in both accuracy and robustness, maintaining stable anomaly detection performance under domain shifts and thereby enhancing the reliability of DFOS-based monitoring systems.

Title: Business dynamism, reallocation, and growth: Evidence from China
Authors: Wenhan Liu, Ruiwen Liu, Junqian Wu, Ying Wang
Affiliations: Business School Chengdu University Chengdu China; School of Public Administration Southwestern University of Finance and Economics Chengdu China; Institute of Western China Economic Research Southwestern University of Finance and Economics Chengdu China
Abstract: Abstract This study presents an empirical investigation regarding the role of business dynamism (BD) in driving economic development. The results reveal that BD has an escape‐competition (positive) effect and the Schumpeterian (negative) effect on incumbent firms. Mechanism analysis indicates that market competition, innovation intensity, and knowledge spillover are the channels through which BD affects incumbent firms. Moreover, the impact of reallocation is heterogeneous among city's market entry barriers and enterprise type. A decomposition analysis demonstrates that the contribution of BD to incumbents' aggregate productivity growth exhibits a steady increase over time, and this decomposition result aligns with theoretical predictions.

Title: Cash or upgrade? Trade-in and remanufacturing strategies in a dual-market e-platform supply chain
Authors: Kebing Chen, Hui Wang, Ginger Y. Ke
Abstract: Trade-in-for-upgrade (TU) and trade-in-for-cash (TC) programs have been widely adopted to generate economic and environmental benefits. Despite the existing efforts in investigating how trade-in programs stimulate product sales and facilitate used-product recovery, their applications in e-platform closed-loop supply chains (ECLSCs) remain insufficiently explored. In particular, limited attention has been paid to ECLSCs with coexisting new and secondhand markets under different online modes. Motivated by this gap, this paper investigates trade-in programs in an ECLSC under resale and agency modes by considering TU-only, TC-only, and TU-TC coexistence settings. The results show that trade-in programs influence product recovery, remanufacturing decisions, and competition between new and secondhand products. Moreover, the TU-TC coexistence setting is always beneficial to the trade-in implementer, whereas its impact on the other member depends on the online mode, equilibrium strategy, and production cost of new products. In addition, resale and agency modes may achieve preference alignment between ECLSC members and consumers under certain conditions.

Title: Unlocking the catastrophe mechanism in fresh produce E-commerce supply chain coalitions: An integration of stochastic evolutionary game and catastrophe theory
Authors: Xiaochao Wei, Yanfei Zhang
Abstract: The rapid growth of fresh produce e-commerce platforms has prompted the formation of dynamic supply chain coalitions to improve efficiency and reduce costs. However, these coalitions face significant challenges under uncertainty, resulting in abrupt disruptions, yet their dynamic evolution, driven by stochastic strategic interactions and nonlinear regime shifts, remains underexplored. Accordingly, we develop a stochastic catastrophe model to explore such abrupt changes by combining the stochastic evolutionary game (SEG) and catastrophe theory. Specifically, we employ an SEG with Gaussian white noise to model asymmetric strategic interactions between fresh e-commerce platforms and suppliers, then transform the replicator dynamics into a cusp catastrophe model. We mathematically derive the catastrophe threshold (i.e., singularity set) and distinguish two fundamentally different types: perturbation catastrophes triggered by external shocks, and structural catastrophes arising from gradual internal imbalances. The coalition catastrophe can be accurately controlled by parameter adjustment to form the shortest path to avoid catastrophe (precatastrophe), delay catastrophe (in-catastrophe), and recover from catastrophe (postcatastrophe). Numerical simulations show that excess revenue π negatively impacts the stability of fresh produce e-commerce supply chain coalitions (FPESCCs), but value–freshness elasticity positively impacts FPESCC stability, and value–freshness level has an inverted U-shaped effect on the stability of FPESCCs. When the initial willingness to cooperate is low, a lower service-cost coefficient helps stabilize FPESCCs. Robustness checks using alternative functional forms and product heterogeneity confirm the qualitative stability of these findings. This integrated approach provides a new perspective for supply chain coalition research, offering quantitative insights for guiding policy optimization.

Title: Endogenous networks with constrained public goods
Authors: Zeyuan Wang, Masakazu Fukuzumi
Abstract: This paper incorporates individual effort constraints into a network formation framework with local public goods. Strict Nash equilibria are characterised, featuring complete multipartite networks as a novel class of stratified structures, where agents are organised into distinct layers based on heterogeneous effort levels, with full inter-layer connectivity and no intra-layer links. We further show that such constraints weaken the law of the few by limiting extreme concentration of effort provision. As a result, equilibrium networks exhibit broader participation in production and layered patterns of effort provision.

Title: Social expectations and norm nudging in anti-coordination problems: An El Farol Bar Game experiment
Authors: Pietro Guarnieri, Lorenzo Spadoni
Abstract: Norm nudging interventions seek to influence behavior by shaping what individuals expect others to do (empirical expectations) or regard as appropriate (normative expectations). We study how such interventions operate in an anonymous anti-coordination problem, using an online El Farol Bar Game experiment composed of two studies. Study 1 elicits social expectations (empirical and normative) and personal normative beliefs before subjects make their decision in the El Farol Bar Game. Study 2 implements norm nudges by providing participants with pre-decision messages based on the social expectations elicited in Study 1. Results show that subjects conform not only to their empirical expectations, but also to their personal normative beliefs. Normative expectations exert weaker and less consistent effects. Moreover, norm nudging interventions primarily induce prudence by reducing behavior that jeopardizes social welfare.

Title: (Un)equal and safe: How distributional and defense information shape fuel tax support?
Authors: Ausrine Dirzinskaite, Laura Galdikiene
Abstract: Carbon taxation is one of the most effective tools for reducing emissions, but it often faces public resistance due to concerns about fairness, distributional impacts, and the use of revenue. Experimental evidence on how these factors shape tax acceptance remains limited, particularly outside North America and Western Europe. This study examines how information emphasizing the progressive features of a fuel tax—a proxy for carbon taxation—affects perceptions of fairness and tax acceptance. It also investigates, for the first time, how allocating tax revenue to national defense, at a time when this issue is highly salient, influences tax acceptance. Drawing on Lithuania’s 2025 fuel tax increase, which was partially earmarked for defense spending, we conducted an online survey experiment (N = 2553). Respondents were assigned to one of three conditions: (1) information on the tax’s distributional effects, emphasizing its progressiveness; (2) the same information plus a reminder about revenue allocation to defense; or (3) no information. Providing distributional information, both on its own and in combination with a reminder that revenues would be allocated to defense spending, increased perceived fairness and self-reported support for the tax. Moreover, the combined treatment reduced opposition to the tax. The defense-earmarking reminder also made an independent contribution to reducing opposition. Overall, the results suggest that both distributional considerations and the intended use of revenues shape public acceptance of the policy.

Title: Structural resilience assessment of Alliance-Based liner shipping Networks: A Dismantling-Based approach
Authors: Yang Yang, Kaimin Chen, Hao Wang, Kevin X. Li
Abstract: Liner shipping network resilience is crucial in the face of growing complex disruptions. Studies have shown these networks are resilient to random failures, while vulnerable to targeted attacks. Previous targeted attack strategies, which rely on centrality rankings or fixed-set dismantling, tended to overestimate network resilience. To address this, this study proposes a sequence-based framework to assess network resilience. An Optimized Node Sequence (ONS) strategy, which formulates dismantling as a bi-objective trade-off between minimizing attack cost and maximizing attack damage, is proposed and solved via a domain-tailored evolutionary algorithm with hybrid initialization. The framework is empirically validated using a longitudinal analysis of annual Ocean Alliance liner services (2017–2025) and ONS is benchmarked against rank-based and set-based strategies. Results show that ONS consistently outperforms the two baselines, identifying ports that trigger early-stage disruptions. The findings further indicate that network resilience fluctuates in response to both internal design choices and exogenous shocks. Furthermore, the service adjustments implemented by the Ocean Alliance during the Red Sea crisis effectively maintained network resilience at a level comparable to that of the pre-crisis designed service network. The proposed framework advances resilience analysis by shifting from set identification to dynamic sequence optimization, offering a decision-support tool for enhancing network resilience planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Marching towards maritime decarbonization: Could self-operated fleets hedge cost and consumer payment uncertainty risks?
Authors: Baozhuang Niu, Enkai Zhang, Fengfeng Xie, Hongzhi Wang
Abstract: Maritime transport is the major source of global carbon emissions. While logistics service providers have made substantial investments in decarbonization initiatives, their volatile shipping fees will significantly influence the demand volume, harming the consignor’s ability to jointly achieve profitability and environmental sustainability goals. Such risks can be further enhanced if consumers have reservations when they pay the bill for both goods and their green mindfulness. Therefore, in this study, we investigate whether the consignor’s self-operated fleets could mitigate the negative impacts of cost uncertainty and consumer green concern risks. Although it becomes the consignor who invests in carbon reduction, we reveal that the mitigated cost uncertainty and double marginalization effect help effectively hedge consumers’ payment hesitation when they have uncertain green mindfulness. We find that the consignor’s preference for building the self-operated fleet exhibits a non-monotonic pattern (shifting from self-operated fleet to logistics service providers and then back) as the initial carbon emission intensity increases. We identify an investment failure zone where aggressive carbon reduction via self-operated fleet suppresses sales quantity, thus reducing the consignor’s profitability. Regarding the system’s sustainability performance, we point out that more carbon reductions might boost demand, and hence, increase overall shipping volume and net emissions. These findings underscore the complexities in balancing logistics autonomy and environmental responsibility, offering useful insights for consignors’ developing overseas business.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Beyond efficiency: societal benefit perception as a driver of public acceptance for UAM-based last-mile delivery in Japan
Authors: Dohyung Kim, Sunbin Yoo, Shunsuke Managi, Zheng Chang
Abstract: This study examines the attitudinal drivers of drone delivery acceptance in Japan using a stated-preference discrete-choice experiment in a nationally distributed Japanese survey of 5,113 respondents (with the ICLV estimates based on the 3,592 drone-aware respondents) and a simultaneous integrated choice and latent variable (ICLV) model incorporating six latent constructs. Three principal findings emerge. First, the baseline drone alternative-specific constant is not statistically distinguishable from zero among drone-aware respondents, consistent with acceptance being shaped primarily by the attitudinal and attribute channels in the model. Second, willingness-to-pay (WTP) for institutional trust and equity attitudes represents sizable monetary valuations when their direct and mediated pathways are combined: TRUST ¥34.5 (of which 19.3% is mediated through Perceived Societal Benefit) and EQUITY ¥30.4 (of which 51.4% is mediated). Third, a two-class latent class analysis identifies two distinct preference segments, a TRUST-Affective segment (50.2% of respondents) responsive to institutional and equity attributes, and a Price-Insensitive/Functional segment (49.8%) responsive primarily to operator identity and delivery lead time. These findings suggest that investments in institutional trust and societal benefit communication may generate acceptance returns comparable to operational improvements, offering guidance for socially sustainable UAM logistics policy.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: A framework for enriching survey datasets using passive data and machine learning, with an application to transferring attitudinal variables across transport surveys
Authors: F. Atiyya Shaw, Xinyi Wang, Patricia L. Mokhtarian, Kari E. Watkins
Abstract: Declining response rates make it increasingly critical for survey designers across disciplines to utilize mechanisms that facilitate timesaving and reduce the burden on the part of respondents. In practice, this often means that questionnaires are shortened, yielding increased response rates but reduced information/ variables available for modeling purposes. Here, this challenge is addressed by using machine learning and regression algorithms, alongside passive data augmentation, to develop and apply a predictive transfer learning-based framework for enriching surveys with information from other datasets. We demonstrate the framework by applying it to supplement and enrich the U.S. National Household Travel Survey (NHTS) with psychometric data (e.g., attitudes), which have been shown in the literature to have the ability to explain and predict behavior, but which are often not captured on household travel surveys. It is, to our knowledge, among the first times such an approach has been applied: (1) in a framework-based systematic approach in transportation; and (2) to transferring attitudinal variables across survey datasets. The application shown here explains up to 25% of the variance in observed attitudes, yielding correlations of up to 0.5 between observed and predicted attitudinal variables. Future applications of the framework presented in this paper have the potential to improve travel demand forecasting and behavioral predictions; and, even more broadly, may be used to enrich other large-scale behavior-based surveys with external variables, thereby providing more diverse and robust data streams for use in an array of modeling efforts.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Induced e-bike adoption from income-conditioned rebates in British Columbia: who are the marginal purchasers?
Authors: Polina Polikakhina, Amir Hassanpour, Meghan Winters, Alexander Bigazzi
Abstract: Electric-assist bicycle (e-bike) purchase incentive programs have gained popularity worldwide, yet evidence on their effectiveness in generating new (marginal) e-bike purchases remains limited. The objective of this research is to examine the marginality of e-bike purchases incentivized by income-conditioned rebates (i.e., the likelihood an e-bike would not have been purchased without the rebate), and to determine whether rebate value, household income, and other factors moderate this marginality. We use survey data from 1,110 participants in two e-bike rebate programs in British Columbia, Canada. Rebate values ranged from CA$350 to CA$1,600, with higher rebate values only available to lower-income recipients. A latent class model of purchase motivations identified five types of purchasers, including Cost Minimizers (27%), Mode Substituters (17%), and Effort Minimizers (7%), along with two mixed categories of Cost Secondary (34%) and Cost Indifferent (15%) purchasers. The average likelihood of a marginal purchase was 56%, ranging from 21% to 75% with increasing rebate value. Besides the strong effect of rebate value, rebates were more effective (i.e., likely to generate a marginal purchase) when recipients were from lower-income households, commuted regularly, and were not cycling prior to the purchase. More marginal e-bike purchases were also associated with lower-priced e-bikes and rebate recipients who were younger, had a post-secondary degree, and were Cost Minimizers. The findings are promising for potential mode shift stimulated by e-bike rebate programs and support income-conditioning of e-bike rebates to improve effectiveness and equity.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: EVCS siting and sizing with multi-stakeholder utilities: non-cooperative and cooperative perspectives
Authors: Shang-Wu Wen, Tie-Qiao Tang, Jian Zhang, Meng-Xin Qin, Xiao-Ming Xu, Hai-Jun Huang
