Abstract: To alleviate the imbalance between the construction and utilization of charging infrastructure, this study develops an integrated framework that couples a non-cooperative perspective, a cooperative perspective, and charging demand generation to analyze the siting and sizing outcomes of electric vehicle charging stations (EVCS) among operators, users, and the grid. First, utility functions for the stakeholders and a Nash-product-inspired multi-stakeholder optimization model are formulated from a non-cooperative perspective. Second, a Shapley-value-based imposed utility-transfer mechanism is introduced to extend the model to a cooperative perspective. Third, a Monte Carlo-based charging demand generation method is proposed, which infers the evolution of vehicle state of charge (SoC) using a vehicle energy-consumption model. Finally, the SoC data is used as input, and a genetic algorithm with an elitist strategy is used to solve the problem. Experiments on Hangzhou datasets show that, under the baseline utility-coupling setting, although EVCS siting and sizing can improve utility, they are still accompanied by investment contraction and insufficient accessibility, and stakeholder participation incentives may remain unstable. Meanwhile, user heterogeneity highlights the demand for a higher-quality charging environment. Although expanding the service radius and improving charging capability can enhance utility, the associated marginal gains exhibit a diminishing trend. By contrast, the imposed utility-transfer mechanism can be introduced at an early stage of planning, where it coordinates the utility allocation among the stakeholders, promotes infrastructure deployment, and thereby improves overall system sustainability.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Exploring the determinants of hydrogen bike-sharing adoption among urban residents using explainable machine learning
Authors: Junjie Chen, Yuming Lin, Jianghao Yu, Jianbang Du, Pei Liu
Abstract: Hydrogen bike-sharing is an emerging mode of zero-carbon transport that has recently appeared in some cities. However, salient empirical research remains insufficient, and it is thus unclear how to effectively increase residents’ adoption intention. This study draws on innovation diffusion theory (IDT) to develop a model of the determinants of hydrogen bike-sharing adoption intention, including innovation attributes, social system, communication channels, time, and external environment characteristics. Using data collected from 5,220 residents across 302 cities in China, we employed LightGBM to train and test the model. The results of this model combined with Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) are threefold. (i) In terms of relative importance, the relative advantage of innovation, social system, communication channels, and the external environment are important, whereas the importance of time is limited. (ii) Most determinants exhibit pronounced nonlinear and threshold effects. Particularly, price and maximum riding range reveal a diminishing marginal effect of relative advantage, with adoption intention increasing once they outperform conventional bike-sharing options but rising more slowly as the advantage further expands. (iii) Interaction effects between external environmental characteristics and key IDT factors are observed. The role of price as an economic relative advantage varies with the level of hydrogen infrastructure, while the performance relative advantage of maximum riding range varies across urban areas. These findings provide decision makers and practitioners with more targeted strategies for accelerating the transition toward zero-carbon transport.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Optimizing cycling network design in the city of Parma
Authors: Rafael Praxedes, Anand Subramanian, Stefano Ardizzoni, Luca Consolini, Mattia Laurini, Marco Locatelli
Abstract: Cycling is a sustainable mode of transport that helps address urban challenges such as traffic congestion and high carbon dioxide emissions. However, to encourage citizens accustomed to using private motorized vehicles or public transportation to adopt cycling, it is essential to provide suitable infrastructure that meets expectations regarding factors such as travel distance, safety, and comfort. This paper proposes an optimization strategy for designing the most suitable bicycle network for the city of Parma, Italy, based on a set of possible interventions (e.g., building new bicycle lanes or improving the quality of existing lanes) that can be implemented by the municipality under a limited budget. Given cyclists’ preferences for road characteristics including length, safety, and practicability, the optimization strategy determines both the interventions to implement and the routes to recommend for a set of origin–destination pairs, aiming to minimize the perceived costs of travel according to these weighted preferences. For this purpose, we develop a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation and propose three solution methods: a branch-and-bound algorithm and two heuristic procedures based on knapsack problems, solved using dynamic programming. Computational experiments are conducted using both real-world data from Parma and randomly generated instances to evaluate performance and to provide useful insights for infrastructure planners.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Rentier resource nationalism and overseas investment by multinational corporations: the impact of resource value
Authors: Liuguo Shao, Zhouyi Zhang
Abstract: Characterized by its predatory nature and the institutional uncertainty, rentier resource nationalism (RRN) has emerged as a critical risk factor for overseas investment by multinational corporations (MNCs). However, existing literature rarely relies on theoretical models to analyze the differential impacts of RRN across heterogeneous investment objectives. Furthermore, the underlying role of resource value remains underexplored, particularly from the perspective of “cognitive divergence”. To address these gaps, this study develops a three-stage game model and investigates how RRN and resource value affect the economic variables of MNCs. The results reveal that RRN significantly reduces the residual profit and overseas investment outlay of MNCs, while increasing metal output. Through the lens of investment objective heterogeneity, MNCs targeting residual profit maximization suffer negative shocks. Conversely, MNCs aiming to ensure more resource supply can benefit from the dynamics, and exhibit a higher tolerance threshold for RRN intensity. The ultimate impact of resource value hinges on the relative strength of the market-size driving effect versus the resource-depletion inhibitory effect. Crucially, “cognitive divergence” regarding resource value serves as an important mechanism explaining the simultaneous emergence of intensified RRN and the expansion of investment outlay. This study provides a theoretical foundation for the rational formulation of RRN policies and enriches the theoretical framework of international investment.

Title: A multi-objective dual hyper-heuristic approach for rescheduling in dynamic flexible job shop
Authors: Mengyuan Sun, Xi Zhang, Mingzhou Liu, Lin Ling, Maogen Ge, Jing Hu
Abstract: Predictive-reactive rescheduling combines pre-scheduling with real-time responses to maintain production stability under disturbances, and is extensively used in dynamic production environments. For multi-objective optimization of Dynamic Flexible Job Shop Scheduling Problem (DFJSP), the problem’s complexity increases significantly, challenging traditional algorithms to provide high-quality global solutions with low latency. This study proposes an innovative dual hyper-heuristic (DHH) method for rescheduling in DFJSP, aiming to generate rescheduling solutions in real-time and optimize two practical objectives: rescheduling stability and makespan. A rescheduling framework is proposed to decompose the global optimization problem into the sequence repair decision process based on the operation-to-interval transfer. The framework comprises two-stage hyper-heuristics: rule generation and selection. In the first stage, genetic programming is used to generate local repair heuristics as candidate action set. A double-tree encoding for selecting operations and intervals respectively is designed, and a terminal set combining real-time operating conditions and critical path characteristics is constructed to improve search efficiency. In the second stage, deep reinforcement learning is used to accurately relocate operations based on repair heuristics to achieve global optimization. A knowledge sharing pattern across scenarios is developed to enhance the generality of the algorithm. Comprehensive experiments on benchmark extensions demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms widely used multi-objective meta-heuristic algorithms while significantly reducing computation time.

Title: Improved variable neighborhood search for the min-degree constrained minimum spanning tree problem
Authors: Manisha Israni, Shyam Sundar
Abstract: The min-degree constrained minimum spanning tree (MDMST) problem is a well-known NP[jls-end-space/]-hard problem of finding a minimum-csot spanning tree while ensuring that every non-leaf vertex has degree at least d[jls-end-space/], where d is a constant positive integer. Degree constraints fundamentally reshape the feasible search space, often forcing the inclusion of longer edges to restore feasibility, which makes the problem particularly challenging. Based on these observations, this paper proposes an improved variable neighborhood search algorithm, denoted as (Formula presented), for the MDMST problem. Unlike the four existing VNS variants, which rely on random edge modifications, the proposed approach incorporates four structurally diverse, degree-based neighborhoods (N1 to N4[jls-end-space/]) that explicitly target edge modification associated with degree-critical vertices. These neighborhoods, combined with tailored local search strategies, enable more effective exploration and refinement of feasible solutions by balancing diversification and intensification in the search space. Extensive experimental analysis confirms the superiority of (Formula presented) over previous four variable neighborhood search variants. Its performance is also superior to state-of-the-art approaches particularly on instances of larger size. (Formula presented) discovers new best-known values on 43 out of 105 instances across all four data-sets, underscoring its capability to explore the search space effectively. Also, (Formula presented) requires only 2 tunable parameters, compared to 12 in the recent approach (Wu et al., 2025), highlighting its robustness and practical efficiency.

Title: Resilience planning for power systems under deep climate uncertainty
Authors: Jiarui Wang, Junqi Liu, Lei Zhu, Gang He
Abstract: The rising frequency and intensity of extreme weather events introduce deep climate uncertainties that fundamentally challenge the resilience of urban power systems. Conventional deterministic planning approaches are ill-suited to capture such uncertainties, often leading to maladaptive investments and system vulnerabilities. We develop a data-driven robust planning framework to cope with climate uncertainties in power system. Specifically, a hybrid framework combining a Graph Neural Network and a Conditional Generative Adversarial Network (GNN-cGAN) is utilized to capture the spatiotemporal couplings of multiple meteorological variables, which provides a more realistic characterization of deep climate uncertainties and compound extreme events. According to the Minimax Regret (MMR) criterion, a two-stage robust planning model is proposed to balance economic efficiency with extreme climate resilience, which can effectively mitigates the excessive conservatism and prohibitive investment premiums of traditional robust optimization. Applied to Lvliang City, China, the results demonstrate that the proposed approach improves system resilience by avoiding investment lock-in and reducing the risk of performance degradation under extreme conditions. Compared to conventional planning methods, the framework achieves a more balanced trade-off between economic efficiency and climate adaptability.

Title: Climate policy diffusion across US states
Authors: Mitali Das, Manuel Linsenmeier, Gregor Schwerhoff
Abstract: Climate policy at the subnational level is sometimes framed as counterproductive because climate change is considered a collective action problem that can best be addressed in a coalition that should be as large as possible. Using comprehensive data from US states on climate policy and policy outcomes, we show that state-level policy is effective in accelerating the adoption of solar energy. Crucially, however, state policies also have positive spillovers to other states, making it more likely that neighboring states adopt climate policy as well. By proportionally attributing the spillover effects, we find that many US states achieve more climate benefits through the spillovers to other states than within their own jurisdiction. In a further step, we distinguish between climate policies in the energy sector and policies targeting either other sectors or greenhouse gas emission (GHG) reductions in general. We find that climate policies in the energy sector are distinct from other climate policies in two ways: They have a significant effect on solar capacity growth and diffuse more broadly.

Title: From emission trap to mitigation dividend: The nonlinear impact and mechanisms of rural infrastructure on agricultural carbon emissions in China
Authors: Yonghao Hu, Xiang Li, Xiaoxiao Li, Kunyang Zhang, Peirun Li, Laping Wu, Nanyan Hu
Abstract: Balancing agricultural carbon mitigation with food security has become a major challenge in the pursuit of global carbon neutrality. Rural infrastructure is a key form of public capital, yet its environmental impact remains unclear. Using provincial panel data from China covering the period 2005–2023, this study examines the impact of rural infrastructure on agricultural carbon emissions (ACE) and explores the underlying mechanisms. The analysis employs fixed-effects, instrumental variable, and spatial Durbin models. ACE follows an inverted U-shaped trajectory, peaking in 2015, while rural infrastructure exhibits a similar nonlinear effect. In the early stage, infrastructure increases emissions by expanding production scale and intensifying input use. As infrastructure develops, it reduces emissions through green technological progress. Mechanism analysis shows that infrastructure initially raises emissions by increasing cropping intensity, fertilizer use, and mechanization, but gradually promotes emission reduction by facilitating the adoption of water-saving irrigation. Technological progress thus becomes the dominant force driving transition beyond the environmental turning point. The effects of infrastructure vary across components. Water infrastructure shows a nonlinear transition. Electricity infrastructure supports emission reduction. Transport infrastructure tends to increase emissions. Infrastructure also generates spatial spillovers, with indirect effects exceeding direct effects. Substantial regional heterogeneity is observed. Plain regions and major grain-producing areas reach the turning point earlier. Mountainous regions face a higher risk of emission lock-in. These findings suggest that infrastructure investment should follow a stage-specific strategy. Policies should prioritize the adoption and diffusion of green technologies while strengthening cross-regional coordination to achieve agricultural decarbonization without compromising food security.

Title: Does public debt hinder transport decarbonization? Theoretical analysis and empirical evidence
Authors: Yunhan Zhang, Zhixin Liu, Le Wen, Douglas J. Wilson
Abstract: Transport CO 2 emissions have become one of the fastest-growing sources of global greenhouse gases, posing a major challenge to sustainable development. This study examines whether, and under what conditions, public debt supports or hinders transport-sector decarbonization. We extend the debt-environment model to the transport sector, demonstrating a nonlinear U-shaped long-run relationship between public debt and transport CO 2 emissions, and test it using a panel CS-ARDL approach for 31 economies from 2000 to 2021. The empirical results support a nonlinear U-shaped long-run relationship between public debt and transport CO 2 emissions. Additionally, transport-related climate change mitigation technologies and environmental taxes significantly reduce emissions, suggesting their potential as effective strategies for transport decarbonization. Heterogeneity analysis reveals lower debt thresholds for low-growth and politically unstable economies. Overall, by integrating fiscal and transport sustainability within a unified theoretical framework, this study provides novel evidence and practical policy insights for designing debt-sustainable, climate-aligned transport strategies.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: The role of procurement in (un)locking circular transitions: A case of circular standstill
Authors: Wendy van der Valk, Marleen Habes
Abstract: This study examines the role of procurement in stalling systemic change toward a circular economy. We address a paradox: despite strong ambitions and technically feasible alternatives, in many industries, circular solutions remain at a standstill. Drawing on institutional theory in combination with supply chain theory, we study the lack of uptake of circular synthetics in Dutch construction procurement, particularly how institutional pressures are filtered through procurement routines and with what effects for supply chain governance and systemic change. We leverage meetings of a Special Interest Group and individual interviews with its members to trace the process from initial exploration of circular synthetics to the point where this alternative remains non-default in practice. Our findings reveal that procurement does not merely lag circular ambitions but actively constrains transition pathways. Established practices such as bid scoring logics, certification regimes, and risk-averse evaluation criteria lock supply chain actors into linear routines, preventing experimentation with and adoption of circular alternatives. This challenges the dominant narrative in extant literature that positions procurement primarily as an enabler of circular transitions: instead, we demonstrate how procurement is not simply a lever for circular transitions, but a translation arena in which circular ambitions are reformulated through procurement practices and routines that reproduce institutional inertia and stall systemic change. Our study unpacks the processes through which procurement reflects and reinforces institutional logics in supply chains, highlighting the need for rethinking procurement design if uptake of circular alternatives is to become structural.
Journal: Journal of Purchasing and Supply Management

Title: How to make pricing strategy for the influencer’s self-operated products considering the content switching level?
Authors: Xiaoping Xu, Ying Zhang, Hua Liu, Xiaohang Yue, T. C. E. Cheng, Li Zhou
Affiliations: Anhui University; University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee; The Hong Kong Polytechnic University; University of Greenwich
Abstract: We analyse a supply chain with a manufacturer and an influencer selling products by live streaming. The influencer can introduce self-operated products and choose between competitive pricing strategy (Scenario CM) and sequential pricing strategy (Scenario SQ). The content switching level and influencer power impact the demand, which are crucial factors influencing decisions. Additionally, we consider the long-term effect, where live streaming slices or product recommendation logos continue to drive sales after live streaming. We find that in Scenario CM, the manufacturer's optimal production quantity initially declines and then rises as the long-term effect, while in Scenario SQ, it consistently increases. The influencer's optimal profit initially declines and then rises as the long-term effect in both scenarios. When the influencer adopts Scenario SQ, introducing self-operated products always benefits her. However, in Scenario CM, the decision depends on the long-term effect. The manufacturer's and influencer's preferred pricing strategies vary based on the long-term effect. If the long-term effect is high (low), Scenario SQ is preferred to avoid direct competition, while if moderate, Scenario CM is preferred. This paper is the first examining pricing strategies for influencer-operated products, offering valuable insights on when to incorporate self-operated products into the live streaming.

Title: A systematic review of constraint management studies in construction: current status and future direction
Authors: Zeyu Mao, Vicente A. Gonzalez, Mohammed Abdelmegid, Yang Zou
Affiliations: Infrastructure and Human Tech (IHT) Lab, Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, University of Alberta; Infrastructure and Human Tech (IHT) Lab, Strategic Projects Insight Centre in Engineering (SPICE), Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, University of Alberta; School of Civil Engineering, University of Leeds; Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, University of Auckland
Abstract: Construction constraints are a foundational concept in Lean Construction. They are factors that restrict or regulate the execution of tasks and hinder workflow reliability. Their systematic identification and removal underpin production planning and control processes such as the Last Planner System (LPS). However, current constraint management (CM) has yet to reach sufficient implementation levels in most projects. Motivated by the need to improve CM in current construction practices, this article aims to identify current research gaps through a state-of-the-art review of CM-related research and propose future directions for addressing the gaps. To achieve this, we conducted a systematic literature review (SLR) using a sequential mixed-method design, combining bibliometric analysis (quantitative mapping) with thematic analysis (qualitative synthesis). First, a total of 128 papers were collected using a structured data collection approach from Scopus and the IGLC (International Group for Lean Construction) conference and then fed into a bibliometric analysis to construct science maps. Subsequently, an in-depth thematic analysis combined with the quantitative analysis results is presented to reveal the research topics, trends, gaps, and future directions of CM-related research. As a consequence, five primary research themes, along with their research trends and gaps, have been revealed. This article suggests five areas for improvement to overcome the identified gaps in current CM-related research. Through its findings and recommendations, this article contributes to the body of knowledge of CM-related research and provides future directions to enhance CM implementation in construction projects.

Title: Deep financial planning
Authors: Hyunglip Bae, Jang Ho Kim, Hwayong Choi, Frank J. Fabozzi, Woo Chang Kim
Abstract: Financial planning for individuals jointly determines consumption and investment to achieve multiple prioritized goals over the life cycle and is commonly formulated as a multi-stage stochastic asset–liability management problem. Solving such problems repeatedly for many clients is computationally demanding, which limits the scalability of personalized financial planning services. We introduce Deep Financial Planning (DFP), a decision framework that treats the individual goal-based planning problem as a parametric stochastic program and approximates its optimal policy with deep neural networks. In DFP, we first solve a representative set of multi-stage stochastic goal programming problems under diverse parameter configurations and then use the resulting optimal asset and goal allocation policies as training data for the network. We provide theoretical results that establish conditions under which the optimal policy of the underlying parametric problem can be approximated arbitrarily well by a neural network. Numerical experiments on individual financial planning scenarios show that DFP delivers near-optimal policies in unconstrained and moderately constrained settings with substantial reductions in response time relative to directly solving the stochasticprograms, enabling real-time what-if analysis for end investors. We further demonstrate that transfer learning can enhance the efficiency and accuracy of DFP, reinforcing the practical viability of DFP as a scalable tool for lifelong personalized financial planning.

Title: Toward low-carbon diets: Exploring the role of climate perceptions and household mitigation practices in reducing meat consumption
Authors: Lan Tran, Ye Su
Abstract: Transitioning toward a sustainable food system requires reducing meat consumption, yet global meat demand continues to rise. This study investigates the behavioral mechanisms linking abstract climate perceptions and routine household mitigation practices (e.g., recycling, energy efficiency) to sustainable food choices. Specifically, we examine whether routine pro-environmental behaviors act as a “spillover” mechanism and a behavioral bridge toward lower-carbon dietary changes, such as reducing meat intake or adopting plant-based substitutes. Using a nationwide climate survey of U.S. households (2024–2025), we analyze the drivers of these shifts. The findings reveal that climate change perceptions influence dietary outcomes through both direct and indirect pathways, with household mitigation practices serving as a significant mediating mechanism toward more demanding shifts such as plant-based food adoption. The results further show that climate justice perceptions are significant drivers of high-commitment dietary choices, while specific socio-demographic factors remain persistent barriers to change. By situating food choices within the broader context of household environmental pressure, the study offers a quantified framework for understanding how to align individual consumption with ecological limits. This research also provides actionable insights for policymakers and food marketers in developing integrated strategies to facilitate the transition toward a more sustainable, low-carbon food system.

Title: Does ride-hailing moderate the relationship between public transit preference and transit use?
Authors: Ruijia Sun, Kunbo Shi, Frank Witlox, Tianren Yang
Abstract: It has been widely accepted that people who have a strong preference for public transit tend to use public transit more frequently. However, the growing popularity of ride-hailing systems, by offering door-to-door mobility services, may be correlated with a decline in people's reliance on public transit. Therefore, a critical question arises: Does ride-hailing moderate the positive relationship between public transit preference and transit use? To empirically investigate this question, this study uses data from an online questionnaire survey covering 81 Chinese cities, yielding a total of 7,205 valid participants. The results indicate that a high preference for public transit is strongly correlated with frequent public transit trips (including both bus and metro). However, with ride-hailing frequency increasing, this positive association becomes significantly less pronounced. These findings reshape the traditional understanding of the relationship between public transit preference and public transit use, indicating that the popularization of ride-hailing is potentially linked to lower loyalty among pro-transit users. This poses a new challenge to the sustainability transition of urban transportation systems and calls for strategic policies to address it.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Scarred by nature: How early exposure to natural disasters shapes risk attitudes
Authors: Despina Gavresi, Andreas Sintos
Abstract: Can early-life experiences shape long-term risk attitudes? This paper examines the relationship between exposure to natural disasters during early adulthood and individual risk preferences later in life. Using harmonized survey data linked to disaster records, we find that individuals exposed to natural disasters between the ages of 18 and 25 exhibit significantly greater risk aversion later in life. This relationship proves robust across a range of alternative specifications. We further explore the role of cultural transmission as a mechanism, showing that social connectedness moderates the observed behavioral shift. Our findings underscore the impressionable years as a critical window for the formation of individual preferences. The study offers new insights into how climate-related shocks are linked to long-lasting behavioral patterns, with implications for public policy, economic behavior, and climate adaptation.

Title: Editorial Board
How do temperature and precipitation influence electric vehicle adoption? Evidence from U.S. States
Authors: Fengxiu Zhang, Yuzheng Xie, David W.S. Wong, Wenying Ji
Abstract: Although extensive technical evidence shows that temperature and precipitation affect electric vehicle (EV) performance, less is known about how these factors translate to adoption behavior. This study examines how temperature and precipitation – incorporating both average and extreme conditions – shape EV adoption. Using panel data from 2016 to 2023 on the 48 contiguous U.S. states and the District of Columbia, we find that mean annual temperature exhibits a positive and linear relationship with EV uptake. Mean annual precipitation has no standalone effect but weakens the influence of mean temperature. Among extreme conditions, only low-temperature days (below 10°C) reduce EV adoption, while high-temperature days (above 25°C) show no significant effect. The effects of extreme precipitation are context-dependent: it promotes adoption under high-temperature conditions but shows no significant effect in cold environments. The study highlights the need for climate-sensitive and regionally tailored strategies to promote EVs and offers actionable policy recommendations.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Unveiling amplified socioeconomic disparities in electric vehicle charging infrastructure: Accessibility versus utilization
Authors: Changlong Ling, Peng Chen
Abstract: This study examines user-centered spatial disparities in electric vehicle charging infrastructure by jointly analyzing accessibility (equity) and utilization (efficiency) in Shenzhen, China. It investigates how disparities differ between the two measures, and which factors explain utilization patterns. Using charging-station data, socioeconomic disparities are quantified across income and migrant groups, and a GeoXAI approach identifies nonlinear and spatially heterogeneous relationships. Results show that disparities exist under both measures but are consistently larger during utilization. From accessibility to utilization, Gini coefficients increase by 1.1%–3.4% and Theil indices by 3.0%–9.5%. Charging stations in areas with larger low-income populations exhibit higher energy use, while those in areas with higher migrant shares are associated with longer charging durations and higher occupancy rates. Infrastructure, pricing, and built environment factors are correlated with utilization, with strong nonlinearity and spatial heterogeneity. These findings underscore utilization-aware charging evaluations and user-centered infrastructure planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Programmatic or sponsored advertising? Control, costs, and consumer utility in platform competition
Authors: Dan Gao, He Xu, Stuart X. Zhu
Abstract: User-generated content platforms increasingly rely on advertising for monetization, with programmatic advertising (platform-controlled) and sponsored advertising (producer-controlled) representing two distinct formats. Sponsored advertising not only shifts decision rights from platforms to producers but also raises quality-related costs and alters consumer utility, which may be positive or negative. We develop a game-theoretic model to analyze competing producers’ advertising format choices. The equilibrium outcomes depend on three forces: the sponsorship-induced utility effect, the advertising effect, and the quality cost difference effect. When the sponsorship-induced utility effect is strongly negative, both producers adopt programmatic advertising, while a strongly positive effect leads both to adopt sponsored advertising. For moderate effects, equilibrium strategies hinge on advertising aversion: weak aversion favors asymmetric strategies, while stronger aversion reduces differentiation and may yield multiple symmetric equilibria. Increasing quality cost differences further discourages sponsored advertising. Our results reveal when platforms and producers benefit from delegating advertising control, and under what conditions sponsored advertising enhances platform profits, consumer surplus, and social welfare. These findings contribute to the literature on digital platform operations and provide guidance for platforms in designing advertising models that balance monetization, content quality, and user experience.

Title: Hospital Billing Regulations and Financial Well-being: Evidence from California’s Fair Pricing Law
Authors: Yaa Akosa Antwi, Marion Aouad, Nathan Blascak
Abstract: We examine the financial consequences of the 2007 California Fair Pricing Law, which places a price ceiling on hospital bills for financially vulnerable individuals. Using cross-sectional variation in exposure to the law, proxied by county-level uninsured rates, we estimate its impact on individual financial outcomes. We find that the law reduces the likelihood of incurring non-medical debt in collections and the number of non-medical accounts in collections. In addition, we find evidence that credit scores increased and suggestive evidence that the number of delinquent accounts decreased for individuals in more exposed counties. Our results suggest hospital billing regulations can improve targeted individuals’ financial outcomes.

Title: The impact of credit frictions on immigrants’ labor market outcomes
Authors: Esteban Argudo
Abstract: Exploiting the differential effect of the USA PATRIOT Act on natives and non-citizens, I find that the Act increased credit frictions for non-citizens and was associated with a decline in their wages. I also document a decline in unemployment, although this result is sensitive to the choice of specification and may partly reflect the recovery from the 2001 recession. The estimated wage effect does not reflect occupational downgrading, sectoral reallocation, or changes in self-employment. Instead, it occurred largely within industries and occupations, consistent with non-citizens accepting lower wages for similar jobs following the increase in credit frictions. These findings suggest that credit frictions may be an important yet overlooked determinant of nativity gaps in labor market outcomes.

Title: Coordination in the network minimum game
Authors: Johannes C. Hoelzemann, Hongyi Li
Affiliations: University of Vienna: Universitat Wien; UNSW: University of New South Wales
Abstract: Abstract Motivated by the problem of organizational design, we study coordination in the network minimum game : a version of the minimum-effort game where players are connected by a directed network. We show experimentally that acyclic networks such as hierarchies are most conducive to successful coordination. Introducing a single link to complete a network cycle may drastically inhibit coordination. Furthermore, acyclic networks enable resilient coordination: initial coordination failure is often overcome (exacerbated) after repeated play in acyclic (cyclic) networks.

Title: Uncertainty-aware simulation optimisation for yard template planning in transshipment hubs
Authors: Bonggwon Kang, Taehoon Lee, Zhou Sun, Soondo Hong
Affiliations: Kumoh National Institute of Technology; Major in Industrial Data Science & Engineering, Department of Industrial Engineering, Pusan National University, South Korea; Schoolof Transportation Engineering, Dalian Maritime University; Pusan National University
Abstract: Yard template planning (YTP) is commonly applied at transshipment hubs to reduce transportation costs by assigning storage areas for outbound vessels. With recent advances in digital transformation technologies, terminal operators increasingly rely on simulation-based decision-making to address the uncertain nature of port operations. However, high-fidelity container terminal simulations typically require several minutes to hours per run, and YTP involves a high-dimensional and combinatorial design space. To address these challenges, we propose a domain-informed parallel Bayesian optimisation framework. A Gaussian process (GP) surrogate is presented to efficiently approximate the posterior distribution of terminal performance, thereby enhancing an uncertainty-aware balance between exploration and exploitation. We further integrate a large neighbourhood search (LNS) with the surrogate to navigate the combinatorial design space in parallel. Experimental results show that the proposed approach improves average prediction accuracy by 14.89% and 23.42% over two standard GP surrogates and reduces average vehicle travel time by 4.15%, 1.47%, and 3.27% compared with two Bayesian optimisation approaches and the LNS-based simulation optimisation approach, respectively.

Title: Relief resource allocation with time restrictions in dual reserve humanitarian supply chain
Authors: Daqiang Chen, Lalitha Dhamotharan, Xin Chen, QingXin Chen
Affiliations: Zhejiang Gongshang University; University of Exeter Business School, University of Exeter, Exeter, United Kingdom; School of Public Affairs, Zhejiang Gongshang University, Hangzhou, People’s Republic of China
Abstract: Relief resource allocation is a pivotal component of humanitarian aid during disaster response. The urgency of our work stems from two temporal constraints: time-sensitive medical intervention (golden hour therapeutic window) to prevent infected patient deterioration, and demand dynamics with hourly/daily increments in affected areas. The humanitarian supply chain relies on a dual reserve system (physical stockpiles and production capacity) to meet these demands. We address the interdependency between demand volatility and emergency response activation by developing a prescriptive optimisation framework for relief resource allocation under time restrictions. The framework partitions relief resource pooling stations endogenously into virtual units for modelling and proposes a three-phase solution: baseline (no time restrictions), feasible (with time restrictions) and optimal (with time restrictions) allocation. This method corrects discrepancies between planned and actual resource needs, critical in pandemic scenarios where delays heighten mortality risks and resource misallocation. Simulations on bioterrorism-induced disease outbreaks validate the framework. Results show: (1) optimised resource allocation while maintaining differential time restrictions at each affected area, (2) enhanced dual reserve system performance, operational robustness and resilience and (3) time restrictions directly shape allocation schemes by leveraging available reserves. The framework applies to scenarios like the COVID-19 pandemic, offering actionable managerial insights.

Title: Logic-based Benders decomposition for integrated order acceptance, distributed heterogeneous factories, inventory, and hub-spoke delivery scheduling under make-to-order products
Authors: Xiaoyan Wang, Taoliang Wang, Fei Zuo, Yongling Liu
Affiliations: Shenyang Aerospace University
Abstract: This article investigates an integrated production and distribution scheduling problem considering order acceptance (OA-IPDS) with committed delivery dates. It integrates order acceptance, distributed heterogeneous factories, inventory, and a hub-spoke delivery network within a complex system for producing customised orders, aiming to minimize total operating costs, including rejection, production, transportation, inventory, and overdue costs. Accepted orders are split into jobs and then enter the production system. Completed jobs are transported from factories to service centers, and then orders with all their jobs arrive and are delivered from service centers to customers. A mixed integer programming model is formulated and further enhanced by a proposed dominance rule, for which a logic-based Benders decomposition (LBBD) method and a branch-and-check search framework are also developed. The proposed LBBD method divides the problem into the master problem of order acceptance and job assignment and the subproblem of production and distribution scheduling. A hybrid algorithm, TS_LBBD, integrating tabu search and the LBBD method, is also proposed to further enhance computational performance. Extensive computational experiments demonstrate that the proposed algorithm can generate optimal or near-optimal solutions efficiently and validate the OA-IPDS model, analyze the sensitivity of key cost factors, and provide valuable managerial insights for practitioners.

Title: Correction
Abstract: Article title: Strategic lean practices for Industry 5.0 manufacturingAuthor: Søberg, Peder Veng, Rasmus Sorth and Samuel Brüning LarsenJournal: International Journal of Production ResearchDOI: htt...

Title: Influencer selection under budget constraints: a learning approach
Authors: Zhen Xu, Xinjie Xing, Sunil Tiwari
Affiliations: University of Liverpool; University of Bristol Business School
Abstract: Influencer marketing is becoming the fastest-growing and most cost-effective form of marketing and advertising. In this paper, we consider an influencer selection problem in online learning and adaptive settings: a brand conducts influencer marketing campaigns to promote a product over multiple rounds with a limited promotional budget. We propose a cumulative oversampling (CO) technique for Thompson Sampling (TS) that can be used to construct optimistic parameter estimates using significantly fewer samples from the posterior distributions compared to existing oversampling frameworks. By combining CO with the oracle we designed for the offline problem, our online learning algorithm simultaneously addresses budget allocation, parameter learning, and reward maximisation. We prove that our online learning algorithm achieves a scaled regret comparable to that of the UCB-based algorithms for the Influence Maximisation problem. It is the first regret bound for TS-based algorithms for IM semi-bandits that does not depend linearly on the reciprocal of the minimum observation probability of an edge. Our results provide actionable insights for firms on how to allocate marketing budgets and select influencers in dynamic and uncertain environments.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: The 2‐D Orthogonal Packing Problem With Multiple Levels of Prioritization: A Spatial Optimization Perspective
Authors: William K. Kirschenman, H. Sebastian Heese, Michael G. Kay, Russell E. King, Brandon M. McConnell
Affiliations: Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering North Carolina State University Raleigh North Carolina USA; Poole College of Management North Carolina State University Raleigh North Carolina USA; Center for Additive Manufacturing and Logistics (CAMAL) North Carolina State University Raleigh North Carolina USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper addresses two‐dimensional orthogonal packing within a confined space, integrating bin packing principles with facility layout concepts to address scenarios in which items must not only fit but also be arranged according to spatial priorities. We embed a prioritization matrix into the bin packing framework, enabling items to be clustered with one another or pulled toward certain bin access points based on assigned priority weights. Unlike traditional bin packing, which often minimizes bin count or unused space, our approach balances proximity to bin access points and adjacency among functionally related items already assigned to a given bin, extending the utility of bin packing to applications requiring more nuanced layout preferences. We introduce a single mixed‐integer linear programming (MILP) model and a complementary sliding‐window matheuristic that scales effectively to larger problem instances. Numerical experiments illustrate that this matheuristic approach consistently outperforms a direct MILP solve with a commercial solver in both runtime and solution quality, and also performs best among the adapted heuristic and metaheuristic alternatives considered in our study. This computational study underscores the flexibility and effectiveness of embedding multilevel priorities into orthogonal packing.

Title: Advance selling strategies for reducing food loss: consumer perceptions and retailer decision-making
Authors: Song Wang, Yanping Liu, Na Luo, Herbert Sima
Abstract: Reducing food loss is crucial for global food security and supply chain sustainability. This study examines how advance selling strategies impact food loss and profitability, with a focus on consumer perceptions of product quality deterioration. Unlike traditional models assuming perfect consumer knowledge, we distinguish between effective and perceived quality deterioration, recognizing that consumers often make decisions based on perceptions that may not reflect a product’s true condition. We analyze consumer behavior across high, low, and constant valuation scenarios to understand how perceptions influence purchasing decisions and reduce food loss. The results show that the hybrid selling (HS) model minimizes food loss most effectively when effort costs remain below a critical threshold. However, when effort costs exceed this threshold, or when the appearance change period is long, the pure advance selling (PAS) model becomes more effective in reducing food loss. Compared to the pure spot-market selling (PSS) and PAS models, the HS model consistently results in lower food loss, especially when consumers highly value product quality, although it may not be the most profitable model under certain conditions. Robustness tests, including shared quality information and nonlinear deterioration rates, confirm the effectiveness of the HS model. The findings suggest that improving consumer awareness and perceived value can reduce quality-related losses, enhance inventory management, and improve both profitability and sustainability. This research offers actionable insights for retailers seeking to reduce food loss and improve supply chain efficiency.

Title: The operational effectiveness of a full capacity protocol to ease crowding at an emergency department
Authors: Lu Wang, Mazhar Arikan, Suman Mallik
Affiliations: Lumpkin College of Business and Technology Eastern Illinois University Charleston Illinois USA; School of Business University of Kansas Lawrence Kansas USA
Abstract: Abstract Using detailed timestamp data for patient visits and laboratory test orders from the emergency department (ED) of a large, urban, teaching hospital in the United States, we examine the operational effectiveness of the full capacity protocol (FCP), a set of temporary hospital‐wide guidelines that seek to alleviate crowding at the ED. We use an instrumented difference‐in‐differences approach and construct a comparable treatment group prior to the introduction of the FCP. Our results indicate that the FCP is effective in reducing the patient length of stay (LOS) when activated. Patients who arrived when the FCP was activated experienced an estimated reduction in LOS of 6.23%. This reduction was achieved through shorter waiting and after‐treatment times. The reduction in after‐treatment time helped expedite access to the treatment area for waiting patients, alleviating the bottleneck and improving the throughput, consistent with the theory of swift even flow and the theory of constraints. We also find an inverted‐U‐shaped relationship between boarding census and after‐treatment time when the FCP was on, a pattern not observed under similar crowding levels when the FCP was not on.

Title: Imputing Poverty Indicators Without Consumption Data: An Exploratory Analysis
Authors: Hai‐Anh H. Dang, Talip Kilic, Kseniya Abanokova, Calogero Carletto
Affiliations: Data Analytics Unit, Development Data Group World Bank Washington DC USA; IZA, Luxembourg Institute of Socio‐Economic Research Esch‐sur‐Alzette Luxembourg; Indiana University Bloomington Indiana USA; London School of Economics and Political Science London UK; University of Economics Ho Chi Minh City Vietnam; Survey Unit, Development Data Group World Bank Washington DC USA; Free‐land Researcher Washington DC USA; Deputy Chief Statistician, Development Data Group World Bank Washington DC USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Accurate poverty measurement relies on household consumption data, but such data are often inadequate, outdated, or display inconsistencies over time in poorer countries. To address these data challenges, we employ survey‐to‐survey imputation to produce estimates for several poverty indicators including headcount poverty, extreme poverty, poverty gap, near‐poverty rates, as well as mean consumption levels and the entire consumption distribution. Analysing 22 multi‐topic household surveys conducted over the past decade in Bangladesh, Ethiopia, Malawi, Nigeria, Tanzania, and Vietnam, we find encouraging results. Adding either household utility expenditures or food expenditures to basic imputation models with household‐level demographic, employment, and asset variables could improve the probability of imputation accuracy between 0.1 and 0.4. Adding predictors from geospatial data could further increase imputation accuracy. The analysis also shows that a larger time interval between surveys is associated with a lower probability of predicting some poverty indicators, and that a better imputation model goodness‐of‐fit ( R 2 ) does not necessarily help. The results offer cost‐saving inputs into future survey design.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Advances in statistical modelling for social science: part 2—longevity, risk, and the socio-economic structure
Authors: Leonardo Salvatore Alaimo, Susanna Levantesi, Andrea Nigri

Title: Advances in statistical modelling for social science: part 1—measuring and structuring social complexity
Authors: Leonardo Salvatore Alaimo, Susanna Levantesi, Andrea Nigri

Title: Enabling empowerment over exploitative specialization: The role of total productive maintenance in precarious work contexts
Authors: Maria Joao Coelho Guedes, Mateus do Rego Ferreira Lima, Elliot Bendoly, Pankaj Patel, Daniel Bachrach
Abstract: The growing reliance on contingent workers raises critical questions about organizational practices that shape both firm performance and worker outcomes. We examine how high-performance work practices (HPWPs) focused on specialization versus empowerment influence contingent worker development, organizational returns, and risks of exploitation. We then compare these practices with the more organic, process-oriented principles of Total Productive Maintenance (TPM), emphasizing transparency, cross-training, and discretion as foundations that enable empowerment to deliver mutual benefits. We employ a multi-method, multi-source design: matched-sample surveys of operations and human resource (HR) managers, third-party financial data, and 14 semi-structured post-hoc interviews with HR and operations managers. Our results reveal two distinct paths for firms. A specialization-focused approach enhances task-specific productivity but risks limiting professional growth, with burdens falling on contingent workers. In contrast, when TPM conditions provide knowledge foundations, empowerment practices show a significant positive relationship with return on equity. Interviews further indicate that such empowerment benefits not only firms financially but also contingent workers’ professional well-being. This study highlights the dual-edged nature of HPWPs for contingent workers, distinguishing between potentially exploitative specialization and mutually beneficial empowerment. By demonstrating how TPM conditions enable empowerment to deliver both organizational and worker gains, we contribute to theory and practice on the sociotechnical dynamics of contingent work. Findings underscore the importance of coordinated operations and HR planning, showing that empowerment can only succeed when supported by transparent processes and cross-functional training.

Title: Interest rates and bank runs
Authors: Timur Magzhanov, Anton Polous
Abstract: We study how high short-term interest rates affect depositor withdrawals and bank fragility. In a global games model, depositors choose between bank deposits and money market funds, while bank holds short-term and long-term assets. Higher rates raise the payoff from withdrawing and reduce long-term asset recovery values. The model delivers a critical interest rate threshold above which runs occur, conditional on bank balance-sheet fundamentals. Lower switching cost, weaker long-term asset returns, larger fire-sale loss, and larger long-term asset share lower the threshold and expand the run region.

Title: Target-driven Bayesian stacking of realised and implied volatility forecasts
Authors: Hongfei Guo, J.M. Marín, Helena Veiga
Abstract: We propose target-driven Bayesian stacking for a fixed six-model ensemble of GARCH and stochastic-volatility forecasts with realised- and VIX-based extensions. Two rolling stacking rules target either log predictive density or QLIKE. In S&P 500, the objective changes the preferred information channel: LPD stacking remains centred on GARCH-RV, whereas QLIKE stacking shifts toward GARCH-VIX. Across 56 rolling windows, the QLIKE stack improves certainty-equivalent returns by roughly one to one-and-a-half percentage points per year, depending on the investor’s risk aversion. In the 30 windows where the QLIKE stack assigns material weight to implied volatility models, the gain exceeds two percentage points per year with a 90% win rate. However, LPD stacking delivers tighter 5% Value-at-Risk calibration.

Title: Tax-financed green policies and income inequality in an agent-based model
Authors: Lucca Gustafson Rodrigues, Gilberto Tadeu Lima, Pedro Romero Marques
Abstract: The interdependent dynamics among economic growth, income inequality, and greenhouse gas emissions have attracted attention in both academic and policy discussions on decarbonization strategies. Notwithstanding this expanding body of work, theoretical and empirical contributions underscore the difficulty of simultaneously achieving favorable outcomes across these three dimensions, suggesting the existence of a structural trilemma involving growth, income distribution, and environmental degradation. This paper develops an agent-based model (ABM) to explore these trade-offs and focuses on the impacts of different tax-financed green policies. Financing and environmental policy instruments produce complex effects on key macroeconomic variables, raising questions about whether—and under what conditions—the trilemma holds. The simulations examine scenarios in which either a carbon tax or a wealth tax finance the following green policies: (i) green price subsidy, (ii) public non-patented green R&D, (iii) subsidy for private green R&D, and (iv) green public procurement. While the carbon tax is both a financing and an environmental policy instrument, the wealth tax is primarily a mechanism of income redistribution. Findings suggest that the policy mix is a key determinant of whether the trilemma might occur. On the one hand, carbon taxation is more effective in reducing emissions but at higher social and macroeconomic costs. On the other hand, despite promoting redistribution, wealth taxation must count on specific complementary policies—such as public-led green innovation—to foster a low-carbon economy.

Title: Decoupling transition patterns in the global economy: A multi-regional structural decomposition analysis
Authors: Waka Nishifuji, Shigemi Kagawa
Abstract: This study revisits the decoupling of economic growth and carbon emissions by identifying limitations in conventional state-based classifications and proposing a transition-based framework with endogenously determined thresholds. We use the global multi-regional input–output database (2000−2021) to construct continuous attribute vectors in order to capture the relationship between changes in per capita gross domestic expenditure (GDE) and per capita carbon footprints across 56 countries. Hierarchical clustering reveals seven distinct decoupling transition patterns. The results demonstrate that widely used fixed thresholds such as Tapio's 0.8 boundary between coupling and weak decoupling may separate countries with highly similar trajectories while grouping countries that follow fundamentally different transition paths. Structural decomposition analysis indicates that, although improvements in emission intensity constitute the largest emission-reduction effect and per capita GDE growth remains the dominant driver of emission increases, divergent decoupling outcomes among countries with comparable growth rates are explained primarily by differences in trade structures and shifts in the sectoral composition of final demand. These findings suggest that decoupling should be understood as a development stage-dependent transition process rather than a static state, with important implications for structurally differentiated climate policy design.

Title: Biodiversity benefits of the climate adaptation policy: Evidence from millions birdwatching records in China
Authors: Hantian Sheng, Canfei He, Wenbo Hu
Abstract: Climate adaptation policies are critical for building urban resilience, yet their ecological consequences remain underexplored. We take China's climate adaptation pilot policy (CACP) as a quasi-natural experiment and employ a difference-in-differences approach to examine the biodiversity effects. By using a unique dataset of over four million birdwatching records from 2012 to 2021, we find that the policy significantly increases biodiversity, raising the Shannon diversity index by 0.25–0.40 units in pilot cities. Mechanism analyses reveal three influencing channels, including improved air quality, enhanced vegetation cover, and stimulated green innovation. Meanwhile, the positive ecological effects are more pronounced in disaster-prone and less economically developed regions, and are conditioned by both public concern and governmental attention. Our findings highlight synergies among climate action, biodiversity conservation, and equitable urban development, and provide empirical evidence that climate policies could create win-win outcomes across these policy domains. We also propose that ecological considerations should be incorporated into adaptation planning both in China and globally.

Title: Strategic disclosure of emissions under supplier competition
Authors: Amirmohsen Golmohammadi, Armaǧan Özbilge, Samuel Yousefi
Abstract: Growing concerns about climate change have prompted governments to require firms to disclose greenhouse gas emissions, including those across supply chains (Scope 3). To estimate supplier emissions, firms may rely on secondary data (e.g., industry averages) or primary data reported by suppliers. When a supplier reports emissions below the industry average, the buying firm can reduce its reported Scope 3 emissions, creating a competitive advantage. We develop a game-theoretic model to study how competition shapes suppliers’ emissions measurement and disclosure decisions in a supply chain with one firm and two competing suppliers. We show that disclosure strategies are governed by two thresholds, responsiveness and disinvestment, that together determine when disclosure is unconditionally optimal, strategically conditional, or never beneficial. Counterintuitively, lower measurement costs, higher industry-average emissions, or greater production capacity can lead suppliers to stop measuring emissions, as competitive dynamics can eliminate the informational advantage disclosure provides. The structural properties of this threshold framework are robust across several extensions, including post-disclosure pricing, delayed disclosure, buyer transparency, and fixed adoption costs. These findings reveal that incentive mechanisms targeting individual suppliers can have unintended consequences for overall disclosure rates, offering actionable guidance for firms seeking to improve Scope 3 reporting transparency.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Bi-objective electric vehicle routing with charging–swapping replenishment and location-dependent waiting time
Authors: Xin Zhang, Jiantong Zhang, Tingting Chen
Abstract: The rapid adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) in logistics distribution has created new fleet-routing challenges related to limited driving range, station congestion, and multiple replenishment options. This paper studies a bi-objective electric vehicle routing problem with location-dependent waiting time (BEVRP-LD), in which partial charging and battery swapping are jointly considered under customer time-window commitments. The problem aims to reduce operational cost while improving customer satisfaction. Waiting time is represented as a location- and technology-dependent delay, estimated using an M / M /1 queue for partial charging and an M / D /1 queue for battery swapping. The model jointly determines vehicle routes, station selection, replenishment technology choice, and charging amount under partial charging, while representing customer satisfaction through soft time windows. A mixed-integer linear programming formulation and a clustering-enhanced NSGA-II-based solution framework are developed to generate cost–service trade-off solutions. Computational experiments on benchmark instances and an urban distribution case associated with JD Logistics in China show that the proposed framework can generate diverse Pareto solutions and make the underlying cost–service trade-off explicit. The results indicate that the hybrid use of charging and swapping can improve the balance between cost and service performance, while location-dependent waiting time changes replenishment technology choice and improves the operational realism of routing decisions. The case-based analysis further provides managerial insights into replenishment strategy selection, the use of location-dependent waiting-time information, and the effects of key economic and operational conditions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Learning from risk: LLM-guided generation of safety-critical scenarios with prior knowledge
Authors: Yuhang Wang, Heye Huang, Zhenhua Xu, Kailai Sun, Baoshen Guo, Jinhua Zhao
Abstract: Autonomous driving faces critical challenges in rare long-tail events and complex multi-agent interactions, which are scarce in real-world data yet essential for robust safety validation. This paper presents a high-fidelity scenario generation framework that integrates a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) with a large language model (LLM). The CVAE encodes historical trajectories and map information from large-scale naturalistic datasets to learn latent traffic structures, enabling the generation of physically consistent base scenarios. Building on this, the LLM acts as an adversarial reasoning engine, parsing unstructured scene descriptions into domain-specific loss functions and dynamically guiding scenario generation across varying risk levels. This knowledge-driven optimization balances realism with controllability, ensuring that generated scenarios remain both plausible and risk-sensitive. Extensive experiments in CARLA and SMARTS demonstrate that our framework substantially increases the coverage of high-risk and long-tail events, improves consistency between simulated and real-world traffic distributions, and exposes autonomous driving systems to interactions that are significantly more challenging than those produced by existing rule- or data-driven methods. These results establish a new pathway for safety validation, enabling principled stress-testing of autonomous systems under rare but consequential events. Code is available at https://github.com/echoleaeperw/LRF .
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: A two-layer approach of integrating trajectory planner and motion controller for connected and automated buses under mixed traffic flow
Authors: Tianqi Wang, Weihan Xu, Xin Li
Abstract: This study proposes a hierarchical framework for the trajectory planning and motion control of connected and automated buses (CABs) operating in mixed traffic environments alongside connected and automated vehicles (CAVs) and human-driven vehicles (HVs). Then, a two-layer optimization model is developed, in which the upper-layer maneuver planner optimizes the spatiotemporal positions of CABs and CAVs under bus routing constraints, while the lower-layer vehicle controller is responsible for trajectory planning and the execution of control commands in connection to the spatiotemporal constraints from the upper layer. To solve this constrained optimal control problem and address environmental uncertainties, a customized algorithm integrating a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) with Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP) is designed. Extensive simulations show that the proposed model and algorithm reduce bus schedule deviation by 77.2%, concurrently increase overall traffic throughput by 30%, and lower average delay by 46.4%. Maximum performance is achieved at 60% CAV penetration, highlighting the framework’s potential for cost-effective deployment and significant improvements in both transit punctuality and mixed-traffic efficiency.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: A New Approach to collinearity and elasticity problems in value of travel time savings estimation with multinomial logit models
Authors: Louis de Grange, Matthieu Marechal, Raúl Pezoa, Felipe González, Rodrigo Troncoso
Abstract: The value of travel time savings (VTTS) is a central parameter in transport-project appraisal. When estimated from a multinomial logit (MNL) model of mode choice, the VTTS can become imprecise under two structural conditions of the data: strong collinearity between travel time and travel cost, common in revealed-preference samples where cost is imputed at a fixed rate per kilometer; and low absolute price-elasticity of demand, which makes the estimated cost coefficient close to zero and inflates the variance of the VTTS estimator, formed as a ratio with that coefficient in the denominator. Both conditions share a common cause: the cost coefficient is not well identified by the data. This paper diagnoses both conditions analytically and through simulation, and proposes an elasticity-constrained estimator that addresses this common cause by tying the cost coefficient to a value consistent with external price-elasticity evidence. The estimator is compared through simulations to maximum likelihood and ridge estimation. The results show that under adverse collinearity and demand elasticity conditions, maximum likelihood estimates exhibit high variance and errors, even with large samples, while ridge estimates display less variance and improved stability but also significant levels of bias. By contrast, the proposed method, although it introduces bias if the actual demand elasticity is distant from that of the applied restriction, achieves lower values for mean squared error. The three methods are also compared in an application to the Swissmetro mode choice dataset. The results in this case show that although multinomial logit can, in theory, be consistent, the elasticity-constrained method again obtains the lowest mean squared error by reducing the variance of the VTTS estimates. The ridge estimator, meanwhile, proved to be less competitive. Complementing these comparative findings are the results of the Hausman test. The proposed estimator is recommended for VTTS estimation in revealed-preference contexts where strong collinearity and inelastic demand jointly compromise identification, and we provide guidance on the contexts in which it is most useful and on its relationship with alternatives such as willingness-to-pay-space estimation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: How is online shopping reshaping activity patterns? Modeling activity behavior using discrete continuous models
Authors: Katherine E. Asmussen, Usman Ahmed
Abstract: This paper investigates how the rise of online shopping has reconfigured daily time–use patterns across six activity categories (online shopping, in–store shopping, at–home leisure, outside–of–home leisure, at–home maintenance, and outside–of–home maintenance) using the 2013 and 2023 waves of the American Time Use Survey. We employ a multiple discrete continuous framework to jointly estimate time–allocation parameters, decade-shift effects, and to capture complementarity and substitution effects among virtual and non–virtual, home–based and outside–of–home pursuits. Our results reveal that, while baseline shopping preferences remained stable over the decade, participation in at–home leisure and maintenance rose sharply and outside–of–home engagement declined, a likely legacy of pandemic confinement and shifting consumer expectations. Interaction effects show that online shopping complements in–store shopping and at-home leisure but substitutes for outside–of–home leisure and any type of maintenance activity. These findings highlight the need for activity-based travel demand models that more explicitly incorporate at-home and ICT-mediated behaviors, as well as for transportation and access policies that respond to the changing relationships among online shopping, in-store shopping, freight activity, and daily time use across different household and neighborhood contexts.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Cash transfers and time use within the household: an analysis of the effect of Familias en Acción
Authors: Edgar Marcillo-Yepez, Maira Emy Reimão, Conner Mullally, Pilar Useche
Abstract: Conditional cash transfers (CCTs) have been found to have several benefits, particularly with respect to educational outcomes of targeted children. However, concerns have also been raised that CCTs may further push women into traditional gender norms, as they make mothers responsible for ensuring that their children meet the conditionalities and that their family receives the transfer. We analyze 2020–21 time use data from Colombia, and find that the CCT Familias en Acción increased the time that mothers allocated to domestic work, particularly when they have children aged 6–14. This pattern does not come from a substitution between children's and mothers’ domestic labor, but, rather, reveals that the cash transfer enabled women to decrease their labor force participation during the pandemic – but that their time was then reallocated toward more domestic work, following traditional norms.

Title: Reinforcement learning-guided multi-objective particle swarm optimization with adaptive topology
Authors: Baotong Wu, Zhixiang Chen, Emrah Demir
Abstract: Multi-objective optimization problems often involve a trade-off between convergence toward the Pareto front and diversity along the front. This study proposes a reinforcement learning-guided multi-objective particle swarm optimization algorithm, called RL-MOPSO, which uses adaptive topology selection to manage this trade-off during the search. The algorithm combines three network topologies: global best, dual-population ring, and Von-Neumann topology with an adaptive jump collaboration operator. Q-learning selects among these topologies dynamically using feedback from convergence and distribution metrics. Computational experiments compare RL-MOPSO with 11 algorithms, including six state-of-the-art methods and five topology-based MOPSO variants. The results show that RL-MOPSO improves both convergence and diversity. The ablation experiments further confirm the contributions of Q-learning and the proposed topology structures.

Title: Kinky Europe: Evidence from the regional Phillips curve in the euro area
Authors: Marius Faber, Gabriel Züllig
Abstract: We estimate the slope of the Phillips curve in the euro area, allowing for nonlinearities–or kinks–in the relationship between labor market slack and inflation. We exploit cross-country variation in labor market conditions in the period 2001–2024, absorbing aggregate shocks and endogenous monetary policy reactions with time fixed effects. We find that, while the Phillips curve is usually quite flat, it becomes at least three times steeper when the labor market is sufficiently tight. This kink is more pronounced in the euro area than in the United States, potentially due to more rigid labor markets. Our estimates suggest, however, that despite this nonlinearity, most of the post-pandemic inflation surge is attributable to factors other than labor market tightness.

Title: Collaborative planning framework for heavy-duty truck electrification: corridor-port integrated energy systems
Authors: Ruihua Wang, Xuejun Feng, Suyang Wang, Kaixuan Tao, Yan Zhang, Kum Fai Yuen, Min Wu
Abstract: Deep decarbonisation of heavy-duty truck freight is essential for global carbon neutrality. As vital intermodal hubs, ports can support the development of green freight corridors. However, existing research on port integrated energy systems primarily focuses on internal logistics and vessels, neglecting corridor- port energy-demand coupling. To bridge this gap, we propose a “Corridor-Port Integrated Energy System” (C-PIES) framework and develop a two-stage distributionally robust optimisation model to address uncertainties in renewable energy generation and freight traffic flow. Using high-frequency GPS trajectory data, ambiguity sets are constructed to support robust scheduling of port renewable energy for corridor traffic-driven loads. A case study of Quanzhou Port shows that C-PIES enables source-load-storage coordination through battery swapping stations reducing system cost by 42.89% and carbon emissions by 50.2% compared with the isolated mode. The results demonstrate the potential of ports as regional energy hubs for low-carbon freight corridors.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Port environmental health Risks: Insights from the Tarragona Port-Industrial complex and planning implications
Authors: Jose L. Domingo, Joaquim Rovira, Martí Nadal
Abstract: Ports handle approximately 80% of world trade and concentrate vessels, cargo operations, and logistics that generate substantial pollution affecting nearby populations. Following a structured literature search and a narrative synthesis organized around a source-to-exposure-to-impact conceptual framework, this review evaluates the health risks associated with residential proximity to ports. Evidence consistently links port-related emissions to cardiovascular and respiratory mortality, asthma, lung cancer, adverse pregnancy outcomes, and neurodevelopmental effects. The Tarragona Port is used as an illustrative example of a complex port-industrial setting in which port and co-located petrochemical emissions jointly contribute to a quantified local burden of preventable deaths and disability-adjusted life years, although the fraction attributable to port activities alone cannot be readily isolated from that of the adjacent petrochemical complex and other urban sources. These findings support targeted interventions, including mandatory Health Impact Assessments, health-based buffer zones, optimized freight routing, and real-time air quality monitoring integrated into port operations.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Route efficiency and carbon emissions of commercial UAV delivery: Evidence from Shenzhen
Authors: Jing-Peng Wang, Yong Zhou, Yang Cui, Qiong Tian, Peng Liu
Abstract: Urban commercial unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) delivery is increasingly regarded as a faster and potentially lower-emission alternative to ground-based logistics, yet direct evidence from repeated operations remains scarce. Using commercial telemetry from Shenzhen in 2024, this study empirically characterizes an operational UAV delivery network. We retain 45,256 valid trajectories to examine network structure and route performance. Operations are concentrated on recurrent origin-destination (OD) corridors. Compared with OSRM-routed ground alternatives between matched rounded endpoints, the mean trajectory-level route-saving ratio is 15.78%, and the mean absolute distance saving is 1.08 km per delivery. We then translate the observed route records into scenario-based operational carbon estimates. Under the baseline coefficients, estimated UAV operational emissions are 0.080 kg CO 2 per delivery, compared with 0.243 kg CO 2 per delivery for electric vehicle and 1.022 kg CO 2 per delivery for fuel vehicle. UAV trajectories are observed, whereas ground routes and emissions are modeled under stated assumptions. The results provide an empirical basis for selective UAV deployment in urban logistics planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Firm organization and worker outcomes: The role of occupational specialization
Authors: Guido Matias Cortes, Diego Dabed, Ana Oliveira, Anna Salomons
Abstract: Using matched employer-employee data from Portugal, we show that firms differ starkly in their occupational employment composition, even within detailed industries, with some firms employing workers across a broad range of occupations and others being much more specialized. These differences are robustly predictive of wages: a worker employed in an occupationally-specialized firm earns less than that same worker employed in a less specialized firm. The wage penalty for working in an occupationally-specialized firm is observed across occupations and industries of all skill levels, and is distinct from the penalty associated with working in a firm with fewer organizational layers. Specialization helps account for the role of firms in inequality, as specialization is strongly negatively related to estimated AKM firm fixed effects. Around 40%–50% of the wage penalty from specialization is explained by differences in firm productivity. Specialized firms, however, also engage in lower rates of rent-sharing conditional on productivity, accounting for up to 30% of the difference in wage premia between high- and low-specialization firms.
