Finally, we show that being employed in a specialized firm is also associated with worse longer-term career outcomes for workers.

Title: Anti-bullying laws and youth risky health behaviors
Authors: Caterina Muratori, Joseph J. Sabia
Abstract: The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services has urged a coordinated “public health approach” to combatting bullying in schools, in part due to concerns that bullying victimization causes teens to turn to risky behaviors as a coping mechanism. This study provides new evidence on the effect of anti-bullying laws (ABLs) on youth risky health behaviors. Using data from the Youth Risk Behavior Surveys and a generalized difference-in-differences approach, we find little evidence that ABL adoption leads to statistically significant or economically meaningful reductions in binge drinking, tobacco use, marijuana use, risky sex, or body weight for the average teenager. However, for some historically marginalized youth—particularly those who identify as lesbian, gay, bisexual, or questioning—we find some evidence of ABL-induced improvements in behavioral health, especially with respect to binge drinking. This finding is consistent with disproportionate ABL health gains for queer youth.

Title: Electric vehicle routing problem with multi-visit drones considering time windows and battery swapping stations
Authors: Shanshan Meng, Hongwei Ma
Abstract: In this study, the conventional vehicle routing problem is extended by introducing an integrated electric vehicle–drone system. Within this framework, electric vehicles stop at customer locations to concurrently deploy multiple drones for making time-constrained deliveries, aiming to minimise the total cost with the inclusion of battery swapping expenditures. In contrast with existing vehicle routing problems involving drones, the proposed approach allows drones to conduct multiple deliveries per trip and incorporates battery swapping stations to support electric vehicle operations. A detailed mixed-integer bilinear programming formulation is developed to enhance the realism of the model. On the basis of an adaptive large neighbourhood search framework, a hybrid metaheuristic algorithm is designed for large instances; this algorithm features tailored removal and repair operators, complementary local search procedures, and a station relocation mechanism. Additionally, preprocessing procedures are integrated to preclude infeasible moves, and an effective algorithm is dedicated to determining electric vehicle waiting times. Various numerical simulations are employed to validate the model, confirm the superior performance and applicability of the proposed approach, and quantify its advantages in terms of optimising waiting times, enabling multiple drone trips and integrating battery swapping stations. A case study further corroborates these findings and provides additional operational and managerial insights into the practical implementation of these strategies. These features highlight the cost advantages of the integrated system over an electric vehicle-only paradigm, achieving an average cost reduction of approximately 30%. Furthermore, compared with benchmark algorithms from the literature, the proposed algorithm improves the quality of the output solutions by more than 10%.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Flexible yard template planning with variable size sub-blocks in container terminals
Authors: Haixia Wu, Junliang He, Caimao Tan, Yu Wang
Abstract: To address the rigidity caused by fixed sub-block capacities in container terminal yards, this study proposes a flexible yard template planning method based on variable size sub-block. In this method, sub-block capacity is modeled as a decision variable, and sub-block boundaries are dynamically adjusted according to route specific container volumes and vessel operation time windows, enabling flexible space allocation. Based on this approach, a mixed-integer programming model is developed to jointly optimize sub-block partitioning and allocation, with the objective of minimizing operational costs while maximizing yard space utilization. To efficiently solve the model, an improved Benders decomposition algorithm is designed, incorporating heuristic initial solutions and Pareto-optimal cuts. Numerical results show that, compared with fixed size strategies, the proposed method can reduce yard bay requirements by approximately 16% to 21.7% across different problem scales. Sensitivity analysis further indicates that vessel operation time is a key factor affecting optimal sub-block sizing, and that a nonlinear trade-off exists between transportation costs and delay penalty costs.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: A quantitative analysis of multidimensional changes in unemployment insurance policies
Authors: Lei Fang, Jun Nie, Zoe Xie
Abstract: The US government has historically expanded unemployment insurance (UI) during economic downturns along three policy dimensions: benefit amount, duration, and eligibility. We study how these elements affect the labor market, focusing in particular on the interaction among them. Specifically, we quantify the impact of the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (CARES) Act UI package, which combined all three during the COVID-19 pandemic. The package raised average unemployment rate by 1.05 percentage points during April–December 2020. Two-thirds of this effect resulted from amplification by economic shutdown policies and COVID-19 infection risk. Decomposing the CARES Act UI package reveals that interactions between the three policy dimensions accounted for one-fourth of the total effect, highlighting that policy components do not operate in isolation.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Reconfiguring supply chains amid geopolitical risks: a systematic review of emerging topics
Authors: Xinyue Liu, William Ho, Hugo K.S. Lam, Srinivas Talluri
Affiliations: The University of Melbourne; University of Liverpool; Michigan State University
Abstract: In recent years, geopolitical events such as Brexit and the U.S.–China trade war have become increasingly frequent and have had significant impacts on supply chains. Supply chain reconfiguration has been recognised as an effective approach to addressing geopolitical risks (GPRs). However, existing literature reviews in this field exhibit several limitations that motivate us to advance the understanding of supply chain reconfiguration amid GPRs. Accordingly, we conduct a systematic literature review of 92 high-quality journal articles published between 2015 and May 2026 to identify key emerging topics, their antecedents–decisions–outcomes (ADO) frameworks, and the associated research gaps and future research directions. Specifically, we apply a topic modelling technique combined with a semantic validation approach to classify the articles into five topics and rank their scores of emergence. This process identifies three emerging topics: supply chain reconfigurations in advanced technology sectors, adaptive risk management approaches, and diversification strategies. For each emerging topic, we develop topic-specific research frameworks using an ADO framework incorporating moderators. Based on identified gaps, we propose tailored future research directions for each emerging topic. Overall, this study advances the understanding of supply chain reconfiguration amid GPRs and provides actionable insights for future researchers and practitioners.

Title: Seeing Beauty in Ugly Produce: Do Ugly Produce Retailers Reduce Food Waste?
Authors: Zheng Han, Bin Hu, Milind Dawande
Affiliations: Driehaus College of Business DePaul University Chicago Illinois USA; Naveen Jindal School of Management University of Texas at Dallas Richardson Texas USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Ugly produce refers to cosmetically unconventional yet taste‐ and nutrition‐wise perfectly edible produce. Advocates of ugly produce retailers claim that they help reduce food waste, but skeptics argue that ugly produce is often not wasted but meets alternative demands such as from restaurants and processed food manufacturers. Given such complications, it is necessary to model the entire produce supply chain to properly evaluate the impact of ugly produce retailers on food waste. We model an agricultural cooperative producing, pricing, and selling produce to a retailer and an alternative buyer and find that the retailer selling ugly produce indeed strictly reduces food waste. However, doing so also weakly reduces the retailer's profit, which explains traditional grocery chains' hesitancy to carry ugly produce. Fortunately, we find that a dedicated ugly produce retailer competing with a traditional retailer yields the same food waste reduction. This research reveals supply‐chain level insights into the debate about ugly produce retailers and alludes to the sustainability value of dedicated ugly produce startups.

Title: Risk-aware trading portfolio optimization
Authors: Marco Bianchetti, Gabriele D’Acunto, Gianmarco De Francisci Morales, Yuko Kuroki, Marco Scaringi, Fabio Vitale
Abstract: We investigate portfolio optimization in financial markets from a trading and risk management perspective. We term this task Risk-Aware Trading Portfolio Optimization (RATPO), formulate the corresponding optimization problem, and propose an efficient Risk-Aware Trading Swarm (RATS) algorithm to solve it. The key elements of RATPO are a generic initial portfolio $$\mathcal {P}$$ P , a specific set of Unique Eligible Instruments (UEIs), their combination into an Eligible Optimization Strategy (EOS), an objective function, and a set of constraints. RATS searches for an optimal EOS that, added to $$\mathcal {P}$$ P , improves the objective function respecting the constraints. RATS is a specialized Particle Swarm Optimization method that leverages the parameterization of $$\mathcal {P}$$ P in terms of UEIs, enables parallel computation with a large number of particles, and is fully general with respect to specific choices of the key elements, which can be customized to encode financial knowledge and needs of traders and risk managers. We showcase two RATPO applications involving a real trading portfolio made of hundreds of different financial instruments, an objective function combining both market risk (VaR) and profit&loss measures, constraints on market sensitivities and UEIs trading costs. In the case of small-sized EOS, RATS successfully identifies the optimal solution and demonstrates robustness with respect to hyper-parameters tuning. In the case of large-sized EOS, RATS markedly improves the portfolio objective value, optimizing risk and capital charge while respecting risk limits and preserving expected profits. Our work bridges the gap between the implementation of effective trading strategies and compliance with stringent regulatory and economic capital requirements, allowing a better alignment of business and risk management objectives.

Title: Strategic interactions of platform information sharing and supplier encroachment in a multi-tier supply chain
Authors: Nenggui Zhao, Jing Wang, Panpan Xia
Abstract: This paper considers a multi-tier supply chain comprising an online platform, a supplier, and a retailer. The platform possesses a market information advantage and decides whether to share this information with either the retailer or the supplier, thereby forming asymmetric and symmetric information structures. The supplier determines its encroachment and the sequence of sales quantity decisions, leading to three supply chain structures. Under asymmetric information structures, the uninformed player makes operational decisions based on signals transmitted by the informed player, resulting in signaling games. We develop a series of Stackelberg and signaling game models to examine the individual, joint, and mutual effects of encroachment, information sharing, and the sequence of quantity decisions on supply chain performance. The findings indicate that the platform consistently exhibits a willingness to share information with other players. A separating equilibrium is proved to be the optimal strategy under asymmetric information structures, except when the supplier refrains from encroachment. In such cases, players may distort information to achieve the separating equilibrium. The supplier can strategically adjust the sequence of sales quantity decisions, making encroachment beneficial for both itself and the platform while detrimental to the retailer. Additionally, if the supplier chooses to encroach, it will always determine sales quantity after the retailer has made its decision, which in turn compels the platform to fully share information with the other players. In such a case, a Nash equilibrium emerges between the platform and the supplier.

Title: Strategic interactions and operational efficiency in supply chain networks: A game-theoretic network directional distance function approach
Authors: Sheng-Wei Lin
Abstract: This study develops an integrated Game-Theoretic Network Directional Distance Function (DDF) framework that bridges the gap between operational efficiency measurement and strategic interaction analysis in complex supply chain networks. While existing literature treats these dimensions separately, our research demonstrates their fundamental interdependence through a novel methodology that combines network DDF models with game-theoretic analyses of competitive (Nash equilibrium) and cooperative (Shapley value) scenarios. Using comprehensive data from NVIDIA's supply chain network (53 firms across four tiers, 2018-2021), we uncover three critical findings. First, pervasive operational inefficiencies exist with 30-40% improvement potential across all tiers despite intense competition. Second, substantial strategic asymmetries emerge in competitive equilibrium, with payoff differentials of up to 103%. Third, under the baseline calibrated synergy scenario the model-implied upper-bound cooperation gain is 70% relative to the Nash-grounded baseline (sum of singleton coalition values = 36.87, equal to the Nash equilibrium welfare); we emphasize that this figure is parametrically determined by the assumed synergy coefficient, and a sensitivity analysis over that coefficient yields a scenario range of 35% to 105% rather than a statistically estimated effect. Malmquist-Luenberger productivity analysis reveals concerning stagnation (average index of 1.0002), with technical regression rather than advancement constraining performance. The Shapley value analysis reveals a structurally asymmetric but core-stable allocation (coefficient of variation 0.163), with the materials-tier player receiving the largest share consistent with its competitive dominance. The research provides a rigorous methodological framework for analyzing strategic-operational interactions, offers empirical evidence that challenges assumptions about competitive efficiency in technology supply chains, and delivers actionable mechanisms for implementing value-creating collaborative strategies. These findings have immediate implications for supply chain optimization, innovation policy, and the design of fair benefit-sharing mechanisms in network production systems.

Title: Why efficient systems fail spectacularly: A unified theory of systemic risk
Authors: Bhagwan Chowdhry
Abstract: I develop a unified model of resource and risk sharing in which N agents pool against a common crisis threshold subject to transaction costs. Three results follow. As transaction costs fall: the welfare-optimal pool expands and individual buffers shrink; average welfare improves strictly; and expected crisis scale — the number of agents simultaneously unable to access the shared resource — grows, even if crisis probability falls. The mechanism is identical across financial risk pooling, supply-chain management, and transportation networks. Large systemic crises are the necessary consequence of welfare-optimal pooling. The correct policy response is a Pigouvian charge on each participant’s marginal contribution to expected crisis scale.

Title: Effects of oil price uncertainty on the stock returns of oil and gas companies
Authors: Elena Maria Diaz, Juncal Cunado, Fernando Perez de Gracia
Abstract: This paper investigates the distinct effects of oil-specific and global uncertainty shocks on the stock returns of international oil and gas companies. Using monthly data from May 2007 to August 2025, we employ a Dynamic Factor Model on high-frequency volatility indices to construct separate proxies for global uncertainty and idiosyncratic oil uncertainty shocks. The dynamic effects of these shocks are estimated using Smoothed Local Projections. Global uncertainty shocks generate an immediate and homogeneous decline in stock returns across integrated, upstream, and downstream firms. In contrast, the effects of oil-specific uncertainty depend on a firm’s position within the value chain. Upstream firms exhibit the most pronounced responses, integrated firms display intermediate and mixed effects, while downstream companies appear comparatively insulated from oil-market uncertainty. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing global from sector-specific uncertainty when assessing the financial consequences of uncertainty shocks in energy markets.

Title: Geopolitical risk and inflation: Does central bank independence matter?
Authors: Whelsy Boungou, Stevy Darel Moussavou Moussavou, Bossoma Doriane N’Doua
Abstract: Does central bank independence shape the inflationary impact of geopolitical risk? Using a panel of 29 countries over 1990–2023, we show that geopolitical risk significantly increases inflation, but that this effect depends on the degree of central bank independence. Higher institutional credibility substantially attenuates, and in some case offsets, the inflationary impact of geopolitical shocks. This moderating effect is stronger for geopolitical threats than for realized actions and is considerably more pronounced in advanced than in emerging economies. These findings highlight the importance of credible monetary institutions in enhancing resilience to geopolitical inflation.

Title: Diagnostic testing a time series regression with zero-one dummies
Authors: Philip Hans Franses, Mikhail Muradov
Abstract: We consider tests for normality, residual autocorrelation, and autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity for a time series regression, which includes various zero-one dummy variables for individual observations. The sizes of these tests are distorted as the residuals associated with the dummies are equal to zero. We propose a simple solution which amounts to dismissing the observations with these zero-valued residuals, that is, treat these observations as missing. With simulations we show that the resulting tests have the proper size.

Title: From scarcity to strategy: Designing hay markets to mitigate feed shortages and income shocks
Authors: Julia Kunkel, Jonathan Haag, Robert Finger, Sergei Schaub, Jürgen Groeneveld, Christian Klassert, Birgit Müller
Abstract: Grassland-based forages — such as grass, silage, and hay — are a key feed source for dairy cows. In the transition to more sustainable dairy systems, grassland-based production is increasingly valued for its contributions to biodiversity and regional resilience. However, droughts reduce grassland yields and raise feed prices, challenging farmers to secure feed and stable incomes. Existing coping strategies, such as early slaughter or livestock sales, can have long-term consequences beyond the drought event. In this study, we propose hay markets as a short-term buffer for drought-induced feed shortages and income shocks. We compare potential trading networks differing in trading radius and trading partners in terms of effectiveness, efficiency and possible side effects using a stylised network model. For farm units aggregated at the German county level, we simulate cost-minimal trading schedules and derive remaining feed shortages and income shocks. Results show that forage trading can reduce shocks by around two-third during nationwide droughts and fully mitigate localised shocks. Effective mitigation requires either a broad trading radius or sufficient trading partners. However, poorly connected nationwide networks can lead to inefficient transport, while segmentation at state level may lock in shortages and reduce both effectiveness and efficiency. We also observe unintended side effects: trading may shift income shocks to unaffected farm units and increase overall transport distances. Overall, we show that hay markets could enhance dairy farmers’ drought resistance, but must be designed carefully. Policy makers, farmer associations, and agricultural chambers can support this by providing a well-designed market infrastructure.

Title: Between resistance and readiness: Segment-specific reactions to consumption reduction
Authors: Charlotte Baar, Saskia Flachs, Petra Riefler, Oliver B. Büttner
Abstract: Limiting global warming to 1.5 °C requires not only technological innovation but also substantial reductions in individual consumption, particularly in high-income societies. Yet, sufficiency lifestyles evoke divergent expectations among individuals including gains and losses that act as enablers or barriers to adopting such lifestyles. Effective communication efforts aiming at promoting lifestyle uptake should be informed about existing consumer stances on this idea. Using a sample of Austrian consumers and latent class analysis, we identify five consumer segments that differ in their engagement with sufficiency-oriented lifestyles, from highly engaged to highly disengaged. These segments vary systematically in the benefits versus costs they anticipate from changing their lifestyles to support environmental goals. Anticipated satisfaction or frustration of autonomy, competence, and relatedness needs is linked to the likelihood of belonging to specific segments. The findings reveal distinct psychological profiles associated with individuals' position on sufficiency as a demand-side mitigation strategy and emphasize the importance of audience-tailored communication.

Title: Enhancing pedestrian-automated vehicle interaction using external human-machine interfaces (eHMI): an experimental study considering vehicle-eHMI, Road-eHMI, and secondary task complexity
Authors: Hailin Shi, Feng Chen, Yunjie Ju, Yanni Huang, Yitian Lin, Yudi Wu
Abstract: Automated vehicles (AVs), by lacking conventional interaction cues derived from human driver feedback, introduce greater uncertainty in pedestrian interactions, especially when secondary task engagement heightens safety risks. External human–machine interfaces (eHMI) are widely recognized as an effective means of simulating human driver communication, but current research largely remains vehicle-oriented. With the advancement of intelligent road infrastructure, it has gradually gained the capability to convey information to road users. In the context of vehicle-infrastructure cooperation, this study considers vehicle-eHMI and road-eHMI as an integrated system to explore their potential in pedestrian-AV interaction. A video-based experiment was conducted to investigate the effects of vehicle-eHMI, road-eHMI, and secondary task complexity on pedestrian crossing behavior and subjective responses. The results indicate that both vehicle-eHMI and road-eHMI improve interaction safety and enhance trust, but their influence on behavioral decisions depends on the risk level conveyed by implicit cues such as vehicle motion. Furthermore, the combined presentation of vehicle and road eHMIs yields the best performance. Increased secondary task complexity significantly elevates cognitive workload, reduces situational awareness and trust, and leads to more hesitant crossing decisions. Notably, road-eHMI demonstrated a pronounced compensatory effect under high cognitive load, as its location within the central visual field enables more efficient detection and interpretation when attention is constrained. This study highlights the necessity and feasibility of eHMIs in pedestrian-AV interaction and suggests that future designs should consider pedestrians’ cognitive states and integrate intelligent infrastructure and cooperative communication to support multi-agent interaction, providing new design insights and theoretical support for safe and efficient interaction.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Development approaches for preventing violent extremism: A systematic review of the empirical evidence
Authors: Leanne M. Kelly, Greg Barton, Anthony Ware
Abstract: This systematic review examines English-language publications documenting primary-level community programming for preventing and countering violent extremism (P/CVE) undertaken by development civil society and non-government organisations (CSO/NGOs). The objective is to identify and critically analyse the strengths, problems, gaps, and opportunities in incorporating P/CVE into international and community development work. This focus is necessary because primary-level interventions target broad community resilience, unlike secondary and tertiary interventions, which focus on at-risk or radicalised individuals. Given that development CSOs working on P/CVE programs operate independently from government-led counterterrorism efforts, this review provides insights specific to non-securitised, community-level, development-driven approaches. Source inclusion parameters were set to require empirical studies on primary-level P/CVE programs run by development CSOs. Studies of secondary and tertiary interventions, government-led programs, and initiatives by educational or religious institutions were excluded to maintain the focus on non-state, community-level, development-driven approaches. There was no restriction on location, publication date, or publication type, with both peer-reviewed and grey-literature publications included. As the P/CVE field is relatively new, it was expected that the search would mostly find publications from the 2010s and 2020s, which proved to be the case, with the earliest publication being from 2008. Records were identified using Google Scholar, Google, JSTOR Security Studies, 3ie, ALNAP, OECD iLibrary, and institutional websites, with a final search occurring on 31 January 2024. Bias was assessed by recording authors’ affiliation with the evaluand (although internal evaluations were not excluded on that basis). Extracted data was analysed using grounded theory to inductively determine themes. The systematic review incorporates 129 studies reported in 137 papers: 64% qualitative, 32% mixed-methods, and 4% quantitative. Of these, 53% were industry and evaluation reports, 31% articles, 10% books/chapters, and 6% theses. Limitations include the heterogeneity of included studies and limited evaluation rigour, which constrain reliable conclusions of program effectiveness in many papers. Grounded analysis identified three overarching thematic groupings: interconnections, power and relations, and impact. Common findings across papers highlighted the opportunities for P/CVE programming to enhance the work already being conducted by development CSOs, although papers cautioned that this needs to be carefully designed, implemented, and assessed with consideration of context, objectives, appropriate terminology, local agency, sustainability, marginalised groups, and potential for perverse outcomes. The need for consistent, long-term, untied funding of development CSOs’ P/CVE programs was frequently raised, as was the importance of prioritising local participation in all aspects of programming. Many papers noted the value of effective coordination and collaboration horizontally between communities and CSOs as well as vertically between global and local authorities and academia. Evidence of effectiveness was heterogeneous, with some studies measuring impact and others measuring satisfaction. This likely underlies a particular problem with monitoring and evaluation in this nascent field rather than necessarily representing problematic programming. Key issues with monitoring and evaluation typically include unclear and infeasible theories of change, poor monitoring practices, and limited ability to conduct rigorous evaluation due to insufficient funding and capacity. The most promising practices centred on the evaluation of changes in knowledge, attitudes, social cohesion, and wellbeing. Rather than trying to evaluate the impact of a development program on a reduction in violent extremism, these evaluations demonstrated how

Title: Conflict-aware seat assignment in classroom environments
Authors: Bruna Cristina Braga Charytitsch, Mariá Cristina Vasconcelos Nascimento
Abstract: Determining an effective seating plan is a key challenge in classroom management, as the spatial arrangement of students directly influences interpersonal dynamics and the overall learning environment. This paper introduces the Student Seat Allocation Problem (SSAP), which consists of strategically assigning students to seats in a traditional classroom, to minimize interpersonal conflicts while satisfying operational constraints. We propose a mathematical model and an Iterated Local Search (ILS) heuristic to address the SSAP. Computational experiments on a benchmark of 131 instances show that both methods converge to the optimal solution in 78 small- and medium-scale instances. For large-scale instances, Gurobi frequently exceeded the time limit, yet achieved very low optimality gaps, outperforming the heuristic’s average gap in 45 instances. ILS, in turn, outperformed Gurobi in 8 instances, and, when analyzing individual runs, successfully reached a gap of zero in multiple executions for several large-scale instances — within a fraction of Gurobi’s computational time. These results position ILS as an effective and accessible alternative for educational institutions where commercial solver licenses are unavailable or cost-prohibitive.

Title: Research on multi-resource flexible job shop scheduling considering flexible matching of pallets and workbenches
Authors: Zhifeng Liu, LinJing Wang, Jun Yan, Yueze Zhang, Yanhong Cheng, Qiang Cheng
Abstract: Pallets and workbenches are one of the main factors affecting production efficiency in multi resource flexible production during the preparation phase. The flexible matching of pallets and workbenches is key issue and directly affects production scheduling. For this purpose, a flexible job shop scheduling model is developed to address multi-stage operations involving setup, processing, and unloading, incorporating specific constraints on workbenches and pallets. An improved genetic algorithm for multi-stage resource-driven scheduling (IGA-MSRDS) is proposed, featuring three-layer encoding, dynamic optimization strategies, and resource-sensitive operators. The algorithm enhances task sequencing and resource coordination through cooperative crossover and load-aware mutation, and refines multi-resource handling via dynamic strategies. The experimental results of multiple benchmark instances demonstrate that IGA-MSRDS excels in scheduling performance. Especially in terms of solution quality and system adaptability under complex resource constraints.

Title: A small volume reduction that melts down the market: Auctions with endogenous rationing
Authors: Karl-Martin Ehrhart, Ann-Katrin Fleck, Marion Ott
Abstract: Auctions with endogenous rationing have been introduced to stimulate competition. Such (procurement) auctions reduce the volume put out to tender when competition is low. This paper finds a strong negative effect of endogenous rationing on participation when bid-preparation is costly, counteracting the aim to stimulate competition. For multiple auctioneer's objectives mentioned in directives, we derive optimal mechanisms, which differ due to different evaluation of the tradeoff between participation and bid-preparation costs. Thus, the auctioneer needs to decide on an objective. However, reducing bid-preparation costs improves the optimal values of multiple objective functions.

Title: Foreign direct investment and greenhouse gas emissions: Evidence across income groups and technological contexts
Authors: Narek Mirzoyan, Jennifer Brodmann, Mahmoud Salari, Sunghoon Joo
Abstract: This paper examines the relationship between foreign direct investment (FDI) and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in middle- and high-income countries. Particular attention is paid to income-group heterogeneity and the context of green technology. Using an unbalanced panel of 74 countries from 1975 to 2021, we estimate static and dynamic panel data models. The static analysis includes pooled OLS, random effects and two-way fixed effects specifications, incorporating income group and FDI-patent interactions. To address dynamic persistence and potential endogeneity, we also employ one-step and two-step system GMM estimators with lagged dependent variables and income-specific FDI effects. The results suggest a generally positive association between FDI and GHG emissions, although the magnitude and statistical significance of this relationship vary across different models. Dynamic system GMM estimations provide further evidence of a positive association between FDI and emissions. In the main interaction specifications, estimated effects are somewhat larger for middle-income economies than for high-income ones, though this difference is not consistent across all specifications and should be interpreted as suggestive rather than conclusive. Analysis of disaggregated green patent categories reveals substantial technological heterogeneity. Some patent classes are associated with a weaker FDI–emissions relationship, whereas others appear to strengthen it. In contrast, aggregate patent activity shows either positive or statistically insignificant relationships with emissions, suggesting that broad patent measures may obscure important technology-specific effects. Overall, FDI does not automatically lead to environmental improvement. Its consequences appear to vary with income-related structural conditions and the technological orientation of the host economy. These findings support broad policy caution: FDI attraction strategies should be evaluated together with environmental monitoring, and green innovation should be assessed at a more disaggregated technological level.

Title: Thinking machines, shrinking footprints? The impact of Artificial Intelligence on energy consumption in regions
Authors: Robert Dehghan, Nils Grashof, Sebastian Schmidt, Alexander Kopka, Michael Woywode
Abstract: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) becomes more widespread, concerns about its environmental impact, particularly its energy demand, are growing. At the same time, AI is often regarded as a key driver of industrial optimisation and efficiency. This paper examines this tension by analysing the impact of AI adoption on regional industrial energy consumption in Germany between 2012 and 2023. To do so, we combine a novel web-based machine learning approach that identifies AI and sustainability adoption based on company websites with regional data on energy consumption, technological knowledge, and economic structures. Using a system GMM approach, our results show that regions with a higher rate of AI adoption have significantly lower levels of industrial energy consumption. However, this energy-saving effect has weakened over time, being more pronounced in the period 2012–2017 than in the period 2018–2023. The energy-saving effects are also more pronounced in regions where a higher proportion of firms, both large and small, adopt AI. Furthermore, although interaction terms between AI adoption and knowledge relatedness to AI and green technologies are not statistically significant on average, marginal effects analysis uncovers substantial heterogeneity. The energy-reducing impact of AI adoption becomes stronger and statistically significant only at higher levels of relatedness to AI and green technologies, with effects emerging earlier for green-related knowledge bases. Our findings offer a novel perspective on the role of AI in promoting sustainable industrial development. They also emphasise the importance of capturing both the usage and creation of digital technologies within regional innovation systems.

Title: Predicting energy ETF prices: The impact of Google Trends and investor attention
Authors: Zihui Xia, Xiaotao Zhang
Abstract: From the perspective of investor attention, this study constructs an attention indicator based on Google Trends (GT) data and employs three types of models—Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Rotation Forest, and ARIMA—to forecast the prices of energy exchange-traded funds (ETFs), including clean energy (ICLN), upstream traditional energy (XOP), and the overall energy sector (XLE). Overall, the inclusion of GT data significantly enhances the predictive performance of the CNN model, particularly for clean energy ETFs, with the CNN also demonstrating strong stability, making it the most suitable model among those examined. Moreover, the study reveals a marginal effect of GT information volume on model performance: the CNN model exhibits improved forecasting accuracy as GT information increases, whereas the Rotation Forest model may be subject to an information “threshold effect.” These findings offer valuable insights for quantitative investment and policy formulation in the context of green finance.

Title: Research on new energy vehicle diffusion via multi-subsidy trade-in policy analysis
Authors: Yu’e Wu, Zeyun Liu, Xinyu Wang, Anran Yin, Shuhua Zhang
Abstract: The development of new energy vehicles (NEVs) has become one of China’s pivotal strategic initiatives for achieving low-carbon goals. Considering the renewal and further implementation of the vehicle trade-in policy in 2025, this research establishes a system dynamics model based on evolutionary game theory to analyze the market evolution of NEVs under multiple subsidy mechanisms. Through numerical simulations and sensitivity analysis, we investigate how critical model parameters influence the system, including multiple subsidies under trade-in policies, the initial strategy proportions of various stakeholders, and the composition of different consumer segments. The results demonstrate that under the current multi-subsidy mechanism, consumers ultimately show a clear trend toward participating in trade-in programs. Moreover, subsidies provided by enterprises to trade-in consumers exert a pronounced positive effect in promoting green automotive consumption. The policy recommendations proposed in this study provide clear directions for China’s NEV market amid the emerging wave of vehicle trade-in program.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Beyond connectivity: Travel behavior and hidden inequities in human mobility resilience
Authors: Jingke Hong, Bingsheng Liu, Ran Wei, Yang Jia, Chengchen Guo
Abstract: As climate-related extreme events intensify in frequency and severity, sustaining access to employment, healthcare, and other essential activities increasingly depends on the resilience of human mobility. This study advances mobility-resilience assessment by explicitly incorporating behavioral constraints that shape how travelers adapt under disruption. While conventional approaches largely equate resilience with transportation network connectivity, we conceptualize resilience as a behaviorally grounded outcome that depends on whether technically feasible trips remain acceptable within travelers’ limited tolerance for disruption-induced detours. Using large-scale mobile phone origin–destination data from Chongqing, China, we develop a behaviorally informed framework that integrates empirically estimated detour tolerance into resilience measurement, enabling the quantification of functional mobility loss under flood-induced network disruption. Results show that ignoring travel behavior systematically overestimates realized mobility resilience and masks critical spatial and social inequities, with low-income populations exhibiting consistently lower mobility resilience, particularly under more severe climate scenarios.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Auction design and operational strategy for hybrid recycling platforms under information asymmetry
Authors: Dongmei Xue, Ruud H. Teunter, Stuart X. Zhu, Weihua Zhou
Abstract: Online platforms for used products operate either as marketplaces that earn commission fees or as remanufacturers that purchase and refurbish items. An emerging hybrid structure integrates these roles, allowing platforms to capture both transaction-based and remanufacturing revenues. This paper develops an auction-based analytical model to examine how such a hybrid platform optimally designs its reservation price while internalizing dual revenue streams under product heterogeneity and information asymmetry. Within an independent private-value framework, the analysis shows that the optimal reservation price increases with the number of bidders—contrasting with classical auction predictions under limited competition. The results further characterize the conditions under which the platform optimally adopts a pure commission model, a pure remanufacturing model, or a hybrid structure, depending on its valuation and commission rate. By linking auction design to platform governance in reverse logistics markets, the study provides new insights into how digital intermediation shapes profitability and strategic configuration when managing heterogeneous used products.

Title: A hybrid cost efficiency model under fixed and non-fixed prices: A case study on the Polish justice courts
Authors: Magdalena Kapelko, Dimitrios Sotiros, Sebastian Klaudiusz Tomczak
Abstract: Measuring and improving public sector efficiency is key to delivering fair and effective services. As part of the public sector, justice courts, beyond handling legal matters, should pursue the efficient allocation of public resources. Therefore, their economic efficiency should be regularly assessed. However, studies evaluating the performance of justice courts rarely focus on the economic dimension of efficiency at the micro level. To fill this gap, the contribution of this study is twofold. Firstly, from the methodological point of view, relying on data envelopment analysis, we propose a new hybrid framework for measuring cost efficiency that is capable of handling exogenously fixed and non-fixed prices and allowing the latter to be endogenously optimized. Other advantages of the proposed framework include estimating realistic targets for non-fixed prices and utilized resources, exploring reallocation opportunities for resources, and identifying cost–demand relationships. Secondly, from the empirical perspective, we show the applicability of this new framework to Polish district courts over the period 2017–2021. The results reveal that only 10% of the courts are cost efficient. Interestingly, on average, the model suggests an increase in the number of all employees and in non-fixed salaries, as well as a reduction in the volume of capital. The results also suggest that the reallocation of resources can lead to significantly fewer pending cases or can eliminate them entirely. A further reduction in the number of pending cases can be potentially achieved by redistributing all registered cases under a centralized management system.

Title: The effect of health insurance expansion on price and demand for medications among the uninsured
Authors: Chuanzi Yue
Abstract: Social health insurance expansions can affect not only new beneficiaries but also those who remain outside the program. This paper studies these spillovers in the context of Medicare Part D. Increases in insured demand can raise or lower price depending on market conditions: they may increase price when pharmaceutical firms face less elastic demand, but reduce price when demand concentration strengthens bargaining and pass-through in competitive markets. I find that Part D lowered the out-of-pocket unit price paid by Americans under age 65 without prescription drug insurance. Price declines are larger in therapeutic classes more exposed to Part D and in classes with stronger within-class competition, consistent with a demand-concentration channel. Demand increases mainly for generic drugs and among existing users. The implied consumer-surplus gain is roughly $76 per person per year, comprising about $65 from lower price on inframarginal consumption and $11 from additional consumption. Demand responses appear strongest among lower-income, younger, and healthier uninsured individuals, consistent with greater pre-existing non-adherence. Although price fall across several drug classes, demand does not increase significantly for medications associated with greater overuse in the United States, suggesting potentially positive net health spillovers.

Title: Enhancing supply chain resilience through green investment under emerging contaminants risk: a network game theory perspective
Authors: Daipeng Ma, Jian Guan, Rui Li, Xiaohong Chen
Affiliations: Central South University; Xiangjiang Laboratory
Abstract: As emerging contaminant risks intensify, supply chains in pollution-sensitive industries have become increasingly uncertain and vulnerable. Containing pollution risk diffusion and enhancing supply chain resilience therefore constitute urgent theoretical and practical challenges. Based on inter-firm supply and demand relationships, this study constructs a network game model incorporating firm pollution sensitivity, economic exposure, and green investment. By comparing independent firm decision-making, homogeneous decision-making with network effects, and heterogeneous decision-making, this study conducts numerical simulations using data from 391 firms across six typical pollution-sensitive industries. The findings show that complementary business relationships alter the marginal returns to firms’ green investment and may induce free-riding-like strategic dependence under network externalities, thereby weakening preventive green investment incentives and increasing supply-chain network vulnerability. Firms’ green investment decisions are jointly driven by their own pollution sensitivity, potential economic losses, and partners’ risk exposure. Supply-chain topology further moderates the green investment–resilience relationship: when cooperation is limited, higher business concentration strengthens network resilience; when cooperation is intensive but structurally imbalanced, improving the green governance capacity of vulnerable firms and reducing structural asymmetry more effectively curb pollution-risk diffusion. These findings provide implications for stakeholders’ green governance and supply chain risk management decisions.

Title: Research on cascade coal procurement model based on Bi-objective and integer optimization with virtual coal blending calibration
Authors: Guangbo Wang, Jun Li, Xiaodi Huang, Yanchen Jiang, Qiansheng Li, Yongfu Wang
Affiliations: Northeastern University; HUANENG Power Intl Inc
Abstract: China’s thermal power enterprises generally rely on manual experience while lacking robust modelling and optimisation support for coal procurement, leading to non-optimal economic performance and limited feasibility of procurement schemes. To address these issues, a cascade coal procurement model with two layers is constructed. The outer loop comprehensively considers the effects of pollutant emission on coal cost, as well as seasonal-variation effect from procurement to blending on coal quality, and an improved non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm-II (INSGA-II) is proposed for optimisation. The inner loop further considers vessel capacity and freight charges, and introduces a coal quantity adjustment and substitution mechanism to improve the original inner-loop model against the situation of “low planned coal quantity using high-capacity vessels”. Finally, a virtual coal blending model is constructed to calibrate the inner-loop scheme. Case results show that, compared with the experience-based scheme, the model-based inner-loop scheme reasonably adjusts the procurement quantity in the outer loop while ensuring supply requirements, reducing the cost by 5.75%, and the model-based virtual coal blending scheme not only optimally matches the planned load but also achieves greater economic efficiency. In addition, INSGA-II outperforms NSGA-II in cost–quality trade-off under different weights.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: A neo-institutional response matrix for explaining governance dynamics influencing infrastructure project cost misperformance
Authors: Peter E. D. Love
Affiliations: School of Civil & Mechanical Engineering, Curtin University
Abstract: This paper operationalizes the Fifth Hand, an emergent theory of project behavior explaining cost misperformance in infrastructure projects, through a neo-institutional response matrix that captures institutional pressure and behavioral enactment across two governance regimes: (1) the pre-contract regime, where funding commitments are established at the decision-to-build; and (2) the post-contract regime, where delivery proceeds under contractual enforcement and audit oversight. Two indices—the Mode of Action Index and the Institutional Pressure Index—classify cost-relevant decision episodes and identify patterns of dominance, transition, entrenchment, and suppression across regimes. An illustrative case, the New Perth Bunbury Highway, shows how cost trajectories emerge from governance responses to divergence between approved funding and updated cost projections. Under heightened institutional pressure, adjustments are deferred, increasing the likelihood of discrete increases in funding. Under moderated pressure, revised projections are incorporated earlier through incremental adjustment. The response matrix explains how cost misperformance develops through successive governance decisions.

Title: Blockchain technology affordances in the supply chains: a systematic literature review
Authors: Md Rokonuzzaman, Trevor Clohessy, Graham Heaslip, Sandy Schumann, George Onofrei
Affiliations: Faculty of Engineering and Computing, Atlantic Technological University Galway City; Department of Security and Crime Science, University College London; Atlantic Technological University, ATU Donegal Letterkenny

Title: Digitalisation empowering firm inventory management: a lean inventory perspective
Authors: Yang Xu, Yang Wu, Yanyan Zhang, Xu Tian
Affiliations: School of Finance, Anhui University of Finance and Economics; School of Public Policy and Administration, Nanchang University
Abstract: Drawing on a lean inventory perspective, this study examines how digitalisation empowers inventory management. Using panel data on firms listed on China’s A-share market, we find that firm digitalisation significantly increases inventory leanness, which in turn enhances firm value. Mechanism analyses show that digitalisation improves inventory management efficiency primarily through an internal optimisation channel (increasing production efficiency), and an external integration channel (enhancing supply chain efficiency). In addition, digitalisation improves inventory management efficiency by reducing sales uncertainty. This study provides empirical evidence on the mechanisms through which digitalisation empowers inventory management and enables firms to optimise inventory management and enhance firm value through digital transformation.

Title: Long short-term memory network with adapted attention mechanism for credit risk modeling
Authors: Hao Wang, Anthony Bellotti
Abstract: In recent years, survival models have received increasing attention in credit risk. Unlike classification models typically used to model defaults, survival analysis can model not only whether a borrower will default but also the time to default. Since loan transaction data are discrete time-series information, it is natural to apply a discrete-time survival model (DTSM). At the same time, there have been significant advances in deep neural networks. In this paper, we extend the DTSM using long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, incorporating an adapted LSTM-based attention mechanism to better uncover temporal features that influence the probability of default, along with a washout phase, which is used to iterate several dummy LSTM prediction steps and hence addresses the LSTM state initialization problem. Finally, instead of using a standard attention mechanism that linearly encodes the input, we adapt it with an LSTM layer that captures non-linear temporal features from the sequential data. This model shows great improvement in model fit and predictive ability, in comparison with baseline linear DTSMs and standard LSTM with attention, when evaluated on US mortgage data. Moreover, we show that our proposed model gives good forecast performance, providing practitioners with a practical and powerful early warning service to manage potential credit loss.

Title: Detecting Favoritism in Public Procurement
Authors: Joosua Virtanen, Janne Tukiainen, Susmita Baulia
Affiliations: Department of Economics Hanken School of Economics Helsinki Finland; Boulevard Tech Helsinki Finland; Department of Economics University of Turku Turku Finland; VATT Institute for Economic Research Helsinki Finland; RBB Economics Helsinki Finland
Abstract: ABSTRACT Favoritism as a mode of corruption is a major concern in public procurement (PP) in many countries. We propose a regression discontinuity design (RDD) test arguing that the winning history of marginal winners and losers can be used to detect favoritism. We apply the empirical test to PP of cleaning services in Finland and find evidence of favoritism even in this relatively low corruption environment. First, winners of close races in terms of win margin tend to have won more also in the past, which is in contrast to competitive environment. Second, to rule out an alternative explanation of collusion based on incumbency, we show that these winners also tend to submit their bids the last, indicating information sharing about rival bids from the buyer to the favored bidder.

Title: Inequality of Opportunity in Wealth: Levels, Trends and Drivers in Germany
Authors: Daniel Graeber, Johannes König, Viola Hilbert
Affiliations: DIW Berlin, IZA@LISER, CEPA Berlin Germany; BAuA/Minimum Wage Commission Information Office Berlin Germany; University of Leipzig and DIW Berlin Leipzig Germany
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper studies inequality of opportunity (IOp) in individual net wealth in Germany from 2002 to 2019 using the Socio‐Economic Panel (SOEP). Applying the ex‐ante IOp framework, we quantify the share of wealth inequality attributable to immutable circumstances and benchmark it against IOp in gross labour earnings. Relative IOp in net wealth is high—slightly above one half of total wealth inequality—and stable over time, whereas relative IOp in labour earnings declines and converges towards the wealth level by the end of the study period. Decomposing net wealth into financial, real estate and business components shows similar and stable IOp levels for financial and housing wealth, but substantially higher and more variable IOp for business wealth. Across all components, childhood and parental circumstances are the dominant drivers of wealth IOp, while place effects matter most for real estate wealth and gender for business wealth. In contrast, gender and demographics are the main contributors to IOp in labour earnings.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Technology as the material ‘how’ of socio-ecological (re)production: Reflections on Wassily Leontief's ‘technological structure of the economy’
Authors: Miriam Boyer, Carlos López-Morales, Mathis Favre
Abstract: Wassily Leontief is widely known for his development of an applied approach in economics known as input-output (IO). In this paper, we turn to Leontief's analysis to reconstruct a concept of technology based on his work. The concept rests upon an analysis of Leontief's epistemological-methodological assumptions and the premises of his input-output model regarding interdependence. We argue that Leontief's concept of technology highlights the physical process of technology in two senses: As concrete flows of material stuff used in economic production in the sense of a particular ‘recipe’; but also as emergent systemic effects of that particular ‘recipe’ throughout an economy, or indeed throughout a socio-ecological system. This contrasts with other approaches in the social sciences that understand the materiality of technology largely in terms of objects, artifacts, and infrastructure. We argue that future research could benefit from incorporating Leontief's approach with work elsewhere in the social sciences. On the one hand, IO depictions of quantitative and systemic effects could be complemented by aspects that are not explicit in Leontief's framework, including specific social relations such as power, and the role of certain actors or conflicts. On the other, Leontief's emphasis on physical material aspects and their systemic effects can also link nicely with ecological research, even beyond the now common environmental extensions of the IO model. We argue that such work could yield interesting synergies in the future, not least in the field of ecological economics.

Title: Corrigendum to ‘The distributional impact of climate policy stringency in the European Union, Ecological Economics 249 (2026) [109118]’
Authors: Syeda Aimen Abbas, Thomas Kopp
Abstract: The authors regret that the footnote associated with the first author was incorrect. The published article states: “Work was carried out at University of Siegen.” This is incorrect. The work was carried out at Justus Liebig University Giessen (JLU Giessen). The footnote should therefore be deleted.

Title: The integrated time slot pricing and on-demand food delivery routing problem with demand and travel time uncertainty
Authors: Yuchen Zhang, Runliang Dou, Meng Zhao, Peng Sun
Abstract: In this paper, we address the integrated problem of differentiated time slot pricing (DTSP) and order dispatching for on-demand food delivery platforms, with a focus on managing both demand and travel time uncertainty and complex operational constraints. A robust two-stage stochastic programming model is proposed. In the first stage, delivery fees for different time slots are selected and combined with a dynamic pricing mechanism that accounts for delivery distance and order value. In the second stage, a budget uncertainty set enables the multi-wave pickup and delivery plan to explicitly withstand fluctuations in trip duration while integrating factors such as restaurant preparation time, rider waiting time, and vehicle load capacity. To solve large-scale instances efficiently, we develop a Robust Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search (RALNS) algorithm enhanced with tailored operators and a hybrid dispatching engine. This engine combines heuristic order bundling with a compact set-partitioning mixed-integer linear program to ensure optimal assignment. Extensive computational experiments using the Meituan TSL Challenge dataset demonstrate that the proposed hybrid approach achieves an average optimality gap of less than 1% for small-scale instances while maintaining computation efficiency for larger-scale instances. Sensitivity analysis indicates that the robust framework increases realized profit by 5% to 15% over deterministic approaches by significantly reducing delay penalties. Furthermore, the dynamic pricing scheme achieves approximately 20% higher overall profitability compared to fixed pricing strategies.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Robust heterogeneous bus-assisted drone delivery under transit uncertainty and drone failures
Authors: Xuefeng Jin, Mingyang Pei, Lingshu Zhong
Abstract: Bus-assisted drone delivery can extend drone service range by using existing public transit resources, but its practical deployment is challenged by heterogeneous drone capabilities, customer time windows, bus transit uncertainty, and drone failure risk. This paper studies the Heterogeneous Bus-Assisted Drone Delivery Routing Problem with Time Windows and Drone Failures and incorporates a robust optimization framework to handle bus transit uncertainty. A mixed-integer nonlinear programming model is developed to minimize the worst-case total cost, including fixed dispatch cost, working time cost, and expected loss of demand (ELOD). Bus transit uncertainty is described by a polyhedral uncertainty set, while drone failure risk is quantified through a Weibull-based failure probability model. To solve the problem efficiently, a JOIH-ALNSLS algorithm is designed by combining a joint optimization insertion heuristic, adaptive large neighborhood search, and variable neighborhood descent local search. Computational experiments show that the proposed algorithm outperforms Gurobi and benchmark metaheuristics. Out-of-sample simulations further demonstrate that robust planning reduces time-window violation risk, and incorporating ELOD lowers both failure risk and actual total cost.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Heterogeneous drone-truck routing problem with En-route operations
Authors: Shuhong Liu, Shaoxuan Zhu, Canrong Zhang
Abstract: The rapid expansion of e-commerce and the increasing complexity of urban logistics have placed unprecedented pressure on last-mile delivery systems. While the integration of drones and trucks offers a promising solution, most existing research restricts drone launch and recovery to fixed customer locations and overlooks the operational flexibility afforded by drone heterogeneity and the multi-visit characteristic. This paper introduces the Heterogeneous Drone-Truck Routing Problem with En-route Launch and Recovery (HDTRP-ELR), which allows multiple heterogeneous drones to launch from and land on a moving truck while performing multi-visit sorties. We formulate a Mixed-Integer Second-Order Cone Programming (MISOCP) model with a payload-dependent energy consumption function. To solve this computationally challenging problem, we propose a Reinforcement Learning-guided Decoupled Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search (RLD-ALNS) algorithm, in which a Deep Q-Network (DQN) agent dynamically selects destruction operators based on the structural features of the current solution. Numerical experiments demonstrate that RLD-ALNS outperforms heuristic baselines by up to 18.0%. The HDTRP-ELR model yields substantial gains over traditional node-restricted models, with en-route launch and recovery alone reducing makespan by 18.5% to 36.5%, and multi-visit capability yielding an additional 8.8% to 13.9%. A heterogeneous drone fleet cuts energy consumption by 23% to 28% versus a homogeneous heavy-duty fleet while preserving makespan. These results demonstrate that the combination of en-route operations, multi-visit sorties, and fleet heterogeneity is key to maximizing the efficiency of next-generation autonomous logistics ecosystems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Determinants of investment risk: A comparative analysis of China’s port and manufacturing investments along the maritime silk road
Authors: Dongxu Chen, Yawen Jin, Feng Lian, Fuyu Lai, Zhongzhen Yang
Abstract: Under rising geopolitical tensions, trade conflicts, policy uncertainty, and host-country risks, global logistics systems increasingly require diversified and resilient corridors to maintain trade continuity and transportation efficiency. In this context, China’s port and manufacturing investments along the Maritime Silk Road (MSR) may support corridor resilience by improving logistics node capacity, maritime connectivity, industrial support, and cargo-generation potential. However, investment failure risk may constrain this expected resilience-enhancing role by affecting logistics capacity, industrial support, and corridor diversification. To address these challenges, this study develops a risk analysis framework for port and manufacturing investments along the MSR, incorporating the dimensions of socioeconomic condition, bilateral relations, institutional distance, and sector-specific risk. A binary logit model is used to assess their associations with investment returns, while historical data are used to estimate the probability of investment failure. The results show that: (1) the risk attributes of the port and manufacturing investments differ substantially, i.e., for ports the risk is more closely associated with capital amount, whereas for manufacturing it shows a stronger association with macroeconomic indicators such as Gross Domestic Product (GDP), economic growth rate, openness, and railway network scale; (2) regarding bilateral relations, high-level reciprocal visits demonstrate a long-term cumulative effect, with a four-year lag being more pronounced than a two-year lag; (3) interactions between institutional distance and indicators such as capital amount and logistics performance are significantly associated with variations in risk levels. These results provide evidence-based insights for identifying key risk drivers and for supporting more resilient decision-making on port and manufacturing investments under uncertain geopolitical and trade environments.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: When cash enters local markets: local economic spillover effects of cash transfers, remittances, and insurance
Authors: Constantin Johnen, Michael Ross Carter
Abstract: Insurance payouts, remittances, and government cash transfers all share one feature: they inject cash into local markets. While these interventions typically aim to improve the welfare of recipients, they can also affect the economic welfare of non-recipients. Yet our understanding of such economic spillover effects remains limited. Empirical studies report mixed findings, ranging from welfare-increasing to welfare-decreasing spillover effects, while the theoretical literature discussing potential mechanisms remains fragmented and lacks an integrated framework. This study develops a structured conceptual synthesis that integrates dispersed theoretical and empirical insights on the spillover effects of cash injections. We first develop a unified theoretical framework identifying the key mechanisms and moderating factors shaping spillovers, and then review the empirical literature through its lens. The framework highlights that spillover effects emerge through changes in local prices, wages, and resource sharing within social networks. We further show that the magnitude and direction of these effects depend on the interaction between cash-injection-specific parameters and the local environment, including its local economic structure and the constraints that recipient and non-recipient households face. By integrating insights across studies on cash transfers, remittances, and insurance programs, the paper provides a conceptual foundation for understanding spillover patterns of cash injections more broadly. Our analysis generates policy-relevant insights and highlights several important gaps in the current literature.

Title: Editorial Board
Capital reallocation under climate policy uncertainty
Authors: Makram Khalil, Felix Strobel
Abstract: In a structural dynamic model that incorporates two broad production sectors with different carbon emissions, we find that climate policy uncertainty (CPU) shocks (i) lower the market value of the highly carbon-emitting sector relative to the low carbon-emitting sector, and (ii) reduce real investment and the capital stock in the highly carbon-emitting sector, while real investment in the sector with low carbon emissions tends to fare better. To apply the theoretical predictions to the data, we employ a news article-based measure of climate policy uncertainty to identify CPU shocks as well as quarterly balance sheet data of listed firms in the United States. In line with the predictions from the theoretical model, we find that in response to CPU shocks (i) financial markets markedly revalue strongly carbon-emitting firms relative to firms with low carbon emissions, and (ii) substantial investment reallocation takes place, in particular from the manufacturing sector towards services.

Title: Damping-enhanced tire-pavement noise mitigation of thermoplastic polyurethane/crumb rubber composite-modified asphalt pavements
Authors: Zehua Zhu, Keke Lou, Peng Xiao, Jun Zhou, Chenying Li
Abstract: Road traffic noise is a major environmental burden of urban transport, and tire-pavement interaction is a key source-control pathway. This study developed a damping-oriented noise-mitigation strategy for SMA-13 mixtures prepared with thermoplastic polyurethane/crumb rubber (TPU/CR) composite-modified binders. Laboratory damping and acoustic tests were combined with a coupled tire-pavement-air finite element model incorporating explicit tread patterns to link material damping, vibration attenuation, and transition in the dominant noise source. The results showed that TPU/CR modification enhanced the critical damping ratio, with the optimum response obtained at 6 wt% TPU + 10 wt% CR, representing an increase of up to 14.46% over the CR-modified mixture. Enhanced damping promoted viscoelastic energy dissipation and reduced vibration-induced sound pressure levels. Simulations revealed a speed-dependent transition: vibration noise dominated at 60–90 km/h, whereas air-pumping noise became the main contributor above 90 km/h. TPU/CR modification therefore provides a damping-oriented source-control strategy for reducing tire-pavement noise while maintaining pavement performance.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Which probability measures are strict correlated equilibria?
Authors: Can Kizilkale, Anthony Rodriguez, Rakesh V. Vohra

Title: Sustainable Steel Supply Chain Network Design under Export Taxes and Import Tariffs: A Multi-objective Stochastic Programming Framework
Authors: Navid Sahebjamnia, Vedat Verter, Amir Hossein Azadnia
Abstract: This paper introduces a two-stage stochastic programming model featuring multi-objective recourse functions to address the economic, environmental, and social dimensions of sustainability in steel supply chain networks. The model integrates strategic decisions (facility location, capacity acquisition, and technology selection) with tactical material flow coordination. The dynamics of steel industry-specific characteristics are captured through multi-scale time periods, technology compatibility requirements, and sustainability metrics based on location-technology-flow configurations. Furthermore, the model incorporates export taxes and import tariffs to optimise material flows between nationwide and global networks, enabling comprehensive analysis of how these policy tools influence strategic and tactical decisions whilst impacting sustainability objectives. A solution approach is developed using the ε-constraint and Sample Average Approximation methods to address demand uncertainty and the trade-offs among multiple recourse objectives. Novel algorithms are introduced to determine the upper and lower bounds of the constrained objective functions and to form the loops of the ε-constraint method. The model's application to a real-world case study demonstrates its effectiveness in achieving balanced material flows across the steel SCN after four strategic periods. Through sustainability assessment and analysis of various tax and tariff policies, we derive eight policy insights regarding their impacts on strategic and tactical decisions. The results confirm the model's capability to generate robust solutions that effectively balance network capacity against demand patterns while achieving sustainability objectives.

Title: The effects of neighborhood redevelopment on housing markets and beyond: Evidence from HOPE VI Revitalization Program
Authors: Lizhong Liu
Abstract: Many advocates highlighted place-based housing policies as a remedy for urban decay despite mixed evidence on their long-term effects. This paper presents a national-level study investigating changes in the trajectory of local housing markets caused by the Housing Opportunities for People Everywhere (HOPE VI) Revitalization Program, the largest federal investment in public housing redevelopment. I combine a stratified version of the synthetic difference-in-difference method with a stacked event study model to identify the effects of HOPE VI redevelopment and the underlying mechanisms. The analysis finds that HOPE VI led to long-lasting changes of housing markets and socioeconomic conditions in target neighborhoods. Housing values and rents increased by 8 and 11 percent, respectively, more than 20 years after redevelopment. These effects varied systematically with both the scale of redevelopment and baseline neighborhood characteristics. Distinguishing mechanical from non-mechanical channels reveals that only a portion of the rent increase reflects compositional replacement, while the majority is associated with improvements in housing quality and positive spillovers to nearby neighborhoods.

Title: Mobility, segregation and inequality: Who gains from urban transportation improvements?
Authors: Prottoy A. Akbar, Victor Couture
Abstract: Urban transportation projects are massive public investments that can transform cities. This article reviews how they shape where people live and how they affect the rich and poor differently. Existing empirical evidence and a simple model point to three factors that matter most: who uses the new mode, where it is built, and how easily people can relocate. Projects serving a narrow group in a specific area tend to raise income segregation and inequality. These effects can be severe if poorer households face barriers to relocation, as with the Interstate Highway System. Projects with broad ridership and broad spatial coverage, like Bus Rapid Transit in developing countries, have smaller segregation effects and more widely shared welfare gains.

Title: A novel scenario generation method for optimal energy management in a system with uncertain energy yields and prices
Authors: Robert Hanusa, Stijn De Vuyst, Birger Raa
Affiliations: Ghent University

Title: Allocating the right intervention to the right patient: a robust approach using stratified clinical evidence
Authors: Huaxiao Shen, Zhilin Yong, Xiaoli Yan, Qingpeng Zhang, Youhua Frank Chen
Affiliations: Sun Yat-sen University; Sichuan University; Southwest Jiaotong University; The University of Hong Kong; City University of Hong Kong
Abstract: Allocating limited resources (like medicines, professional cares, or hospital beds) across multiple treatments for diverse patients is challenging, especially when choices must be made under uncertainty using grouped data from published clinical studies, such as Sample Average Treatment Effects (SATEs) and Conditional Average Treatment Effects (CATEs). Existing frameworks are often limited to single-intervention settings and do not exploit the value of granular subgroup data. This paper bridges that gap by adapting robust allocation to the summary-evidence regime in which a multi-intervention planner must work with marginally stratified SATE/CATE summaries. Specifically, we propose a tractable approach that maximises the worst-case aggregate patient benefit under a budget constraint. We formulate a hierarchy of models, from a baseline SATE-informed model to an advanced CATE-informed model, and further extend it to capture pre-specified second-order interaction effects. They can be solved through mixed-integer linear programming. Using a case study of COPD vaccination grounded in clinical and population data, our numerical experiments show that allocations based on stratified CATEs achieve substantially higher performance than those based on aggregate SATEs or a stylised risk-based heuristic. The results highlight the significant benefit of systematically incorporating detailed clinical evidence to create more effective and reliable healthcare allocation strategies.

Title: Process operating performance evaluation for IC packaging in smart manufacturing
Authors: Kuen-Suan Chen, Chun-Min Yu
Abstract: Improving the quality and yield of integrated circuit packaging processes is crucial for reducing scrap rates and component failures. Among all stages of the packaging chain, gold wire bonding is widely considered a critical process with a clearly defined role. According to the Taguchi loss function, insufficient gold wire bonding capability significantly degrades the performance of integrated circuit components, leading to premature failure. Due to the indispensable role of integrated circuit components in applications such as network communications, consumer electronics, and the automotive, industrial, aerospace, and defense sectors, any failure could disrupt operations, cause economic losses, and increase carbon emissions. This makes rapid decision-making essential and has led to a growing trend towards decision-making based on small sample sizes. Furthermore, the increasingly mature smart manufacturing environment and the continuous advancements in the Internet of Things as well as production data collection and analysis technologies have facilitated the accumulation of past professional data experience within the industry. This study thus proposes a confidence interval-based fuzzy evaluation method to establish a fuzzy evaluation model for the operational performance of integrated circuit components based on gold wire bonding process capability. Given that this method integrates previously accumulated professional data and experience and is based on confidence intervals, not only can the accuracy of decision-making be maintained, but the risk of misjudgment due to sampling errors even with a small sample size can also be reduced.

Title: Asymmetric Pass‐Through and Competition
Authors: Christos Genakos, Yuan Lyu, Mario Pagliero
Affiliations: Cambridge Judge Business School, CEP and CEPR University of Cambridge Cambridge UK; School of Applied Economics Renmin University of China Beijing China; Center for Research on Global Energy Strategy (CROGES) Renmin University of China Beijing China; Collegio Carlo Alberto, and CEPR University of Turin Turin Italy
Abstract: ABSTRACT We study the retail price pass‐through of four major tax changes in petroleum products using daily pricing data from gas stations on small Greek islands. We find that (i) the pass‐through of the tax hikes is five times higher than for the tax decrease, (ii) the pass‐through of the tax hikes increases with competition, while that of the tax decrease does not, (iii) there is significant asymmetry in the speed of price adjustments, and (iv) the asymmetric price adjustment can be rationalized by either tacit collusion or consumer search behavior, as the most plausible explanations.

Title: Economic Growth Vulnerability Across Euro Area Countries
Authors: Claudio Lissona, Esther Ruiz
