Affiliations: Department of Economics University of Bologna Bologna Italy; Department of Statistics Universidad Carlos III de Madrid Madrid Spain
Abstract: ABSTRACT We analyse growth vulnerability in the four largest Euro Area (EA) economies, measured as a lower quantile of the growth distribution conditional on EA‐wide and country‐specific macroeconomic/financial factors. Growth densities are obtained under a normal activity scenario and under stressed conditions. We find that vulnerability is higher in Germany, more exposed to EA‐wide conditions, and in Spain, with large country‐specific dynamics. Under stress, financial factors amplify adverse macroeconomic conditions, and even severe individual shocks fail to fully explain the vulnerability observed under systemic stress. Our results underscore the importance of monitoring local and EA‐wide macro‐financial conditions to mitigate vulnerability.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Building resilient product portfolios in B2B manufacturing: A multi-criteria decision-making framework for managing disruptive factors
Authors: Till Gramberg, Aron Burgel, Andreas Eggert, Thomas Bauernhansl
Abstract: This study develops a methodologically grounded decision-support framework for product portfolio management (PPM) in manufacturing business-to-business (B2B) firms, aimed at systematically addressing the growing challenges posed by disruptive change, particularly those arising from digital and sustainable transformations. A preliminary study and systematic literature review reveal that current evaluation approaches fall short in addressing these emerging challenges. To address this gap, the proposed PPM-specific framework integrates established multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) methods: the analytic hierarchy process (AHP), the decision-making trial and evaluation laboratory (DEMATEL), and the weighted sum model (WSM). In addition to the three established PPM target dimensions – value maximization, strategic fit, and balance – the proposed methodology introduces a fourth dimension: resilience to disruptive factors. This expanded framework enables a structured derivation and weighting of evaluation criteria, identification of interdependencies within the product portfolio, and a systematic assessment of the strategic value contribution of individual portfolio elements. A case study with a global automation technology provider and evaluation workshops with three additional globally operating B2B industrial firms demonstrate the framework's practical relevance. The results indicate enhanced transparency, more objective decision-making, and systematic portfolio governance. This research contributes a formal and transparent decision support tool that facilitates strategically robust portfolio design in times of disruptive transformation, thereby addressing critical gaps in existing literature.

Title: Impact of return shipping insurance in live-streaming retailing
Authors: Yan Zhou, Xue Zhao, Shuai Liu, Feng Tao
Abstract: The growing prevalence of return shipping insurance (RSI) in live-streaming commerce presents a critical strategic dilemma. While RSI can stimulate demand by lowering consumers’ return costs, it simultaneously increases the seller’s operational costs and return rates. This paper develops an analytical framework to examine the impact of RSI in two dominant modes: self-operated and third-party live-streaming sales. We derive equilibrium outcomes with and without RSI and compare them to uncover its impacts. Our findings indicate that the seller chooses to provide RSI only under specific conditions: when the product dissatisfaction rate is high, but consumer sensitivity to return costs remains low. This finding suggests that offering RSI does not necessarily signal high product quality. Moreover, the effect of RSI on promotional effort is highly mode-dependent. In self-operated live-streaming, RSI may lead to lower seller effort for most cases, as the accompanying rise in return rates diminishes the marginal benefit of aggressive promotion. In contrast, third-party streamers, who do not bear RSI or return-related costs, are incentivized to increase effort to capitalize on heightened consumer demand. Additionally, in both modes, the introduction of RSI does not necessarily lead to higher prices. In fact, when RSI significantly raises return rates and reduces effective demand, sellers may strategically lower prices to stimulate orders. These insights provide valuable guidance for sellers and streamers in understanding RSI and designing RSI strategies aligned with their operational models and market environments.

Title: Improved Andrews’ formula for testing changing mean
Authors: Wei Li, Xinyue Zhang, Yang Zu
Abstract: We propose a robust bandwidth rule for the classical CUSUM and QS tests for shifts in the mean of a time series: the AR(1) coefficient entering Andrews’ (1991) data-driven HAC bandwidth is truncated at a fixed threshold (Formula presented), with ρ0 selected by a simulation-based procedure that controls empirical size against a user-specified persistence robustness target. The truncated bandwidth is shown to be free from the asymptotic power reversal problem under the diverging-alternatives framework of Juhl and Xiao (2009). Monte Carlo evidence indicates that the CUSUM and QS tests implemented with this bandwidth deliver good size control and monotonic power across a range of break designs and persistence levels.

Title: Efficiency bounds for incomplete information social interaction models with network structures
Authors: Ryota Ishikawa
Abstract: This paper studies incomplete information social interaction models with exogenous network structures under rational expectations, where an agent’s outcome is affected by the expected outcomes of other agents through a network. Incomplete information models are suitable for cases where an agent’s outcome is not fully observed or precisely predictable to others. Under an asymptotic framework with many small networks, we derive efficiency bounds for the model. The derivation requires the information matrix to be non-singular. We show that the information matrix is non-singular under an identification condition based on observed network structures.

Title: Weighing growth uncertainty and regime shift risk in a resource extraction game
Authors: Bruno Nkuiya
Abstract: In this paper, we design a stock-recruitment framework to examine non-cooperative conservation decisions made by players exploiting a common-pool renewable resource, such as a shared fish stock. The players face two sources of uncertainty. First, the resource population is subject to growth uncertainty caused by environmental variability like fluctuations in ambient temperature. Moreover, the biological growth function may undergo a permanent downward shift at an uncertain future date. We capture this regime shift risk through a hazard process within a discrete-time framework. Despite their impacts on management, the extent to which both types of uncertainty affect fishing communities is a matter that has surprisingly received little attention. Here we derive Markov Perfect Nash equilibria and show that each player’s harvest responses to stock growth uncertainty may change qualitatively when a stock-dependent hazard of regime shift is introduced. The harvest effect of regime shift risk may change qualitatively when growth uncertainty is allowed. Escapement may be monotonic or not in the variance of growth uncertainty. We identify scenarios in which competition to extract the resource gives rise to novel equilibrium outcomes relative to the optimal management case.

Title: Within-group inequality and caste-based crimes in India
Authors: Kanishka Bhowmick, Indraneel Dasgupta, Sarmistha Pal
Abstract: We examine how within-group inequality, by influencing the group bias of state institutions, affects the cost-benefit calculus of individuals engaging in identity-assertive behaviour, that results in police complaints regarding hate crimes. We develop a two-stage contest model of between-group conflict, where the relative influence of a group over institutions, determined by an initial contest, affects subsequent hierarchy-establishing interaction between individuals belonging to opposing groups. Applying this model to caste conflict in India, we find that greater inequality among non-Scheduled Caste and non-Scheduled Tribe (non-SC/ST) Hindus reduces the registered rate of crimes against SCs by non-SC/ST Hindus, and the rate at which such registered crimes lead to conviction. Using state-level annual crime and household consumption data over 2005–2021, we find empirical support for these hypotheses. Our analysis suggests that greater equality within dominant groups might reduce institution-capture by them and thereby improve both reporting and punishment of aggression against marginalized groups.

Title: Preferences for redistribution policies among politicians and citizens
Authors: Javier Olivera, Christian Breunig, Troy S. Broderstad, Patrick Dumont, Maj-Britt Sterba
Abstract: This paper compares the “mental maps” of redistribution among politicians and citizens across seven parliaments, using original in-person surveys of sitting MPs and nationally representative citizen samples. Fairness beliefs and ideology are the strongest correlates of support for redistribution in both groups, while misperceptions of wealth concentration matter for citizens but much less for politicians. A central finding is that politicians hold markedly more polarized views on redistribution than citizens, including within the same party families. We also find systematic elite-voter gaps: left MPs are more supportive than their voters (notably on inheritance taxation), whereas right/liberal MPs are less supportive than theirs. These patterns point to a representation concern and to a narrower bargaining space among elites than in the electorate.

Title: The effect of network degree on bargaining: Experimental evidence from the field
Authors: Ben D’Exelle, Christine Gutekunst, Arno Riedl
Abstract: We conduct an artefactual field experiment in real-existing trade networks to analyze how individual network degree affects bargaining demands and outcomes. We combine data from a bilateral bargaining experiment with data of trade networks in 24 villages in Uganda. To identify the effect of individual degree in the village trade network we experimentally vary the disclosure of participants’ identities in a bargaining pair. We derive hypotheses on how degree should affect behavior and find partial support for them. Specifically, we observe that individual degree affects bargaining demands in the predicted direction when one of the bargainers is informed about the network positions but not when both sides are informed. Moreover, network degree affects the likelihood of agreements and earnings, irrespective of the knowledge of the network positions of bargaining partners.

Title: The demographic impact of weather disasters: Evidence from extreme rainfall exposure in rural China
Authors: Wenjie Tian, Jinci Liu, Kang Zhou
Abstract: Using monthly rainfall data, we study the demographic consequences of extreme rainfall variability, focusing on extreme dry and wet events in rural China. We find that both types of extreme rainfall events increase fertility, with a stronger response for male births, between 1990 and 1999. More than a decade later, children who were exposed to extreme rainfall events in utero, especially extreme wet events, attain fewer years of schooling than unexposed cohorts. The second trimester of pregnancy emerges as the critical exposure window, with shocks during this period generating the largest negative effects on adult educational outcomes. Examining potential mechanisms, we show that extreme rainfall events reduce household income and increase child mortality. These results highlight the persistent demographic impacts of extreme weather shocks.

Title: Routing coordination optimization for modular electric vehicles in intensive passenger flow evacuation
Authors: Jiarui Yu, Ximing Chang, Qingyun Tian, Huijun Sun, Jianjun Wu
Abstract: For intensive travel demand at transport hubs, commercial districts, or large-scale activity venues, public transportation requires frequent transfers due to fixed stations, routes, and timetables, leading to increased travel uncertainty and time cost. While ride-hailing services offer greater flexibility, the concentration of vehicles exacerbates road congestion and reduces overall transport efficiency. The emerging Modular Electric Vehicles (MEVs) present a promising solution, as they can couple and decouple dynamically along their routes in response to spatiotemporal demand variations and provide door-to-door delivery service. This paper proposes a route collaborative optimization strategy for the efficient evacuation of intensive passenger flows with MEVs, aiming to minimize distance cost while enhancing service efficiency. An integrated clustering-based optimization algorithm (IntCO) is designed to seamlessly integrate demand point clustering and decision-making through policy gradient. Unlike traditional methods, IntCO dynamically adjusts clustering to iteratively refine decision-making, ensuring better alignment with optimization objectives. Real-world case studies demonstrate that MEVs can increase occupancy by 16.2% compared to fixed-capacity shuttle buses and reduce travel distance by 37.7% compared to ride-hailing services. By enabling rapid evacuation of high passenger volumes while providing door-to-door service, MEVs show significant potential for enhancing transportation efficiency and delivering personalized mobility service.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Corrigendum to “Event-driven dynamic ambulance dispatch: A transformer-based reinforcement learning approach with model explainability” [Trans. Res. Part E: Logist. Trans. Rev., 213 (2026) 104981]
Authors: Yimo Yan, Bo Zou, Theja Tulabandhula, Linhui Fu, Yong-Hong Kuo, Songyi Cui, Chengshuo Ying
Abstract: The authors regret that the funding bodies were not appropriately acknowledged in the published version. The following acknowledgement should be added: Yimo Yan, Linhui Fu, and Yong-Hong Kuo are supported by the General Research Fund of the Hong Kong Research Grants Council (Ref: 17204823). The authors would like to apologise for any inconvenience caused.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Can policy design build trust in local taxation? Experimental evidence of property taxation in Mexican municipalities
Authors: Aurora Echavarria
Abstract: Property taxes, the primary source of local revenue for municipal governments, are essential for improving urban service provision and resident welfare. Yet this tax is widely unpopular and often politically contentiuous. This study's descriptive findings reveal that property owners are not currently motivated to pay their property taxes by the promise of collective benefits, but rather by the desire to secure their property rights. Thus, this study asks: What dimensions of property tax design do property owners prioritize? How do they negotiate trade-offs? And can policy design establish credible commitment? I address these questions using an experimental conjoint survey with over 2,000 property owners in 34 urban municipalities in Mexico. I find that property owners are largely indifferent to the progressivity of property tax increases yet strongly prioritize policies that enhance accountability in how government administers, spends, and enforces taxes. Specifically, the presence of active oversight strategies in the use of funds increases the support for a policy by 11 percentage points, an effect greater than that of policies that offer more direct benefits. Individuals with high perceptions of government corruption disproportionately favor tax policies that incorporate active transparency strategies even if this implies a higher fiscal burden. Overall, this study demonstrates that public support for property taxation is not entirely inelastic and that adopting accountability measures that signal how funds are spent can make property owners more accepting of tax increases. This study contributes to literature on the fiscal contract by demonstrating how policy designs that enhance accountability can help establish credible commitment.

Title: Partisan politics and sectoral policy in Africa’s agro-export commodity chains
Authors: Catherine Boone, Michael Mugisha
Abstract: Even after economic liberalization in the 1990s, the role of the state in Africa's traditional tropical commodity export sectors has remained extensive. This paper argues that post-liberalization, these patterns of state regulation have often been shaped by the pressures and incentives of partisan politics, just as they were in earlier decades. We compare and contrast the changing institutional structure and patterns of state regulation in four agricultural commodity export sectors: Côte d'Ivoire-cocoa, Ghana-cocoa, Kenya-coffee, and Uganda-coffee. In spite of important differences, all four sectors are critical in providing resources, organizational structure, and policy mechanisms for building and maintaining electoral and other forms of political support for historically powerful political parties and/or power contenders. Post-1990s, each of the four cases presents an alternative pattern of alignment between export-sector organizations and partisan politics. Comparison across cases reveals the depth and variety of the ways in which domestic politics in African countries, including electoral politics, can shape state intervention in commodity chains for agro-exports, even in the neoliberal era. One implication for development studies is that domestic political and partisan dynamics are likely to continue to influence how governments use their “policy space” in supply chain governance in the future.

Title: Migration opportunities and human capital investments
Authors: Esther Gehrke
Abstract: We examine how shocks to migration opportunities affect schooling outcomes in origin communities. We focus on the migration between Mexico and the United States, and exploit the expansion of the Secure Communities program in the US—a federal data-sharing program that substantially increased the risk of deportation for illegal migrants—as an exogenous shock to the attractiveness of illegal migration. Our results suggest that the Secure Communities program increased attendance, enrollment, and educational attainment in municipalities that had stronger migration-network links with counties in the US that adopted the program early-on relative to municipalities that had ties with US counties that introduced the policy somewhat later. These results are consistent with the interpretation that the Secure Communities program raised the returns to education for prospective migrants by making low-skill migration to the US less attractive.

Title: Energy prices, inflation, and the ECB’s monetary policy during the 2021–22 energy crisis
Authors: Stefano Neri
Abstract: This paper quantifies the effects of energy price shocks in the euro area and examines the role of ECB monetary policy during the energy crisis. Using a Bayesian VAR identified with sign and narrative restrictions, local projections, and counterfactuals, I show that energy shocks induce persistent and broad-based inflationary pressures while reducing real activity. The pass-through to inflation is state-dependent: it is sizeable and persistent only when inflation is already elevated and when the shock originates from gas and electricity prices. A counterfactual exercise shows that an earlier and more forceful monetary policy tightening would have reduced inflation only at the cost of a sizeable output loss.

Title: Regulating investments when both costs and need are private
Authors: Daniel F. Garrett, Elena Panova
Abstract: Large-scale infrastructure investments are often carried out in settings where their eventual usefulness or importance is difficult to predict. This paper studies optimal incentives for investment when the agent undertaking the investment has superior information on two dimensions: the cost of investment and the likelihood it is useful or beneficial to the principal. Usefulness eventually becomes public, but punishments are limited as the regulator aims at ensuring the agent earns non-negative profits in each period. We characterize the optimal incentive scheme and show it involves either: (i) investments by the agent even though he knows they are useless and rents to only cost-efficient types, or (ii) rents to all types. The possibility that rent is left to all types contrasts with the usual prediction in static (and also dynamic) mechanism design and arises even though the agent’s preferences are stable over time.

Title: Policy pathways for low-carbon transport in Ireland: Carbon taxes and ICE bans
Authors: Daniel Cassidy, Kelly de Bruin
Abstract: This paper develops I3E-Transport, a new Irish passenger transport model that integrates behavioural, technological, and macroeconomic drivers to assess the effectiveness of carbon taxation and internal combustion engine (ICE) phase-out policies on emissions from private cars and public transport. The model is soft linked to the Ireland Environment-Energy-Economy (I3E) CGE framework, allowing for a comprehensive evaluation of how these policy measures influence transport demand, vehicle stock composition, energy consumption and emissions within the passenger transport sector. Simulations for 2024–2050 indicate that, under a business-as-usual scenario, emissions rise by 2050 despite modest gains in energy efficiency and alternative vehicle uptake. A carbon tax yields only limited abatement, whereas a comprehensive ICE ban from 2035—banning hybrids—reduces CO 2 emissions by over five million tonnes relative to the baseline by 2050. However, the results show that the sector remains off track relative to implied carbon budget ceilings under a 2035 implementation, with only an earlier and comprehensive ban delivering substantial progress towards compliance, pointing to the need for timely and coordinated policy action to align Ireland’s transport sector with its long-term climate commitments.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Typhoon and bike-sharing: Non-linear built environment associations with activity recovery in Shenzhen
Authors: Yi Long, Haoran Jiang, Shaozhi Hong, Yangyang Su
Abstract: With extreme weather becoming more frequent, transportation resilience is critical. However, evidence remains limited regarding how built-environment and urban-context conditions are associated with grid-level bike-sharing activity recovery under disruption. We analyze dockless bike-sharing recovery during Typhoon Cempaka in Shenzhen using Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), Generalized Additive Model (GAM), and model-based 3D response surfaces. The outcome captures service-use recovery, not individual cycling safety, welfare, or causal resilience. Results show that: (1) nighttime light intensity, population density, and distance to the nearest planned urban functional center are the leading diagnostic predictors; (2) several predictors show non-linear fitted responses, so recovery associations vary by range; and (3) the strongest interaction patterns connect activity intensity with population concentration, polycentric location, and transit accessibility. Robustness checks indicate sensitivity to baseline demand and meteorological exposure, and spatial validation shows residual spatial structure.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Financing constraints and structural drivers of maritime decarbonization
Authors: Jau Yang Liu
Abstract: Maritime transport accounts for nearly 3% of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet decarbonization research often assumes that stronger regulation will automatically accelerate transition. This study examines how financial, technological, and regulatory conditions jointly shape the feasibility of capital mobilization in shipping. Using integrated factor extraction, perception-based causal mapping (DEMATEL), and Importance–Performance Analysis (IPA), the study identifies perceived structural interdependencies influencing maritime decarbonization finance. The results suggest that financial viability, liquidity conditions, risk-sharing mechanisms, and digital verification infrastructure are perceived as key enabling conditions, while regulatory and stakeholder factors tend to operate as reinforcing elements. Rather than indicating regulatory insufficiency, the findings highlight the interdependence between policy signals and financial-system readiness. This study contributes by integrating structural diagnostics with prioritization logic and provides policy-relevant insights for sequencing interventions in capital-intensive transport systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Subsidize rent or subsidize homeownership? Evidence from a Hong Kong experiment
Authors: Michael B. Wong
Abstract: Governments often provide homeownership subsidies, but their effects may depend critically on institutional context. This paper estimates the impacts of Hong Kong's Tenants Purchase Scheme, an unusual program that allowed 183,700 regularly income-tested public housing tenants to buy restricted ownership rights. Leveraging its incomplete roll-out between 1998 and 2006, I find that the program increased the share of “well-off” households in treated housing estates by 44 percent from 11 p.p. Further evidence suggests that incumbent households purchased units to avoid regular income tests and reconfigured co-residence among family members to obtain additional public housing units. The unintended consequence was to exacerbate hardship for excluded low-income populations.

Title: What are the benefits of metro rail in Mumbai, India?
Authors: Palak Suri, Maureen L. Cropper
Abstract: We estimate the effects of the first metro rail line in Mumbai using administrative data on assessed property prices from 2011–18 for 723 subzones in the city. Comparing areas within 1 km of the metro with those beyond 1 km but within 3 km, we estimate the effects on property values for commercial, industrial, and residential properties. We find a significant and persistent increase in prices of 6%–8% for residential and commercial land use categories in treated areas relative to control areas after Metro Line 1 opens. We show that commute time savings and improvements in employment accessibility are plausible mechanisms underlying these effects.

Title: Drivers of Digital Traceability System Adoption for Greenhouse Gas Emissions in Complex Supply Chains
Authors: Sukrit Vinayavekhin, Aneesh Banerjee, Feng Li, Davide Luzzini
Affiliations: Thammasat Business School Thammasat University Bangkok Thailand; Bayes Business School (formerly Cass) City St George's University of London London UK; EADA Business School Barcelona Spain; Business School LUT University Lappeenranta Finland
Abstract: ABSTRACT The global climate crisis is pushing firms toward sustainable supply chain practices, with digital technology offering a vital pathway to track greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. This research investigates the factors influencing the adoption of digital traceability systems for managing these emissions, focusing on implementation scope and supply chain complexity (SCC). Drawing on Institutional Theory and Transaction Cost Economics, we conducted a choice‐based conjoint experiment with managers in manufacturing sectors to capture the trade‐offs in their decision‐making process. Our results show that firms are more likely to consider technology solutions when (a) those solutions cover Scope 1, 2, and 3 GHG emissions, and (b) there is greater SCC due to ‘detail‐numerousness’ (number of elements in a system) and ‘detail‐variety’ (heterogeneity of these elements). However, dynamic complexity (changing nature of elements) has an ambiguous impact on technology adoption. “Detail‐numerousness” (e.g., number of products produced) is the most critical attribute for internal operations, while “detail‐variety” (e.g., geographical dispersion and supplier heterogeneity) has the greatest impact on upstream supply chains. This research extends the supply chain technology adoption literature by providing a nuanced empirical understanding of how distinct dimensions of SCC at both internal and upstream levels shape the adoption of digital traceability.

Title: “Girls with girls”: gender composition and team performance in survey data collection
Authors: Qing Huang, Yingyue Quan
Abstract: We investigate the impact of gender composition on team performance in a real-world setting using a large-scale survey conducted within Chinese firms. We study the performance of two-person interviewer teams, with gender composition randomly assigned, tasked with complex survey data collection. Our analysis shows that two-female teams outperform both mixed-gender and two-male teams in interview completion and refusal-based questionnaire quality. Specifically, assignment to an all-female team increases the likelihood of completing an interview by 2.4%, and reduces refusals to answer key questions by 5%. This performance difference is likely driven by improved task coordination and a more favorable communication environment in all-female teams. This leads to increased effort input and ultimately enhances team effectiveness.

Title: Why are the youngest in class more often prescribed pharmacological treatment for ADHD?
Authors: Catia Nicodemo, Cheti Nicoletti, Joaquim Vidiella-Martin
Abstract: Abstract Children who start school at a younger age are more likely to receive pharmacological treatment for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). This pattern is widely attributed to peer-comparison biases, but the relative importance of different underlying mechanisms remains debated. We use administrative data from England to study how school starting age affects ADHD prescription rates from ages 5 to 15. Exploiting a sharp school-entry cutoff and comparing children born just before and after September 1, we estimate both age- and grade-specific effects of early school entry. We find that early starters are 40–50% more likely to be treated for ADHD by age 15. This long-term gap is entirely driven by first-time prescriptions among children aged 5 to 8. Using a novel decomposition strategy, we isolate the roles of relative age, absolute age, the length of school exposure, and age at school entry. We find that relative age is the primary long-term driver, aligning with previous evidence on peer-comparison bias, while absolute age and the length of school exposure have only short-lived effects. Our findings suggest that early starters are more likely to receive marginal diagnoses due to their relative immaturity, and we recommend refining diagnostic guidelines and classroom grouping practices to reduce diagnostic gaps.

Title: Integrated large language models and digital twin-based decision support in closed-loop supply chain operations: green steel transition case study
Authors: Chi An Le, Devika Kannan, Kannan Govindan, Truong Thinh Nguyen
Affiliations: Adelaide University
Abstract: The green steel transition requires corporates to operate closed-loop supply chains (CLSCs) that involve operational decisions under heterogeneous data. Although decision models have shifted CLSC operations towards advanced analytics and optimisation, challenges remain in automatically interpreting natural-language requests, enabling data-driven reasoning, and communicating outcomes for actionable decision-making. Motivated by recent progress in large language models (LLMs), we propose an intelligent digital twin-based decision-support method (LMiDTSC) to automatically interpret, reason, and address CLSC operational tasks, and synchronise physical and digital CLSC resources. We develop a knowledge graph, a benchmark, and an accurate query-explanation consistency (AQEC) metric to operate the method and evaluate its effectiveness in supporting decisions on steel distribution and scrap collection. Across focal operational tasks, LMiDTSC outperforms baselines (e.g. GPT-5.2) by 82.73% in AQEC, while its fine-tune outperforms backbones using proprietary models by 93.17% in AQEC. This study advances decision support systems and AI-enabled operations research by integrating LLMs and digital twins for computerised decisions in CLSC operations. This study suggests supply chain practitioners should consider high-performing LLMs for complex operational tasks and exercise caution in scaling in-context learning prompts. Finally, policymakers can accelerate the implementation of such integrated decision support systems by promoting industrial symbiosis and workforce training.

Title: Supply-demand uncertainty in bone China supply chains: distributionally robust optimization with voluntary and recycled resources
Authors: Hadi Hassanzadeh, Hossein Neghabi
Affiliations: Ferdowsi University of Mashhad
Abstract: This paper dvelops a mathematical model for designing a multi-echelon Bone China Supply Chain (BCSC), aiming to minimise total costs minus revenues through decisions related to facility location, supplier selection, and material flow quantities across the network. The model explicitly incorporates simultaneous uncertainty in both raw material supply and product demand, which is addressed using a Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) approach. Additionally, part of the required raw material is obtained through voluntarily contributed recycled sources. To solve the proposed model, we employ the L-shaped Benders decomposition algorithm and an enhanced version that incorporates a warm-up strategy to improve computational efficiency. Computational experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves higher profitability and better demand fulfillment rates under various uncertainty scenarios compared to traditional stochastic optimisation methods. Moreover, the inclusion of voluntary recycled inputs significantly reduces operational costs and enhances the overall economic performance of the BCSC. The results also confirm the effectiveness of the warm-up strategy in accelerating convergence and improving solution quality, particularly in large-scale instances.

Title: A review of process planning from an operations research perspective: models, algorithms, and benchmarks
Authors: Yiming Ma, Kaiping Luo, Qiuhong Zhao, Lianyu Zheng
Affiliations: Beihang University; Management and Decision (Beihang University), Ministry of Education
Abstract: Process planning bridges product design and manufacturing and increasingly involves multiple types of flexibility. As an NP-hard combinatorial optimisation problem, it poses substantial methodological challenges, yet effective optimisation is critical for improving production performance. This paper presents a review of process planning from an operations research perspective, covering models, algorithms, and benchmarks. We systematically classify mathematical programming models according to key characteristics, including model class, flexibility types, and objective settings, and highlight recent advances in linearisation techniques and compact formulations. From an algorithmic standpoint, we review and categorise solution paradigms, encompassing metaheuristics, multi-objective optimisation, deterministic methods, heuristics, and reinforcement learning, and analyse their respective strengths and limitations. In addition, we compile benchmark test cases together with technical specifications and best-known solutions to support systematic performance comparison. Finally, we identify research gaps and outline promising future directions, with particular emphasis on advanced optimisation methods and practically relevant modelling.

Title: Hierarchical collaborative scheduling in cloud manufacturing based on dynamic contract net protocol and deep reinforcement learning
Authors: Xi Wang, Yongkui Liu, Chunfu Zhong, Lihui Wang, Bin Zi, Yueqin Huo, Wenxue Wang
Affiliations: Xidian University; KTH Royal Institute of Technology; China National Heavy Machinery Research Institute Co., Ltd.; Chongqing University
Abstract: Cloud manufacturing facilitates collaborative production by integrating distributed manufacturing resources via service-oriented platforms. However, its scheduling process is constrained by resource heterogeneity, complex task dependencies, and inefficient platform-enterprise coordination. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approach for multi-task scheduling that integrates a contract net protocol (CNP) with graph neural networks (GNNs). First, a platform-enterprise collaborative scheduling framework is proposed. Then, two CNP-based schemes are designed and extended into a Dynamic CNP (DCNP) which updates evaluation weights to improved service selection. Moreover, an RGCN-LDDQN algorithm is proposed, which integrates relational graph convolutional networks (RGCN), long short-term memory (LSTM), and double deep Q-network (DDQN) to model inter-task dependencies and support global scheduling decisions. A bi-level priority constraint is integrated to mitigate conflicts, and a priority-aware P-RGCN-LDDQN is obtained, which enhances feasibility and stability. Subtasks are autonomously scheduled using a genetic algorithm at the enterprise layer based on platform-issued objectives and constraints. Simulations with respect to automotive parts assembly tasks are conducted. Results indicate that, under DCNP, RGCN-LDDQN reduces makespan by 21.88% and comprehensive cost by 15.64% compared to conventional DDQN, while maintaining service quality. Additionally, P-RGCN-LDDQN achieves further reductions of 9.15% and 6.69% over RGCN-LDDQN.

Title: From reference class forecasting to decomposed contingency in infrastructure projects
Authors: Peter E. D. Love
Affiliations: School of Civil & Mechanical Engineering, Curtin University
Abstract: Reference class forecasting (RCF) has become a central tool in infrastructure investment governance, primarily supporting funding approval by comparing outcomes with those of completed projects. Cost overruns that arise between funding commitment and contract award, and subsequently during construction, are often tied to how risk and uncertainty are managed after project approval, particularly when RCF is used to set or control contingency allowances. These patterns point to a problem in post-approval uncertainty management rather than a limitation of cost-estimation methods alone. While RCF provides a useful assurance mechanism for testing the plausibility of proposed cost estimates, it is not designed to manage uncertainty during the pre-contract phase, when project-specific information remains incomplete and subject to revision. A decomposed contingency approach (DCA) is proposed as a conceptual and methodological framework for managing uncertainty during this period. The DCA distinguishes among risk and aleatory uncertainty, epistemic uncertainty arising from incomplete or provisional information, and residual uncertainty associated with system-level effects that cannot be fully anticipated. It links different forms of uncertainty to decision approaches suited to their informational characteristics and provides a structured basis for adjusting contingency as information becomes more complete. Within this framework, contingency is determined through a decomposed treatment of uncertainty, while RCF is retained solely as an independent assurance mechanism.

Title: Group buying strategy in dual-channel with consideration of two selling formats: reselling and agency
Authors: Mengyao Zhang, Zenghui Su, Ke Han
Abstract: Group buying platforms have emerged as well-structured marketplaces, attracting a significant number of consumers with attractive prices. While these platforms boost sellers’ sales through the group buying channel, they also create channel conflict by competing with the seller’s original channel. Consequently, sellers and group buying platforms must carefully deliberate on their cooperation modes: reselling or agency contract. Previous research has insufficiently explored how sellers and platforms select cooperation contracts in dual-channel settings. To address this gap, we construct a game-theoretical model to analyze the strategic interactions between sellers and platforms in a dual-channel structure under two different contracts. Our findings reveal several notable insights. First, under both contracts, prices in both channels decrease as peer influence efficiency increases. However, the impact of group buying effort costs on prices is nonuniform, diverging from prior findings. Second, both sellers and platforms benefit from peer influence, shedding light on the emphasis stakeholders place on leveraging peer influence in group buying strategies. Most importantly, we find that both parties are more inclined to adopt the agency contract only when the fixed commission rate is moderate. Finally, while competition between the group buying and direct channels intensifies under the agency contract, the overall performance of the supply chain improves.

Title: Mergers when price and quality are set by bargaining
Authors: David J. Balan, Jeremy A. Sandford
Affiliations: Econ One Research Washington DC USA; Econic Partners Washington DC USA
Abstract: Abstract We study the effects of horizontal mergers on product quality in a bilateral bargaining environment. In our model, a competition‐reducing merger reduces equilibrium quality as long as the buyer's marginal rate of substitution of quality for price declines with price, holding quality constant. This condition is closely related to quality being a normal good. This result holds when price and quality are jointly negotiated, and it extends to a sequential setting in which sellers first choose quality and then bargain with buyers over price. We discuss applications to procurement and healthcare markets, as well as several extensions.

Title: Financial suicide: Debt and death across US counties during the Great Recession
Authors: Scott Abrahams, Bulent Unel
Affiliations: Department of Economics Louisiana State University Baton Rouge Louisiana USA
Abstract: Abstract Exploiting variation in debt‐to‐income ratios across US counties at the onset of the Great Recession, we investigate the impact of debt exposure on suicide. We find that more indebted counties saw a significant rise in suicide rates, with effects double for men and triple among adults ages 40–64. These patterns align with financial responsibilities: men are primary borrowers on mortgages, and middle‐aged adults hold the most secured debt. The impact of debt on suicide behavior, with annual costs of several billion dollars, underscores the welfare implications of inflexible household debt instruments.

Title: From catastrophe to culture: The role of historical disasters in shaping long-term orientation
Authors: Meng Liu, Jun Wang, James B. Ang, Per G. Fredriksson
Abstract: Natural disasters expose societies to an external environment that requires forward-looking adaptation. This paper argues that societies with greater historical exposure to natural disasters are more likely to develop long-term-oriented norms that emphasize preparation, saving, and future well-being. We test this hypothesis by linking historical exposure to earthquakes, tsunamis, and volcanic eruptions from 4360 BC to 1980 CE to contemporary long-term orientation. Disaster exposure is proxied by a distance-based measure that aggregates proximity to major catastrophic events over long horizons. Long-term orientation is examined using folklore traditions at the ethnic level and survey-based evidence at the individual and country levels. Across all levels of analysis, we find that greater cumulative disaster exposure is associated with significantly stronger long-term orientation. Evidence from folklore and second-generation migrants suggests that these effects operate through cultural adaptation and intergenerational transmission.

Title: Who drives inequality?
Authors: Domenico Moramarco, Olivier Sterck
Abstract: Which countries drive global inequality? Which states drive US inequality? We characterize the class of inequality measures that can answer these questions, permitting both an additive decomposition by subgroup and a multiplicative decomposition into within- and between-group components. Its central measure is simply the expected ratio of incomes between two randomly selected individuals. We show that global inequality fell since 1990, driven by declining disparities between countries. Inequality is primarily driven by large middle-income countries (India, China) and poor countries (Democratic Republic of Congo, Ethiopia). In the US, rising inequality is explained by widening gaps within states, while between-state inequality remains limited.

Title: Property rights and market frictions: Evidence from the universe of land dispute files in China
Authors: Jiong Zhu
Abstract: This research demonstrates how securing land property rights can mitigate frictions in rural land rental markets, specifically in the form of landlord-tenant disputes. By combining a comprehensive data set of land rental dispute records, farm-level panel data, and complete agricultural firm registration data, we find that rental disputes decreased following China's land titling reform. We corroborate this finding by distinguishing between property rights-related disputes (e.g., ownership ambiguity, boundary issues, or expropriation) and contractual enforcement disputes (e.g., rent collection). Further analysis reveals that the effect is particularly pronounced in rental agreements between farmers and agricultural firms, especially those involving non-local entities.

Title: A decision support system to dynamically align supplier portfolio management decisions and actions across levels and time horizons
Authors: Pamela Danese, Marco Formentini, Pietro Romano, Marco Boem
Abstract: Supplier portfolio management is essential for organizations to achieve their strategic goals. However, there is a lack of decision support systems (DSSs) that can support purchasing managers simultaneously at the strategic, tactical and operational levels, while ensuring consistency of supplier portfolio management decisions and actions across different levels and time horizons. Existing DSSs based on purchasing portfolio models (PPMs) are static and typically address supplier or purchasing category segmentation and analysis at a single point in time. Following a design science paradigm, we specified, implemented, and evaluated NorthStar, a novel DSS for supplier portfolio management designed to align decisions and actions across levels and time horizons through a structured three-step procedure. Ex-ante and ex-post evaluations, conducted in both artificial and naturalistic settings, demonstrate the novelty, relevance, and utility of this artifact. Our study contributes to the theoretical debate at the intersection of supplier portfolio management, PPMs and DSSs, and sourcing strategy literatures. First, it demonstrates how a PPM-based DSS can align supplier portfolio decisions and actions across multiple levels, as well as across time horizons, while remaining consistent with category strategies. Second, it addresses the static nature of traditional PPMs by supporting a shift toward dynamic models that enable continuous monitoring and adaptation. Third, NorthStar operationalizes key theoretical constructs, such as dependence by suppliers, competition, and supplier portfolio complexity, translating them into measurable indicators within a structured decision process, thereby bridging theory and practice. Finally, it provides a flexible, data-driven procedure that enhances the applicability of portfolio approaches in real-world settings.

Title: Three horizon-specific drivers of gold prices with Iterated Dynamic Model Averaging
Authors: Sihan Chen, Shenggang Yang, Xiaomei Lan
Abstract: This paper identifies three monthly horizon-specific drivers of gold prices using Iterated Dynamic Model Averaging (IDMA), a new machine-learning method that optimizes DMA by cyclically selecting predictors and updating forgetting factors. IDMA and standard DMA outperform other benchmarks, validating the variable selection mechanism. Predictor selection reveals three main drivers: stock market spillovers over short term, interest rate factors over the medium to long term, and safe-haven effects against geopolitical risk over long term. With the financialization of commodities, spillover effects from equity markets have become more prominent in gold price dynamics, challenging gold’s traditional safe-haven role in financial markets.

Title: Do non-financial risks compound? Evidence from U.S. industry returns
Authors: Corrado Botta
Abstract: Non-financial risks affect asset prices individually, yet they are typically studied in isolation. Using 49 Fama–French industry portfolios over 1990–2026, we show that pairwise compound channels among geopolitical risk, climate policy uncertainty, and financial stress carry significant pricing power beyond individual exposures. Climate policy uncertainty emerges as the nexus variable: its interaction with financial conditions is the most consistent channel, surviving all standard error methods, sub-sample splits, and predetermined (lagged) financial conditions, with an effect roughly four times larger for carbon-intensive industries. A Wald test confirms the joint significance of the interactions while individual risks lack joint significance.

Title: Omitted instrument bias
Authors: Bora Kim, Myoung-jae Lee
Abstract: Researchers often have access to multiple instrumental variables for a single treatment, yet empirical practice frequently relies on only one instrument while ignoring the others. We show that this approach generally identifies a noncausal parameter. We characterize the resulting “omitted-instrument bias” and show that it vanishes in special cases, such as when instruments are independent of each other or treatment effects are homogeneous. We propose a simple alternative two-stage least squares specification that identifies a causal estimand.

Title: Maximum resale prices across heterogeneous local markets
Authors: Øystein Foros
Abstract: We study maximum resale prices across heterogeneous local markets that share a common target retail price. A sufficiently small retailer margin can make the ceiling bind across markets, allowing common terms to implement this price. Two-part tariffs instead require the marginal wholesale price to align the retailer’s unconstrained optimal price exactly with the target. If the ceiling already binds, changes in market structure require no contractual recalibration. Apple’s use of list prices as de facto maximum resale prices, combined with discounts from those prices for independent resellers, illustrates a setting in which the mechanism may be relevant.

Title: On the inefficiency and coalitional manipulability of stable mechanisms
Authors: Gabriela J. Denis, Juan Pablo Torres-Martínez
Abstract: In the context of school choice, Ergin (2002) shows that Pareto efficiency and group strategy-proofness are equivalent properties for the student-optimal stable mechanism. We show that this equivalence holds at each preference profile and for every stable mechanism, providing a simple test for coalitional manipulability.

Title: Corporate earnings announcements and stock market bubbles
Authors: Elie Bouri, Ufuk Can, Oguzhan Cepni, Rangan Gupta
Abstract: We examine how corporate earnings announcement shocks influence US stock market bubbles using daily data from January 1990 to June 2025. After identifying positive and negative bubbles, we derive corporate earnings announcement shocks using a heteroskedastic vector autoregression model and estimate their dynamic effects on bubble indicators using local projections, with vector autoregression-based impulse responses reported as a robustness check. Positive earnings shocks boost positive bubbles, particularly at the medium to long-term, while reducing negative bubbles at the short-term. Therefore, favorable earnings news can fuel prolonged speculative episodes by increasing investor optimism, and lead to deep crashes but mild recoveries.

Title: Measuring the Sources of Taste-Based Discrimination Using List Experiments
Authors: Ariel Listo, Ercio A. Muñoz, Dario Sansone
Abstract: This paper examines how attitudes among supervisors, co-workers, and customers are related to discrimination against sexual minority individuals in the workplace. Participants from a large, nationally representative online sample in Chile took part in double list experiments  which reduce social desirability bias when eliciting views on sensitive topics  followed by direct questions on attitudes toward sexual minority individuals. The findings reveal a discrepancy between reported and actual levels of comfort with gay individuals in the labor market. The respondents underreported their discomfort by 15-23 percentage points, with the largest bias and lowest comfort levels observed when they were asked about supervising gay employees. These attitudinal patterns were mirrored in incentivized donation behavior: individuals who chose not to donate any amount from a lottery to a local LGBTQ-related nonprofit reported lower comfort levels and exhibited greater misreporting. Finally, the respondents consistently underestimated the broader societal support for gay employees and co-workers.

Title: Puzzles and dynamics in resource allocation: An introduction
Authors: Changxia Ke, Lucas Rentschler, Shane D. Sanders
Abstract: The papers collected in this special issue address two enduring difficulties in the economics of resource allocation. The first concerns the cost of allocation itself: contestants routinely expend resources in pursuit of a prize far in excess of what equilibrium reasoning would suggest, and conflict over resources destroys a portion of the value it reallocates. The second concerns the consequences of allocation: control over a valuable resource frequently fails to translate into improved welfare for the party that secures it. The nine contributions approach these problems from theoretical, experimental, and empirical directions, and several of them bear on the connection between how resources are contested and what follows once control is established. This introduction situates the papers within the contest-theoretic and resource-economics literatures from which they draw, identifies the questions they leave open, and sketches a theoretical bridge between issues of puzzle and dynamics in the resource allocation literature.

Title: Editorial Board
Behaviorally informed optimization of mobility-as-a-service bundle and fleet design for car users
Authors: Si Zhang, Niloufar Javanbakht, Khoa D. Vo, Prateek Bansal
Abstract: Mobility-as-a-Service (MaaS) is widely regarded as a promising strategy for reducing private car dependence. However, existing system-design studies typically rely on simplified or exogenous demand assumptions and often treat fixed-route public transit as the backbone, limiting their ability to capture the behavior of private car users. This is a critical gap, as car users who constitute the primary target for mode shift exhibit strong preferences for door-to-door convenience, reliability, and flexibility that traditional transit systems often cannot satisfy. To address this limitation, we study a demand-responsive multimodal MaaS system centered on shared micro-transit (MoDS) and ride-hailing (RH), two service types capable of replicating key attributes of private car use. We develop a behaviorally grounded optimization framework that jointly determines fleet configuration, service provision, and bundle pricing while endogenizing user subscription and modal choices. On the demand side, we estimate a discrete choice model using stated-preference data from private car owners in Singapore, capturing heterogeneity in sensitivities to travel time, cost, modal composition, waiting, and transfer inconvenience. On the supply side, we formulate a mixed-integer nonlinear program that maximizes a weighted objective combining operator profit and consumer surplus under operational constraints. To ensure computational tractability, we propose an iterative supply-demand optimization method in which supply decisions are updated iteratively with demand responses. We demonstrate the framework through city-scale simulations for 1.2 million car users in Singapore. The results show that up to 43.8% of car trips can be shifted to MaaS and that each MoDS vehicle can replace approximately 2.64 private cars in trip-equivalent terms. These findings highlight the importance of explicitly modeling behavioral responses in MaaS system design and suggest that demand-responsive, car-oriented service configurations can play a central role in reducing private vehicle dependence.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Truck-drone collaborative routing optimization: a unified framework and systematic review
Authors: Yansheng Chen, Jieling Jin, Helai Huang, Wei Liu, Said M. Easa, Yuanwen Lai, Shuyi Wang, Ye Li
Abstract: The collaborative operation of trucks and drones has increasingly emerged as an area of focus in both academic research and industrial applications, driven by the potential to revolutionize logistics and other sectors. This review presents a comprehensive and structured framework designed to systematically categorize and synthesize the existing body of research based on a review of 185 papers published between 2015 and 2025. It encompasses application domains, operational models, fundamental models, solution algorithms, current challenges, and future research directions relevant to truck-drone collaborative operations. The applications of truck-drone collaboration across various sectors are first explored, including logistics, emergency response, and monitoring systems. Three primary operational models of truck-drone collaboration are then analyzed, namely, single-truck and single-drone mode (STSD), single-truck and multiple-drone mode (STMD), and multiple-truck and multiple-drone mode (MTMD). Subsequently, this review classifies the existing mathematical models. It discusses collaboration mechanisms, optimization objectives, constraints, and uncertainty modeling, accompanied by a thorough examination of exact algorithms, approximation algorithms, heuristic algorithms, metaheuristic algorithms, artificial intelligence algorithms, and hybrid algorithms. Finally, the challenges and potential issues encountered in the truck-drone collaboration are summarized, and future research directions are proposed. This review proposes a unified framework for systematically classifying and integrating existing research on truck-drone collaborative routing optimization.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Rolling-horizon UAV dispatch for urban traffic incidents with preparedness-aware repositioning
Authors: Linghui Han, Yue Wu, Chengjuan Zhu, Huijun Sun
Abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) enable rapid aerial response for urban traffic incidents, yet existing work rarely integrates real-time dispatch with anticipatory positioning in an operationally tractable decision model. This study develops a preparedness-aware single-window UAV dispatch model embedded in a rolling decision process. At each scheduling window, the model optimizes current incident response while incorporating a one-step-ahead preparedness term based on predicted regional demand and expected UAV availability in the next window. A mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model jointly optimizes (i) response time and deadline-tardiness penalties in the current window, (ii) next-window preparedness shortfall, and (iii) diversion penalties associated with en-route retasking of returning UAVs and return-depot rebasing penalties. The model captures heterogeneous UAV availability (standby, mission-completed, returning), cross-window state transitions, endurance and service-time constraints, and depot operations. To satisfy online timeliness, we design a two-stage adaptive algorithm: adaptive large neighborhood search (ALNS) produces a dispatch plan, and a MILP repositions idle/returning UAVs; the two stages are coupled via adaptive resource-usage penalty parameters to provide interpretable trade-offs. The method delivers high-quality feasible solutions within minutes. It matches Gurobi’s best feasible solutions on small and medium instances. On large instances, it improves time-limited Gurobi solutions by up to 2.91% and reduces runtime by about one order of magnitude. Sensitivity analyses reveal diminishing marginal returns from fleet expansion and overly conservative repositioning when preparedness is over-weighted, offering guidance for risk-preference calibration and dynamic resource allocation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: HELP-RL: Real-time policy optimization with hierarchical decoder for heterogeneous and stochastic disaster response logistics
Authors: Hadi Aghazadeh, Xin Wang
Abstract: Disaster response logistics plays a vital role in reducing existential risk in relief operations by ensuring that essential resources reach affected communities promptly during emergencies. Although its significance is widely recognized, existing studies tend to focus primarily on pre-disaster planning, leaving notable gaps in addressing the complex, dynamic, and unpredictable challenges of real-time disaster response. This paper introduces a new framework called HELP-RL ( Humanitarian Emergency Logistics Planning with Reinforcement Learning ) to address these challenges, which are grouped into three main categories: heterogeneous fleet types, diverse demand types, and stochastic travel times. Together, these reflect the real-world complexities of disaster response logistics, all of which require real-time management. The HELP-RL framework incorporates a unique hierarchical decoder to manage the intricate action space, paired with an efficiently designed attention-based policy optimizer using the REINFORCE algorithm. This fully integrated model is built to adapt dynamically to changing disaster conditions, providing reliable and real-time solutions. To assess its performance, we tested the framework using both synthetic and real-world data from wildfire response logistics, drawing on actual data to replicate realistic scenarios. The findings show that HELP-RL produces adaptable and optimal policies that effectively handle rapid changes, surpassing other reinforcement learning approaches in terms of both efficiency and practical applicability.

Title: On disperse generalized linear models
Authors: Emilio Carrizosa, Renato De Leone, Marica Magagnini
Abstract: Generalized Linear Models (GLMs) are a key tool in Explainable Machine Learning, since they provide an easy-to-understand explanation of their coefficients and the impact of the different features in predictions. However, not all accurate GLMs may be equally appealing due to presence of secondary objectives such as sparsity or other measurement costs. For this reason, several methods have been proposed in the literature to address the multiobjective problem of joint optimization of accuracy and other secondary criteria, sparsity being the most popular objective if explainability is pursued. In this work we explore how different GLMs with good accuracy can be. We consider a biobjective P -Dispersion Problem, in which P models are sought jointly maximizing an overall accuracy measure as well as a dispersion measure. Several metrics are used to measure dispersion, such as a function of the distance between their parameters or the set of features used to predict. Moreover, different scenarios for the feasible region are considered, e.g., whether the P models are to be chosen from, or added to, a list of pre-selected GLMs. All these variants are expressed as biobjective nonlinear mixed integer optimization problems. Numerical tests are also presented, showing the effectiveness and the relevance of the proposed methodology.

Title: Instance scaling and metamodel-based sensitivity analysis for rolling horizon optimization with application to postal letter delivery services
Authors: Fabian Dunke, Stefan Nickel
Abstract: In many real-world planning settings, optimization problems are not only large in scale but also must be solved repeatedly as new data becomes available — most notably in rolling horizon schemes. However, this repeated solution process can quickly become computationally prohibitive, especially when assessing the sensitivity of outcomes to model parameters. We address this challenge by integrating two complementary methodological components: First, we propose an instance scaling technique using approximate linear scaling, which systematically reduces problem size to ensure computational tractability with limited loss of solution fidelity. Second, we develop a metamodel-based sensitivity analysis that efficiently displays the relationship between model parameters and solution process outcomes. Using surrogate models such as regression and neural networks, this approach enables fast estimation of both local and global sensitivities, even in complex sequential optimization processes where direct evaluation would require excessive computational effort. Together, these methodological advances form the foundation of a framework for efficiently analyzing the input–output relationships of optimization models used in rolling-horizon schemes. From a practical perspective, the framework enables informed decision-making through systematic alignment of strategic parameter setting in accordance with operational performance. The effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated for the postal letter delivery services, where it is used to examine the influence of different strategic measures, such as requiring specific delivery service levels or (dis-)incentivizing postponed and express deliveries, upon actual postal operations.

Title: Evaluating railway pressure on ecological corridors: From local disturbance to network-level risk
Authors: Yutian Liu, Zhengying Liu
Abstract: Railways increasingly affect ecological corridors that support landscape connectivity and species movement, with effects that can include both negative and context-dependent positive influences. Existing studies mainly focus on local effects such as crossings, fragmentation, and barriers, while system-level understanding of railway ecological pressure remains limited. To address this, we developed a local-to-network simulation framework to examine how segment-level railway ecological pressure is organized and how it relates to ecological network resilience loss. The results show that railway ecological pressure is spatially limited but strongly concentrated in a small subset of segments. Among them, some segments generate substantial network-level resilience loss, with different forms including structural, functional, and coupled decline. Regular and high-speed railways also exhibit distinct ecological resilience-risk organizations, indicating different modes through which railway disturbance can affect ecological corridors. These findings provide a basis for identifying priority segments for ecological mitigation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Economic implications of EVs in Europe: A scenario analysis of value added
Authors: Timm Hoefer
Abstract: The transition from internal combustion engine vehicles to electric vehicles changes where value is captured in the automotive supply chain. This study introduces a vehicle-level model of passenger cars (2020–2032), linking global production data, price breakdowns, and trade flows to map gross value added across eleven value chain segments. The results show that, in 2024, the European Union captures a 12.9 percentage point lower share of gross value added from battery electric vehicles than from comparable internal combustion engine vehicles. If this gap persists in the 2032 fleet, the implied shortfall is €3,575 per vehicle. Across 2032 value chain configurations, European Union outcomes range from −€92 billion to +€63 billion relative to baseline, with local assembly and battery manufacturing as the largest levers. The study shows how the electric vehicle transition reallocates value creation across components, regions, and firm ownership, offering a granular view of Europe’s industrial and regional exposure.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Tracking walking change post-relocation: A big data quasi-experiment of built environment effects
Authors: Nuoxian Huang, Daming Lu, Wenbo Guo, Wenjia Zhang
Abstract: Understanding how changes in built environment (BE) affect walking behavior remains a central issue in transport research. Residential relocation offers a useful quasi-experimental setting, yet post-relocation behavioral adjustment process is largely unknown. Using year-long daily mobile-phone data from relocators in Shenzhen, this study combines Interrupted Time Series (ITS) and comparative ITS with propensity score matching to estimate both immediate and gradual effects of BE changes on walking distance. Our results reveal temporal dynamics after relocation. Higher road network density, subway density, and open space consistently promote walking, whereas land use mix shows only an initial positive effect and population density and bus stop density show only gradual effects. The study extends conventional before-and-after relocation approaches by leveraging high-frequency longitudinal data to provide a more nuanced and complete picture of BE effects. These findings highlight the importance of adopting flexible, context-sensitive and temporally informed perspectives in transport planning and policy evaluation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Corrigendum to “Bridging socio-physical impacts, restoration efficacy and neighborhoods’ social vulnerability facing road flooding” [Transp. Res. Part D 159 (2026) 105506]
Authors: Jie Jiang, Yifan Yang, Yongsheng Yang, Weiping Wang, Jingkong Hong, S. Thomas Ng

Title: Measuring carbon mitigation potential from a network perspective: Evidence from Changsha
Authors: Dazhi Zhao, Pu Wang, Rihong Ke, Qi Liu, Ling Liu
Abstract: Promoting green travel is essential to reducing transportation-related carbon emissions, yet evidence remains limited on how to identify neighborhoods that should be prioritized for decarbonization and how to design effective policy packages. Using Changsha, China, as a case study, we integrate mobile phone data with license plate recognition data to estimate green travel demand and construct travel-related carbon emission networks to assess neighborhood-level carbon mitigation potential. We then apply an XGBoost model with SHAP analysis to examine how built-environment factors shape this potential and to design spatially differentiated policy packages. The findings reveal a clear center-periphery gradient in carbon mitigation potential. Central urban areas should be targeted with travel demand management measures, whereas peripheral areas require strengthened infrastructure. The proposed framework quantifies differences in carbon mitigation potential across urban neighborhoods and provides a basis for deploying customized low-carbon transport policies.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Corrigendum to “Power plays in the jungle: Political alignment and environmental degradation in Colombia” [J. Environ. Econ. Manag. 138 (2026) 103335]
Authors: Juan Miguel Jimenez, Lizeth Melissa Molina Alvarez, Santiago Saavedra
Abstract: The authors regret that the author contribution statements in the published version of the article were incompletely reported. The correct author contributions are as follows: Juan Miguel Jimenez: Project administration, Investigation, Methodology, Formal analysis, Data curation, Conceptualization, Writing - Original Draft, Writing - Review & Editing.
