Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: The regional economic impact of weather shocks: Evidence from Portugal
Authors: Dhruv Akshay Pandit, Paulo M.M. Rodrigues, João Seixo
Abstract: Weather extremes shape short-run economic activity through both market and nonmarket channels, yet evidence on local consumer-side activity remains limited. Using a municipality-level panel of Portuguese data (2010–2021), we estimate panel VAR and local-projection responses to weather shocks of point-of-sale purchases (a measure of merchant-location transaction activity, not resident household consumption), together with unemployment and house prices. Our central methodological finding is that hourly rather than daily measurement of rainfall variability raises the estimated semi-elasticities by an order of magnitude, suggesting that the existing climate-economy literature systematically understates the importance of high-intensity rainfall. Substantively, the local-projection responses indicate that hourly rainfall volatility raises purchases on impact and reverses the following quarter, consistent with intertemporal reallocation; temperature variability generates a sharp positive impact effect followed by a contraction; and high fire-danger days raise contemporaneous purchases. Unemployment and house prices follow the same patterns more weakly. Regional heterogeneity is substantial, the Lisbon Metropolitan Area and the Algarve sometimes display effects opposite in sign to those in the North.
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: Editorial Board
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: Housing market pressures and post-earthquake displacement: Evidence from the 2023 Türkiye earthquakes
Authors: Muhammed Hamza Kayrıcı, Yusuf Emre Akgündüz
Abstract: This paper investigates the impact of the February 2023 Türkiye earthquakes on housing markets in unaffected regions using online real estate listings and a time-based Regression Discontinuity Design. We document a sharp post-disaster demand shock driven by large-scale population displacement, with effects concentrated in the residential rental market. Consistent with a residential displacement shock, no significant effects are detected in commercial property markets. Price increases were highly segmented: pressures were strongest for multi-room units, reflecting the larger family structures of displaced households, and for newly constructed units, indicating a post-disaster flight-to-safety. Cross-sectional province-level and difference-in-differences estimates show that pre-existing migration networks and geographic distance are the primary determinants of rental price pressures.

Title: Beggars cannot be choosers: Labor market tightness, hiring standards, wages, and hiring costs
Authors: Carolin Linckh, Samuel Muehlemann, Harald Pfeifer
Abstract: This study analyzes how hiring standards, entry wages, and hiring costs are associated with labor market tightness. Using unique linked employer-employee data for small- and medium-sized firms in Germany, we find that pre-match search costs represent only 16 percent of total hiring expenditures, while post-match costs account for the remaining 84 percent. Instrumental variable regressions show no evidence that tighter labor markets are associated with higher entry wages. Instead, we find differences along two non-wage dimensions. First, firms hire workers whose general ability is lower relative to their existing workforce. Second, firms incur higher post-match hiring costs for these hires. A one standard deviation increase in labor market tightness is associated with a 0.1 standard deviation decrease in hiring standards, an 11 percent longer adaptation period, and 15 percent higher informal training hours for new hires. These findings suggest that, in tight labor markets, variation in hiring outcomes is reflected more strongly in hiring standards and post-hire training investments than in entry wages.

Title: Motherhood timing and the child penalty
Authors: Anikó Bíró, Steven Dieterle, Andreas Steinhauer
Abstract: Abstract Age at first birth has increased over time, which is likely to create many benefits in the labour market. Applying a number of alternative estimation approaches to administrative data from Austria, we estimate small to moderate effects of delaying motherhood on earnings, employment, and attachment to pre-birth firms in the medium run. However, even the largest of these effects are small relative to the average age effects, implying that delay leads to only small changes in child penalties. Much of the career return to later first birth comes from delaying the child penalty rather than changing how careers respond to children.

Title: A hybrid model proposal and an application for solving the problem of solid waste collection
Authors: İzzettin Hakan Karaçizmeli, Serkan Kaya
Abstract: The increasing amount of municipal household solid waste generated due to population growth and rising consumption has become a major environmental and economic problem for local governments. Waste collection and transportation activities constitute a significant portion of municipal solid waste management costs and are commonly formulated as vehicle routing problems. This study addresses a real-world municipal household solid waste collection problem involving 280 waste container locations in the Veysel Karani neighbourhood of Şanlıurfa, Türkiye. To solve the problem, a hybrid particle swarm optimisation algorithm combining particle swarm optimisation and local search strategies is proposed. The performance of the proposed algorithm was compared with linear programming, ArcGIS, real-life routing results, and previously developed metaheuristic approaches in the literature. The experimental results demonstrated that the proposed algorithm produced superior results, particularly for medium- and large-sized problem sets. Overall, the proposed method achieved 7.81% improvement over the linear programming model, 5.23% over the ArcGIS method, 33.46% over actual operational routes, and 0.24% over the improved hybrid firefly and particle swarm optimisation algorithm. In addition, statistical analyses based on Friedman and Wilcoxon tests confirmed that the proposed algorithm significantly outperformed the competing methods. The findings indicate that the proposed approach can provide an effective and practical solution for real-world municipal household solid waste collection problems.

Title: Integrating internal and external attributes in clustering: a goal programming-data envelopment analysis model
Authors: Hashem Omrani
Abstract: Conventional clustering methods group objects based on similarities in external data, often overlooking internal characteristics of decision-making units (DMUs), such as their production functions. In contrast, data envelopment analysis (DEA), a data-oriented nonparametric methodology, enables clustering based on the production frontier. However, traditional DEA models do not account for the distance between DMUs, and the resulting clusters are often non-unique, allowing a DMU to be assigned to multiple clusters. To address both internal and external characteristics, this paper proposes a goal programming–DEA (GP-DEA) model that clusters DMUs using both the production function and the distances between them. First, an envelopment form of the DEA model is applied to identify the initial clusters. Then, a GP-DEA model is used to determine a set of common weights for the input and output variables of the DMUs within each cluster. In each cluster, the efficiency scores of DMUs are recalculated using the new common weights. If the new efficiency of a DMU does not match the efficiency generated by the traditional DEA model, the DMU is removed from the cluster. In addition, a DMU initially assigned to multiple clusters is ultimately allocated to the cluster where its efficiency score remains unchanged. To illustrate the effectiveness of our approach, we present numerical examples and analyze a case study of 288 hospitals using the proposed GP-DEA model.

Title: Social Effects of the Vote of the Majority: An Experiment on the Brexit‐Vote
Authors: Fernanda Leite Lopez de Leon, Markus Bindemann
Affiliations: School of Economics, Politics and International Relations University of Kent Canterbury UK; School of Psychology University of Kent Canterbury UK
Abstract: ABSTRACT The 2016 EU referendum result was widely perceived as a statement against immigration. This paper investigates whether information about majority voting outcomes influences attitudes towards immigrants. Using a survey experiment conducted in England in 2017–2018, we randomly exposed participants to truthful information indicating that local constituencies had predominantly voted either to Leave or to Remain in the 2016 EU referendum. The intervention substantially shifted beliefs about local Brexit vote shares. Although we find no statistically significant effects on most individual survey questions, exposure to a Leave‐majority signal leads to more restrictive immigration policy preferences relative to exposure to a Remain‐majority signal. Effects are concentrated among participants for whom the information was politically dissonant or unexpected. Overall, the pattern of results is consistent with a conformity mechanism operating through perceived majority views, suggesting that referenda may continue to shape expressed policy preferences beyond their immediate aftermath.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Scalable state change detection for stimulus-aware digital twins
Authors: Abhishek Tiwari, Vibhor Pandhare
Abstract: One of the fundamental functionalities of a Digital Twin of any production system is its ability to serve as a ‘twin’, i.e. effective synchronization between the physical state and the digital state. This ability of being stimulus-aware through effective detection of state change forms the foundation to realistically model production behavior in real-time for improved production planning, simulation, execution, and management. Application-based top-down approaches to developing Digital Twins generally consider pre-calculated states or known data conditions, limiting their scope. In contrast, real-life production presents a myriad of possible states. Thus, a bottom-up scalable state change detection method and a systematic four-phase learning framework using minimal data are proposed for realizing stimulus-aware Digital Twins at the beginning of equipment operation. The proposed solution uses two-stage pattern recognition and change detection learning using a single state, followed by new state detection and adaptation using a novel implementation of a custom loss function to maximize the distribution discrepancy between the latent representation of the two states. Validation is performed over three experimental datasets, including a newly created gearbox dataset that varies in type of equipment, signal, operating parameters, etc. 80 experiments are conducted across different scenarios and repeated five times each, along with statistical testing to benchmark performance with the traditional approach. The proposed method detects a change in state with over 97.5% accuracy and an F1 score of more than 95.2%, irrespective of the dataset or the states used for modeling, narrowing the gap between localized success stories and the large-scale use of Digital Twins in production industries.

Title: Channel strategy to launch community group-buying channels for instant retail platforms
Authors: Chenchen Zhao, Jianghua Wu, Zepeng Wang
Abstract: Community group-buying, based on pre-sales and self-pickup, has rapidly expanded in recent years, posing a challenge to the instant retail mode, which is characterized by online ordering and instant store delivery. This study investigates whether an instant retail platform should introduce a community group-buying channel and, if so, whether it should adopt a self-run or third-party mode. In the self-run mode, employees hired by the platform serve as group leaders, with the platform determining their effort levels and paying fixed wages. Conversely, the third-party mode involves recruiting residents or community stores as group leaders, with the platform paying commissions. Although community group-buying utilizes group leaders to address the last-mile delivery issue and reduce operating costs, consumers have a higher acceptance of instant retail channels because of their superior delivery efficiency and product freshness. Our findings reveal that the platform considers introducing a self-run group-buying channel when consumer acceptance of group-buying channels is extremely high or low. When consumer acceptance is moderate, the platform prefers to establish a third-party group-buying channel if the commission rate is low; otherwise, it does not establish a group-buying channel. Interestingly, under a high commission rate and moderate consumer acceptance of group-buying, the group leader in the third-party mode may exert more effort than in the self-run mode. Furthermore, the platform's optimal commission rate initially increases and then decreases as consumer acceptance of group-buying channels increases.

Title: Low-cost AI and the value of compute scarcity: Evidence from the DeepSeek shock
Authors: Lingteng Zeng
Abstract: We study whether the DeepSeek-R1 shock changed the market value of scarce AI compute. Using U.S. stock returns around January 27, 2025 and compute-supply exposure from pre-event 10-K filings, firms more exposed to supplying AI compute earned significantly lower abnormal returns. In the preferred specification, higher compute-supply exposure predicts a 2.37 percentage-point lower three-day cumulative abnormal return (CAR[-1,+1]). Results survive industry fixed effects, risk and financial controls, alternative benchmarks, placebo dates, and text-validation checks. The evidence suggests DeepSeek was priced as a shock to AI compute scarcity rents, not only a broad technology-sector shock.

Title: Valuing improvements in native fish populations from river restoration projects: Evidence from a choice experiment in the Murray-Darling Basin in Australia
Authors: John Rolfe, Megan Star, Nicole Flint, Rodrigo Zilleruelo, Jeremy De Valck, Darshana Rajapaksa, Azad Rahman, Matthew Gordos, Boyd Blackwell
Abstract: There is increasing focus on restoration projects to improve environmental health of native fish, but the high cost of these interventions requires careful assessment of the benefits in project justification. While engineering projects such as fish ladders and fish screening in river systems are expensive, the benefits are more immediate and targeted on native fish than generic conservation approaches. This study reports a discrete choice experiment used to value improvements in native fish populations from river restoration projects in the Murray-Darling Basin in New South Wales. As well as considering improvements to native fish, the choice experiment also framed potential changes in river health to benefit water birds, recreational fishing opportunities and the length of the waterway that was improved. The results add to the small pool of primary valuation studies focused on improvements to native fish populations through river restoration projects, providing one of the first economic analyses of this issue. The choice experiments also tested for differences in values between in-catchment and out-of-catchment populations. The present value of each 1 % improvement in native fish populations is estimated at $5.73 per household. Over an estimated 3,228,000 households in New South Wales, this translates to $18.5 M for each 1 % improvement. The consistency of these value estimates with results of other comparable studies indicates that the values for improving fish populations have remained stable over time as well as being consistent across different management options for river restoration.

Title: Food system actors perspectives on Swedish agricultural preparedness -a Q-methodology study
Authors: Hanna Eneroth, Helena Hansson, Amanda Wood, Iman Raj Chongtham, Georg Carlsson, Elin Röös
Abstract: Profitability and environmental sustainability have long been central to agri-food policy. Increasing geopolitical tensions, however, have shifted attention toward the food supply in times of crisis, challenging actors to place greater emphasis on food preparedness. The aim of this study was to assess food system actors' perspectives on the challenges and issues related to the role of Swedish agriculture to ensure supply of food commodities in times of crises. Using Q-methodology, 47 statements drawn from policy documents and media sources relating to food production, sustainability, and preparedness were prioritized by 26 food system actors based on how closely each statement aligned with their individual perspectives. Seven interviews provided further clarification for interpretation of the results. Factor analysis identified four factors, including one bipolar factor, which we interpreted as five distinct perspectives. 1) “Focus on the environment” is a perspective in which respondents emphasize environmental sustainability and low-input solutions. 2)“Strengthen current production”, focuses on prioritizing domestically produced inputs and cattle production. 3) “Ensure profitability and long-term solutions”, highlights profitability and diversification of cropping systems. In the remaining two perspectives, the focus is on preparedness and responsibility of individual businesses: 4) “Go for contingency planning” stresses the importance of authorities' roles, while 5) “Keep up international trade” emphasizes maintaining international trade connections. These perspectives reflect broader societal debates on food system transformation relating to resilience and sustainability. The plurality of perspectives provides insights to guide future policy development in Sweden and in other countries in the European Union facing similar challenges.

Title: Welfare implications of no net loss policies with heterogeneous cultural ecosystem services
Authors: Cathrine Hagem
Abstract: No net loss (NNL) targets for nature are increasingly implemented at both national and subnational levels. While these policies are typically framed in terms of area or biophysical equivalence, they may overlook heterogeneity in the cultural ecosystem service (CES) values associated with undeveloped land. This paper develops a parsimonious economic model to analyze the welfare implications of alternative NNL policy designs when CES values differ across municipalities. We distinguish between local CES values, such as recreational and amenity benefits accruing to nearby populations, and a national CES value associated with the existence of undeveloped nature. We compare unilateral and cooperative municipal policies and examine the performance of taxes and subsidies versus offset markets under area-based and CES value-based NNL targets. We show that area-based NNL policies are generally welfare suboptimal in the presence of heterogeneous local CES values, even when implemented cost-effectively through offset markets. By contrast, NNL targets defined in CES value terms can achieve constrained welfare optima using appropriately designed fiscal instruments or ambient permit markets. Although inter-municipal cooperation reduces aggregate costs, distributional effects may prevent mutually beneficial outcomes without side payments. Numerical illustrations based on Norwegian data support the analytical results and highlight implications for subnational and national offset policy design.

Title: The appearance of democracy: How conditional payments reshape behavior among local leaders
Authors: Ivo Steimanis, Esther Blanco, Björn Vollan
Abstract: Monetary incentives are widely considered to promote democratic practices in local governance. We test this proposition by providing causal evidence from a lab-in-the-field experiment with local leaders (n=64) and their constituents (n=384) in rural Namibia's hybrid governance setting. Using a within-subject design, we introduced conditional payments to leaders for allowing constituents to vote on how to distribute a collective fund. A majority of leaders (64%) chose a democratic rule at baseline, and the payments did not significantly increase this share. The incentives caused a significant reduction in openly autocratic behavior, primarily through a shift toward a pseudo-democratic practice of appearing democratic while retaining unilateral decision-making. This reveals unintended consequences of the conditional incentives, fostering symbolic compliance where leaders appear democratic while retaining control. Exploratory analysis shows payments "crowd out" democracy among initially democratic leaders but "crowd in" pseudo-democracy among autocratic leaders, moderated by governing motivations. Our findings illustrate that conditional payments can fail to foster genuine democracy and caution against their prescriptive use in complex governance environments.

Title: Big push to export: Unintended consequences of China’s domestic regulations in digital game sector
Authors: Xiaofan Li, Ke Meng
Abstract: We document that China’s 2018 domestic regulations, which suppressed the future growth potential of its game app market, unintentionally triggered an immediate and significant export expansion in this sector. This expansion was largely accounted for by apps already established in foreign markets, and was significantly stronger among high-quality firms. To rationalize these patterns, we develop and calibrate a dynamic model featuring customer accumulation under capacity constraints. In response to the regulatory shocks, firms proactively reallocate resources toward foreign markets, with higher-quality firms exhibiting a stronger reallocation response. This proactive behavior further amplifies the welfare losses borne by domestic consumers.

Title: A strategic analysis of narcoterrorism: counterterrorism, terrorist extortion, and illicit drug trafficking
Authors: Subhayu Bandyopadhyay, Todd Sandler
Abstract: The paper presents a novel strategic analysis of narcoterrorism where a developing country's terrorist group extorts home drug farmers to finance terror attacks.A developed country's counterterror actions are motivated by the harm its residents endure from those attacks.The developed country's counterterrorism involves efforts to destroy the drug crop abroad.The analysis begins with the drug price being exogenously fixed, followed by a "large-country case'' with a market-determined drug price.The extension introduces a fourth participant, consisting of the developed country's consumers whose purchases determine the drug demand.A subsequent extension allows for two drug-exporting countries along with their resident terrorist groups.Now, the drug price depends on terrorist extortion rates and the developed country's counterterrorism associated with the two drug-exporting countries.With the last extension, novel drug-based counterterror transfers of terrorism occur between the drug-producing countries.

Title: An ∊-logic-based Benders decomposition algorithm for the bi-objective weekly home health care scheduling problem with patient satisfaction
Authors: Juan Du, Yue Xu, Peng Zhu, Xiuli Wang
Abstract: This paper addresses a bi-objective weekly home health care scheduling problem that incorporates patient satisfaction with respect to their preferred service patterns, where a service pattern is defined as a combination of service days and time slot for multiple visits within a week. The objectives are to maximize the number of patients assigned to their preferred patterns and minimize operational costs. In order to provide the trade-offs between the two objectives for decision-makers, we propose an exact ∊-logic-based Benders decomposition (∊-LBBD) algorithm, which embeds the LBBD algorithm in an ∊-constraint framework to generate the Pareto front. In the algorithm, we construct a dynamic cut pool and propose its reuse mechanism to inherit Benders cuts from previously solved ∊-problems exploiting the ascending ∊-iteration framework. For solving each ∊-problem, we introduce the service-pattern conflict inequality into the master problem, and develop a dynamic programming algorithm to solve the resulting subproblems. Computational experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed ∊-LBBD algorithm. By conducting sensitivity analysis on enterprise data, we derive some managerial insights: i) Lowering operational costs comes at the expense of patient satisfaction, and the marginal benefit of cost savings diminishes as satisfaction declines. ii) For a given level of patient satisfaction with preferred patterns, operational costs can be substantially reduced by encouraging patients to specify multiple acceptable service patterns. iii) In response to patients’ service needs, enhancing nurse-patient compatibility through measures such as targeted training can significantly reduce operational costs and/or improve the fulfillment of patients’ preferred service patterns.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Enhancing port channel logistics safety: An asynchronous distributed DRL approach for waterborne ASVs trajectory tracking under dynamic disturbances
Authors: Chongwei Gong, Zhen Tian, Yusheng Zhou
Abstract: Port channel safety is essential for reliable vessel movements and efficient logistics operations in intelligent ports. Waterborne ASVs can support inspection, monitoring, and auxiliary transportation in restricted port waters, but their deployment requires accurate trajectory tracking to avoid additional port-channel navigational safety risks. However, reliable ASV tracking remains challenging under dynamic disturbances and strict ship-to-shore communication constraints. This study proposes an Asynchronous Distributed Deep Reinforcement Learning (AD-DRL) control scheme for robust ASV trajectory tracking under dynamic marine disturbances. Unlike traditional centralized training, the proposed framework enables distributed ASVs to collaboratively update policies by exchanging model gradients rather than raw sensor data, thereby reducing communication requirements. To improve decision-making in dynamic waters, a gated hybrid attention mechanism is integrated into the Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) architecture. This mechanism helps the agent capture spatiotemporal disturbance features and delayed vessel responses caused by hydrodynamic lag. Moreover, an ERA5-informed data-driven simulation environment is constructed using real-world ocean current, wind, and wave data to train and evaluate the controller. Experiments across five representative international ports show that the proposed method achieves lower tracking errors and higher success rates than baseline methods under varying environmental disturbances. Additional safety-corridor analysis further confirms its ability to maintain reliable trajectory execution in port channels. These results demonstrate the robustness and practical relevance of AD-DRL, providing technical support for safer and more reliable ASV operations in intelligent port logistics scenarios.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: A claim cost assessment method of lifetime warranty products with limited usage rate
Authors: Jingqi Liu, Keyao Zhao, Yan Meng, Deyin Jiang, Huan Pang
Abstract: This paper develops a general theoretical framework for claim cost assessment of the lifetime warranty with limited usage rate (LUR-lifetime warranty) in the automotive transportation sector. Firstly, to address limitations in describing consumer heterogeneity, we develop a two-layer nested probability description method that analyzes vehicle usage rates at the overall, group, and individual levels. Secondly, we study the evolution of the usage rate distribution for in-warranty vehicles and propose a warranty rate calculation method. Furthermore, a claim cost assessment model for products with two-dimensional degradation characteristics is established. Finally, the framework reveals the following theoretical properties, illustrated by a case study: (1) usage rate distribution of in-warranty vehicles gradually shifts toward lower usage rates over driving time; (2) instantaneous warranty rate decreases during the first 12 time periods, then increases thereafter; (3) total claim cost per unit increases with higher annual mileage limits under the same driving time, for a 30,000 km limit, the cost after 60 months is about 64% lower than a pure lifetime warranty. The proposed theoretical framework enriches warranty strategy design theory and provides a general analytical tool for vehicle manufacturers and transportation operators.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: A two-stage stochastic programming approach for the time-dependent vehicle routing problem with stochastic demands: a dynamic space–time network perspective
Authors: Chenhao Zhang, Lin Xie, Yaoxin Wu, Tao Feng, Lin Cheng
Abstract: Urban delivery operations increasingly face dual uncertainties from stochastic customer demands and time-dependent traffic, challenging the adequacy of classical vehicle routing models. This study addresses the Time-Dependent Vehicle Routing Problem with Stochastic Demands (TD-VRPSD) with service time windows by constructing a dynamic space–time network aligned with real-world road topology. A two-stage stochastic programming model is developed, integrating preventive and reactive recourse strategies to handle capacity violations under uncertain demands, while explicitly accounting for time-dependent travel times in both routing and round-trip recourse operations, along with service time windows, vehicle waiting and service times. We solve the problem using an improved integer L-shaped method that separates expected-demand routing from scenario-specific recourse and embeds Benders cuts directly into branch-and-bound, dynamically generating cuts during branching. Computational experiments on benchmark instances and a real-world JD.com case show that the proposed method yields adaptive, cost-effective routes, with an average optimal gap of 2.98%, reducing runtime by 39.0%-88.9% while narrowing the optimality gap by 34.1%-84.8% compared to commercial solvers and classical decomposition techniques. Sensitivity analyses on problem scale, demand distribution, deteriorated traffic conditions, and time windows are further conducted, providing relevant managerial insights. This work represents a first attempt to integrate space–time modeling, stochastic demand, hybrid spatiotemporal recourse, and exact decomposition in the TD-VRPSD, providing a framework that can support robust and scalable solutions for urban logistics under uncertainty.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Ride-hailing markets with mixed autonomy: how will path choice modes of idle vehicles affect repositioning schemes?
Authors: Yingying Ma, Ziyan Guan, Xiaoran Qin
Abstract: In recent years, several companies have attempted to apply autonomous vehicles to on-demand ride-hailing services. The on-demand ride-hailing market is expected to present a scenario of shared autonomous vehicles (SAVs) mixed with human-driven vehicles (HVs) soon. Operational differences between SAVs and HVs present significant impacts on road traffic and raise challenges for ride-hailing platforms in terms of scheduling and managing SAVs. To derive the optimal repositioning scheme of SAVs, we propose a bi-level model considering interactions between road traffic operation and ride-hailing market conditions in the mixed-fleet scenario. A profit-maximization model is established at the upper level for the SAV repositioning schemes under market equilibrium conditions. With the mixed-fleet size and market indicators derived from the upper level, we develop network equilibrium modes at the lower level in which idle SAVs follow the system optimality (SO) and the rest follow the user equilibrium (UE). These models differentiate not only the types of vehicles, but also their occupancy status to guarantee passengers’ experience. By solving the complex bi-level model with a tailored algorithm, we show the advantages of idle SAVs following the SO principle in terms of market operations and user experience. Our results demonstrate that by following specific SAV management strategies, the platform can achieve a balance among system efficiency, passenger experience, and market fairness. This provides new insights into the scheduling of SAVs.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Transit network design and frequency setting with elastic demand: a mixed-integer linear programming approach
Authors: J. Albuquerque, M.C. Gomes, J.M. Olivé, A.R. Andrade
Abstract: This work introduces a new single-level mixed-integer linear programming framework for the Transit Network Design and Frequency Setting Problem that successfully integrates discrete choice models into a linear formulation. The model aims to capture demand by taking into consideration the travellers’ preferences and activates or deactivates routes at a certain frequency accordingly, from a given pool of possible routes. This work was applied both to an illustrative example and to a case study of the existing bus and Bus Rapid Transit network in an area of the Barcelona Metropolitan Area, comprising 9 lines and 319 origin-destination pairs. For each origin-destination pair, each possible itinerary within the network is pre-computed and is compared against the best itinerary of each of the competing modes of transport, which are obtained using Google Maps. For each itinerary in the network, it is computed its probability of being chosen, based on its utility, using a multinomial logit model, that takes into consideration the access, waiting and travel times, cost, and number of transfers. The coefficients were calibrated using a Stated Preferences Survey. The goal is to maximise the total network demand by tuning the active routes and frequencies, activating the itineraries with the highest probability of being chosen, allocating most or a pre-determined percentage of the demand to them, constrained by number and capacities of buses. The formulation allows for different assumptions on traveller assignment and coverage. The models are solved with exact methods within reasonable computational time and low optimality gaps.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Is irregular migration responsive to recent German asylum policy adjustments?
Authors: Bernd Beber, Cara Ebert, Maximiliane Sievert
Abstract: We investigate the extent to which asylum policies that aim to deter individuals from migrating irregularly in fact do so. We specifically consider effects of Germany’s 2023 asylum policy adjustments, which include accelerated asylum decision processes, the prospect of asylum processing outside of Europe, the introduction of a payment card to replace cash benefits, and an extended waiting period for native-level benefits. To estimate the effects of these policy measures on irregular migration intent, we implement a conjoint experiment with 989 men aged 18–40 in four cities in Senegal, a country where irregular migration to Europe is highly salient. Offshoring the asylum process substantially lowers irregular migration intentions, and extending the waiting time for native-level benefits only has a small effect on intent. Neither reducing asylum processing times nor replacing cash benefits with a payment card alters intentions. Our study does not resolve political and normative questions concerning these policies.

Title: The contributions of community forests to rural prosperity in the United States
Authors: Reem Hajjar, Susan Charnley, Gregory E. Frey, Kathleen McGinley, John Schelhas, Frederick W. Cubbage
Abstract: Community forests (CFs) are a forest ownership and governance approach that enable community members and other key stakeholders to cooperatively manage local forests to produce a range of benefits that align with local community priorities. While well-studied internationally, there is a lack of research that systematically documents how CFs can contribute to rural prosperity in the U.S. amidst ongoing socioeconomic and environmental change. We adapt a framework developed to characterize the contributions of forests to rural prosperity in the international context to investigate the environmental, economic, and social benefits from CFs. In examining 18 in-depth CF case studies, we find that establishing CFs increases access to and control over local forests by local communities, allowing them to manage forests according to local priorities and needs. Economically, many CFs bring in earned income and employment, directly and indirectly, from forest products and services, and support local businesses through tourism and recreation. Social benefits of CFs include access to recreation opportunities, enhancing social relations, and building community identity, security, and empowerment. In extending existing rural prosperity frameworks, we propose that environmental benefits of CFs, including forest protection and restoration and reducing wildfire risk, also play a key role in enhancing rural prosperity. Evidence from these cases suggests that local governance of forests for the production of local benefits using a CF model is a promising approach to enhancing rural prosperity in the U.S.

Title: Fickle fossils: Economic growth, coal, and the European oil invasion, 1900–2015
Authors: Miriam Fritzsche, Nikolaus Wolf
Abstract: Fossil fuels have shaped the European economy since the industrial revolution. We use new long-run panel data to analyse the effect of both, coal and oil on economic growth between 1900 and 2015, exploiting variation at the level of European NUTS2 and NUTS3 regions. We show that the reversal of fortune of coal regions resulted from the second energy transition. Specifically, an “oil invasion” in the early 1960s turned regional coal abundance from a blessing into a curse. Human capital accumulation contributed to this reversal of fortune and fully explains the negative effects until today. Moreover, we find substantial heterogeneity between former coal regions that is in line with Glaeser’s “reinvention hypothesis”: regions with a higher skill-level adjusted much better to the decline of coal. In particular, we show that coal regions with a higher urban density before 1800 were much more resilient than others.

Title: No remote, hybrid remote, and full remote: Additional insights from telework intensity
Authors: Peng Chen, Changlong Ling
Abstract: This study investigates the factors of telework intensity, no telework, hybrid telework, and full telework, using a generalized ordered logit model. The analysis integrates commuting characteristics, employer-based travel demand management strategies, and industry/occupation factors. Results indicate that telework intensity is primarily associated with occupational characteristics, workplace policies, and commuting conditions. Knowledge-intensive industries exhibit substantially higher levels of telework participation, whereas socio-demographic and built-environment factors contribute limited explanatory power. Elasticity analysis shows that automobile dependence significantly decreases the probability of teleworking, while longer in-vehicle travel time is negatively associated with higher telework intensity. Among employer-based strategies, flextime significantly increases telework participation, whereas compressed workweeks function as a substitute. These findings highlight the dominant role of job-related constraints and workplace flexibility in shaping telework intensity and illuminate the importance of differentiating telework participation by intensity level.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Information paths and learning in games: Experimental evidence
Authors: Peiran Jiao, Heinrich H. Nax, Jichuan Zong
Abstract: Information in repeated real-world interactions is rarely fixed. Instead, over time, players typically learn more about the game structure, understand more about their own payoff correspondences, and find out what others did and earned in the past. However, how this dynamic information path influences learning and which aggregate outcomes are reached as a result have not been investigated to date. To study this, we conducted a series of laboratory experimental games where we provided more information over time in different orders and along different paths. These games span two strategically distinct classes: a Cournot game with a unique symmetric Nash equilibrium, and step-level public-goods (coordination) games with multiple Nash equilibria of differing Pareto efficiency. Our evidence confirms a natural mapping from information to predominant learning rule: information about own payoffs triggers payoff-based learning, feedback concerning others’ realized payoffs triggers imitation, and structural information about the game triggers best response. In addition, when multiple learning rules are feasible, which one dominates depends on information paths. In particular, feedback about others’ actions and payoffs, especially when supplied marginally, may trigger persistent imitation that locks into Pareto-inferior Nash equilibria, even when more information later becomes available.

Title: Testing for spillovers in resource conservation: Evidence from a natural field experiment
Authors: Lorenz Goette, Zhi Hao Lim
Abstract: This paper studies whether behavioral interventions designed to promote resource conservation in one domain generate spillovers in another. Using a natural field experiment involving over 2,000 residents, we identify the direct and spillover effects of real-time feedback and social comparisons on water and energy consumption. We implement three interventions: two targeting shower use and one targeting air-conditioning use. We find significant reductions in shower use from both water-saving interventions, but no direct effect of the energy-saving intervention on air-conditioning use. For spillovers, we estimate precise null effects of water-saving interventions on air-conditioning use, and of the energy-saving intervention on shower use.
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: Sponge city and impermeable housing value: Evidence from London
Authors: Yihao Wu
Abstract: Climate change has intensified flash flooding, prompting cities worldwide to implement green stormwater infrastructure as a scalable adaptation strategy. This paper evaluates the economic consequences of London's Sustainable Drainage Systems (SuDS) program on the local housing market. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design and an LSOA-by-year panel dataset from 2010 to 2024, I find that neighborhoods receiving green infrastructure record 3.2–3.7% increases in housing prices on average but no discernible rise in transaction volumes. Event study estimates reveal a hump-shaped temporal profile, with effects peaking around the fifth year before partially attenuating. The price responses exhibit a non-monotonic pattern across flood risk categories, largely because infrastructure salience drives value creation more than hydraulic performance. My findings suggest that successful climate adaptation requires balancing engineering effectiveness with public perception, and that green infrastructure can generate sufficient returns to self-finance through property tax revenue.

Title: Collaborative negotiation and auction protocols for multi-agent supply networks
Authors: Frederik A. Weber, Shimon Y. Nof
Affiliations: Purdue University

Title: The Curvilinear Impact of Environmental Sustainability Strategies on Cost and Profit Growth: The Moderating Influence of Operations, R&D, and Logistics Capabilities
Authors: Siavash Rashidi‐Sabet, Sreedhar Madhavaram
Affiliations: Department of MIS, Marketing, and Analytics| Saunders College of Business, Rochester Institute of Technology Rochester New York USA; Department of Marketing and Supply Chain Management| Jerry S. Rawls College of Business Administration, Texas Tech University Lubbock Texas USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Research linking environmental sustainability efforts and firm performance provides equivocal evidence of negative, neutral, or positive effects. Drawing on myopic management theory, this research develops and tests a time‐contingent, nonlinear account of how corporate environmental sustainability performance shapes cost growth and profit growth. This research conceptualizes environmental sustainability initiatives as requiring up‐front process redesign and coordination investments that elevate short‐run cost growth and compress profitability, but yield delayed benefits as implementation stabilizes and learning accumulates. This research further examines how three core functional capabilities relevant to logistics and supply chain execution—operations capability, R&D capability, and logistics capability—condition these curvilinear trajectories. Analyses of data from 498 U.S. public firms over 2012–2024 show an inverted U‐shaped relationship between environmental sustainability performance and cost growth and a U‐shaped relationship with profit growth, with both relationships evolving over time. Analyses indicate that core functional capabilities meaningfully condition these curvilinear relationships, shaping the magnitude and timing of sustainability‐related cost escalation and profitability improvement. The findings position sustainability as a staged logistics and supply chain implementation challenge and indicate that investing in logistics execution effectiveness and innovation scaling helps firms manage transition frictions and translate sustainability initiatives into more stable long‐horizon performance improvements.

Title: The costs of access: Freeway disamenities across US cities
Authors: Jeffrey Brinkman, Jeffrey Lin
Abstract: We construct city-level measures of freeway disamenities and examine their association with metropolitan growth. We combine neighborhood-level estimates from Brinkman and Lin (2024) with calibrated spatial models for U.S. metropolitan areas. Each city measure is based on a counterfactual that removes estimated disamenities while holding modeled travel times fixed. Cities with larger estimated disamenities grew more slowly, conditioned on total freeway mileage and initial population. Total freeway mileage is positively associated with growth in the same specification. Estimated disamenities are larger in cities with greater 1950 populations, more centralized freeway networks, and coastal geography. These patterns are consistent with local quality-of-life costs attenuating regional access-related growth benefits.

Title: When brands go live: AI host or profit-popularity driven influencer?
Authors: Baozhuang Niu, Xingyun Yue, Fanzhuo Zeng, Nan Zhang
Affiliations: South China University of Technology; University of Southampton
Abstract: Livestreaming sales (LSS) has become one of the fastest-growing formats in digital commerce, yet rising commission rates render influencer-led livestreaming increasingly costly. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) now offer a promising alternative: AI-powered virtual hosts that engage consumers and promote products without commission payments, albeit with lower interactional efficiency. This paper examines the brand's strategic choice between influencer-led and AI-hosted LSS. We develop an analytical model involving a brand and a dual-purpose influencer who values both commission and popularity-related benefits such as follower-base expansion. Our analysis uncovers two opposing mechanisms shaping how cost dynamics affect livestreaming choices. The influencer interactional-compensation effect captures the influencer's tendency to raise interactional richness as product cost increases, thereby helping stabilise demand. In contrast, the AI price-stabilisation effect results in lower interactional investment but more stable pricing. We show that when the influencer cares only about commission earnings, AI hosting is optimal only for low-cost products. If the influencer is profit-popularity driven, however, AI hosting may remain profitable for mid-to-high-cost products when AI is inefficient and popularity incentive is strong. Our results highlight the importance of tailoring livestreaming mode with product cost structure and the moderating role of the influencer's profit-popularity motivation.

Title: Resource allocation and patient care: a two-stage network-DEA model for optimising rural hospital operations
Authors: Guilherme P. Afonso, Dinesh R. Pai, José Rui Figueira, Diogo Filipe Cunha Ferreira
Affiliations: CERIS, Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa; Penn State Harrisburg; CEGIST, Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa
Abstract: We propose an evaluation framework to enhance U.S. rural hospital efficiency and sustainability amid rising costs and staffing shortages. Moving beyond ‘black-box’ evaluations, we utilise a two-stage Network-Data Envelopment Analysis (N-DEA) Slack-Based Measure model - Resource Allocation and Patient Care Delivery – to analyse internal inefficiencies. To ensure validity, 57 rural hospitals were segmented by size. To capture performance evolution, we integrate the Hicks-Moorsteen Productivity Index to evaluate annual Total Factor Productivity (TFP) shifts. We model hospitals as production systems converting resources into health outcomes. Applied to a 2018–2023 dataset, the model reveals that Patient Care Delivery consistently outperforms Resource Allocation. Longitudinal analysis indicates that while 48 of 57 hospitals recorded net TFP increases, volatility persists, particularly among small and medium facilities. This suggests performance gains are achievable by addressing Resource Allocation bottlenecks. Slack analysis reveals divergent profiles: small hospitals frequently operate with zero slack, whereas the broader sample shows 20% average excess for physicians and certified nurse practitioners. Scenario testing confirms modest reductions (25%) in these roles would enhance efficiency by 1.8%. Conversely, we recommend protecting registered nurse staffing due to minimal slack (6%), as potential efficiency gains are outweighed by patient care risks. This study offers data-driven insights for healthcare decision-makers.

Title: A scheduling problem in a reconfigurable manufacturing system with stochastic worker availability: a hybrid L-shaped decomposition method
Authors: Hessam Bakhshi-Khaniki, Reza Tavakkoli-Moghaddam, Zdenek Hanzalek, Behdin Vahedi-Nouri
Affiliations: University of Tehran; Istinye University; Czech Institute of Informatics Robotics and Cybernetics, Czech Technical University in Prague
Abstract: Modern manufacturing faces growing challenges from market volatility, resource uncertainty, and the need for quick adaptation. Reconfigurable Manufacturing Systems (RMSs) offer a flexible adaptable solution; however, scheduling becomes more complex when worker availability is uncertain. Workers in RMSs represent limited and mobile resources, whose uncertain availability can severely disrupt production efficiency. This paper investigates the non-identical parallel machine scheduling problem in an RMS under stochastic worker availability. To tackle this complex optimisation problem, a two-stage stochastic programming model is developed. In the first stage, job-to-machine assignments are determined as here-and-now decisions. The second stage involves optimising job sequencing, machine configurations, and worker assignments after the worker availability scenarios are revealed. To solve this problem, a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model and an L-shaped Decomposition (LD) method are developed to minimise the expected makespan. To enhance solution efficiency, a novel CP-LD is proposed, where the master problem uses MILP while subproblems employ Constraint Programming (CP). Computational results show that the proposed CP-LD method outperforms the MILP and LD methods in terms of solution quality and computational efficiency. The sensitivity analysis provides insights into the impact of various system parameters on the expected makespan performance, highlighting the critical importance of workforce management.

Title: A hybrid solution approach for the joint optimisation of skeleton cut line layout and cutting path planning
Authors: Yuanpeng Lai, Shaowen Yao, Meng Tian, Hao Zhang, Congyi Wang, Jiewu Leng, Qiang Liu
Affiliations: Guangdong University of Technology; CSSC Huangpu Wenchong Shipbuilding Company Limited
Abstract: In CNC cutting scenarios such as large-scale shipbuilding, net-like scrap skeletons formed by cutting often lead to difficulties in separating nested parts, and their dimensions frequently exceed the handling limits of automated equipment or scrap containers, thus necessitating further segmentation. Existing ‘skeleton cut line’ (SCL) processes heavily rely on manual experience, making it difficult to balance scrap disposal requirements and processing efficiency. To address this, we propose the Joint Optimisation Problem of Skeleton Cut Line Layout and Cutting Path Planning, aiming to synergistically determine the SCL layout, cutting sequence, and entry points to minimise total processing costs under process constraints. We construct a mixed-integer linear programming model that integrates the Extended Precedence-Constrained Generalised Travelling Salesman Problem with the Weighted Set Covering Problem, and propose a two-stage heuristic hybrid solution approach of ‘geometry generation–dynamic optimisation’. The first stage constructs a finite high-quality candidate SCL set via geometric rules; the second employs a hybrid heuristic integrating Adaptive Large Neighbourhood Search, Simulated Annealing, and Local Search for efficient joint dynamic optimisation. Experiments on standard benchmarks and real-world industrial instances verify the model accuracy and demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches in solution quality, efficiency, and robustness, confirming its practical applicability.

Title: Profit-oriented dynamic scheduling for disassembly flexible job shops: dealing with structural uncertainty and operation skipping
Authors: Zengyu Kuang, Hui Xie, Yinghui Ren, Xiaojun Zhuo, Minghao Shi
Affiliations: Hunan University; Changsha Research Institute of Mining and Metallurgy Co Ltd
Abstract: Disassembly scheduling for End-of-Life (EOL) products, particularly EV batteries, exhibits dynamic structural uncertainty and physical degradation characteristics. However, existing scheduling models are predominantly static and fail to fully capture the distinctive stochastic features and operation skipping patterns of such disassembly systems. To address these gaps, we formulate the process as a Markov Decision Process and propose a Hierarchical Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning (H-MADRL) framework. To enhance practical applicability, a Hierarchical State Embedding module acts as a digital perception layer to quantify physical risks. Meanwhile, a Physics-Informed Dual-Agent mechanism coordinates task-machine assignments, and a Constraint-Compliant Masking layer ensures strict adherence to Standard Operating Procedures. Averaged over multiple independent runs, the framework achieves a 45.6% increase in profit rate and a 16.9% reduction in makespan compared to standard reinforcement learning and heuristic baselines. Ultimately, this approach secures shop-floor adaptability and significantly advances managerial precision in balancing economic density with operational throughput under stochastic constraints.

Title: A fix-and-relax matheuristic method for lot-sizing and scheduling problem in a dairy industry
Authors: Parisa Pourabdollah, Saeed Emami, Ebrahim Asadi-Gangraj
Affiliations: Department of Industrial Engineering, Babol Noshiravani University of Technology
Abstract: The lot-sizing and scheduling problem (LSP) focuses on determining the production quantities and the sequence of production activities, simultaneously. This article addresses the LSP in a flexible flow shop environment within the real-world dairy industry in Iran. We consider perishability, which is a common issue in the food industry, as well as cleaning in place (CIP) of the machines. The problem can be described as multi-product, multi-level, multi-period, with sequence-dependent setup and CIP time. To maximise profits, we present a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that subtracts total revenue from the total cost, including tardiness, inventory holding, sequence-dependent setup, CIP, and disposal of perished products costs. Due to the NP-hardness of this problem, we propose a fix-and-relax (F&R) matheuristic method to solve it. The numerical experiments on randomly generated instances with up to 40 products on the proposed model show that while the exact MILP model becomes computationally intractable for large-scale instances, the proposed F&R method is able to generate high-quality feasible solutions within reasonable computation times.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Operationalizing circular supply chains through integrating product development and supply chain design: a multi-phase framework grounded in multiple case studies
Authors: Sobhan Mostafayi Darmian, Sotirios Panagou, Fabio Sgarbossa
Affiliations: Department of Mechanical and Industrial Engineering, NTNU
Abstract: Manufacturing firms seeking to implement circular economy strategies often face a practical challenge in translating R-imperatives into coordinated decisions on product development and supply chain design. Although prior studies and conceptual frameworks have highlighted the importance of integrating these domains, there is limited guidance on how to operationalise such integration in practice. In response, this study develops a three-phase operationalisation framework for integrating R-imperatives, product development, and supply chain design. The framework comprises an As-Is phase, which identifies the current product and supply chain configuration and assesses the existing level of integration, a To-Be phase, which identifies feasible R-imperatives and the redesign requirements they imply, and a To-Do phase, which identifies implementation challenges, capability gaps, and action priorities. The framework is built on the existing knowledge in the literature and empirically grounded through multiple case studies of Norwegian manufacturing companies. The findings show that the feasibility of R-imperatives depends strongly on product architecture, reverse logistics capabilities, and the synchronisation between product redesign and supply chain adaptation. The study contributes by moving beyond conceptual recognition of integration towards a practical framework that supports design for circularity in industrial settings.

Title: Supply strategies in live stream supply chains: The role of market overlap
Authors: Shaofu Du, Yuzhu Guo, Junsong Bian, Xiaolong Guo
Abstract: Selling in live-stream channels can stimulate market demand by providing lower prices than manufacturers’ online channels. Cooperating with streamers can bring extra markets for manufacturers. However, manufacturers should pay slotting fees to streamers before cooperating, and they may face market overlap and competition. One way to alleviate competition is to control the quantity of products for streamers. We develop an analytical model consisting of an online store channel operated by the manufacturer and a live-stream channel that may run out of stock operated by the streamer. Firstly, the results show that the manufacturer should base the quantity decision on the market overlap between the manufacturer and the streamer. When the market overlap is sufficiently low, the manufacturer should supply the streamer with an adequate quantity of product to enlarge the streamer’s market. When the market overlap is sufficiently high, the manufacturer should supply the streamer with a limited quantity of products to promote consumer transfer. Secondly, the results show that as the slotting fee increases, the manufacturer requires a lower market overlap if cooperating with the streamer. Finally, we extend our basic model to the Nash Bargaining scenario. Negotiation will decrease consumer surplus, but increase social welfare compared to the basic model.

Title: Integrating returnable and disposable packaging to balance efficiency, resilience, and sustainability in automotive supply chains
Authors: Jesús García-Arca, Mar Vazquez-Noguerol, Borja Ponte, J. Carlos Prado-Prado
Abstract: : The adoption of returnable packaging systems (RPSs) is widespread in supply chains across many industries due to their potential economic and environmental benefits. However, designing and managing RPSs effectively remains challenging, particularly in volatile, uncertain, and disruption-prone environments such as the automotive sector. To better understand these challenges, we conduct an exploratory analysis involving professionals from one of Europe’s largest automotive assembly plants. Drawing on the insights gathered, we develop an empirically grounded simulation model that captures the dynamics of these closed-loop supply chains (CLSCs). The model integrates the RPS with an alternative, non-returnable packaging system (NPS), used as a contingency when returnable items are not available. Through designed experiments, we investigate the operational and economic behaviour of this hybrid packaging system, demonstrating its potential as an effective strategy for achieving both efficient, sustainable and resilient supply chains. The study further shows that determining the optimal quantity of returnable packaging items is a complex decision shaped by the interplay of costs, defective item rates, disruption probabilities, and renewal policies. Interestingly, intermediate renewal periods can outperform more frequent replacement cycles in terms of total packaging costs, highlighting the need for a balanced and integrated approach to packaging management.

Title: Market selection of strategic thinking types
Authors: Lawrence Choo, Todd R. Kaplan, Xiaoyu Zhou
Abstract: Markets are often used to allocate decision-making, from selecting voting rights of shareholders to hiring workers in the gig economy. We study how market selection can influence the composition of strategic thinking types in strategic interactions. Using auctions as the selection mechanism, we demonstrate that after-market decisions in the p[jls-end-space/]-Beauty Contest Game can result in either higher or lower numbers, depending on the incentives. Furthermore, we pinpoint the cause of differences to the market selection of strategic thinking types, rather than the decision-maker altering behaviour due to beliefs about the selection of other players. This highlights the role of institutional factors in determining “who plays the game”.

Title: Sexual identity, industrial segregation and earnings
Authors: Samuel Mann, Nigel O’Leary, David Blackaby
Abstract: Using longitudinal data from the UK, we study the role of industrial segregation for sexual identity-based pay disparities, while controlling for fixed unobserved heterogeneity. We show that industries that have a greater proportion of sexual minorities pay their male employees less. This is of an order of magnitude of a 0.6% marginal reduction in earnings as industrial representation of sexual minorities increases by 1 percent. This compares to an equivalent marginal figure for occupational segregation of approximately 0.9%. In contrast, there is a protective element present for females in the public sector who benefit from a within industry premium to locating in industries with greater LGB representation. However, such effects do not remove the substantial wage penalty faced by gay men, and by lesbian women in the private sector.

Title: Universalization and the origins of fiscal capacity
Authors: Esteban Muñoz-Sobrado
Abstract: This paper proposes a model of tax compliance and fiscal capacity grounded in universalization reasoning. Citizens partially internalize the consequences of concealment by imagining a world in which everyone acted similarly, linking their compliance decisions to the perceived effectiveness of public spending. A selfish elite chooses between public goods and private rents, taking compliance as given. In equilibrium, citizens' moral internalization expands the feasible tax base and induces elites to allocate resources toward provision rather than appropriation. When the value of public spending is uncertain, morality enables credible reform: high-value elites can signal their type through provision, prompting citizens to increase compliance and raising fiscal capacity within the same period. The analysis thus identifies a moral channel through which states may escape low-capacity traps even under weak institutions.

Title: From regulation to valuation: Carbon pricing signals and eco-technology diffusion
Authors: Hyun-Jung Nam, Doojin Ryu
Abstract: Using monthly data for major tanker and dry bulk segments from 2018 to 2025, we examine whether carbon-pricing signals, measured by European Union Allowance (EUA) prices, are associated with eco-vessel diffusion, measured by eco-vessel share and eco-vessel price premiums. We find that stronger carbon-pricing signals are associated with increases in both dimensions of eco-vessel diffusion. A USD 1 increase in the EUA price is associated with a 0.02 percentage point increase in eco-vessel share over horizons ranging from three to twenty-four months. Over the twelve- to twenty-four-month horizon, the same increase raises eco-vessel price premiums by approximately USD 40,000–60,000.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: A dual GCN–MCTS framework for yield-aware scheduling in multistage manufacturing
Authors: Sugyeong Lee, Dong-Hee Lee
Abstract: Yield in semiconductor manufacturing is strongly path-dependent, as lots processed through different machine sequences can achieve substantially different final yields even under comparable throughput conditions. Yet conventional scheduling research has focused almost exclusively on productivity metrics, leaving quality-aware scheduling largely unexplored. This paper proposes a dual Graph Convolutional Network (GCN)-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) framework for yield-aware scheduling in a multistage manufacturing process with parallel machines, where the objective is to maximize product yield while preserving production throughput. The framework integrates two complementary GCN components—a Regression GCN (RegGCN) that learns a path-to-yield value function from historical path-yield records, and a Policy GCN (PolGCN), trained through offline policy distillation from RegGCN, that provides state-conditioned action priors over feasible machine assignments for MCTS under real-time machine availability. These components are integrated into a Progressive Value Integration PUCT (PVI-PUCT) selection mechanism that adaptively blends RegGCN value estimates with simulation statistics as tree search matures, enabling informed decisions from the earliest search iterations. Experiments are conducted on a simulated semiconductor dataset incorporating machine-level main effects and adjacent-stage interaction effects that preclude purely additive yield prediction. Results show that RegGCN achieves an R2 of 0.9984 using only 5% of all feasible paths, and that the proposed framework improves yield by +11.18 percentage points over a random baseline while maintaining comparable throughput, matching the performance of parameter-tuned heuristics without requiring sensitivity analysis or parameter selection. The analysis further reveals that the GCN value function provides the primary yield-improvement signal, while MCTS lookahead prevents throughput degradation by accounting for future machine availability in early dispatching decisions. These results demonstrate that process-path data can be transformed into actionable scheduling decisions for yield improvement without requiring additional sensors or inline inspection data.

Title: Editorial Board
Evidence of firm-level pollution leakage resulting from China's 2013 Clean Air Plan
Authors: Chang Liu, Jingrong Wang, David M. Reiner
Abstract: Spatially differentiated environmental regulation can induce pollution leakage through intra-firm relocation of pollution-intensive activities to less-regulated regions. This mechanism remains underexplored, especially in developing countries, where data limitations make intra-firm relocation difficult to measure and existing investment-based proxies often miss expansions within existing subsidiaries. Using manually collected subsidiary-level investment data for 411 listed pollution-intensive firms in China and a difference-in-differences framework, we examine whether regionally differentiated regulation under the 2013 Clean Air Plan led to intra-firm investment reallocation consistent with production relocation and potential domestic pollution leakage. We find that regulated firms increased pollution-related investment in subsidiaries located in less-regulated areas following the policy, accompanied by declines in parent-firm output and rising PM₂.₅ concentrations around subsidiary locations. Adjustment patterns differ across regions: firms in the three key regions centered on Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou reallocate investment from eastern regulated areas to distant western regions, mainly through new subsidiary entry, whereas firms in ten other major city clusters mainly expand existing subsidiaries located nearby. Reallocated investment is disproportionately directed toward regions with stronger agglomeration economies and transportation advantages rather than environmentally fragile areas. These findings suggest that investment flows offer a valuable lens for detecting potential pollution leakage and that unintended east-to-west transfers may undermine environmental gains, highlighting the need for stronger disclosure requirements and targeted pollution-control policies in recipient regions.

Title: Optimal climate and monetary–fiscal policies in a climate-DSGE framework
Authors: Lorenzo Forni, Mehrab Kiarsi
Abstract: This paper studies the optimal design of climate, fiscal, and monetary policies in response to climate-specific shocks within a climate-DSGE framework. We show that carbon taxes significantly mitigate the effects of climate shocks on output, consumption, and welfare, while optimal monetary policy is largely unaffected and fiscal policy adjusts via lower labor taxes. Extending the model with a richer climate module and abatement costs, we find that the assumed damage function is crucial: under a standard quadratic specification, climate policy has little effect on conventional macroeconomic shocks, but a highly convex, Weitzman-type damage function makes carbon taxation materially relevant. Accounting for climate fiscal outlays further raises optimal abatement and reduces emissions. Our results highlight the importance of integrating both macroeconomic and environmental considerations when designing policy.

Title: Roadside native species seeding practices of Midwestern US departments of transportation
Authors: Wesley J. Bollinger, Rabin Bhattarai, Jeffrey W. Matthews
Abstract: To counteract environmental problems associated with road construction and maintenance, road agencies have developed vegetation management plans that incorporate native seeding. We reviewed the specifications manuals from the Departments of Transportation of eight US states to synthesize information on native plant species used, seed mixes, site preparation, seeding methods, and maintenance to provide recommendations for roadside vegetation management. Manuals varied among states in terms of the species composition and functional diversity of plants listed for use. Individual mixes included an average of 14 native species, although some had as few as 3, and many lacked functional diversity or early blooming forbs that would benefit pollinators. We identified several early-blooming, low-cost, conservative plant species that could be incorporated into seed mixes. Compared to other states, Minnesota listed more native species and seed mixes, and provided detailed specifications for seeding, establishment, and maintenance, aligning well with recommendations based on ecological restoration research.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment
